Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?
- Published
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

‘Gen Z wants good opportunities, education, and infrastructure’: Dipke on Uttar Pradesh polls
Abhijeet Dipke also said that the CJP will not side with any party in the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.
CJP convenor Abhijeet Dipke on Wednesday mocked the ruling BJP over what he described as "Meta and Instagram censorship" and the purported removal of more than "five million" posts by playing a "Modi Chalisa" song at his press conference and placing the PM's photo.
"Censorship in the country is so rampant in the country that excluding PM Modi's photo, any other political content is being suppressed on Instagram and Meta. Taking this into account, we have kept the PM's photo and 'Modi Chalisa' for Instagram and Meta," he said while addressing the press conference in Nagpur.
The Cockroach Janta Party founder claimed that more than "five million" posts with political content were removed from Instagram between January and June.
"Hence, we thought that if we keep Modiji's photo during media interaction, Instagram may not remove this press conference from its platform.
"I and CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka are addressing you in the presence of "Aadarniya, Sanmanniya and Mahamanav Prime Minister," he said with Modi's photo placed in the background.
When asked about whether this "Modi Chalisa" audio would hurt the sentiments of Hindus, Dipke said an FIR should be immediately registered against the singer of the concerned song and against the BJP social media platform from where they have picked up the audio.
ALSO READ: CJP’s Saurav Das claims his passport leaked, blames ‘BJP-aligned’ social media handles
Speaking on the contribution of Gen Z, Dipke said the young people have brought accountability back in the country, citing the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan amid protests against the NEET paper leak.
"The country has been afraid of raising questions for the last 12 years; however, Gen Z has given courage and voice to the people, which is the most important contribution," he added.
Dipke said the CJP has no plans to form a political party.
"We are not here to side with any party. We are not inclined towards any party; our commitment is towards the youth of this country," he added.
He said the CJP will not side with any party in the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.
"The CJP is not here to side with any party. We want the elections to be contested on issues concerning young people. Gen Z wants good opportunities, education, and infrastructure. They don't want caste and religious issues, which are often raked up during polls. We will talk about education, employment, healthcare, and public infrastructure," Dipke added.
Addressing the media, Ranka rejected allegations that CJP's recent tour in poll-bound Goa was a pressure tactic ahead of the elections.
"The CJP's intention is not to topple any government or replace it with another. We want elections, including in Goa, to be contested on real issues concerning the people. The CJP will draft a citizen manifesto in the coming weeks in association with the local civil society organisations, activists and people of Goa and will make every political party agree with that manifesto," he said.

Sachin Bansal-led Navi continued to strengthen its position in the UPI ecosystem in October 2026. The fintech platform’s share in the UPI market crossed the 5% mark over the past month, data released by NPCI revealed. Of the 25.47 Bn processed by UPI, transactions processed by Navi platform rose to 5.04% from 4.76% in September. Overall, Navi hosted 1.27 Bn UPI transactions during the month, an 11% increase from 1.14 Bn in September The fintech platform processed around 1.27 Bn UPI transactions during the month, up from 1.14 Bn in September. Navi's gains came as the UPI leaders — PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm — continued to see some decline in their market share in October. Taken together, the three platforms still combine over 85% of India’s UPI market. PhonePe remained the largest UPI app, with a 45.34% share of transaction volume, down from 45.57% in September. Google Pay's share fell to 32.09% from 32.23%, while Paytm's share declined to 7.96% from 8.12%. Navi Overtakes CRED In UPI Transaction Value Navi's growth was also visible in transaction value. The platform processed UPI transactions worth ₹62,492 Cr in October, marginally ahead of CRED's ₹62,102 Cr, according to NPCI data. This made Navi the fourth-largest UPI app by transaction value, ending CRED's position in the ranking after more than five years. Among other emerging platforms, WhatsApp's share increased to 0.85% in October from 0.80% in September. FamApp by Trio also recorded a rise to 0.99% from 0.95%, while BHIM's share edged up to 1.07% from 1.06%. On the other hand, super.money's share declined to 1.65% from 1.69%. CRED maintained its share at 0.59%, while Amazon Pay's share increased marginally to 0.40% from 0.38%. The data indicates that while PhonePe and Google Pay continue to control a large part of India's UPI market, smaller players such as Navi are gradually expanding their presence. Navi's latest gains also come amid growing competition among fintech platforms to capture a larger share of India's digital payments market.

For Rauf Rumi, a 38-year-old writer, translator and educator from Kannur, Kerala, translating a book rooted in Christian teachings became an experience that went beyond language and literature.
A Muslim woman, Rumi translated Adam, Where Art Thou?, a collection of speeches on Biblical teachings by Congress leader V D Satheesan, from Malayalam into English. Her work brought together the perspectives of a Hindu politician who spoke about the Bible and a Muslim translator who found herself deeply moved by Christian teachings.
Speaking to PTI, Rumi said she was touched by the Christian teachings and ideas expressed in the book. “I belong to the Islamic faith, which teaches us to respect all religions and their scriptures. This work gave me an opportunity to understand Christian beliefs and Biblical teachings more closely,” she said.
The English edition of Adam, Where Art Thou?, translated from the Malayalam original Adam Nee Evide Aakunnu?, was released by DC Books on November 5.
Rumi had undertaken several translation assignments for the publisher before it approached her to translate Satheesan’s book. “I wanted to read the book even before they approached me. When DC Books contacted me, I was happy to take up the assignment. It was an interesting experience, and every speech of the leader offered something different,” she said.
‘Prayers of all communities hold significance’
Although she was not a regular reader of the Bible, Rumi said her academic background in English literature had given her some familiarity with Biblical references. “For me, that was significant. Here is a Hindu who deeply respects Christian teachings. Similarly, I am a Muslim, but I could engage with and translate a book rooted in Christian beliefs. We do not have to belong to a particular religion to appreciate its teachings or respect its scriptures,” she said.
One passage that particularly stayed with Rumi was Satheesan’s observation that people who pray are a source of strength for society and that the prayers of all communities hold significance. “That portion touched me deeply while translating the book,” she said.
Speaking at a church programme in Changanassery, Satheesan highlighted the religious inclusiveness of Kerala’s social fabric. “I am a Hindu who delivered speeches on the Bible and later compiled them into a book. A Muslim woman translated it into English. Such things are possible in Keralam,” he said.
For Rumi, the assignment became much more than a translation project. Satheesan also personally called her after the release of the English edition to express his appreciation for the work.
“He said he liked the translation very much and that the essence of the original Malayalam book had been retained. I was extremely happy to hear that,” she said.
The original Malayalam book is a compilation of 32 speeches Satheesan delivered at programmes organised by various Christian organisations across Kerala. The speeches explore Biblical stories and the teachings of Jesus Christ in the context of contemporary society.
Inputs from PTI

As far as trailblazers go, Kadambini Ganguly will figure right on top of several lists. She was a pioneering woman physician, the first to practise successfully in India, a gynaecologist and a social reformer who, equally efficiently, managed a large family as well. The story of Kadambini Ganguly is one of extraordinary achievement, and if told widely, will continue to inspire the young women of today.
In a profile published in Cureus in 2024, the authors point to the influence of the progressive Bramho Samaj movement, initiated by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that helped Kadambini emerge from the shackles of conservative orthodoxy that might have stiffled her immense talent. “This environment, which championed the values of education and gender equality, contributed significantly to shaping her exemplary career and lifelong dedication to social justice,” the article reads. Records of her life acknowledge that she was partly recognised during her lifetime, but also mercilessly criticised and defamed for being a progressive, working woman. The full recognition of her contributions in medicine and the social sector came much later, only in recent decades.

Nothing’s Ear (note) is a pair of earbuds with built-in AI notetaking
I was more excited for Nothing’s latest device when I thought it was an AI vape pen.
Ahead of December 8 and too many coordinated leaks to count, Nothing has officially announced its first "AI-native" device. Somewhat anticlimactically, the Ear (note) is a pair of earbuds with built-in AI notetaking. As the company told Bloomberg, the earbuds can transcribe and summarize in-person conversations, calls, online meetings and voice memos, in addition to offering traditional audio playback with Hi-Res audio support.
"Ear (note) is part of Nothing's vision to build the hardware context layer of AI, bringing intelligence closer to the moments, conversations and experiences that shape our everyday lives," the company wrote in a press release it shared with Engadget.
No information on pricing or specs just yet, but Nothing promised to share more details soon. The company describes the Ear (note) as a "new approach to personal productivity," but Nothing is not the first to announce earbuds with built-in AI transcription. This past August, Plaud debuted its own pair of AI-forward earbuds in the form of the Plaud One. That said, if you're a fan of Nothing's design, you'll be sure to appreciate the Sony Walkman-like design the company has gone for, especially when it comes to the new Record and Talk buttons along the bottom of the aluminum case.
The Ear (note) will launch on December 8.

Tata Trusts, ‌which owns a 66% holding in Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata Group, has decided to move to the ‌Bombay High Court to challenge the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as ‌chairman of Tata Sons.
Tata Trusts filed two separate suits in Bombay High Court against Tata Sons. The hearing has been scheduled at 3 p.m. on Friday (November 27, 2026).
On September 17, 2026, the Tata Sons board approved his third term beginning in February 2027 by a majority vote.
The Tata Trusts termed this reappointment illegal, as it violated Tata Sons’ Articles of Association.
Sir Dorab Tata Trust (SDTT) has sought ₹50 crore damages while RD Tata Trust (RDTT) seek ₹15 crore, with 18% interests.
The suits have been filed against Tata Sons and six directors including Noel Tata. The suits have challenged the September 17 resolution of Tata Sons board reappointing Chandra for 5 more years.
The trusts have sought immediate relief seeking to prohibit Mr Chandrasekaran from using casting vote at the forthcoming November 30 board meeting if Trust nominees split again.
The suits were first mentioned before Justice Arif S. Doctor who recused himself. Then re-mentioned before Justice Abhay Ahuja who has scheduled the hearing on November 27 at 3 PM. Tata Trusts are represented by lawyer Abhishek Manu Singhvi. With this the Tata Sons has now moved from the board room to court room.
On Wednesday (November 25, 2026), SDTT and RDTT authorised legal action against the Board’s decision leading to the matter being dragged to court.
The petition is leant and will seek Mr. Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as invalid. The Trusts will seek an injunction prohibiting Tata Sons from acting on the reappointment or passing resolutions without an affirmative vote as required by the Articles of Association.
As per this, the nominated members of Tata Trusts on Tata Sons’ board must vote in unison.
During the last board meeting, while the nominated member Noel Tata voted against the resolutions, the other nominated member Venu Srinivasan voted in favour, thus invalidating the outcome as stated by the Trust.
Reportedly, Tata Sons is going ahead with listing formalities as required by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The Trusts are opposed to it.
The latest flare-up comes ahead of the Tata Sons board meeting, now rescheduled to November 30, 2026. The listing of Tata Sons is the main agenda for resolution and approval.

Health Canada issues warning on rare risk of vision loss with semaglutide GLP-1 drugs
Federal team's safety review found possible link between use of drugs and 'very rare' eye condition
Health Canada has issued a public warning about the "very rare but serious" risk of vision loss tied to semaglutide GLP-1 drugs, best known by brand names such as Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.
On the heels of similar warnings in the U.S. and Europe, the federal department announced on Wednesday that it had completed its own safety review, which found a possible link between prescription semaglutide drugs and the risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).
The condition causes sudden blindness or vision changes due to reduced blood flow to the optic nerve, which carries information from the eyes to the brain. It's a permanent condition, with no known treatment.
"If you experience sudden vision loss or rapidly worsening eyesight while taking semaglutide … seek urgent medical attention," the new warning reads.
'Black veil over your eye'
Montreal resident Jeffrey Gilman, 71, welcomed the move from Health Canada, since he experienced near-total vision loss in one eye after just a few months of taking semaglutide as a diabetes treatment in 2024.
"I just woke up one morning and couldn't see out of my right eye. I called my optometrist, who said come on in now. Like not tomorrow — now," he recalled.
After seeing multiple specialists within just a few days, including ophthalmologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, Gilman was told there was "irreparable" damage to the optic nerve at the back of his right eye. He now has only 10 per cent vision in that eye and wishes he'd been aware of the potential risks.
"I've described it as almost like putting like a black veil over your eye and trying to see through it," he told CBC News.
Multiple studies show links to vision loss
Both Health Canada and other international medical experts have stressed the rarity of NAION, even as millions of individuals around the world are now taking GLP-1 medications, including an estimated three million Canadians.
Yet multiple studies have also suggested there may be increased risk of the condition among those using these drugs, which are approved in Canada for a variety of uses, including chronic weight management and treating Type 2 diabetes.
"This is an extremely rare side effect — might be one in 5,000, one in 10,000 or even less common — and we need to be cautious until we know for sure," said leading Canadian GLP-1 researcher and endocrinologist Dr. Daniel Drucker.
- Should kids living with obesity be on GLP-1s? New guidance says yes — in some cases
- Everyone’s going on — and off — GLP-1s. What’s that doing to your health?
One headline-making 2024 study in JAMA Ophthalmology found a "potential risk" of NAION associated with prescriptions for semaglutide, but the researchers stressed more research was needed to assess causality.
Earlier this year, other observational research published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology found the risk of vision loss varied between semaglutide formulations, and was three times greater among men than women. The findings highlighted a "potential dose-dependent safety concern," the authors wrote.
Risk-benefit ratio may vary between patients
Given this growing body of research, Dr. Mahyar Etminan, a drug safety epidemiologist in the Regulatory Science Lab at BC Cancer Research Institute, told CBC News that patients should carefully weigh the possible risks and benefits of GLP-1 use with their physicians.
"When your sample size is very large, even a rare event — especially one as serious as this one — can be very significant," he said following Health Canada's announcement on Wednesday.
The risk-benefit ratio may be different depending on why people are using these drugs, Etminan added.
Drucker agreed, and encouraged patients to heed Health Canada's caution.
"If you're a casual user who has no other health problems and is trying to lose weight, maybe this is something that's really important for you to balance against the benefit you're going to achieve," he said.
"On the other end, if you have serious health concerns with Type 2 diabetes or obesity, the numbers are overwhelmingly favourable for benefit."
Vision loss usually painless, sudden
NAION usually affects one eye at a time, Health Canada noted in its new notice, and often occurs as cloudy, blurry or worsened sight across part of the field of vision — usually in the lower half — of the affected eye.
Most people notice the vision loss when waking up, though it can also happen gradually over about two weeks.
"It is usually painless, though mild headaches or discomfort around the eye may occur," the department's warning adds.
So why does the condition happen?
Although it is not fully understood how semaglutide may contribute to NAION, Health Canada's safety review explained that a "rapid drop in blood sugar levels following the use of semaglutide may cause swelling of the optic nerve and reduce its blood supply, especially in individuals with other risk factors."
But Drucker said researchers might never be able to prove the exact mechanisms, or the role these drugs may play. NAION also occurs in individuals with diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
"We probably will never have any clear causation," Drucker said, "given the rarity of the condition."
Health Canada recommended any Canadians experiencing sudden vision loss or eyesight changes while taking semaglutide GLP-1 drugs should quickly get medical attention, while health-care providers should urgently refer those patients for ophthalmological examination and discontinue semaglutide treatment if NAION is confirmed.
In cases where someone doesn't have direct access to an ophthalmologist, Halifax-based optometrist Dr. Allison Scott, from the Canadian Association of Optometrists, said other specialists such as optometrists or emergency department physicians can provide a referral.
The notice applies to all types of prescription semaglutide drugs used in Canada, including brand names such as Ozempic, Plosbrio, Poviztra, Rybelsus and Wegovy, along with generic offerings such as apo-semaglutide injection, aspen-semaglutide, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories Ltd. semaglutide injection, Sandoz semaglutide and Sevmia.

How to watch every 2026 NFL Thanksgiving game on streaming
Cutting cable should never stop a tradition.
Death, taxes and vegging out on the couch to watch Thanksgiving football are three givens in America. This year's holiday slate is jam-packed with major storylines, including division rivals, star players, big-name halftime performers and, for the first time, an extra matchup on Thanksgiving Eve.
With games spread across both streaming services and TV networks, knowing how, where and when to stream the NFL has become a sport of its own, but we've got you covered.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving Eve
Today, you can stream Packers at Rams exclusively on Netflix, kicking off at 8:15PM ET/5:15PM PT. If you don't have an active subscription, you can sign up for the ad-supported tier at $8.99/month. Signing up today will also get you access to this year's Christmas Day games.
Since this is the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game, the league is bringing out a big name for halftime: U2 will perform at SoFi Stadium fresh off the release of its new album, Carnaval De Luz. Unlike 2014's Songs of Innocence, it didn't show up on your iPhone overnight, so you may have missed it.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving
On Turkey Day itself, the action kicks off at 1PM ET/10AM PT with Bears at Lions, airing on CBS and streaming on Paramount+. You can get Paramount+ starting at $8.99/month to watch the game and see Wu-Tang Clan swarm the stage for a halftime show executive produced by Michigan-bred icon Eminem.
Next on the docket is Eagles at Cowboys, starting at 4:30PM ET. The game airs live on Fox, but it's the one matchup you can stream at no cost on Tubi. It's also available on the Fox One streaming service for $19.99/month. Texas native Miranda Lambert is set to perform at this year's Salvation Army Red Kettle Kickoff Halftime Show, marking 30 years of the annual tradition.
Then, two of the league's premier quarterbacks, Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, face off to close out the night with Chiefs at Bills. This matchup airs live on NBC and streams on Peacock at 8:20PM ET. You'll need the Premium tier to watch on Peacock, which starts at $12.99/month. Like the prior game, the NFL tapped a local act, the Goo Goo Dolls, to headline halftime in Buffalo.
If you cut cable a while ago but don't want to sign up for individual subscriptions, you can watch these three NFL games on live TV streaming services, including YouTube TV (starting at $49.99/month for the Sports tier), Hulu + Live TV (starting at $99.99/month) or DIRECTV (starting at $94.99/month). Eagles at Cowboys and Chiefs at Bills will also be available to stream on Sling TV Select ($19.99/month) or a higher tier.
Where to stream on Black Friday
On Black Friday, you can stream Broncos at Steelers on Prime Video at 3PM ET. If you're not a Prime subscriber, you can score a standalone subscription for $8.99/month. This matchup will not feature a halftime performance, but two of the league's top teams should suffice.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.
Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.
Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.
To be fair, biotechnology raises real national security questions, from genomic privacy to research that could be misused for nefarious purposes. Imposed limits on capital flows are a legitimate tool. I am certainly not arguing that U.S. investors should fund Chinese state-linked companies without scrutiny. Nor do our data indicate that all Chinese products are comparable in terms of quality or originality. Higher counts may overstate the number of genuine breakthroughs.
Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.
Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.
The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.
A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.
Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.
First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.
Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.
Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.
Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.
Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.
Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

SpaceX said Tuesday that it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account.
Elon Musk, SpaceX's CEO, will also personally match the number of shares donated by the AI and rocket company, SpaceX said. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, also pledged more than 2 million SpaceX shares.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
In July, the Trump administration launched Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children born between 2025 and 2028. Once an account is opened, the US Treasury Department will make a one-time $1,000 contribution.
The Treasury Department has said that the accounts are designed to help families build long-term financial security.
SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts. Dell, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Charles Schwab, and BlackRock have also pledged contributions to the accounts.

First phase of gram panchayat polls in AP today; voting for 23 ULBs also begins
In the first phase of gram panchayat elections, polling will be held in 3,240 gram panchayats, excluding Visakhapatnam and Guntur districts
The first phase of gram panchayat election and second phase of municipal polls in Andhra Pradesh will be conducted on Thursday.
According to state election commissioner (SEC) Anil Chandra Punetha, a total of 99,43,895 voters are eligible to exercise their franchise at 34,312 polling stations, with around 70,000 election officials and personnel deployed to oversee the process.
The SEC and district administrations have completed elaborate arrangements to ensure the smooth and peaceful conduct of polling in both rural and urban areas.
In the first phase of gram panchayat elections, polling will be held in 3,240 gram panchayats, excluding Visakhapatnam and Guntur districts. As many as 74,45,583 voters are eligible to cast their votes at 31,614 polling stations.
Also Read: Back to ‘Nau-maas da rishta’: SAD, BJP reunite for Punjab polls after 6-year split
A total of 62,863 candidates are contesting for 3,189 sarpanch and 25,101 ward member posts, excluding the seats declared unanimously elected.
Polling will begin at 7am and continue till 1pm. Counting of votes will commence at 2pm, immediately after the completion of polling, and results will be declared subsequently.
The authorities have made arrangements for the deployment of polling personnel and other officials to facilitate voters and ensure that the election process is completed without disruption.
23 urban local bodies (ULB) polls
Simultaneously, polling will be conducted in 23 urban local bodies comprising four municipal corporations and 19 municipalities and Nagar Panchayats.
The four municipal corporations going to polls are Srikakulam, Rajamahendravaram, Kakinada and Mangalagiri-Tadepalli. A total of 170 candidates are contesting for the posts of mayors and chairpersons, including 36 candidates for four mayor posts and 134 candidates for 19 chairperson posts.
Of the 260 divisions in the four municipal corporations, two have been declared unanimously elected, while polling will be conducted in the remaining 257 divisions.
Similarly, of the 750 wards in the 19 municipalities and nagar panchayats, 39 have been declared unanimously elected. A total of 2,968 candidates are in the fray for these 964 divisions and wards.
Punetha said 24,98,312 voters are eligible to exercise their franchise in the 23 urban local bodies. The electorate comprises 12,04,819 men, 12,93,084 women and 409 voters belonging to the other category.
The commission has identified 2,801 polling stations for the elections, of which polling will take place at 2,698 centres.
Security and counting arrangements
Punetha said comprehensive arrangements had been made to conduct the municipal elections in a free, fair, peaceful, impartial and transparent manner.
Of the 2,698 polling stations where polling will be held, 819 have been classified as sensitive and 597 as hyper-sensitive. Special security arrangements have been made at these centres to prevent clashes and other untoward incidents.
Also Read: In Punjab polls, huge stakes for Opposition
Returning officers, polling personnel, zonal officers and route officers have been appointed to supervise the electoral process. As many as 5,602 CCTV cameras will be deployed to monitor polling activities continuously.
The commission has also made elaborate arrangements for the subsequent counting of votes, with 23 counting centres, 115 counting halls and 842 counting tables being arranged.
The counting of votes in the 23 urban local bodies will be counted on November 30.
In view of clashes and law-and-order incidents reported during the first phase of municipal elections and the MPTC and ZPTC elections, the authorities have decided to deploy a massive police force of 46,080 personnel to ensure peaceful polling.
Surveillance will be strengthened through drones, body-worn cameras and CCTV cameras to monitor sensitive locations and prevent any untoward incidents.
The police have been directed to remain alert throughout the polling process and take necessary measures to maintain law and order in both rural and urban local bodies.

We weren't able to confirm, as of this writing, precisely how many barrels of lead azide would be exploded.
In mid-November, a rumor spread online that the U.S. Army had plans to set off two detonations to destroy an old cache of lead azide — a highly explosive compound — in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 20.
"The Army found 68 barrels of the explosive that had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years," one Facebook post read (archived). "Lead azide becomes more unstable as it ages and can detonate with slight movement or friction, making it unsafe to move off site."
The claim spread across other platforms, with several Snopes readers also contacting us for answers.
In short, the claim is true. Here's what we know:
Army confirms explosions will take place
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant launched a campaign to inform the public about the upcoming explosions, including an open house on Oct. 15 and a notice (archived) on Nov. 15 warning people in the affected area to evacuate and inviting residents to shelter at the Armed Forces Reserve Center during the explosions if needed.
In a document titled "Keeping Our Community Safe," the Army described how plans to reduce harm from the explosion by using specialized water misters and cleaning and removing affected soil and debris once the operation ceases.
(U.S. Army)
The public warnings issued by the Army to residents in the area were as follows:
- Consider avoiding the affected area.
- If you are inside of the affected areas, avoid outdoor air by staying indoors.
- Keep windows and doors closed.
- If it is safe to do so, set heating and cooling systems to "recirculate" to minimize outdoor air exposure and maximize indoor air filtration until the plume passes by your community.
- Avoid unnecessary travel through impacted areas.
- After the US Army determines the air exposure period has ended, consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces such as play surfaces for children and windowsills.
- If your car was parked outside, consider washing your car at a car wash to minimize your contact with potentially exposed surfaces.
Is the circulated 'blast zone' map accurate?
In the circulated map shown in the Facebook post above, the blast zone appears to stretch approximately 100 miles northeast from the blast site. We compared this map to maps the Army released ahead of the planned detonations and found they aligned.
(Facebook user Live Storm Chasers and U.S. Army)
As Nov. 20 draws closer, the Army's maps will be updated. Residents in the area were encouraged to regularly check for updates.
What is lead azide and how did it get there?
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lead azide is a "hazardous waste that exhibits the characteristic of reactivity (energetic) and exhibits the characteristic of toxicity for lead." In a public notice (archived) Nov. 16, the EPA wrote:
The recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation. The Army's evaluation of a range of potential alternatives for the treatment of lead azide culminated in the secretary of the Army selecting in-place, controlled, intentional detonation for the treatment of lead azide.
The material is used to initiate munitions, according to a Q&A document the Army published.
It's unclear precisely how the lead azide stores came to be stored at that underground location. While a number of media outlets reported that 68 barrels would be detonated, we were unable to confirm that amount. We contacted the Army seeking more context and information about the history of the lead azide stores and will update this story if we receive a response.
In March, the Army announced that experts were conducting a safety review for the "safe removal of a chemical compound currently at the plant."
On Nov. 17, local ABC affiliate KCRG reported that local activists were planning a "peaceful demonstration" against the planned detonations.
Group organizers were reportedly demanding:
- An immediate halt to the Nov. 20 lead azide detonation, at minimum until affected communities have had an adequate opportunity to review the risks and alternatives.
- Full transparency regarding the potential environmental and public health consequences.
- Independent environmental experts to review the proposed disposal method and evaluate safer alternatives.
- A comprehensive plan for independent air, soil, and surface testing in potentially affected communities.
- A commitment to clean up and remediate any lead contamination resulting from this operation, at no cost to affected residents and property owners.

The recent weeks have seen Australian cricket in turmoil with Usman Khawaja’s allegations in his autobiography ‘Sabr’ about the rest of the Australian team knowing that sandpaper was being used on the ball in the 2018 Newlands Test match against South Africa as well statements by Cameron Bancroft about how the whole team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper the ball in the Newlands Test and how the team had used the sandpaper for the first time in the second Test of the series at Port Elizabeth.
While Australian captain Pat Cummins called Khawaja’s allegations as ‘100% wrong’ and ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Bancroft statement as well the 12th man in the Newlands Test Chadd Sayers supporting Khawaja’s version led Cricket Australia to set up a forum that will allow the players and the support staff involved in the ball-tampering incident to share their experiences. Former England captain Ben Stokes, on the ‘That’s Not Cricket’ podcast which he co-hosts with former teammate Mark Wood, has compared the situation in Australian cricket to the situation in Marvel movie Captain America: Civil War.
“This is in Marvel Universe. This is the scene of Captain America Civil War, when they’re at the airport and then they’re all just flying in and then they’re just fighting amongst each other. This is literally a civil war in Australia at the moment. It’s completely utter chaos. It’s just civil war. That’s what I mean. It’s just complete and utter chaos because of how a situation was handled back in 2018. And I don’t think back then they ever thought about the situation happening because why would you think about someone doing releasing something in a book with these big claims when they handle it, they had to handle it in the way that they thought fit back then. They would never have thought that it is further down the line that something else would come from it. It’s just chaos and there’s a lot of people saying some things that, you know, I just think can have an effect on people who don’t deserve to be affected by it,” Stokes said on the podcast That’s Not Cricket.
With Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg along with Cricket Australia chair David Boon addressing media in recent days about the setting up of the forum for the players and support staff involved in Sandpaper gate to come and share their experiences, the recent days have also seen Cricket Australia talking with players. Usman Khawaja has shared on The Grade Cricketer podcast about how he spoke with Greenberg about finding the middle ground to the Sandpaper gate. Stokes further shared how he believes then Cricket Australia CEO James Sutherland and chairman David Peever could have resolved the situation post the ball tampering incident. “I think when this situation happened, there were two people in charge of Cricket Australia at the time. And regardless of what had happened back then in terms of what the players did, what they said, and what they’re seeing now, that’s two different things. What happened back in 2018 in terms of the process after Cameron was seen with sandpaper on his hand? I think people were acted in aware, but were instructed by whoever. But those are the two guys in charge of Cricket Australia back then (James Sutherland and David Peever). So they would have been the ones heavily involved in the process of what we’re going to do, you know, were they involved in the press conference, how that was conducted. And now it’s on the new regime with the new CEO and Chairman. So they’re in a difficult situation. I just think at the moment there is quite a few people who are answering for things that not necessarily they should be, but they are because of the situation that they now find themselves in. Pat being captain, you know, a new coach, a new CEO or a new director or whatever it is. It’s like, they weren’t involved in what happened in terms of the big decisions back then,” added Stokes.
The former England captain also shared that all the talk about Sandpaper gate should stop for now. “I just I don’t think we, in the close future, we were ever going to hear what truly happened because it’s just so deep. And for the sake of players, the staff, the management who were involved in this whole situation, for the sake of their families, for the sake of their friends, the best thing for it to do now would for just to stop because it’s affecting people who do not deserve to be affected by this. I think what I’m saying, because I’m coming from that, because I’ve been through something like this when you are so heavily in the media for something — that I’ve seen what it’s done to people who don’t deserve to be put through stress, put through anxiety,” said Stokes.

When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to prime minister Narendra Modi seeking a ban on releasing the Pakistani series “Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo” on Netflix India on December 4, 2026. The body has also demanded a "strong, permanent law" to keep Pakistani content off Indian television, OTT platforms and cinema. The letter, dated November 24 and signed by AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, was shared by news agency ANI on X. It is copied to information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and to Netflix India. AICWA’s four demands are listed below: that the series is not released or streamed in India on December 4 or any other date that all OTT and streaming platforms strictly comply with the May 8, 2025 advisory that the permanent law be enacted that platforms be made to understand that commercial interest can never come before national security and the sentiments of the martyrs' families The letter also appeals to Netflix India and other OTT platforms to state clearly in their social media posts that such content will not be shown in India. It ends with the line: "No Pakistani face, voice or story has a place on Indian screens." Netflix is yet to issue a statement on this. Inc42 has reached out to the company and the story will be updated based on their response. AICWA claimed that the series stars Pakistani actors — Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hania Aamir — have spoken against India at times of high tension between the two countries. The association said its letter speaks for the "140 Cr people" of the country. The letter's central argument is that Netflix's release would run directly against the government's stance. AICWA pointed to the information and broadcasting ministry's May 2025 advisory, which asked OTT platforms and streaming services to stop streaming Pakistan-origin web series, films, songs and podcasts. Back then, the ministry said that several terrorist attacks in India have been established to have cross-border linkages with Pakistan-based state and non-state actors. ICWA highlighted that the government itself had banned Pakistani artists from working in the Indian film industry after the recent Pulwama attack. Notably, this pattern of cancelling things associated with Pakistan is not only limited to content. Last year, trade body CAIT asked the government to ban Pakistani flags and merchandise on ecommerce platforms. The Central Consumer Protection Authority then issued notices to Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy and three other platforms over the sale of such products.

The situation in the India-China border areas remain “generally stable”, China’s Defence Ministry spokesperson and PLA Senior Colonel Chen Xi said on Thursday (November 26, 2026) adding that China “does not recognize the so-called Arunachal Pradesh illegally set up by India.”
“China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels, including general-level talks, to jointly implement the consensus reached by the two sides and safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas”, he said in response to a question at a press briefing on recent tensions in the Eastern sector of the border, Chinese state media reported.
On November 24, 2026, India and China concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks aimed at easing tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and putting in place measures to prevent friction between troops deployed along the frontier ahead of the onset of harsh winter conditions.
Sources in the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the closely guarded discussions, which began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between. The talks were described as cordial, though it remains unclear whether the measures discussed will be implemented on the ground before winter sets in fully.
The latest round of talks primarily focused on establishing engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, maintaining open communication channels and reducing tensions in the eastern sector. Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.

Deepavali, the festival of lights, left a trail of dark smoke across large parts of India’s northern plains, especially around the national capital, Delhi, where 80 million people, particularly infants and the elderly, are struggling to breathe. The Air Quality Index (AQI) at several locations in the National Capital Region (NCR) had touched 400, indicating the severity of the conditions. Other cities and towns in the north, south, east and west, though better off than the NCR because of favourable weather and geographical advantages, do not have pristine air either. Air in most Indian cities contains pollutants, including particulate matter, at levels about eight times higher than the threshold set by the World Health Organization. The worst part of the problem is its dire predictability, except for concessions from the weather. The costly lessons from the capital have implications for the entire country.
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) swiftly moved up the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) from Stage I to Stage III within 15 days. The Commission, a statutory body established as an emergency response to toxic air conditions, has been cracking down on farm fires in Punjab, with its teams visiting fields to check incidents of stubble burning. PAVAN-I3C, the CAQM’s new Integrated Command and Control Centre, seeks to capture non-compliance in industries, traffic and transport systems and trigger immediate action against pollution spikes. Construction and demolition (C&D) activities have been halted until the 20th of this month. Inspections of construction sites and checks of Pollution Under Control Certificates (PUCC) are also vigorous. Last week, in an unprecedented move, CAQM directed Delhi and other NCR States to plan reduction of annual pollution levels by 15-20% forthwith.
Regulatory moves, however essential, are not enough. Fines and work stoppages offer only partial deterrence, while obstructions and congestion on roads are an outright failure of enforcement. Institutional compliance, enforcement and monitoring by agencies are paramount, but civic behaviour is equally critical.
The asks of people are not any great sacrifices, but some lifestyle retuning: use public transport and minimise use of personal vehicles, work from home, avoid construction activities for a few weeks, clean air filters at homes and in vehicles, avoid activities which generate dust, heat and smoke, and avoid open burning of solid waste and biomass. It would be unimaginable in many other countries for vehicle owners to be reminded of the pollution caused by their vehicles only during the months when the air becomes unbreathable. If clean air is part of the right to life, citizens also have a charter of duties to follow.
The causes of pollution are well known. These straddle sectors, including industry, roads and buildings, vehicles, agriculture, shrinking green cover, municipal waste and urban living. However, citizens and their behaviour, in their varied roles as farmers, car and house owners, builders, contractors, and urban residents, remain at the centre. People complain and curse, and even silently suffer sickness from foul air, but sensitive and responsive behaviour remains elusive. The expansion of metro services and the availability of more public transport have not persuaded private car owners to switch. The Supreme Court went the extra mile by allowing firecrackers this Deepavali, while imposing justifiable restrictions on their toxic content and duration of use. Yet, citizens’ responses have not remotely matched the severity of the problem. It might seem contradictory, but many would like to reap all the dividends of GRAP without complying with its requirements.

Two-time Olympic medallist P.V. Sindhu has been named international event ambassador for the 11th edition of the Vedanta Pink City Half Marathon, scheduled to be held here on November 29.
The badminton star will lend her support to the Anil Agarwal Foundation's 'Run for Zero Hunger' campaign, under which Vedanta has pledged to provide one meal to a child or an animal in need for every kilometre covered by participants.

(Bloomberg) -- A rent freeze backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration was cleared by a state judge who dismissed a lawsuit filed by a group of landlords seeking to void the measure, which went into effect last month.
The landlords sued the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in July, arguing that Mamdani improperly influenced the vote and ignored evidence of rising operating costs for building owners. A judge on Wednesday threw out the case, saying the decision to implement the freeze was not “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious” and must be upheld.
But the judge, Brendan T. Lantry, sharply criticized Mamdani’s campaign promises to freeze the rent. The mayor’s comments were “reckless and irresponsible” because only the board can raise, freeze or adjust the rent of stabilized units in the city, the judge wrote. Correspondence between the mayor’s office and the board about the measure was “troubling” and “puts a dark shadow over the purported ‘independence’ of the board,” but it doesn’t show that the mayor dictated the decision, Lantry said.
“The court recognizes that political candidates routinely comment on prevalent policy issues while running for an elected position, but to guarantee a rent freeze to millions of New Yorkers without the authority to do so, is irresponsible and, quite frankly, invited” the lawsuit, the judge wrote. Still, there is “nothing to suggest the guideline-setting process was an orchestrated ‘sham process,” Lantry said.
In a statement, Mamdani cheered the decision. “This is a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in,” he said. “Because housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity. This holiday weekend, more than two million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier.”
Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords and a former deputy mayor in the Giuliani administration who has also challenged the pied-a-terre tax backed by Mamdani, didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.
The suit came weeks after the board voted for the first time ever to freeze rents for both one-year and two-year leases for roughly 1 million stabilized apartments. The last one-year rent freeze was during the pandemic in 2020.
Courts have historically deferred to the Rent Guidelines Board. A state court judge dismissed a challenge by landlords to a 2016 rent freeze. While that lawsuit claimed the board didn’t account for finances of the building, this challenge focused on the mayor’s involvement.
Mamdani made the freeze a centerpiece of his mayoral campaign, contending that tenants squeezed by years of rising housing costs needed immediate relief. After taking office, he appointed a majority of the board’s members. A member of the board who represented landlords, Christina Smyth, resigned in protest hours before the vote.
Tenant advocates hailed the vote as a long-overdue reset after inflation and housing shortages left many renters facing mounting financial pressure. Landlord and housing industry groups have warned that the freeze will make it harder for owners to maintain aging buildings and finance fixes as insurance, taxes and repair costs have surged amid a tight rental market.
The case is Kenilworth Holdings LLC v New York City Rent Guidelines Board, 453580/2026, New York State Supreme Court, New York County.

EXCLUSIVE: Lauren Ash (Superstore) and Mae Martin (Wayward) have been cast in Dirts, an ensemble adult animated high-school comedy series for New Metric Media‘s streaming service Shozer.
They will appear alongside the likes of Ash’s Superstore co-star Mark McKinney, Mark Little (Gary and His Demons) and Ryan Belleville (Workin’ Moms).
The show, set to premiere in winter 2027, follows Gus (Little) and Brus (Belleville), two deeply unpopular vegetable teenagers trying to survive life at Leguma Beach High, where high-society vine vegetables mingle with scrappy root transplants. The unlikely friends have to navigate the indignities of adolescence in a world where school politics can get particularly rotten.
Ash plays Sproutabella, Martin is Trevin Stems and McKinney Principal Corny. Also in the voice cast are Kyle Dooley (Cupcake & Dino: General Services) as Eggmilio and Butternut; Evany Rosen (Total Dramarama) as Cheryl and Snap Pea; Kayla Lorette (Doomlands) as Pep and Ms. Jicama; Rodrigo Fernandez-Stoll (BlackBerry) as Janitor McKale and Theatre Squash; and Chelsea Clark (Ginny & Georgia) as Gabe.
Dane Clark, Viveno Caldinelli and Mark Montefiore co-created the show, with Caldinelli directing. New Metric Media is the producer in partnership with Little Black Stone Studios. Ariel Yang and Max Wolfond are the producers for New Metric, with Tysen Potter in the same role for Little Black Stone. Production will cater for vertical and horizontal viewing, and you can watch a first-look clip above.
Dirts toplines the latest slate for Shozer, the YouTube comedy channel brand that Shoresy and Letterkenny producer New Metric launched last year.
Also greenlit is The Historical History of Canada, a mockumentary series that takes a twisted and satirical look at the most infamous moments in Canadian history. These will include the mysterious fire that destroyed the Parliament building in 1916 and the Toronto Maple Leafs’ latest Stanley Cup win. New Metric’s Lana Maclin, Alona Metzer and Liv Berkowitz are producing.
Elevator Comedy is a 30-part series of 45-second episodes that will give emerging comedy talent a platform, with performers put in close quarters with the audience. As with Dirts, it’s being produced for vertical and horizontal viewing.
The Eh-List, New Metric’s stand-up comedy strand, is also getting specials from Just For Laughs regular Daniel Tirado, veteran comic Alex Wood and viral sensation Drew Behm.
Shozer debuted last year with a slate of shows and films including Lionsgate’s Running Wilde, Van Wilder: Party Liaison and Zack and Miri Make A Porno, along with Letterkenny‘s first YouTube outing, LetterkennyProblems.
“We’ve spent years building comedy franchises and seeing what happens when audiences connect with great characters and creators,” said Montefiore, CEO of New Metric. “With Shozer, we’re applying that experience to a D2C model where we can discover new talent, invest in original ideas and build audience communities.
	“We want Shozer to become a trusted destination for comedy, where people come to discover their next favourite creator or series. And by developing and owning that IP from the outset, we have the flexibility to grow those properties across multiple platforms, formats and consumer experiences.”

Industrialist Lakshmi Venu has demanded partition of joint family assets belonging to the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family, intensifying the ongoing dispute over family wealth and succession rights.
Lakshmi is the daughter of TVS Group Chairman Emeritus Venu Srinivasan and Tractors and Farm Equipment Limited (TAFE) Chairman Mallika Srinivasan. She is also the great-granddaughter of TVS founder TV Sundaram Iyengar.
In the latest development, Lakshmi has moved to the Madras High Court to initiate legal proceedings to secure her claimed share of the joint family wealth.
Who Is Lakshmi Venu?
The 42-year-old industrialist holds an economics degree from Yale University and a doctorate in engineering management from the University of Warwick. She has been associated with the family's business operations from a young age.
According to TAFE's website, Lakshmi serves as the company's vice chairman and is also a director of TAFE Motors and Tractors Limited (TMTL). TAFE ranks among India's largest tractor and agricultural equipment manufacturers.
She is married to technology entrepreneur Mahesh Gogineni, an alumnus of BITS Pilani and the London School of Economics.
Invokes Hindu Succession Act
In her partition notice, Lakshmi urged her father to fulfil his fiduciary responsibilities as family head and facilitate an equitable division of assets.
Citing Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, amended in 2005, she asserted her independent right to seek partition and receive an equal share of joint family property.
Her claim covers family interests held through the VS Trust and other ownership structures, including assets allocated to the Srinivasan branch under the 2020 TVS family arrangement. These include interests in TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton.
Lakshmi maintained that the broader family arrangement did not amount to a partition within her immediate family. She argued that managerial authority cannot override the ownership rights of other family members.
She alleged that beneficial interests had been concentrated in her brother's favour, depriving her of her lawful entitlement.
Describing the alleged exclusion as a breach of law and trust, Lakshmi reiterated her preference for an amicable settlement that respects the legitimate rights of all family members.
