NASA's DART mission left a stadium-sized crater in an asteroid, the ESA finds
The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.
In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to new images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids. The 2022 controlled crash created an "impact crater the size of a sports stadium," according to Patrick Michel, the Director of Research at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Hera's principal investigator.
The crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid. Besides physically altering the surface of Dimorphos, the ESA found that the DART impact sent the asteroid tumbling in its new orbit. Hera also revealed that both Dimorphos and Didymos are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders.
All of these new details were captured by Hera's monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, multi-spectral Hyperscout H and JAXA-developed Thermal Infrared Imager from about 25 to 30km away from the asteroids, the ESA says.
"NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet."
NASA and other space agencies are exploring altering asteroids' orbits as one way of protecting the Earth from potentially dangerous future impacts. In December, the ESA plans to move Hera closer to Dimorphos and Didymos to capture even higher-resolution images of the impact site. In January, Hera will also deploy shoebox-sized CubeSats to collect other types of data. The Juventas CubeSat, created by a Luxembourg-led research team, will use radar to probe the asteroid's interior and eventually land on its surface. An Italian-led team will use the other CubeSat, Milani, to prospect asteroid dust and other surrounding materials.

Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

Srinagar- Amid the controversy over the playing of Vande Mataram at the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board’s Waqf Day function, Dr Kamal-ud-Din Farooqui has called for a balanced and respectful approach, saying that patriotism should not come at the cost of religious convictions.
In a statement, Farooqui, former Imam of Dargah Hazratbal, said the issue called for calm and principled reflection rooted in both Islamic teachings and constitutional values.
He said the Islamic principle of Tawheed, or the absolute Oneness of Allah, formed the foundation of Muslim faith, with worship and ultimate spiritual devotion belonging exclusively to God.
However, he emphasised that Islam also encouraged love for one’s homeland, goodwill towards fellow citizens and respect for all communities.
Citing Surah Al-Mumtahanah (60:8), he said the Quran encouraged kindness and justice towards those who did not fight Muslims on account of their faith.
“There is a vital distinction between civic loyalty and religious worship. Respecting one’s motherland is a noble duty; attributing divinity to it or treating it as an object of worship crosses into the realm of shirk,” he said.
Farooqui said certain expressions in the later stanzas of Vande Mataram, particularly those invoking the motherland through imagery of goddesses, posed a genuine theological difficulty for Muslims.
He stressed that such concerns should neither be dismissed nor misconstrued as a lack of patriotism.
Referring to Article 25 of the Indian Constitution, which guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess and practise religion, he said the constitutional framework also recognised an individual’s right to religious convictions.
He further cited the Quranic injunction, “There is no compulsion in religion,” arguing that matters of faith and conscience deserved sensitivity and respect.
Farooqui said the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board, being entrusted with the stewardship of Muslim religious endowments, had an added responsibility to remain sensitive to the religious beliefs of the community it represented.
He also urged members of the Muslim community to exercise restraint and avoid publicly condemning individuals or questioning their faith merely because of their presence at a public function.
“Matters of intention, awareness and spiritual accountability rest with Allah alone,” he said.
Appealing to religious scholars, public representatives and administrators, Farooqui said matters of conscience should not be turned into instruments of political polarisation.
“True patriotism never demands the compromise of one’s faith, just as genuine faith never permits the denial of justice and respect to others,” he said.
He said remaining steadfast in one’s religious convictions while upholding fairness and dignity for all was the path advocated by the Quran.

Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.
Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.
One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.
It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".

The warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner. Instead, the jailer insisted, Rom and his fellow deportees from the United States were “the king’s guests.”
Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa. Then he was made to stand at attention as the country’s national anthem, “Nkulunkulu Mnikati Wetibusiso temaSwati,” reverberated through the halls of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Most meals consisted of a portion of rice splashed with thin broth. It was late 2025, and the weather was warm and wet. For 15 minutes a day, Rom and the other men were allowed to go outside. Before they were locked up for lights out, the anthem played again; thick clouds of mosquitoes kept Rom thrashing all night.
Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene. If I’m a guest, then why am I being held in a prison with criminals? Rom would ask. Why aren’t I allowed to leave? But Rom knew these exchanges with the warden were absurd, like everything else about his situation.
Before the second Trump administration, the practice of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties was a rare and tightly restricted move in US immigration enforcement—reserved mainly for cases where a person simply could not be returned to their nation of origin due to risk of persecution or torture. It has since expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal. Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US. The kingdom of Eswatini, which agreed to take up to 160 migrants for a fee of $5.1 million, is one of them. Some of the other destination countries—the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan—are so violent and unstable that they rank on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.
Often making a spectacle of its own transgressiveness, the administration has steamrolled past public outcry, an investigation by Democratic lawmakers, and a warning from the United Nations about a “cascade of human rights violations” resulting from these removals. At least twice in the past two years, US federal courts have ordered the Department of Homeland Security to stop shipping migrants to third countries with insufficient due process. Both times, the Supreme Court has quickly stepped in to let the administration resume.
In September, during one of those brief, court-ordered pauses in removal flights, DHS general counsel James Percival went on X to publish the most comprehensive figures yet on how many migrants have been affected by the practice. He posted a GIF of Taylor Swift mouthing the words “That’s my husband” and pointing excitedly at her wedding ring. Percival’s caption: “How my wife looks at me when I tell her we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations.”
Rather than slowing down in the face of resistance, in fact, President Trump’s third-country push appears to have inspired imitators. Five European Union countries announced in November that they are working toward a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda. In the past two years, Italy has begun sending asylum seekers to Albania. The United Kingdom quietly sent an asylum seeker to Eswatini earlier this year; the man, originally from Sri Lanka, died last month, the government of Eswatini reported. According to local media, the apparent cause was suicide.
Rom’s lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen—who is himself the child of refugees from Vietnam—predicts that, if the administration keeps getting away with these expulsions, additional wealthy countries will be emboldened to offload their undesirables to poorer nations for a price. “This is going to be the new model for the West, not only for the United States,” says Nguyen, who also represents three other men currently held in Eswatini and Rwanda. “It’s just kind of out of sight, out of mind for these Western countries.”
But as Rom’s experience reveals, some of these removals may rest on little more than bureaucratic fiction. The US claims it has followed due process with every one of the 25,000 migrants deported to unfamiliar lands. “Their own countries say, ‘We do not want them back,’” US attorney general Todd Blanche told Fox News in early October. Yet in Rom’s case—among countless other Kafkaesque details—his own country never even appears to have been asked.
An American in virtually everything but citizenship status, Rom came to the United States as a 3-year-old refugee from Cambodia. Around 1979, his parents fled their home to escape the horrors of the Khmer Rouge, a genocidal regime that seized power in the wake of Richard Nixon’s carpet-bombing of the country. From there, the family went to a Thai refugee camp—where Rom was born in 1982—and then to a resettlement center in the Philippines. As Rom’s father was selling off possessions to raise money for their ultimate move to America, he was killed by roadside thieves. Rom sat by his side after the attack, his mother later told him, trying to wake his father up.
Rom’s first memories of America are of a cramped, dimly lit bedroom in a small apartment in the Bronx, where he arrived with his mother and six siblings in 1985. “There was just one mattress, and we all slept on that,” he says. “It was a new world to us; everything was new.”
Rom and his family had arrived in the middle of the largest resettlement effort in US history. As America’s chimerical war efforts in Southeast Asia faltered in the 1970s, hundreds of thousands of people began arriving in the US from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. Of the nearly 158,000 Cambodians who gained entry between 1975 and 1994, the majority, like Rom and his family, were refugees deeply marked by the atrocities of the Khmer Rouge.
Around 10,000 of them came to be resettled in areas of the Bronx that were blighted by high crime and poverty. Many were placed in dilapidated housing, with limited job opportunities. Rom’s mother, who didn’t speak English, relied on government support checks and whatever extra income she could make sewing and scavenging. As a child, Rom would help her collect cans and carry the overstuffed bags to the grocery store to return for cash.
With the help of an uncle, the family eventually relocated to Philadelphia, where an adolescent Rom was enticed by a newly formed gang—a Cambodian clique within the Crips called the Blue Dragons. “If you don’t want to get bullied,” older members of the gang told him, “you need to link up with us.” Rom was barely a teenager. An older gang member dubbed him Menace, after Dennis the Menace, because he was “funny and bad at the same time.”
By the time he was 18, Rom had done three stints in juvenile detention and was caught in ever-escalating street beefs. At a New Year’s Eve party in 2008, rival gang members jumped him. Rom waited for a day off from his job—caring for abandoned dogs at a local rescue—to seek revenge. He parked outside the gang’s hangout, and when his targets exited, he opened fire from his car. Rom contemplated running when he heard that the police were looking for him but decided against it largely because he had a young daughter. In jail he would be able to see her, even if it was from behind glass. On the lam, he’d have to disappear. He pleaded guilty in April 2010 to multiple charges, including attempted murder.
Rom was a legal permanent resident of the US, a status he had been granted as a refugee. Though refugees are entitled to obtain full American citizenship, Rom had been told he didn’t stand a chance due to his juvenile record, an obstacle that would greatly alter the trajectory of his life.
Under US immigration law since the 1990s, legal permanent residents who commit crimes that qualify as “aggravated felonies”—an expansive and, critics say, somewhat arbitrary legal category—can lose their immigration status and become subject to deportation after they’ve served out their sentences. In a case of what immigrant advocates call “double punishment,” Rom’s conviction for attempted murder meant he would lose his green card. And he knew that in the post-9/11 era, his home country had bowed to US pressure to accept the repatriation of deported Cambodian refugees.
Rom likes to say that prison saved his life. He spent much of his time in lockup reading, exercising, and making cents an hour working in the kitchen to save up for small gifts for his daughter. As he served out his sentence, a generation of shifts in America’s immigration policy flew by—from President Obama’s support of the Dreamers and record-high deportation numbers to Trump’s policy of family separation to Biden’s border crisis to Trump’s return to the White House. But in Rom’s mind, none of that made a difference for him: His fate was already sealed. He was fully prepared to be deported to Cambodia, a country he had never visited, once his sentence was finished.
Rom’s reserved mood as his prison term neared its end confused fellow inmates. “Yo, why are you not happy?” they asked. “You’re about to be released, you made parole.” On November 13, 2024, Rom walked out after serving 15 years. He was immediately transferred to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) holding, where what he believed would be a straightforward process turned into a bewildering journey through the American deportation machine.
From detention, Rom did what he could to hasten the process of his own removal. He frequently called the Cambodian embassy in Washington, DC, seeking information on his departure process. He was told that his questions should be directed to the Department of Homeland Security. Officers in Pennsylvania, he says, had no updates. They told Rom they were swamped by the number of cases they were trying to handle. At one point, they told him he would be deported to Thailand, his country of birth, which he told them was incorrect. After six months of detention, Rom filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he was being unlawfully detained.
He continued to wait for another three months. On September 24, 2025, his daughter’s birthday, Rom saw on a tablet device that his commissary account had been zeroed out. Among ICE detainees, this is a telltale sign that deportation is imminent. The following day, Rom was transferred to Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in Louisiana. He was moved again a few days later to Alexandria, Louisiana, where the airport hums with obscure charter airlines that ferry deportees abroad. He waited there for another 72 hours before he started, again, asking officers what was happening.
At first, they said they didn’t know, a claim Rom found hard to believe. When an officer checked his case on the computer system and then quickly clammed up, Rom’s suspicions grew. Finally they told him to pack up, and Rom caught a look at the immigration paperwork. It listed Eswatini as the country of deportation. Confused, Rom turned to another detainee: “Hey, bro, is Eswatini another ICE facility in Louisiana?” he asked. The man responded that it was in southern Africa.
Rom ran to the phone and made a panicked call to his sister in Las Vegas. She searched online and confirmed that Eswatini was indeed in Africa. Rom asked her to call the Cambodian Embassy. Another detainee’s lawyer suggested the group request “reasonable fear” interviews: US Citizenship and Immigration Services conducts these interviews through their asylum officers to ascertain if a person has a reasonable fear of persecution or torture. Immigration agents seemed amused by the suggestion, Rom says. What could the men be afraid of? they asked. “Y’all a bunch of murderers,” Rom recalls them taunting.
Rom pleaded with the guards. Eventually, one officer told him and the others that if they agreed to be shackled, he would take down their request in writing. They stepped into the restraints, and the officer set about filling out some paperwork. As they sat waiting, their feet and hands in chains, Rom gave the request for a “reasonable fear” interview one last try. “Hey,” he asked, “you think you are going to give us that interview?” He realized it was “all fake” and that the officers never intended to file anything.
One by one, under heavy guard, the men were loaded onto a small airplane. When the door closed it was “like my coffin is closing,” says KV, another deportee on the flight who asked to be identified by his initials because he remains detained. The plane flew from Alexandria to Puerto Rico. The officials accompanying the men gave them no information. They tried, and failed, to disable the small TVs that showed the plane’s flight path.
The plane carried on to Senegal, where they were delayed as officials sought permission to travel onward. “They were basically smuggling us through Africa,” Rom says. When the flight touched down at King Mswati III International Airport early on the morning of October 6, the runway was lined with dozens of armed military personnel. Rom was loaded into a paddy wagon. As the van turned onto a dirt road, Rom was overcome with fear. Oh yeah, they are going to kill us, Rom thought. They’re definitely going to kill us.
Eswatini, a country about the size of New Jersey surrounded almost entirely by South Africa, is the continent’s last remaining absolute monarchy. In April 1973, King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and banned all political parties. The ban remains in place. His son, King Mswati III, took power in 1986, at just 18 years old. Challenges to the monarchy have been met with violence. In June 2021, security forces cracked down on pro-democracy protests, killing 46 people, including two children, according to a government inquiry. Civil society organizations say this is an undercount. A leading human rights lawyer and pro-democracy activist was assassinated at his home two years later. No one has been held accountable for his death.
Eswatini has the highest HIV prevalence rates in the world. Poverty in the country is pervasive. A 2024 report from the US State Department describes Eswatini as having “significant human rights issues,” including torture, media restrictions, and the worst forms of child labor. The king is reportedly married to a cohort of wives and lives a life divorced from his country’s brutal reality. At an April event to mark his 40 years on the throne, he held an extravagant party at a luxury convention center that included a performance by Grammy-nominated singer Davido.
The men, none of whom had committed any crime in Eswatini, were deposited in a high-security area of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Rom’s cell sat behind a large metal door with a barred window painted forest green. When the detainees arrived, the cells were dirty. They asked for cleaning products but were told that none were available. Basic hygiene supplies took four months to arrive. In a dirt courtyard outside, the men had access to a row of concrete sinks to hand-wash their clothes during their 15 daily minutes of outdoor time. One detainee was allowed to retrieve the clothes in the evening.
Rom’s 15-year sentence in the US proved to be a useful experience. He fell back into his workout routine from prison, knocking out 500 pushups a day along with burpees and sit-ups. He read books donated to the prison, churning through the Hunger Games and Twilight series. His lawyer sent him a copy of First They Killed My Father, a memoir about surviving the Khmer Rouge. Rom had expected the weather to cool down at night, but there was little reprieve from the heat. He was given heavy blankets, which meant choosing between sweltering or being swarmed by mosquitoes. He asked jailers the same question he had been asking the guards in the US. “How long am I going to be here?” No one had an answer.
Gradually, the men were granted a few freedoms. They were brought to a mobile store so those without phones could buy them using money from their families. On the way back, they were allowed to eat at KFC and buy two beers apiece. These were the first excursions Rom had taken outside of detention facilities in more than 15 years.
In a post on X, a DHS official had said that the men being deported to Eswatini were “depraved monsters,” and those statements had spread in local media. So Rom smiled and waved, saying hello to the people who stopped to gawk.
The men were permitted to make one phone call a week using WhatsApp. The calls were broadcast in a common room; a prison official would sit nearby, scribbling notes. When Rom wanted to discuss something sensitive with his sister, the two would switch to speaking in Khmer. Local lawyers were barred from visiting. Shortly after Rom was deported, his sister saw a post on Facebook that mentioned Tin Thanh Nguyen, the lawyer in North Carolina. She got in touch, and Nguyen agreed to take Rom’s case.
Thanks to a TV in the common room that was set to the news, Rom was well aware of the controversy surrounding his fellow deportees. He watched a report about one fellow Matsapha inmate from Cuba, Roberto Mosquera del Peral, who had arrived earlier and was on a hunger strike. Each morning, when officers checked Mosquera del Peral’s cell, Rom says, they would shout, mockingly asking if he was still alive.
How Rom and the others came to be trapped in Eswatini is still unclear. According to a report from Reuters, the deal was brokered in February 2025 between Caitlin Piper, a diplomat who was leading the US embassy in the capital of Mbabane, and Russell Dlamini, the country’s prime minister, who sought and received approval from the king. Neither Dlamini nor the acting government spokesperson, Thabile Mdluli, responded to requests for comment. In May, a spokesperson for King Mswati told Reuters that “the king embraced the deal as Eswatini’s contribution to world order.”
Piper has since departed Eswatini. She was most recently based at the US Consulate in Erbil, Iraq, according to social media posts from the consulate. The consulate did not respond to requests for comment on her current position.
In November 2025, more than a month after Rom arrived and four months after the first deportees were deposited at the prison, Eswatini’s finance minister confirmed that he had received a $5.1 million payment from the US. He said the money would be funneled toward Eswatini’s National Disaster Management Agency. The country said it would accept 160 deportees as part of the agreement. The State Department eventually posted a copy of the memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries on May 14, 2025, which confirmed these details. The signature of the US official includes a looping C, but no name is printed underneath. Asked for comment, the Eswatini Press Inquiries Team at the embassy directed questions to the Department of State in Washington. The Department of State did not respond to questions regarding who signed the agreement.
This payment disclosure led the men in detention to charge that they had been trafficked. “You are moving people around, and money is exchanged,” says KV. “So what is that?” If Eswatini got all that money, Rom wondered, why was he having to spend his own on basics like a fan for his cell?
The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC), a human rights NGO, joined several other groups in filing a legal challenge against Eswatini in 2025, aiming to declare the deportation agreement unconstitutional, obtain the terms of the agreement, and secure an order stopping further arrivals until the matter was legally resolved. The initial challenge was dismissed. SALC and the other groups filed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Eswatini in March. (Just weeks before her reported meeting with Eswatini’s prime minister to facilitate the deportations, Piper had addressed an SALC workshop, urging participants “to bring injustice to light, to demand the respect of those in power, to advocate for a world in which our most cherished freedoms are secured.” )
Rom’s personal path to Eswatini appears to have come about through a combination of cruelty and bureaucratic ineptitude. Nguyen points out that Cambodia has been accepting deportees for more than two decades and that the country is generally responsive and professional in issuing the requisite travel documents. He says that the Cambodian government moved to begin rectifying the situation within a week of his contacting them in October 2025.
Nguyen believes that the US erroneously thought Rom should be sent to Thailand, the country of his birth, not citizenship, but never bothered to contact government officials from that country or from Cambodia. Chann Rotana, a spokesman for Cambodia’s foreign ministry, says they also do not understand why Rom was sent to Africa. He adds that the US did not contact the country’s embassy in Washington, DC, regarding Rom’s case before he left the country. Rotana described the deportation to Africa as “strange” and said the embassy only became aware of the situation when Rom’s sister got in touch. Asked about Rotana’s comments, the Department of Homeland Security directed questions to the Department of State, which declined to respond.
“There’s no rhyme or reason as to why any of my clients were picked to go to Eswatini versus the clients that I have who are actually in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia,” Nguyen says. “There’s nothing that makes them distinguishable.”
After an interview with Cambodian officials, Rom’s case for removal progressed while the other men sat hoping for similar developments. When he was cleared to be sent to Cambodia in early February, he requested that he be escorted by a representative from the UN’s International Organization for Migration as a form of insurance. Rom finally arrived in Cambodia on March 26, becoming the second US deportee freed from Eswatini. (The first, a Jamaican man named Orville Isaac Etoria, was deported to Eswatini in July 2025 and repatriated to Jamaica in September of that year.)
When I met Rom in June, at a restaurant in the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh, he was dressed in all black. The sleeves of his polo shirt were taut around his thick, tattooed arms. We met within walking distance of S-21, a Khmer Rouge torture and interrogation center that is now a museum dedicated to the genocide that set his family on its path to America. He is contemplative about his journey and speaks softly.
After arriving in Cambodia, Rom enrolled in a creative writing class, hoping to detail his experience. He was taking teacher training courses, hoping to land a job at an international school, and picked up work fixing air conditioners when he could.
The jarring transition to life in Cambodia was made harder when his older sister—who had been his lifeline in detention—died in July. “Im trying to hold it together,” he texted me. In August, Rom sent a string of messages saying he’d gotten a job teaching English to a rambunctious group of third graders.
Once a week, Rom calls the deportees who remain in Africa. There are more now. A few weeks after Rom and I met, Eswatini announced that it had received a fourth batch of 11 deportees. Another group followed. Thirty-two have been forced to the country in total. KV remains imprisoned. “With the holidays around the corner,” he texted in late September, “it feels I’m wasting my life sitting here for no reason.” It is unclear when he will be released.
The fate of all third-country deportees stands to be clarified in the coming months. After at least twice granting the Trump administration temporary stays to keep deporting migrants to third countries, the US Supreme Court will start hearing oral arguments on the ultimate legality of the practice in December.
Shortly after he arrived in Cambodia, Rom noticed that Kuenene, his warden at Matsapha, had added him as a contact on Telegram and WhatsApp. Another Eswatini official requested to connect on Facebook and follow Rom on Instagram. Rom accepted some of the invitations and declined others; he couldn’t tell why they were trying to befriend him. Maybe Kuenene wanted to keep tabs on what Rom might say publicly. “He was one of those guys that tell you what you want to hear, smile at your face, make you believe that he is the most supportive guy in the world, and then he will stab you in the back,” Rom said. “I didn’t trust him.” Before he was released, Rom told the guards and other deportees that he might return to Eswatini to visit as a tourist. In reality, he has no intention of ever returning. One visit as a royal guest was enough.

For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology. Today, nearly every radiologist uses AI tools, whether that’s to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day.
But last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI. Business acquisitions and debates centered on technology, powered by vision-language models, that can do the core work of a radiologist: looking at an image, and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it.
“Last year’s RSNA was mainly focused on whether it’s actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report, and that would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist,” said Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc.

India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
- Published
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," Das wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

Frustration reigns for Pochettino in chaotic start to Man Utd job
- Published
Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?
United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.
Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.
This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.
Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".
That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.
Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.
United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.
Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.
A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.
A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.
"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."
Pochettino searching for first Man Utd win
Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.
The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre.
Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.
Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.
"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.
"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."
United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.
Pochettino defends Lammens over error
Young said Lammens may be one mistake from being dropped.
The Belgian's performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount.
It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy.
Darlow did end last season as first choice at Leeds but started just 30 league games in his three seasons with the Elland Road club. Tom Heaton, 40, who was also on the bench against Sporting, has not played in a senior game since February 2023.
Could Pochettino contemplate leaving Lammens out.
"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.
"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.
"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."
It has been a whirlwind week for Pochettino, who last Wednesday morning UK time was still United States boss.
There have been a few blows to absorb, and lessons are having to be learned quickly.
But despite the clear frustrations, the 54-year-old is glad he accepted the challenge.
"I am happy to be here," he said. "I'm so excited to be the face representing this club.
"We are here because the situation wasn't the situation all the fans and people expect. We are here to take the responsibility from one week, and we are going to improve for sure.
"It's going to be tough, of course. Nothing is easy. But we have the energy and I think we have the capacity, and, most important, we have the players and the power and the energy from our fans, which is massive."

Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.
Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.
Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.
The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.
Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.
Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry
Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.
In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.
Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.
These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.
The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."
The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.
In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.
Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.
Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.
Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.
The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.
RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."
The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.
The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

A video showing a woman holding a weapon and trying to protect her house and child as a mob attacks and vandalises the house is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it depicts an attack on Hindu homes in Bangladesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a mob attacking Hindu homes in Bangladesh, while a woman tries to protect her house and child.
Fact: The video shows a mob attacking the houses of two men accused of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh, on 25 March 2026. The woman seen holding a child and a sharp weapon while trying to protect her house is the wife of one of the accused. Police confirmed that theft cases had been registered against the accused but condemned the mob attack. Bangladeshi fact-checkers also clarified that the woman is Muslim and that the incident stemmed from allegations of cattle theft, not communal violence. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) from March 2026, which identified the incident as one involving allegations of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Dolar Bazar Union, Chhatak Upazila, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh.
According to these reports, villagers were angered by repeated cattle theft. A man named Saifur Rahman was reportedly caught stealing cattle in neighbouring North Kurshi village. During questioning, he allegedly named Ali Hussain, his son-in-law Tarek Mia, and several others as being involved in the thefts. Following this, an agitated mob attacked the houses of Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia in South Kurshi village on 25 March 2026.
The reports stated that more than a hundred people gathered following the allegations and vandalised and looted the houses of the accused. The mob threw bricks and stones, damaged tin walls and household belongings, and attacked women and children. The viral video shows Tarek Mia’s wife, who is also Ali Hussain’s daughter, holding a child and a sharp weapon as she attempts to protect her house from the mob. She tries to fend off the attackers, but they continue to vandalise the house.
Reports further stated that Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia had previously faced theft allegations. Sub-Inspector Abdur Rahman of the Zahidpur Police Investigation Centre reportedly said that police had registered multiple theft cases against the accused and filed a case in connection with the latest incident. However, the officer condemned the mob attack, stating that vandalising someone’s house was unjustified, despite the villagers’ frustration over repeated thefts. The viral video, therefore, depicts an incident arising from allegations of cattle theft in Bangladesh and has no communal angle.
We also found an X post by Bangladeshi fact-checker Shohanur Rahman dated 1 November 2026, stating that the woman is Muslim and the wife of Mohammad Tarek. He clarified that she was trying to protect her father’s house during an attack triggered by allegations of theft.
To sum up, the video of a mob attacking houses in Bangladesh over cattle theft allegations is falsely shared with a communal spin.

Separately, a senior U.S. Department of War official, speaking on background, warned the Pentagon was prepared to "up the ante" on recent restrictions it had imposed on interaction with the Canadian military unless Ottawa took Washington's concerns more seriously.
"I won't get drawn on what other nations may say," said Stringer.
"What I do look at in Canada now is a nation putting significant forces into Europe, most obviously, but not exclusively the multinational brigade in Latvia. I look at a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its forces."
In a background briefing this week, senior officials with the U.S. Department of War said Canada's contribution to NATO was exaggerated.
"I would say that the gap between rhetoric and reality in Ottawa is the widest in all of NATO,” said one Pentagon official.
"It’s an unquestioned fact that Canada's commitment to NORAD is not backed by needed defence investment and its readiness is well below what is expected. The United States makes up the gap. And in the context of NATO, Canada’s minimal contributions barely make a dent."
Asked directly whether he was satisfied with the readiness of the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia, Stringer responded: "I'm happy when I look at Canada."
At the moment, there are roughly 2,200 Canadian troops in Latvia with a plan to increase the number to 2,600 in the near term.
Aside from contributing a battle group, Canada serves as the commander of the 3,000-strong NATO multinational brigade, a deployment which Carney recently extended until 2031.
The commitment to Operation Reassurance, according to the recent federal budget, will amount to $7 billion during that timeframe.
Canada isn't alone in terms of where it is on the curve of rebuilding its forces and is making the necessary investments, said Stringer, who is next in line to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich.
"Everybody had that wonderful moment of — we won the Cold War and it created both physical disinvestment and it also created a bit of conceptual disinvestment," Stringer said.
"A bunch of nations now are coming out of some relatively low spends and I look at Canada as one of those nations that's spending well."
On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a "fact sheet" that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and that military spending is unfocused. The document pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics and deferred modernizations of key equipment.
"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer," the fact sheet said.
But Canada is hardly alone among NATO allies in struggling with military readiness, including the United States itself.
The U.S. Government Accountability Office told Congress in March that American military readiness had deteriorated over the past two decades. Twenty-five of 27 types of its army and air force aircraft failed to meet their operational availability targets in 2024.
A separate audit, published in June, found the mission-capable rate for the American F-35 fleet had plunged from 67 per cent in 2021 to 44 per cent last year. Only 25 per cent were capable of performing all their assigned missions.
Senior U.S. Navy officials said last year that readiness across their fleet of ships, submarines and aircraft hovered between 67 and 70 per cent.
Britain, meanwhile, refuses to publicly disclose detailed military readiness figures, citing national security. Parliamentary research published this year showed all three branches were below their trained personnel targets.
France has similarly restricted publication of readiness data. Its 2023 figures projected operational availability of 69 per cent for combat aircraft, 59 per cent for frigates and 87 per cent for battle tanks.
Germany has also classified detailed equipment readiness figures, making direct comparisons with Canada's military particularly difficult.
"If I look at where Canada is in that mix, it looks a lot like a lot of other nations," said Stringer.
"Readiness can always be improved. You can always be better tomorrow than you are today. And indeed that's one of the focuses we've got with all the nations in the alliance."
Going into a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Wednesday, the prime minister weighed in and dismissed the controversy with the Pentagon.
"I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we're focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently," Carney said.
"Canada is taking responsibility for our defence. We're at the front lines of NATO's defence, Operation Reassurance in Latvia. We're working with our NATO partners, including the U.S. but very much with the Nordics — with Germany, with France — through the High North, the Arctic."
As Canada and the U.S. debate commitment and investment, Stringer and the rest of NATO's supreme command has focused on Russia's rising campaign of grey zone warfare in Europe.
Last week, three Russian KH-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during a large-scale overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. There were no injuries or infrastructure damage. One missile landed about 35 kilometres from where troops from 11 allied countries were conducting military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the airspace violation an "intentional provocation" by Russia.
Stringer was not prepared to go that far, saying an investigation was still being conducted.
"What we're really looking at is, why did they go there? And fundamentally … was it deliberate or was it accidental?" Stringer told CBC News.
"And by the way, even if it's accidental, what does it tell us about a recklessness in warfare five years into their three-day special military operation?"
He said Russia is always seeking to provoke. The question for NATO is how to respond.
"What we don't need to do is do Mr. Putin's job for him by overreacting," Stringer said. "What we need to do is be calm and measured and resolute in the approach to provocations. And by the way, not every military act needs, even warrants, some form of military response."

New Delhi- The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has asked Netflix to ensure that content originating in Pakistan is not streamed in India, official sources said.
The directive came after the I&B Ministry received several complaints and representations regarding the possible release in India of Pakistan-based web series ‘Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo’.
The ministry has asked Netflix to adhere to its advisory dated May 8, 2025, and ensure that streaming content originating in Pakistan is not available in India, sources said.
In June last year, Netflix informed the ministry that it had made no film or series originating in Pakistan available to subscribers in India.
The ministry has asked Netflix to stand by that commitment it gave then and maintain the position it conveyed at the time.
The trailer for the show dropped on Tuesday, and it is supposed to be streamed on December 4.

WhatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.
WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send
You can schedule WhatsApp texts you might forget to send up to two weeks ahead of time.
If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too.
Meta:
To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.
Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.
Scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
- Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results? 
  - Published6 November
- Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back 
  - Published6 days ago
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
- The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon 
  - Published10 April 2025
Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.
It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".
It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".
Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients
The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the company’s LINK device.
Elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the company announced. The study represents a more advanced step in the company's efforts to develop a brain implant that allows people with paralysis to control devices using their brain alone. It will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement.
"We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink announced on X. "This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date."
Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the company revealed that its first participant with ALS named Bradford Smith was able to communicate using brain signals alone. "Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people," Smith said at the time.
We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.
Those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more:https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR pic.twitter.com/Vor7iXXCBA
— Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026
The FDA authorization was granted on an experimental basis, but it's a key step forward for Neuralink's LINK brain-implant system. The study will evaluate the ability of patients to control digital devices through thought, "with a focus on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life," Neuralink wrote. It will also assess the system's long-term safety and reliability.
WIth Neuralink's latest system, the company's N1 implant is surgically placed in the skull, then the company uses its R1 robot to insert flexible electrodes into the brain. Neural activity from the brain associated with movement is then interpreted by software, which translates signals into commands for controlling computers or digital devices. The technology is designed to help patients communicate with the outside world, with the eventual goal to let them operate devices without keyboards or other physical controls.
Neuralink said patients with ALS may be eligible for the LINK trial, but it didn't specify other requirements or the number of participants. It now has approval recruit participants, then conduct the study under an approved clinical protocol. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

B.C.'s new premier outlines 3 immediate priorities after first cabinet meeting
Lorne Doerkson's top 3 to-dos: George Massey replacement, removing SOGI materials, return-to-office
B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson has announced he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting.
Doerkson listed his first priority as posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to replace the George Massey Tunnel between Richmond and Delta.
He said at a news conference Wednesday afternoon the notice would be posted later in the day and will ask the current contractor to do the work.
He said cabinet would review the numbers before making a final decision to ensure the project is the most cost-effective.
"Our responsibility is to ensure taxpayers get the best value for their money," Doerkson said.
He said British Columbians want access over the river, and he wants the space to understand the project.
"I am, obviously, very big on 'bridge' right now, but I do want to understand a few things just before that final decision happens, and I hope that to happen before Christmas."
The previous B.C. NDP government had planned to replace the tunnel, rather than build a bridge.

Secondly, Doerkson said SOGI 123 materials will be taken off government websites "as of today."
SOGI (which stands for sexual orientation and gender identity) 123 has been a resource teachers and educators can turn to to make schools safer and more inclusive for students of all gender identities and orientations, according to its website.
Doerkson said the Ministry of Education will work with school districts to take SOGI 123 materials out of schools.
"We are starting that work right now."
He said parents should have a say in how and when "sensitive topics" are introduced in schools.
"We want our schools to be safe and welcoming places, of course, for every student, with a strong focus on reading, writing, arithmetic and on teaching kids to think for themselves," Doerkson said.
He said he wants to "better understand how our schools were not safe prior to SOGI" and "how we will make sure that our student body is safe."
He added: "SOGI, of course, has been conflated with so much now — I'm not certain that I've even been able to get a good explanation from ministry staff or from teachers, frankly, on this topic."
Doerkson responded to a reporter's question on what would happen if teachers continue to use the SOGI resource.
"We've asked for it to be removed from the rooms, so it's not just that they'll get pushback from parents, but they'll get pushback from me as well."
Return-to-office planned for public servants
Doerkson's third priority is for B.C. Public Service workers to return to the office in a phased plan.
Those who can work from the office "will be back at it, five days a week," Doerkson said.
He said he's written to the head of the public service to start planning for the return-to-office policy.
He said thousands of public servants, such as nurses, teachers, correctional workers and those providing frontline services, have never had the choice to work remotely.
"I think it's reasonable to ask for people in our offices to do the same," Doerkson said, adding people collaborate better in the same room.
