Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.
"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."
The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.
Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.
"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.
Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)
One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.
"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."
The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.
Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.
"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."
The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.
June Hersh, a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.
"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

The United States (US) proposed a tariff rate of up to 25 per cent on Indian imports, but said it could be reduced to 17 per cent if a long-pending trade deal between New Delhi and Washington is struck. India and the US agreed a framework for an interim deal in February, which set an 18 per cent rate, but have not signed an agreement.
Most Indian goods have faced an additional 10 per cent US tariff since July 24, imposed following a separate investigation into forced labour. The new duty will not be added to it. The proposal is "net of existing Section 301 tariffs". A senior US trade official told the Hindustan Times that importers will pay the higher of the two rates.
India is among 14 countries for which the US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs on Wednesday. The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Quick answers to key questions
The proposed rate is 17% if India and the US finalize a trade agreement. Without a deal, Indian imports could face a rate of up to 25%.
No. The article says the proposed duty will not be added to the separate 10% tariff; importers would pay the higher of the two rates.
The tariffs are not expected to take effect until next year and must go through public consultation and potentially hearings. Written comments and hearing requests are due by January 5, 2027, with hearings scheduled to begin January 25.
At 17% with a trade deal, India’s proposed rate is below the 18% rates listed for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, and the 20% rates for China and Vietnam.
The proposal follows a USTR Section 301 investigation into manufacturing policies, structural excess capacity and market-access barriers. India has rejected the claim that it has structural excess capacity in any sector.
The 14 economies mentioned in the report by the office of the United States Trade Representative are: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time.
At the proposed 17 per cent rate contingent on a much-awaited India-US trade deal, India's tariff will be a little lower than rates planned for many key countries with which India competes, potentially giving Indian exporters a competitive advantage.
The Trump administration has proposed a rate of 18 per cent for Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia. Meanwhile, Vietnam faces 20 per cent rate with a deal and up to 35 per cent without one.
China, too, faces a 20 per cent tariff, which complies with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent. China's 20 per cent rate would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.
The potential 17 per cent rate for India is also a notch lower than the 18 per cent agreed by the US and India in a framework for a trade deal in February. That was before the US Supreme Court invalidated President Donald Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to the current 10 per cent baseline rate.

Without a deal with the US, India's 25 per cent ceiling matches that of Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand (18 per cent). The EU, Japan and Switzerland face 15 per cent, including their existing most-favoured-nation (MFN) duties, rising to as much as 20 per cent.
South Korea and Taiwan (net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs) face 15 per cent, with a ceiling of 25 per cent, HT reported.

The story so far: On November 22, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s apex food-safety regulator, sanctioned prosecution against packaged drinking water manufacturer Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd. after a sample of its water was found to be non-compliant with prescribed safety standards, with the regulator declaring it unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The public-health stakes are significant. In 2023, bottled water was the principal source of drinking water for 15% of urban and 6% of rural households, as per Data For India. For consumers buying it at railway stations, airports, highway eateries and neighbourhood shops, a sealed bottle is often taken as an assurance of safety. Yet, the data submitted in Parliament in February 2025 revealed that 333 of 1,300 enforcement samples of packaged drinking water tested in 2023-24 failed to meet prescribed standards. Similarly, in 2022-23, 650 of 1,776 samples had been found non-compliant.
According to the FSSAI, a sample of packaged drinking water (other than mineral water) collected from Bisleri’s premises was found to be non-compliant with the prescribed limits for “bromate” and was declared unsafe under the 2006 Act. Following an appeal by the food business operator (FBO), the sample was referred to a Referral Food Laboratory for further examination, which also declared the sample unsafe, citing the detection of “polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons” (PAHs).
In its response, Bisleri has maintained that its water is safe for consumption, saying the matter concerned a batch manufactured at its Goa facility in September 2025, one of 143 manufacturing plants in its network. In a statement issued on November 23, the company said the FSSAI had collected six samples from its Goa facility on September 30, 2025. While five samples met the prescribed standards, the sixth recorded a “bromate” level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre. Further, Bisleri said it appealed on November 22, 2025, following which the sample was sent to a referral laboratory for retesting. The laboratory, as claimed, found the bromate level within the prescribed limit but separately detected PAHs. Citing the divergent test findings, the company reportedly arranged an independent examination of the same sample at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which, according to Bisleri, also found the bromate level within limits. The company said it submitted these results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office on February 2, 2026, but received no further communication and understood that the matter had been closed.
Water is essential for digestion, blood circulation, temperature regulation and kidney function, but its safety cannot be judged by its appearance, taste, odour or sealed packaging alone. Contamination may be microbiological, causing illnesses such as diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid, or chemical, with some substances posing risks through prolonged exposure. In India, packaged water broadly falls into two categories: (1) “packaged drinking water”, which may be sourced from surface water, groundwater or seawater and treated through processes such as filtration, decantation, reverse osmosis (RO) and disinfection; and (2) “natural mineral water”, drawn from protected underground sources and characterised by a relatively stable mineral composition. Both must meet prescribed chemical and microbiological safety standards.

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.
It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.
Tackling Riemann
The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”
The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.
But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.
Proof factories
It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.
But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.
When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.
AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.
The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.
Deriving worries
Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.
Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.
But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.
By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.
Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.
How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.
This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.
But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.
Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."
Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well
"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."
Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"
This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.
Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan.
Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies.
With the precipitous decline in the cost of whole genome sequencing, it’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed.
As research has shown, patients face many challenges to accessing genomic testing including financial barriers, limited access to providers, geographic limitations, and clinician biases. Since the genome can enable diagnoses and care for so many health conditions, a more streamlined and uniform approach to genomic testing would likely benefit many patients. I call it “test once, evaluate often.”
Is one test really enough?
A “test once, evaluate often” approach could start at any age. For some families, that might be at birth, as an optional add-on to the newborn screening their baby already gets. A single whole genome sequence could be stored, along with other medical records information, for future analysis. Any time a clinician orders a new genomic test, the lab would simply reevaluate the relevant genes and issue a report.
This approach would dramatically lower the cost and turnaround time needed to answer genomic questions by eliminating the sample handling and wet lab processing of patient samples, potentially improving access to genomic information for patients who would otherwise choose to forgo testing due to costs.
Such a paradigm would only apply to tests looking at germline DNA (the DNA we are born with). Clinical genomic tests seeking to understand the genetics of other biological characteristics, such as somatic DNA in a cancer tissue, circulating fetal DNA in a noninvasive prenatal test, or circulating tumor DNA in liquid biopsy panels would still be needed to look for genomic variants beyond germline DNA when patient circumstances dictate.
What about newborns?
Newborn screening is one of public health’s great successes. For more than 60 years, nearly every U.S. baby has had a heel-prick blood test for dozens of serious, treatable conditions, catching thousands of babies each year who look perfectly healthy.
For many, early diagnosis is the difference between life and death. Infants with severe combined immunodeficiency who receive a transplant by 3.5 months survive 94% of the time. Babies destined for the most severe form of spinal muscular atrophy who receive gene therapy before symptoms emerge go on to sit independently and breathe without permanent ventilation. Any interruption to newborn screening would cost children their lives.
Genome sequencing builds on that foundation. In the BabySeq Project, 9.4% of newborns had an unexpected genetic risk for childhood-onset disease. In New York’s GUARDIAN study, 72% of families opted in and 3.7% of babies screened positive, including for treatable conditions that standard screening misses. Because sequencing alone misses some cases that biochemical tests catch, it should add to the heel prick, not replace it.
In childhood, reporting can stay focused on conditions where knowing early changes care; the rest of the genome can wait until there’s a question to answer. And as with any public health program, clear consent and transparent data use must be built in from the start.
Regular evaluation of the genome is critical
The need for genomic information changes with patient circumstances and throughout their lifespan. This is why regular evaluation of the genome is needed in place of the piecemeal approach to ordering individual tests today.
Unfortunately, genomic science is not yet in a place where a single point of evaluation is practical. Evidence about emerging gene-disease relationships and new understandings of variants associated with hereditary cancer and other diseases continue to be adopted into clinical practice, meaning that an analysis conducted 20 years into the future would likely deliver more information than is currently possible.
The genomics community has honed a version of this practice, termed reanalysis, in the rare disease space. There, it is commonplace to reexamine a patient’s exome or genome based on emerging clinical evidence about gene-disease relationships.
Reevaluation is a bit different. Reanalysis is done for the same testing indication (i.e., finding the genetic cause of a rare disease) and reevaluation is studying the same genome for a new testing indication.
The National Human Genome Research Institute envisions a future where genomic data is systematically collected and used more regularly and efficiently for patient benefit. Getting there means moving clinical and laboratory medicine toward a system in which a genome sequenced once, whether at birth or later in life, helps a person’s clinicians manage their health throughout their life.
Making this vision a reality will require several changes to the way medicine is practiced and paid for today.
First, health systems, laboratories, and policymakers need to agree on how genomic data will be stored securely for decades and who can see it. Patients already trust online patient portals with their lab results and medical records, and genomic data can be held to the same standards of security and transparency.
These questions are already being actively worked on. Leading newborn sequencing programs, such as New York’s GUARDIAN study and England’s Generation Study, ask parents for opt-in consent, keep data under strict access controls, and are studying how long it should be kept. Leftover newborn screening blood spots have also been stored for years in many states, often without parents knowing, which is why consent and transparency have become central to this work. Any program that stores genomes, at birth or later, must start with fully informed consent: patients and parents should know what is kept, where, for how long and who may use it, and be free to say no.
Second, additional genetic counseling resources would need to support patients along their genomic health journeys, helping balance clinical needs, desires for information, and the familial implications of genomic insights. That support matters even more as care becomes increasingly patient-driven, with more people ordering tests themselves, reading their own results, and coming back with new questions.
Finally, and perhaps most important, insurers need a way to pay for evaluating a genome that has already been sequenced. Today, insurance can cover reanalysis, but there is no clear path to pay for reevaluation, the step that makes “test once, evaluate often” work. Paying for it would save insurers money, too, since it could replace repeat sequencing over a patient’s lifetime. Without reimbursement for prevention-oriented sequencing, genetic counseling, and genomic evaluation, we can’t improve equity in genomic testing.
Sharing data, finding answers
Something I’ve seen again and again in the rare disease setting is that parents of a child without a diagnosis are almost always eager to share their child’s genetic data. They know that a match with another family somewhere in the world may be what finally explains what’s happening, and many new gene discoveries start exactly that way.
If we protect genomic data well and show people what sharing makes possible, more of us may come to see it the way these parents do: not as a risk to minimize, but as a path to answers, prevention, and cures.
Kelly Hagman, M.S., is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company. She led the launch of the industry’s first clinical exome and has authored more than 55 peer-reviewed publications.

Hello there from STAT’s London bureau, with reporter Andrew Joseph here filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for a few days. It may be a holiday week stateside, but the news, at least for now, has yet to let up. So grab your choice cup of stimulation and settle in. …
Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs, STAT tells us. The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its blockbuster inflammatory drug Dupixent. Sanofi has been upfront that it was searching for takeover targets with late-stage or clinical assets, and with the deal, it will get New Jersey-based Insmed’s two lung disease drugs.
Roche touted the blockbuster potential of a new breast cancer pill after winning two U.S. regulatory approvals within a week, Bloomberg shares. The new medicine, called Wilserdly, is central to the drugmaker’s plan to regain its footing in the fast-growing cancer market. The company is positioning the pill to replace decades-old hormone therapies that are taken for years in an effort to reduce the risk the cancer will return. Estimates from analysts placing its peak annual sales potential at $9 billion are roughly in line with its own expectations, the Swiss drugmaker said.

Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

- The Supreme Court has directed the Centre and FSSAI to mandate separate pictorial warning labels for high-fat, high-sugar and high-salt packaged foods
- The move aims to make nutritional information more visible and help consumers identify unhealthy food products
- The court said each nutrient exceeding prescribed thresholds must have its own hexagonal warning label, and called for stricter enforcement of existing rules
- The Supreme Court has directed the Centre and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to ensure that packaged foods carry separate pictorial warning labels for high levels of fat, sugar and salt. A bench comprising Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said each warning under the front-of-package nutrition labelling (FOPNL) framework must include a standard pictorial representation of the nutrient of concern, alongside the corresponding words “HIGH FAT”, “HIGH SUGAR” or “HIGH SALT”. According to a Live Law report, products exceeding prescribed thresholds for more than one nutrient must carry separate hexagonal warnings for each, rather than a single combined label.
- The direction tightens FSSAI’s proposal, which provided for the relevant nutrients to be identified within one hexagon.
- The court also directed the Centre to ensure strict implementation of existing regulations, including the 2020 rules.
- Alongside the labelling directions, the court asked the Centre to strengthen nutritional literacy among children through changes to school curricula and practical learning initiatives, including interactive workshops and co-curricular activities.

Air pollution helps cause dementia by changing the genes that are switched on in microglia, the brain's immune cells, in ways that disrupt their normal functions, a new study has found.
The study, published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation, combined health records from nearly half a million people from the UK Biobank with experiments in mouse models.
"By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain's immune cells," senior author Sanjay Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at the Case Western Reserve University's school of medicine, said.
"These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world's population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it," Rajagopalan said.
Mice were exposed to outdoor Cleveland (US) air for five months. The fine particles in the air, known as particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), were concentrated to levels similar to those found in the world's most polluted cities.
Otherwise healthy mice developed memory problems, a leaky blood-brain barrier and brain inflammation. Their brains also showed a lower chemical balance reflecting its energy status and ability to withstand injury and disease.
The mice's brains also showed an increased death of newborn neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's centre for learning and memory.
The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third.
Further, in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer's, air pollution caused the same harm and also sped up amyloid plaque buildup -- a hallmark of the neurodegenerative disease.
The authors wrote: "These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure."
"We've identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer's disease," co-senior author Andrew Pieper, professor in translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, said.
"This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can't avoid those stressors," Pieper said.

Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.
Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.
As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.
Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal says it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.

An 18-second-long video has been circulating on social media, which shows Sandeep Khirwar, Special Director General (SDG) of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), making a remark regarding the transportation of the bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs) in a dumper truck.
In the viral clip, Khirwar can be heard saying, “All military trucks and vehicles in the area were occupied. So we had no choice but to transport the bodies of our two martyred SPO personnel in a dumper truck. But the real issue is not whether they were transported in a dumper or a garbage truck. Their families received the bodies of their loved ones. What more could they possibly want?”
X user @cutegirlindia21 shared this video and wrote, “Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred Kishtwar Police officers had to be transported in a garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the Indian Army refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police.”
🛑 Heartbreaking 💔 😢
Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred @KishtwarPolice officers had to be transported in a #garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the #IndianArmy refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police. https://t.co/Jm9i7bScN0
— A N U S H I ❤️T I W A R I🇮🇳 (@cutegirlindia21) November 16, 2026
According to an NDTV report published on November 14, the bodies of SPOs Bobby Chand and Rashpal Kumar — who lost their lives in a recent terror attack in the Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir — were transported to their native village Kiyar in a dumper truck without coffins. This incident sparked significant outrage among locals, with many questioning the manner in which the bodies were transported.
Against this backdrop, the purported video of SDG Sandeep Khirwar began to circulate. Several other users on X, including @RedDeFactoIND, @NetaNamax, and @unknownnewss, also shared the video with similar claims.
The video is also circulating on Facebook with similar assertions.
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral clip, Alt News used relevant keywords to search for information regarding statements made by Khirwar. We did not find any credible news reports or official statements that substantiate the claims made in the viral clip.
We observed that the viral video bears an ANI logo. Performing a ‘reverse image search’ using keyframes from the clip, we found the original video, which was posted by ANI on its official X account on November 16, 2026. In the video, Sandeep Khirwar, SDG of the CRPF’s Jammu & Kashmir Zone, is seen speaking to the media in Srinagar regarding the deaths of two SPOs in Kishtwar.
#WATCH | Srinagar, J&K: On the mortal remains of two missing SPOs recovered in Kishtwar, SDG, CRPF J&K Zone, Sandeep Khirwar says, “Every loss of life to any jawan in the security forces is a huge loss to all of us… We stand with their families, and we will make sure that they get justice.”
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
While the visuals of the video matches, the audio is different. In the original footage, Khirwar states: “All I can say is that, every loss of life to any Jawan, of any security forces are huge loss to all of us and we owe our utmost respect to all the fallen. And we stand with their family. We will make sure that they get justice, the families get justice.” He does not make any mention of the bodies being transported in a dumper truck, nor did he claim that the families were ‘grateful’ upon the recovery of the bodies.
Further, we found that the Khirwar’s voice and manner of speaking in the viral clip does not match the way he is heard speaking in the ANI footage, indicating that the original audio has been digitally altered or manipulated. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 98.9% likely to contain AI-generated speech.
On November 17, the official X handle of the CRPF’s Srinagar Sector addressed the viral claim. They stated that the video had been digitally tampered with and that false statements had been attributed to Sandeep Khirwar, clarifying that no such statements were made by him.
This claim is false and misleading. The video was digitally manipulated, with fabricated remarks attributed to CRPF Special DG Sh. Sandeep Khirwar, who is not the Kashmir Police Chief. The original footage contained no such statement. This is an attempt to spread misinformation and create an anti-India narrative.
— Srinagar Sector CRPF 🇮🇳 (@crpf_srinagar) November 17, 2026
Thus, the viral clip has been digitally manipulated using AI, falsely attributing statements about the transportation of SPOs’ bodies in a dumper truck to Sandeep Khirwar. The original footage by ANI does not carry any such comment.
Sajahan Ali is an intern at Alt News.

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Quick Answer
To schedule a message on WhatsApp, open a chat, compose your message, press and hold the send button, select a date and time, and confirm. You can schedule texts, images, and videos in individual and group chats from 10 minutes to 14 days in advance, even if your phone will be offline or switched off.
Ever been in a situation where you wanted to text someone on WhatsApp on a particular day, but forgot when the day arrived? Well, you can rejoice, as the Meta-owned chat app is finally introducing the ability to schedule messages on WhatsApp.
Message scheduling is one of the most requested features, WhatsApp says. And quite rightly so, since apps like Google Messages, Signal, and Telegram have had it for a while. Nevertheless, it’s good to see it finally catching up with the competition. Here’s everything you need to know about scheduling messages on WhatsApp.
How Do Scheduled Messages Work on WhatsApp?
Scheduled messages, like standard WhatsApp messages, support text, images, and videos. You can schedule a message anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days ahead of time, in both individual (one-to-one) and group chats.
Once scheduled, WhatsApp automatically sends the message at the set time, even if your phone is offline or switched off. The recipient sees it as a standard message; there are no indicators to tell that the message was scheduled.
How to Schedule Messages on WhatsApp
WhatsApp hasn’t introduced a separate button to schedule messages for later, nor has it nestled it under multiple menus. Instead, it has built the functionality directly into the send button, which you currently use to send messages. If you’ve used scheduled messages on apps like Signal, Telegram, and Google Messages, you’ll feel right at home with scheduling WhatsApp messages.
Once message scheduling is available, you can schedule a WhatsApp message like this:
- Open WhatsApp and go to the individual or group chat for which you want to schedule your message.
- Type your message or attach photos or videos, like you normally do.
- Now, instead of tapping the send button, press and hold it until you see the date and time picker pop-up on the screen.
- Set the date and time when you want the message to go out.
- Confirm by tapping the green send button (with your scheduled date and time) at the bottom.
That’s it! Your message will now be sent on the specified date and time.
WhatsApp says all your scheduled messages appear in one place, and you can delete the ones you no longer want to send if you change your mind. (We’ll update this guide with instructions on how to do that once we get our hands on the feature.)
Scheduled messages are also protected by end-to-end encryption, just like regular WhatsApp messages, meaning no one outside the chat, including WhatsApp itself, can read them.
Who Can Benefit From Scheduling Messages on WhatsApp?
Being able to send a message at a future point is quite useful, and different people will find it useful in different ways. An obvious use case is wishing someone on their birthday or anniversary, especially if you don’t share the same time zone. But other than that, scheduling can make life easier in many other ways. Say someone asked you to remind them about something at a specific time tomorrow. Instead of setting a reminder for yourself to send that message, you can schedule the message in WhatsApp today and forget about it.
Similarly, if you coordinate with a team on WhatsApp and have an update to share late in the evening but don’t want to disturb everyone right away, you can schedule the message for the next morning instead. You could also schedule nudges for deadlines or upcoming meetings. Another handy use case for scheduling is reminding yourself. If you use WhatsApp for notes and reminders, you can now combine that with the scheduling feature to remind yourself about something later.
Limitations of Scheduling Messages on WhatsApp
- No WhatsApp Business support: The feature is currently limited to regular WhatsApp accounts.
- Group membership restrictions: People who join a group after you schedule a message won’t receive it.
- Limited editing options: WhatsApp’s documentation currently describes deleting scheduled messages, but doesn’t confirm editing or rescheduling them.
When Is Message Scheduling Coming to WhatsApp?
Message scheduling is said to roll out globally in the coming weeks on both Android and iOS. The rollout started on November 25, 2026. Make sure you’re running the latest version of WhatsApp on your phone. If you still don’t see the option to schedule messages, you’ll need to wait until WhatsApp enables the feature for your account. WhatsApp hasn’t mentioned whether scheduled messages will be available on the web version, too.

Extending human life is a popular pursuit in Silicon Valley. At Nvidia, Jensen Huang appears to have little interest in planning for the inevitable.
A day after being reinstated as CEO on Monday, Huang reportedly told colleagues he didn't "believe in succession planning," because it would suggest some executives were more important than others. The idea is consistent with the unusually flat structure at the top of Nvidia — yet also remarkable given the company's recent leadership upheaval.
"If the CEO is hit by the proverbial bus, somebody has to be in charge," said Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at the executive search firm Kingsley Gate.
Assuming Huang is as mortal as the rest of us, Nvidia will eventually need a new leader. While he may not believe in succession planning, experts in corporate governance say it's the board's responsibility to prepare for a future without him.
"Life goes on beyond one individual, and when a board is so wedded to one individual, they're making a terrible mistake," said Charles Elson, founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.
Avoiding a lame duck
On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing concerns about its management and governance. It said a downgrade could come within 90 days if S&P determines governance deficiencies remain.
"Weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the 'key man' risk to the forefront," S&P said. "The departure, then reinstatement of the CEO, does not sufficiently answer our questions regarding board oversight of executive code of conduct."
It's not unusual for a company to lack a succession plan. In a 2025 Nasdaq survey of about 700 board members, CEOs, executives, and governance professionals, 21% said their boards didn't have one, while another 16% said they had only an emergency plan.
Companies that do prepare for a leadership change tend to keep their plans quiet to avoid turning the sitting CEO into a lame duck or prompting passed-over contenders to leave, said Ramakrishnan. Boards should get started well before a crisis, he added, by developing two or three serious internal candidates, giving them substantial operating responsibility, and creating incentives for them to stay through a transition.
At Nvidia, Huang has around 60 direct reports, an unusual structure he has credited with keeping information flowing and empowering employees. The downside, some leadership advisors say, is that executives who oversee individual pieces of the business may not be prepared to run the whole company.
"It's hard to imagine any of those direct reports are able to get the scale, scope, and experience to even be qualified to be the CEO," David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership consulting firm RHR International, previously told Business Insider.
'A house of cards'
The decision by Nvidia's board to put Huang back in charge just 11 days after announcing his resignation also suggests its directors are unwilling to challenge him, Elson said.
His departure came amid revelations that he had an intimate relationship with a client; concerns raised by US officials that he may have been the target of a foreign intelligence effort; and reports that he had affairs with two employees, including a direct report.
"Given what's happened, he really loses all accountability," Elson said of Huang. "I mean, if that didn't get him out, what will?"
Nvidia's board said it gave Huang his job back because it was satisfied with his "candor" and that it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government."
But Kim Scott, a former Apple and Google executive and cofounder of the leadership-training company Radical Candor, said Nvidia would be vulnerable if it relied too heavily on Huang.
"If it's all dependent on him, then it's a house of cards, and it's going to fall down anyway," she said.
Huang, for his part, has acknowledged that he won't live forever and suggested that his successor can reshape Nvidia to suit their own leadership style. Earlier this year, he told Garry Tan, CEO of the startup accelerator Y Combinator, that he expected to die on the job.
"The next CEO, whatever their personality is, they can figure it out," he said.

2 baby meerkats make their debut at Peruvian zoo, spotlighting conservation
A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima to raise awareness about wildlife conservation
LIMA, Peru -- A private zoo in Peru on Wednesday introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima as part of an effort to raise awareness about wildlife conservation and introduce visitors to the African species.
Eduardo Espíritu, a biologist in charge of mammals at NaviFauna, a private zoo and wildlife refuge, said the initiative aims to educate the public about the importance of protecting biodiversity.
Meerkats are small mammals native to southern Africa that dig underground burrows and often stand upright to keep watch for potential threats.
“Meerkats cannot be pets. They are wild animals,” Espíritu said. “We focus on keeping them healthy, and one sign of that is reproduction,” something the zoo has successfully achieved in Lima.
The zoo is home to 15 meerkats, eight of which have been born in Lima since 2025. The other seven arrived from their native Botswana in 2022 through an exchange between zoos, according to NaviFauna.
The species gained widespread popularity through Timon, the meerkat character in Disney’s “The Lion King.”
NaviFauna is a private zoo authorized by Peru’s forestry and wildlife service. It also houses capybaras, macaws and flamingos.
