Last week, Sarvam AI found itself in the eye of a storm. The poster child of India’s sovereign AI ambitions drew flak for offering access to Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM, through its newly launched inference platform, Token Factory. The point of contention among critics has been whether a startup that received government support to build indigenous AI models should be in the business of selling access to Chinese models. Sarvam clarified that its Token Factory runs on privately procured GPUs, and its inference business does not dilute the ambition to build homegrown AI models. Amid this controversy, the AI unicorn has expanded its product portfolio with two new launches — Sarvam-105B-1711, an upgraded version of its existing large language model (LLM), and Sarvam Dictate, a speech-to-text API that supports English and 22 Indian languages. The launches offer a glimpse into Sarvam’s larger game plan. The unicorn wants to offer Indian enterprises everything they need to build and deploy AI. From homegrown AI models and the infrastructure to run them to voice AI, coding agents and workplace applications, Sarvam desires to become a one-stop shop for enterprise AI in India. Not to mention, Sarvam’s full-stack AI ambition has begun to find commercial traction, particularly in the financial services sector, including Tata Capital and Mahindra Finance. The latter has also deployed Sarvam-powered voice agents across sales, collections and frontline employee engagement. It claims to have executed 1 Cr+ customer calls via its voice stack. At Bolna’s Symphony 2026 last week, Vivek Raghavan, the cofounder of Sarvam AI, claimed that the company was clocking more than 3 Mn minutes a day and had crossed a billion API calls a month for its voice AI business. At its flagship AI event, Epoch, in July this year, Sarvam unveiled a stack spanning foundation models, inference, coding, voice, document intelligence and workplace agents. Its voice agents had already handled 325 Mn minutes of conversations, while its Indus platform brought together voice, work, document, content and coding agents. So, how do the pieces of Sarvam’s existing strategy fit together? Sarvam Punches Above Its Weight Sarvam-105B-1711 is not a completely new model. It is a post-trained checkpoint of the existing 105B, with Sarvam using its upgraded Blackwell infrastructure and reinforcement-learning stack to improve performance on specific workloads. According to Ankit Jha, a machine learning engineer at Warner Bros. Discovery, post-training allows a company to improve its existing model for particular use cases or edge cases. It is also a common industry practice, with major labs routinely improving existing checkpoints rather than training an entirely new model from scratch. In Sarvam’s case, the original 105B was trained on H100 GPUs, while the post-training runs were carried out on newer Blackwell infrastructure. Jha said Sarvam’s investment in its own technology for training, running and compressing AI models has helped it improve its reinforcement learning capabilities. The results are worth looking at. According to Sarvam, its average score across eight conversational-agent benchmarks has grown from 42.6 to 73.9. Its Indic suite score reached 79.1, while the model also posted 89.7 on AIME 26 and 80.4 on GPQA Diamond. On the conversational-agent benchmark average, Sarvam puts the model at 73.9 against 74.0 for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. The significance is not that Sarvam has suddenly overtaken the major global labs. Some of its numbers remain behind larger frontier models on reasoning, coding and knowledge benchmarks. What has changed is the distance between Sarvam and the efficient tier of open models, particularly for workloads where deployment cost, Indian languages and data control matter. Jha said that the model could be a strong option for organisations that want to run AI with less than 100 GB of VRAM. Its roughly 65 GB quantised version can fit into the memory of a high-end workstation-class GPU, opening up a local-AI route that is difficult with much larger models. This is crucial for Indian banks and corporates that may not want sensitive workloads to leave their environments. The engineering underneath the model is just as important. According to Sarvam, its B200 training setup doubled pretraining throughput from 5,500 to 10,900 tokens per second per GPU, while reinforcement-learning steps fell from about 13 minutes to seven. Its 4-bit version can generate around 6,000 tokens per second per B200 across 64 concurrent users. The Expanding Application Layer Sarvam is not just building the brains behind AI but also the tools that put them to work. Dictate is a clear example. The API turns speech into the text a speaker intended to write, rather than simply transcribing every word literally. It supports English and 22 Indian languages and requires 40% fewer character edits than Gemini 3.5 Transcribe in English and 47% fewer in Indian languages and Hinglish. Kivi, Sarvam’s voice-based desktop application, lets users dictate across applications on Mac and is positioned as an alternative to products such as Wispr Flow. Kivi also understands more than 22 Indian languages, including code-switching, while its Epoch roadmap lists Android among the next platforms. Kivi and Dictate sit at different points in the same stack. Kivi is the end-user application, while Dictate turns the underlying speech and language capabilities into an API that developers can embed into their products. Sarvam also offers a document-intelligence API, Extract. It pulls structured information from documents so developers can route it into their own products. With Extract, Dictate and Kivi, the company has extended its playbook to include voice and documents. Finding The Next Thing Sarvam has also raised substantial capital to pursue its full-stack ambition. Its $234 Mn Series B, led by HCLTech at a $1.5 Bn valuation, gives it the financial firepower to build models, infrastructure and enterprise products at the same time. It is also building for enterprises that care about where their AI runs. Its Token Factory provides access to Sarvam’s models, along with other open-weight models, while the company offers India-based inference and dedicated GPU capacity for its BFSI customers. A bank could use Sarvam’s models, run inference within India, deploy voice agents for customer interactions, use document and workplace agents internally, and build specialised applications around the same infrastructure. The value proposition is not necessarily that Sarvam has the best model for every task, but that it is increasingly able to provide several of those layers under one roof. There is, however, a debate around its India-first positioning. The cofounder and CEO of Smallest.ai, Sudarshan Kamath, argues that Indian-language intelligence alone may not be enough to compete in broader knowledge work, where global models benefit from enormous amounts of English-language data. One practical way to judge that is to look at actual developer usage and whether developers choose Sarvam over alternatives such as Qwen or Gemini. “Sarvam can have an advantage in Indian languages and still struggle to become the default model for coding, research or general enterprise knowledge work,” Kamath said. But Sarvam does not need to win every category. The company no longer has to prove that it can train a large Indian-language model. It is increasingly showing that it can build the layers around that model, from inference and deployment to voice, agents and consumer applications. The latest 105B checkpoint and Dictate matter because they extend that strategy rather than replace it. Sarvam spent much of 2026 putting the pieces together. The next phase will show whether those pieces can become a durable enterprise AI stack.

What’s the news: Between January and June 2026, Indian authorities made 9,147 government requests to Amazon, excluding Amazon Web Services (AWS), a 7.1% decrease from 9,846 in July-December 2025, according to Amazon’s government request report.
Amazon, Apple, and the Wikimedia Foundation published their latest reports for July-December 2026, detailing requests from Indian authorities and, where disclosed, the companies’ responses. These are government and legal request reports, not monthly IT Rules grievance reports about user complaints. The figures are not directly comparable across platforms, as reporting categories and data periods vary.
Amazon: 9,147 requests excluding AWS in H1 2026
Amazon published its latest report for H1 2026 (January to June) on July 31, 2026. Requests to Amazon, excluding AWS, totaled 9,147, a 25.2% decrease from 12,225 in H1 2025. AWS received 639 requests, an increase of 5.4% from 606 in H2 2025 and 27.3% from 502 in H1 2025.
India accounted for approximately 32% of the 28,601 government requests Amazon processed globally, excluding AWS. The United States and Germany followed with 4,847 and 4,403 requests, respectively. India submitted more requests than either country, nearly twice as many as the United States.
Amazon reports AWS requests separately from other Amazon requests. Its H1 2026 report provides India’s request counts but does not specify India’s share for either service.
How did Amazon respond to government requests globally?
Amazon disclosed content information in 281 cases (0.98%). In 28,320 cases (99.02%), no content was disclosed. AWS disclosed content information for only one of 2,310 global requests (0.04%).
Amazon’s non-content category covers responses related to subscriber details, billing information, select purchase records, AWS usage data, and cases where no information was disclosed. Therefore, non-content figures should not be interpreted as compliance rates. Content information refers to files stored in customer accounts, such as photographs, and customer data managed through AWS.
What government requests does Amazon accept?
Amazon recognizes three types of legal demands for customer information: subpoenas, search warrants, and court orders, including their international equivalents. The company does not disclose content in response to subpoenas but may do so for warrants or court orders. Amazon requires legally enforceable orders to release customer information and routinely challenges requests that are overly broad or inappropriate.
The report also includes requests made under the Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) process. Amazon classifies these as US requests unless the country of origin is specified. As a result, the reported figure for India may not reflect all requests from Indian authorities through this process.
Apple: device requests led in H2 2025
Apple’s latest transparency report, published on September 4, 2026, covers July to December 2025. Apple received 166 device requests from India, the highest among request types for the country and a 4.0% decrease from 173 in the previous half. These requests covered 2,200 devices, and Apple provided data for 44 requests.
Apple recorded 164 account requests, a 4.1% decrease from 171 in H1 2025. The company specified 355 accounts, down from 517. Apple challenged or rejected 99 requests, provided non-content data in 35 cases, and did not provide any content. It received 135 financial-identifier requests, down from 168, and 17 emergency requests, down from 27. Apple also reported 10 account-preservation requests and 17 accounts preserved; these figures represent different metrics.
Wikimedia: no India content requests granted in H1 2026
The Wikimedia Foundation published its content and user-information reports for H1 2026 (January-June) on September 29, 2026. It received 12 requests from India to alter or remove content, a decrease from 13 in H2 2025 and 26 in H1 2025. None of these requests were granted. The foundation also received two user-information requests from India, up from one in H2 2025, and did not fully or partially comply with either.
The user-information report identifies Cyber Police as the requester for one informal government request from India. The requester for the other user-information request is unspecified, and the 12 content requests lack a breakdown by requesting body.

Kathua, Nov 26: The Jammu and Kashmir Police in Kathua has registered two FIRs against individuals found using Virtual Private Network (VPN) services in violation of the prohibitory order issued by the District Magistrate, Kathua, vide Order No. DMK/IC/2026-27/2275-94 dated 04.11.2026 valid for two months.

He said the FIR No.567/2026 U/S 223 BNS has been registered at Police Station Kathua against Surjeet Kumar, resident of Kathua; and FIR No. 229/2026 U/S 223 BNS has been registered at Police Station Billawar against Neeraj Kumar.

The Best Espresso Machines for Home Baristas
Featured in this article
The Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.
I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don't make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED's counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. For a more classic, all-analog build, we offer the compact, stylish Diletta Mio.
But I also know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For those who want milk-based drinks and a built-in grinder, I recommend the top-selling Breville Barista Express as the Goldilocks machine balancing performance and cost. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.
Note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. Frequently Asked Questions
How Do I Test Espresso Machines?
Over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.
On each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.
I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.
What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.
I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.
On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.
On any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.
I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.
How I Select Espresso Machines to Review
In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.
I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.
But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.
This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.
The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.
But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.
What Beans Are Best for Espresso?
First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.
But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.
Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.
It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.
One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.
Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.
Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups
If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.
An espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.
An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.
The best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.
Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your new frothing pitcher.
Other Machines We Like
Breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the company that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the new Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.
Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.
Meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: Meraki is a young Hong Kong–based company. Last year, it was still Kickstarting funds for its debut Meraki Espresso Machine. But the company started off with a bang, with a premium semiautomatic double-boiler machine offering features you don't find even in machines that cost hundreds more. This means a Timemore grinder that'll grind by weight within two-tenths of a gram precision. PID temperature control. Easy pre-infusion. A quiet rotary pump. Another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. A powerful steam wand that regulates the temperature of froth within about 3 degrees for whatever milk drinks strike your fancy. A tamper with satisfying heft, and a tamping station that feels like luxury. Frankly, despite having to overrotate the portafilter for proper fit, its wondrous aesthetics and ease made it a contender for our top picks. But service is always a worry among newer, direct-to-consumer entrants, and the wackily complicated descaling procedure makes maintenance a concern.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED's mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.
De'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $900: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It's the best De'Longhi espresso machine I've tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.
De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $1,000: De'Longhi's new Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It's also got a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming, as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.
La Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.
De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never showed signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.
Breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.
Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The new Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.
Cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's new espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.
Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $600: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.
Also Tried
Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.
Cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.
De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $675: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category, It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It's a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

New Delhi-The Supreme Court on Thursday directed that front-of-package nutrition labelling should treat “total sugars” and “saturated fat” rather than “added sugar” and “added fat” as the nutrients of concern alongside “salt”.
Front-of-package nutrition labelling (FoPNL) is a nutritional information graphic on food packaging that can assist consumers in making an informed decision about food purchases and healthier dietary choices.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran also asked the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to ensure that each hexagon in the FoPNL carries a standardised pictorial representation of the nutrient of concern, together with the corresponding words “High Fat”, “High Sugar” or “High Salt”, as the case may be.
“The FSSAI shall ensure that the FoPNL provides for a separate hexagon for each nutrient of concern, each containing the words ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’, respectively, alongside their corresponding pictograms, rather than a single combined hexagon,” the bench said.
“The FSSAI shall ensure that the FoPNL treats ‘total sugars’ and ‘saturated fat’, rather than ‘added sugar’ and ‘added fat’, as the nutrients of concern, alongside ‘salt’, in alignment with its own long-standing consensus existing prior to the DGI, 2024 (Dietary Guidelines for Indians),” it said.
The bench said the FSSAI shall revisit and reformulate the threshold levels for each nutrient-of-concern.
It said as regards sweetened beverages that do not exceed the threshold limits for the relevant nutrient of concern, the FSSAI shall ensure that no front-of-pack label which is identical or deceptively similar, in appearance, form or shape, to the warning label required for beverages that exceed the threshold limits, is displayed for the purpose of denoting its food category.
The bench directed that as regards artificial preservatives and other additives, the FSSAI shall closely monitor the reformulation of products following the introduction of the FoPNL.
It noted that the FSSAI, in its affidavit, had stated that it proposes to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of the FoPNL regime.
“The FSSAI shall bring the regulations into force within the timeline proposed by it and shall take all necessary steps, including pre-emptive steps, to ensure that this timeline is strictly adhered to,” the bench said.
The apex court delivered its verdict on an application filed in a petition by public charitable trust ‘3S and Our Health Society’ which sought directions to the Centre, states and Union territories to implement mandatory FoPNL on packaged foods.
While hearing the matter on September 28, the top court had questioned the FSSAI over its proposed timeline for implementation of front-of-package labelling on packaged foods.
The food regulator had told the top court that it would require approximately four months to issue and finalise the draft regulations.
It had told the apex court that the draft amendment regulations would be published for 60 days to invite comments from stakeholders through domestic consultation and the WTO platform.
The top court had earlier asked the FSSAI, which has proposed phased implementation of front-of-package labelling on packaged foods, to come up with more clarifications on the planned labels of “nutrients of concern”, fat, sugar and salt.

Every time I called my cousin Arun* around 9 a.m., his voice would echo, as though he were in a bathroom. “I’m on the throne, I’ll call you in 20 minutes,” he would say. The first time I heard this, it took me a while to understand what ‘the throne’ was, and as if that was not confusing enough, what was he doing there for 20 minutes. Perplexed, I asked him why he had the phone in the bathroom when he was doing his morning business, to which he casually replied that he would sit on the throne solving Wordle, crosswords and reading the news until he ‘downloaded’. A couple of months ago he told me that he was diagnosed with early stages of haemorrhoids and was on treatment. I advised him on this matter, stressing how his morning ritual could be contributing to his condition. This ultimately led to his ‘conscious reduction of phone time in the bathroom’. His words, not mine. Recently, he proudly announced that his scheduled ‘throne time’ was now down to six minutes, every morning after breakfast.
Bathroom humour is universal. Cinema is no exception — it has found humour and dependable plotlines from this predictable ritual. Just one instance is in Lokesh Kanagaraj’s Vikram, where a character pulling the flush coincides with the house exploding. Thankfully, the consequences of spending 20 minutes on the toilet are far less dramatic.

The Keralam government has approved two new initiatives being launched by the Health department which aims at eliminating all preventable maternal and child deaths in the State.
Keralam, through its consistent mortality audit and course corrective measures, has maintained a good track record in minimising maternal and child deaths
“We have had excellent protocols in place to manage the most common causes of maternal and child deaths. We also have 'near-miss' maternal audits which systematically track what went wrong and what we did right to bring mothers back from the brink of death. Achieving the last mile reduction in maternal and child deaths means focussing on every preventable death possible. This involves investment in the continuum of care, right from pregnancy screening and care to making available the services of personnel trained in the management of obstetric emergencies, emergency transport facilities in the periphery hospitals and improved ante-partum and post-partum care,” a senior Health official said.
The action plans have been drawn up by the department in consultation with clinicians and professional bodies, including Kerala Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology and the State chapters of Indian Academy of Paediatrics and National Neonatal Forum.
Risk reduction
The Zero Preventable Maternal Deaths action plan begins with risk reduction before pregnancy and extends to antenatal care, safe delivery, critical care, emergency transport and surveillance.
It proposes preconception screening, risk-stratification tools and links with adolescent health services to optimise maternal health before pregnancy.
A Statewide online High-Risk Pregnancy Registry linked to Unique Health Identification (UHID) and Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) is proposed.
The State is planning to roll out a Keralam Pregnancy Risk Score (KPRS) for the structured follow-up of high-risk pregnancies, along with the implementation of Keralam Maternal Obstetric Early Warning Score (MOEWS), which will help clinicians in the timely recognition of clinical deterioration in obstetric cases.
“We have proposed that while Gynaecology OP clinics can be run in the periphery on select days, deliveries be restricted to a few well-equipped public hospitals in every district so that obstetric emergencies are not rushed from various periphery hospitals to referral hospitals. The services of all trained personnel may be pooled and redeployed in select delivery points in every district, which can be developed as centres with 24 x 7 provision of obstetric services,” an Obgyn specialist at a district hospital said.
Standardised protocols
The plan calls for round-the-clock availability of trained personnel, 24-hour blood bank readiness, intensive care pathways, high dependency units and standardised protocols for management of common obstetric emergencies like post-partum haemorrhage in every district
As many obstetric emergencies take a turn for the worse during transport — the 108 ambulance service does not have advanced life support facilities — the action plan has proposed that a Keralam Maternal-Neonatal Emergency Transport Network with GPS tracking be set up.
Experts have sought the setting up of contingency funds in public hospitals for the emergency transfer of women from vulnerable groups which the hospital Superintendents can directly manage.
Hospitals are required to report maternal deaths within two to four hours, with detailed reviews by experts in the next few days.
Within seven days
The child-death prevention plan mandates that all infant deaths are notified under the Kerala Clinical Establishments Act within seven days.
To improve survival immediately after birth, the plan mandates the presence of providers certified in neonatal resuscitation at every birth. Round-the-clock in-house paediatrician coverage is proposed at designated delivery points, alongside standardised perinatal care protocols across public and private healthcare facilities.
For small and sick newborns, the government proposes a tiered network of Special Newborn Care Units and Neonatal Intensive Care Units, supported by a real-time bed-occupancy dashboard and organised neonatal transport.
The plan also calls for strengthening life-threatening congenital anomaly care pathway and priority interventions for the tribal settlements in the State and migrant families.
The Keralam Child and Maternal Survival Task Force will review overall implementation and strategic milestones quarterly, while a technical steering committee and district child and maternal committees will also monitor the execution and review of the initiatives planned.

People on the internet have been sharing the claim that turkey contains sleep-inducing properties for decades. Snopes first addressed it in 2003.
The factoid's ubiquity may be at least partly the result of a 1997 episode of the sitcom "Seinfeld" in which Jerry and George attempt to make Jerry's girlfriend, Celia, fall asleep with wine and turkey so he can play with her vintage toy collection.
"What is that stuff in turkey that makes you sleepy?" Celia asks at the dinner table.
"Tryptophan," Jerry and George respond in unison.
Tryptophan — one of nine essential amino acids involved in the synthesis of protein — is found in turkey, and some studies show it does have properties that encourage sleep. Purified tryptophan supplements are on the market to treat mild insomnia.
The alleged turkey-tryptophan-sleep connection has become a staple not only of Thanksgiving dinner small talk but social media conversations as well, with examples on platforms such as X, Reddit and Facebook. For example, in 2023, an X user wrote (archived):
By the way, did you know why the consumption of turkey makes you feel satisfied and sleepy? That's because turkey contains high amounts of L-tryptophan, an amino acid that is metabolized into serotonin, a neurotransmitter associated with feelings of well-being and satisfaction. Serotonin can then be converted into melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep, contributing to feelings of sleepiness.
According to one study published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research in 1982, tryptophan (in doses of 1 gram or more) in combination with little to no other food (which limits the absorption of tryptophan by the body) can produce an increase in subjective sleepiness and a decrease in sleep latency (the time it takes to fall asleep). Another 1977 study by the same author called the amino acid a "rational hypnotic with clinical potential."
However, the claim that eating turkey makes people sleepy is wide of the mark and requires more context, as outlined below.
Although tryptophan is a precursor for several bioactive compounds — including serotonin and melatonin, which regulate sleep as well as mood and appetite — it is in competition with other amino acids for access to the brain. Simon Young, a neurochemist who worked at McGill University in Montreal, told National Geographic in 2005: "Brain levels of tryptophan could even go down after a big meal because of the [amino acid] competition."
As Snopes originally reported in 2003, the amount of tryptophan found in turkey is also not enough to produce the alleged sleepiness effect. According to the Texas Medical Center in Houston, a pound of raw turkey contains 410 milligrams of tryptophan. Most tryptophan supplements sold are between 500 and 1,000 milligrams — and in purified form. Experts maintain that one would have to consume an exorbitant amount of turkey to feel the effects equal to those of one supplement. "For example, you would have to eat roughly 20 servings of turkey to ingest as much tryptophan as one supplement would contain," Andrew Wong, a doctor with Hartford HealthCare in Westport, Connecticut, said in 2024.
Many other foods, such as chicken, lamb, egg whites, cheese and pumpkin seeds also have levels of tryptophan similar to, if not higher than, turkey.
Nicolaas Deutz, an expert in nutrition and metabolism at Texas A&M University who studied the effects of tryptophan, told The New York Times in 2015: "Turkey is not special in relation to the other meats. You just eat a lot of meat, but if you would eat a steak you would feel as satisfied as with the turkey."
In sum, there is no evidence the tryptophan content in turkey is enough to make people sleepy. For this to occur, tryptophan would have to be consumed in higher doses and in purified form (separate from other proteins), such as in a supplement.
If people do feel tired after Thanksgiving dinner, it's likely due to the heavy, carbohydrate-rich meal they consumed, alcohol, the general exertion of the day or a combined effect.

The Staff Selection Commission (SSC) aimed to develop an indigenous examination device to hold computer-based tests at locations such as village and district schools, reducing its dependence on privately operated examination centres.
S. Gopalakrishnan, SSC’s chairman, said the commission had floated a request for proposal (RFP) for developing the device and had received expressions of interest from more than 25 bidders. The bidding process was under way, he said, adding that the technology could become a model for examinations in the future.
“We want to develop an indigenous device through which we can conduct the exam anywhere. We don’t need any centre. This device, we can take it to a village school, to a district school, to any centre anywhere,” he said during the inauguration of Tech Verse 2026 in Chennai.
The proposal aims to address the commission’s dependence on private examination centres, where it does not have direct control over the hardware, network equipment, or personnel involved in conducting tests. The chairman pointed to the risks associated with relying on infrastructure that the commission does not own or fully control.
“Do I own the hardware? I don’t know. Do I know anything? What is the switch? What is the router? What is happening? Nothing,” he said, explaining the vulnerabilities in the existing examination-centre model.
The SSC has been working with the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) and four to five other agencies over the past two years to strengthen examination security. Gopalakrishnan said the collaboration had helped establish greater control over examination-centre operations and reduce malpractice.
The proposed device would take this further by allowing examinations to be conducted at locations such as village and district schools, without requiring candidates to travel to dedicated private examination centres. The chairman said the opportunity could extend beyond the SSC, as other examining bodies could also use such a system.
The commission has also proposed developing an indigenous CCTV solution with C-DAC. Mr. Gopalakrishnan said that surveillance devices not owned or controlled by the agency using them could pose a security risk. The proposed system would perform analysis at the edge rather than centrally.
“We are proposing to have an indigenous CCTV solution and edge. All the analysis will be happening on the edge, nothing centrally,” he said.
He argued that government departments and technology institutions needed to work more closely to translate requirements into solutions. Institutions such as C-DAC, the Society for Applied Microwave Electronics Engineering and Research (SAMEER), and the Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology (C-MET) had capabilities that could address problems faced by government agencies, but the two sides did not always connect.
“Whatever they do is to solve problems. And on the other side, there are people more like us who have problems. We come to them with problems. Sir, please solve this problem. There, that connect, that linkage is what helps us to take things ahead,” he said.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows RSS members armed with swords surrounding the Jama Masjid in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside.
Fact: The video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music outside Shahi Jama Masjid in April 2022. The Ghaziabad Police have also dismissed the claim as fake, clarifying that no such incident occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts from April 2022 featuring the same visuals (here, here, and here). According to these posts, the video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music in front of a mosque.
We also found an article published by Muslim Mirror on 12 April 2022, featuring an image identical to a frame from the viral video.
The same video was posted on X by Hindutva Watch on 12 April 2022. The accompanying caption identified the location as Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The incident was also mentioned in a VICE News article published on 22 April 2022, which reported that Hindu groups carrying weapons, including guns and swords, marched through Muslim neighbourhoods during Ramadan, playing provocative and Islamophobic music and raising inflammatory slogans. The article alleged that Hindu extremist groups were linked to some of the processions associated with the violence.
To further verify whether the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid, Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, we checked Google Maps for Street View imagery and photographs of the location, but none were available. We then compared the surroundings visible in the video with an image of Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, published in a Dainik Bhaskar article. The mosque’s architectural features and other identifiable elements matched those visible in the video, confirming that the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The Ghaziabad Police also responded to the viral claim through a post on their official X account dated 19 November 2026. They dismissed the claim as false and misleading, clarifying that no such incident had occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. The police further stated that legal action was being taken against those spreading the misinformation and urged the public not to circulate misleading claims.
To sum up, a video from Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as showing RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh.

The Rotary Club of Madras (RCM) and the Tamil Nadu government have entered into a partnership to provide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination to 3.5 lakh adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
The partnership, valued at approximately ₹200 crore, is among the largest public-private initiatives for HPV vaccination in India. It was acknowledged in the presence of Darez Ahamed, Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Tamil Nadu government.
High-risk HPV infections account for more than 95% of cervical cancer cases. HPV vaccination during adolescence helps prevent infections caused by high-risk HPV types and reduces the risk of cervical cancer later in life.
Bobby Krishna, president of the Rotary Club of Madras, said the partnership was part of Rotary’s efforts to work with the government on large-scale vaccination programmes. The club also aims to vaccinate one million children as it approaches its centenary in 2028-29, building on its work under the Polio Plus programme.

Lajja Gauri idol to Tagore painting: Yuge Yugeen museum takes shape
The gallery will be the first of seven themed galleries planned across the North and South Blocks, with the larger museum expected to display 1.8 m objects.
A section of Delhi’s North Block, once home to key government ministries including Home and Finance, will open to the public towards the end of 2027 as part of the government’s Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum, with its first gallery showcasing up to 1,000 objects tracing India’s traditions of adornment.
The gallery will be the first of seven themed galleries planned across the North and South Blocks, with the larger museum expected to display 1.8 million objects. Other themes include Mathematics and Astronomy, Architecture and Cityscapes, Healing Systems and Medicine, Beliefs and Spirituality, Languages and Scripts, and Bharat Connects -Trade and Ideas.
The exhibits will be sourced from government museums across the country, including the Kolkata-based Indian Museum, the country’s oldest museum. A dedicated team has been appointed to examine collections and select objects for the galleries.
For the Adornment gallery, the Indian Museum has sent rare works, including a Mauryan period stone sculpture of the Earth goddess, called the Lajja Gauri figure, and a 14th century statue of Darpanika (Surasundari) from the Eastern Ganga Dynasty from Puri, Odisha. The Victoria Memorial Hall in Kolkata will send an early 20th century watercolour by Abanindrnath Tagore depicting Vasantasena from Mrichhakatika. A sculpture of the same character from the National Museum collection will also be displayed, as will Saundarya Lahiri, a Sanskrit literary work attributed to Adi Shankaracharya.
The exhibits will include inscriptions, manuscripts, sculptures, paintings and archaeological material, offering what Union culture secretary Vivek Aggarwal described as “hard evidence” of India’s civilisational legacy.
“In the Adornment gallery, we are attempting to show the sophistication of India’s civilisation and the evolution of how we, as a people, presented ourselves, with jewellery, dresses, head gears, tattoos, craft,” Aggarwal said during a walk-through of the section on Wednesday.
The gallery will also explore how adornment and “shringar” evolved through India’s civilisational journey, he said.
The section will include an orientation room and food and beverage facilities, a ministry official said.
Giving North Block a new lease of life
Built between 1912 and 1929 by architect Herbert Baker, along with its twin South Block, North Block was designed as part of the seat of imperial power in British India. Its red sandstone structure, courtyards, corridors and rotunda have since served generations of government officials.
The building is now undergoing extensive restoration and adaptive reuse to accommodate the museum. Wooden window panes have been carefully removed, door frames are being treated for pests and polished, floors are being replaced and walls are receiving lime plaster. Seepage repairs are also under way, while worn out portions of courtyard pillars are being restored using similar red sandstone.
Although the building is not a designated heritage structure, the restoration is being undertaken with minimal intervention, Aggarwal said. Office partitions are being removed and courtyards, corridors and rooms reconfigured for museum use.
“Adaptive reuse means that we have to turn what was once an office into a museum, while preserving the heritage value of the building,” he said.
The conversion will require significant changes to the building’s infrastructure. The museum will need centralised climate control, dehumidification and tighter security to protect artefacts spanning several centuries. At least 70-80% of the 78,000-square-metre built-up area in the section being developed will be converted into gallery space, compared with the estimated 45-50% earlier used for offices, Aggarwal said. The courtyards will be covered without scaffolding touching the original structure and converted into central display areas.
The restoration plan has been developed by School of Planning and Architecture, Bhopal with assistance from the Archaeological Survey of India and heritage experts. Los Angeles-based architect and museographic designer Kulapat Yantrasast is leading the team repurposing the building. Teams of museologists, scenographers, curators and scholars are also working on the new museum.
Announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on May 18, 2023, the museum project received approval from the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs earlier this month. The total project cost is estimated at ₹3,230 crore. The museum is part of the Central Vista redevelopment project.

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.
 In India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany

Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.
Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
Opinion: An alternative more of us should maybe consider
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith
- Published
Liverpool fans have needed to be patient to see the best of Alexander Isak after an injury-hit start to his career, but the striker is now proving the wait has been worth it.
By scoring twice against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Isak took his tally for the season to 10 - more than double his total for his first season at the Reds.
Of course, that campaign was disrupted; he had no pre-season because of his protracted £125m move from Newcastle and then suffered a broken leg in December.
But Isak is now in a hot streak of form, having scored four goals in his past four games for Liverpool.
Asked whether fans were now seeing his full capabilities, Isak told TNT Sports: "It is always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are but I can definitely say I feel good, I am in a good place and the team is in a good place which is the most important thing.
"Hopefully it just gets better."
Isak joins Liverpool greats as scoring run continues
When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.
That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.
Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight – level with Erling Haaland).
His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.
Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper.
But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution.
"He is in a great moment right now," he said.
"In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower."
Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock agreed that Isak had shown he has more to his game than the goals.
"There were a lot of questions about Isak last year, about his price tag and what Liverpool paid for him," he said.
"There were a lot of people saying he doesn't take people on, but now he looks fitter and looks sharper and we are starting to see the quick, nimble feet again that we saw at Newcastle, with his nice touches and link-up play.
"So we are starting to see a different side of him. My big question in this system would be - can he press? Can he close down, can he affect the game in the other way that Iraola likes to do? Now we are starting to see that.
"All of it is coming together, which is great for him."
Isak and Wirtz get best out of each other
It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.
Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany.
"Both are now in a good place," Iraola said of Wirtz and Isak.
"When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better.
"The important part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment."
But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz.
In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position.
"We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports.
"Even when we can substitute some wingers, midfielders or strikers in the 60th minute or later it gives us a lot.
"It shows how good our team is and it is important for a top team to have a strong bench."
Liverpool's win against Club Brugge was their seventh from their last 10 games across all competitions.
"I spoke to Wirtz at the weekend, after the [Manchester] United game, and we were talking about his form - and he said 'well it helps that the team are playing well'," Warnock added.
"It's true because if you try to influence a bad team or a team that's not playing well, then it is much harder.
"With a fitter Isak, Wirtz looks a better player because now he is playing balls in behind that Isak is getting to, and getting in on goal on the back of.
"It has a knock-on effect, which is obviously like Wirtz said, he is playing in a team which is better equipped to suit him."
