Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after the QB rips coach Mike McCarthy on TV
PITTSBURGH — Aaron Rodgers came to Pittsburgh in a Chevy.
He left it sitting atop a flamethrower.
The Pittsburgh Steelers cut the four-time MVP on Wednesday, shortly after he torched Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show."
The move capped a chaotic 18 hours in which the team announced it was benching the 42-year-old future Hall of Famer for backup Mason Rudolph ahead of Friday's visit from Denver.
Rodgers responded by taking an excused absence from the club, then used the unexpected time off to go on McAfee's show and repeatedly call out the 62-year-old McCarthy's mental fitness. Rodgers told McAfee he found out about the surprise decision to bench him while on the phone with teammates, including tight end Pat Freiermuth.
McCarthy said later Wednesday, after Rodgers was released, that there were "continuous efforts" to reach the player he's known for two decades dating to their time together in Green Bay.
While McCarthy declined to get into personal conversations, he said things came to a head Tuesday when Rodgers offered an "ultimatum" that McCarthy felt was "clearly out of his job description."
Asked if the decision to cut Rodgers came after he went scorched earth on national television, McCarthy said he couldn't pinpoint the exact timeline because he was in and out of meetings all afternoon.
A Pittsburgh native hired in January to replace Mike Tomlin, McCarthy also brushed off Rodgers' suggestion that the coach had lost the team, saying he had a "very direct, very honest" meeting with the club's players' council after practice Wednesday and believes the Steelers will respond with the proper urgency.
"This is a growth opportunity that I intend to take full advantage of," McCarthy added.
Rodgers says McCarthy fell asleep and blew off meetings
In a blistering offensive, Rodgers painted McCarthy — whom he played under during a long, successful run in Green Bay earlier in their careers — as woefully out of touch.
He described a quarterback meeting last Wednesday where McCarthy arrived late, sat down "and within 10 minutes began snoring," woke up and nodded off again minutes later, then eventually "walks out of the room like nothing happened." Rodgers also said McCarthy missed an offensive meeting Thursday, missed a walkthrough Friday and a morning meeting Saturday, and did not hold a team meeting that night ahead of Sunday's 19-16 loss at Philadelphia.
"And then comes to Sunday, when obviously we struggled and the product wasn't great," Rodgers said, adding that McCarthy broke up the halftime locker room meeting by saying "1-2-3 Packers."
McCarthy didn't deny he misspoke, citing the emotions of the game and the long hours for what he called an "embarrassing moment."
Rodgers said he felt it was the right thing to bring up the issues to McCarthy as a longtime league star instead of putting it on others with fewer years, shaky roster positions or those who "haven't made 400 million dollars in the NFL."
"Me? I don't care, what are you going to do to me?" Rodgers said. "Like I said, you're going to release me? Cool. You're going to deflect this thing and make it that you were trying to bench me and that I'm at home contemplating whether or not I'm going to accept a benching? Couldn't be farther from the truth.
"That word never came up in our meetings. What came up was: sleeping, habits, game plan, understanding what we're doing, being able to call a play, being able to call a game without the game sheet."
The scene played out bizarrely during Rodgers' extended appearance on the show on which he has been an occasional contributor. McCarthy waded through a throng of assembled reporters in the lobby at the Steelers' facility — most of them huddled over their phones listening to Rodgers — after practice ended.
Minutes later, in a subdued locker room, the Steelers tried pick up the pieces declined to get into specifics about Rodgers' accusations but didn't outright dismiss them, either.
Speculation about McCarthy's habits and commitment to his job is nothing new. A former NFL quarterback confirmed that he saw McCarthy asleep during a meeting at an earlier coaching stop. The player spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the delicate nature of the topic.
Asked if he's confident McCarthy can lead the team going forward, Freiermuth responded with a simple "I'm confident" but little else.
Rudolph, who has developed a good friendship with Rodgers over the last 18 months, called him "nothing but the epitome of a first-class teammate."
Wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who played alongside Rodgers and under McCarthy as a rookie in Green Bay in 2018, acknowledged there was general frustration about the team's recent performance but allowed, "I didn't think it was this."
Steelers cutting a QB of Rodgers' status is unusual in NFL history
Rodgers has already said this will be his last season. Now it's fair to wonder if he'll reach the end of it on an NFL roster after McCarthy turned to Rudolph, a longtime backup, with the Steelers (6-4) trying to snap out of a two-game funk.
There's little precedent for replacing a future Hall of Famer and Super Bowl winner midseason. Johnny Unitas, playing out his final days in a Chargers uniform, got benched for rookie Dan Fouts after four games in 1973.
Joe Namath never played again after throwing four picks in a loss to Chicago during a late-career cameo for the Los Angeles Rams a month into the 1977 season.
More recently, Denver replaced Peyton Manning with Brock Osweiler midway through 2015 even with the club sitting at 7-2, though Manning's health was a contributing factor in the decision. Manning returned in the season finale and then served as a game manager in the playoffs as the Broncos' dominant defense led the franchise to its third Super Bowl victory.
Manning walked off the field with the Lombardi Trophy in tow in his final game.
This is not that.
While the Steelers are currently in playoff position, their next three games are against AFC West-leading Denver, surging Houston and AFC South leader Jacksonville. While they can probably withstand one loss or maybe two, three would be catastrophic.
Enter Rudolph, who rescued Pittsburgh's season and briefly earned folk hero status in 2023 by coming off the bench in December and leading a surge to a playoff berth.
That didn't stop the Steelers from moving on from him immediately, bringing in Russell Wilson and Justin Fields in 2024 and then Rodgers in 2025, a move designed to help Pittsburgh end a postseason victory drought that's nearing a decade.
"Does it put some of us in an awkward space? Yes," Rudolph said. "But again, it's just another sort of opportunity to overcome adversity."
Rodgers took Steelers to the playoffs before returning to play for McCarthy
Rodgers — who first met with Pittsburgh as a free agent in March 2025 while visiting the facility in a nondescript Chevrolet sedan, wearing a hat and sunglasses to deflect attention — was effective if not spectacular last season, which ended with a blowout loss at home to Houston in the wild-card round of the playoffs. His future seemed uncertain until the Steelers hired McCarthy to replace Tomlin, a job Rodgers played a hand in helping McCarthy land, though how big a hand is up for debate.
Rodgers opted to make one last run at a championship while reuniting with the coach he won a Super Bowl with in early 2011.
Any shot at a storybook ending is gone. For Rodgers and perhaps his now-former team.
Pittsburgh is 2-4 on the road, where it figures to be when the playoffs start if the Steelers can't track down Cincinnati for the AFC North title.
And the team's inconsistent play has offered little evidence that it is a legitimate threat to have an extended postseason stay.
Rodgers' performance was a mixed bag. At times he hardly looked like the league's oldest player, even outdueling Cincinnati star Joe Burrow in a victory over the Bengals in late September. During others, his MVP-winning extended prime looked light years away.
He's struggled to make an impact of late, often checking the ball down to running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle or taking sacks behind an inconsistent offensive line when trying to push the ball down the field to a receiving group that has underperformed, particularly two-time Pro Bowler DK Metcalf.
What happens next to a player who has always leaned into doing things on his terms at all times is unclear. Pittsburgh was supposed to be his third and final NFL stop. Whether any quarterback-needy team will be willing to take on the considerable baggage Rodgers brings is anybody's guess.
He seemed content on Tuesday, spending time in the locker room trading jokes with Rudolph and longtime defensive tackle Cam Heyward after addressing reporters.
Barely eight hours later, Rodgers was no longer the starter. Shortly after that, he was no longer a Steeler, the latest and perhaps final twist in a journey that will end with him getting a gold jacket at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, even if this ends up being an inglorious off-ramp for all involved.

Ben Stokes on Sandpapergate, the Ashes, and Joe Root and Stephen Fleming's new era in charge of the England Test team
"I always felt on as England captain. Now I can just be Ben, not Ben Stokes captain of the England cricket team. Looking back, it's not really a healthy place to be at," Stokes told Sky Sports, adding: "I'm still an England cricket fan. I want the players, Joe and Flem to do well"
Tuesday 24 November 2026 17:09, UK
Former England captain Ben Stokes says he hopes they win next year's Ashes 5-0, though he would not be drawn on Sandpapergate or the possibility of him making a comeback for the series.
Speaking to Sky Sports upon the launch of a new podcast he's presenting with former England team-mate Mark Wood called 'That's Not Cricket', Stokes hinted that he might have more to say on the saga dominating Australian cricket on that platform.
"It would be pretty bizarre for it not to be mentioned [on the podcast]", Stokes said. "It's all kicking off at the moment out there, isn't it?
"What Australia have going on there is far beyond anything we had to deal with [as a leadership group].
"I imagine Joe [Root] and Flem [Stephen Fleming] would be thinking, 'imagine if this happened three weeks before the Ashes next year, as opposed to now'."
'Root and Fleming will work really well together'
England's Test team enter into a new era under Root - who returned to the captaincy with a 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan following Stokes' international retirement - and Fleming, who begins as head coach with a three-Test tour of South Africa next month.
The series, against the reigning World Test Champions, serves as an ideal challenge for the new regime as they steel themselves for the visit of Australia next summer where they'll look to regain the Ashes for the first time since winning on home soil in 2015.
"I'm doing a Glenn McGrath here; I hope England win the Ashes 5-0," Stokes said. "I'm not saying they will, but I wish nothing but the best for them.
"I'm still an England cricket fan. I want the players, Joe and Flem to do well.
"There is no animosity whatsoever between any of us, there's no jealousy."
Stokes did add, however, that he was "surprised" to see Root take on the captaincy again, knowing first-hand how much the job takes out of you - as well as the toll it had taken on Root by the time he handed over the reins in 2022 after five years in the role.
"I was a little bit surprised, if I'm being honest, just because he knows what it's like and he's done so well as a player but also, knowing Joe, he feels like he can take the team from where it was and build on it again," Stokes said.
"It's an exciting time for someone to think like that and when Stephen Fleming got appointed, I thought 'these two are going to work really well together'.
"I did a lot of work with Flem in the IPL. He's a great man manager; everyone has already seen how he speaks, which is very impressive. I'm excited to watch them go about it."
Stokes: Everything after Ashes defeat was tough
Stokes' time as Test captain and as an England cricketer came to an end with a 2-1 series defeat to New Zealand, which was on the heels of a disastrous 4-1 Ashes drubbing in Australia during the winter.
"I was in the right headspace for the Ashes," Stokes reflected. "It was all after that. Before the Ashes, I was so confident.
"Everyone was fit, firing and ready to go. Fans and pundits were all confident, and Australia weren't confident, so we couldn't have been in a better place going out there.
"But emotion and the feeling of what you think is going to happen is completely different to getting out there in the heat of the battle. Everything after that was tough."
Stokes added: "Unfortunately, to do that role, you have to immerse yourself in it, have to throw yourself into it.
"For all the positive stuff that comes with it, there is a negative effect that can flow over into your home life and your family.
"I think every England captain will have that. I don't think there is anything you can do.
"You can try your hardest, but when you do that role you just have to do it. I don't think you are doing the role justice if you take it lightly.
"I always felt on as England captain. Now I can just be Ben, not Ben Stokes captain of the England cricket team. Looking back, it's not really a healthy place to be at."
As well as still playing for his county side Durham - helping them clinch promotion back to Division One of the County Championship - and an upcoming stint with the Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League, Stokes is using his newfound freedom to venture into the world of podcasting.
"I have been in the public eye for so long but people who don't know me probably only know 10, 15, 20 per cent of what I am actually like," he said. "That is the exciting thing: I now get a chance to say what I want to be going out.
"I don't feel like you're always necessarily able to give that full account of yourself as a person, because you're wary of upsetting people. The only person I can upset now is myself.
"It's really exciting and I can't wait to get going. We've got a lot to talk about and a lot to say."

The State government has stepped up action against illegal and unsafe cosmetics following reports of a 17-year-old girl from Areekode developing kidney disease after using a mercury-laced fairness cream.
Statewide inspections under Operation Soundarya on Sunday led to the seizure of fake cosmetic products worth more than ₹10 lakh. The Drugs Control department has also seized perfumes containing methanol and initiated action against products that violate cosmetic safety rules.
The department said inspections would continue in the coming days. Health Minister K. Muraleedharan warned of strict action against the sale of fairness creams containing excessive mercury. The government is also considering special inspection teams in all districts.
The crackdown follows the case of the higher secondary girl from Areekode, who developed membranous nephropathy, a kidney disease, after using a cream called F Tune for nearly a year. She bought the product after seeing promotions by social media influencers, particularly on Instagram. She ordered it through WhatsApp after being told that it could remove pimples, dark spots, and pigmentation.
Test results
Laboratory tests reportedly found 1.25% mercury, or 12,500 parts per million (ppm), in the cream. The permitted limit is less than 1 ppm. The girl developed swelling in her legs, fainting spells, low blood pressure and difficulty in walking. Doctors also found that she was losing excessive amounts of protein through urine. She has since recovered from the critical stage following treatment.
The girl said she first learned about the cream after seeing classmates use it. Its packaging listed ingredients such as turmeric but did not provide manufacturer or licence details. She said she would not have used it had she known it contained mercury. She has urged other users to stop using the product.
Her family has handed over the cream’s details and medical records to the police and plans to approach the consumer court. The police launched an investigation and collected details of the product for further examination. Criminal action against the manufacturers and distributors is being considered.
The cream’s Instagram page, which had been promoted by several influencers, is no longer available. The incident has also prompted complaints from others who say they experienced health problems after using similar products.
Mappilapattu singer Saleem Kodathoor said that he too developed membranous nephropathy after using a similar fairness cream. He said the illness forced him to suspend music programmes for months.
CMO’s directive
The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has filed a case and sought reports from the Health department, police and drugs controller. The Chief Minister’s Office has directed the Health department to examine measures to prevent the sale of mercury-containing creams and strengthen inspections.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation had earlier warned about the use of mercury and potent steroids in certain cosmetics. Mercury absorbed through the skin can damage the kidneys and nervous system. Doctors warn that prolonged exposure can cause serious health problems.
The case has raised concerns over the online promotion and sale of cosmetics, particularly products targeting teenagers, without clear information about their ingredients and manufacturers.

Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
Every time Torrie LeBlanc failed to persuade a parent to give their baby a vitamin K injection, she thought about the blood-soaked diaper.
It belonged to a newborn delivered last year, in the bustling labor and delivery unit where LeBlanc worked as a physician at the Corewell Health hospital system in Grand Rapids, Mich.
In the early hours the day after the baby girl was born, she suddenly started bleeding "from everywhere," LeBlanc recalled. Her eyes, nose, and rectum all suddenly oozed blood.
The girl's parents cried out for help from their hospital room. Nurses and doctors on the overnight shift rushed her to the neonatal intensive care unit, where they pumped fresh frozen plasma and other blood products into her small body, trying to replace what she was rapidly losing.
Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.
It worked. The baby survived, largely because she received treatment almost instantly, according to LeBlanc and an attending physician who helped care for the baby. Had the baby been at home when she started bleeding, they believe she would have died.
What LeBlanc witnessed has become much more common in recent years as more parents, influenced by the anti-vaccine movement and broader mistrust of the medical system, refuse to allow doctors to give their babies vitamin K shots at birth.
Nationally, the rate of newborns who do not receive intramuscular vitamin K has more than doubled, rising from 3.1% of newborns in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to research published in JAMA in November.
The spike moved LeBlanc, a pediatrician, and her colleagues to launch an initiative to reduce the rising number of vitamin K refusals at this hospital. On average, at least one family here refuses the injection for their newborn every day.
Two years in, the team won a modest victory: Vitamin K refusal rates are now flat at the hospital, even as refusals of other standard newborn medications, including the hepatitis B vaccine, continue to climb.
Still, doctors at the hospital say parents now regularly argue against everything from the once-routine vitamin shot to antibiotics for a critically ill infant.
"I honestly thought it would be easier," LeBlanc said, sitting by a sunlit window near the end of a 10-hour shift. "The more people I talk to, the more I learn about the misinformation that's online and the different reasons that people are refusing."
She paused. "It's a work in progress."
When doctors struggle to talk with parents
LeBlanc began a two-year fellowship at the children's hospital in 2024, certain she could make an impact on vitamin K refusals. After all, it's a vitamin, not a vaccine. How hard could it be to persuade parents to choose a vitamin that could save their baby's life?
Babies are born with very low levels of vitamin K, which is why the injection has been a routine part of newborn care since the 1960s. The shot is safe, with virtually no severe side effects, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And it effectively prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can involve bleeding in the brain.
Among babies who receive the shot at birth, fewer than 1 in 100,000 develop the most serious form of bleeding. But babies who don't receive it are 81 times more likely to develop the condition, according to the CDC. Of those who do, 1 in 5 die.
The shot was so effective that many doctors encountered a baby with VKDB perhaps only once in a career.
But doctors in multiple hospitals across the U.S. told KFF Health News that they now regularly see babies develop life-threatening bleeding from vitamin K deficiency. Some of those babies have died or been left with lifelong brain injuries.
Solomon Behar, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor in Los Angeles, recently treated an infant with VKDB who died.
"It just made me sad more than anything else," he said. "This was something that literally was a historical footnote up until the recent modern time, when people have decided that Mother Nature is someone that wants to work with them, rather than is trying to kill us."
Vitamin K refusals have increased dramatically in recent years alongside vaccine hesitancy.
Prominent conservative influencers suggest the vitamin K shot is tied to childhood cancer. Online parenting forums are filled with moms worried that the injection could harm their newborns, and wellness influencers on podcasts and TikTok — including some medical professionals — allege that babies have been injured by the shot or say it's unnecessary or unnatural.
When Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was asked at a congressional hearing in April to assure parents that the vitamin K injection was safe, Kennedy demurred. "I've never said anything about vitamin K," he said.
LeBlanc first saw a case of VKDB during her residency training, when a baby came into the emergency room with a nosebleed. Doctors caught it early, and the baby made a full recovery.
But she also watched as other doctors struggled with how to talk to parents who turned down the shot. "A lot of people just felt uncomfortable talking to families about it, or they didn't know what to say," she said.
Part of that was easy to fix: LeBlanc created a basic fact sheet for parents answering some of the most common questions about the vitamin K injection and explaining the risks of not getting it.
Labor and delivery nurses now use a script to offer routine newborn medications: "The standard of care for all babies born here includes vitamin K, hepatitis B vaccine, and erythromycin eye ointment," it says. "Do we have your permission to give these medications to your baby following delivery?"
The harder part is teaching doctors how to talk to parents about the fears that drive refusals.
"We can't walk into rooms where families don't know us from the doorknob and say, 'You have to do this,'" said Jaspreet Loyal, a pediatrician at Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut and a longtime leader in research on vitamin K refusal.
"We have to practice humility, to sit there and listen, and then come back the next day and sort of use that nudge approach."
LeBlanc helped train staffers in motivational interviewing, a technique developed for treating substance use disorders that is gaining popularity for addressing vaccine hesitancy.
It requires doctors to treat parents with a baseline of "unconditional positive regard or acceptance," one study urged. Parents' autonomy is paramount, even if their decisions conflict with medical recommendations. The minute parents feel judged, LeBlanc said, they stop listening.
The most important thing to convey, Loyal said, is "we are on the same team. You're looking out for your child. I'm looking out for your child. We may not fully agree what that looks like, but let's try."
LeBlanc gets only about 50% of parents who initially refuse the shot to change their minds. Other doctors at the hospital said their success rates are closer to 20% to 40%.
A refusal is now included in the patient's electronic medical record, so the family's regular pediatrician can bring it up at the first well-child visit. It also means that if the baby comes into the ER because of bleeding, the staff will immediately be able to see they haven't received the vitamin K shot.
And LeBlanc and Loyal, the Yale expert, argue that the rising rate of refusal means doctors need to be more open to parents who decline the vitamin K injection but want to give their baby liquid drops or crushed supplement tablets instead.
That's controversial: Taking vitamin K orally isn't as effective as the shot and requires multiple doses over several weeks or months, according to researchers. There's also no federally approved oral vitamin K supplement.
"The injection is the gold standard," LeBlanc said. "However, I would rather have them have some protection with the oral than no protection at all."
Finding compromise, with a baby's life on the line
In May, a 2-week-old baby came into Helen DeVos Children's Hospital with symptoms of meningitis, a potentially deadly infection of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
But the baby's parents had declined the vitamin K injection after the baby's birth, which meant the lumbar puncture — in which doctors insert a needle into the baby's lower back to get a sample of spinal fluid — needed to confirm meningitis was risky: What if the baby didn't stop bleeding after the puncture?
Still, as the child's condition worsened, doctors felt it was worth the risk. But then, the parents refused the lumbar puncture as well. LeBlanc recalled the mother telling her that, in her "medical opinion," she did not believe her child had meningitis.
After hours of debate, doctors offered the parents a compromise: They would treat the baby for meningitis, even without a confirmed diagnosis. That meant admitting the baby for two weeks to receive intravenous antibiotics.
Afterward, the mother wrote the medical team a thank-you note, which now hangs on a staff room wall covered with beaming photos of grateful families.
"Almost every single one of you has shown so much grace to us," the mom wrote. "Regardless of differing medical opinions, I'm so grateful for you."
On good days, LeBlanc can see that note as a win, a sign that staff are getting better at working with mistrustful families. On bad days, it feels like a symbol of a losing battle. Both families who watched their baby suffer after not receiving the vitamin K injection — the one whose child nearly died from VKDB, and the one with suspected bacterial meningitis — still declined routine vaccinations when they left the hospital.
At Yale, Loyal has learned not to take any of it personally. "At first, I used to feel like a failure every time: No, I was unable to convince somebody!" she said. Now she takes refusals in stride. "I cannot continue to spend time with someone who I cannot change their mind."
But LeBlanc worries each time she can't persuade a family to get their newborn the vitamin K injection. What if the next time she sees that baby is in the ICU? She would blame herself, she said, for not getting through to the parents.
"I couldn't convince them."
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

India’s cybersecurity agency has flagged a high-severity SQL injection vulnerability in DIGIT, an open-source platform that state governments and municipalities use to deliver public services. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued the advisory on November 25.
The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run arbitrary database queries, according to CERT-In. DIGIT underpins urban governance, public health, water and court systems across several Indian states, so the question is how many deployments run the affected version.
“This vulnerability exists in the DIGIT Platform due to improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system.
Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.” – CERT-In
DIGIT is developed and maintained by the eGov Foundation. The CERT-In note, which is credited to Sarthak Chauhan, does not say whether the flaw has been exploited, and it does not say when eGov was actually informed and the time took for fixing the patch. However, the vulnerability appears to be fixed as the CERT-In asks the users of these platforms to “upgrade DIGIT to latest version v2.9.3.”
What is DIGIT and where is it used?
DIGIT, which is an acronym for Digital Infrastructure for Governance, Inclusion & Transformation, is an open-source platform of reusable building blocks and shared data registries. Local governments, NGOs and market partners can use it to build sector-specific digital public infrastructure.
eGov describes DIGIT as having freely available specifications and standardized APIs, and as “secure by default” with configurable role-based access. It also claims that the personally identifiable information (PII) is encrypted and inaccessible to analytical systems.
The platform is modular and built on microservices. DIGIT Core holds foundational services such as:
- Authentication,
- Payment gateways,
- Notifications, and
- Sector-specific applications for property tax, trade licences, public finance, water and health are built on top of it.
Who owns and runs it
eGov Foundation is a Bengaluru-based non-profit, owns and maintains DIGIT as an open-source, digital public good. Nandan Nilekani and Srikanth Nadhamuni co-founded the foundation in 2003. “The foundation is supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, Nilekani Philanthropies, Omidyar Network India, and Tata Trusts,” a press release indicates.
The software is open source, and thus, no single company controls individual deployments. Governments run their own instances, and the eGov data could possibly sit on government-owned servers. System integrators and IT service providers such as PwC and Deloitte can build on top of the platform.
What could have been exposed:
Whether a service is exposed depends on whether it runs DIGIT Core v2.9. But the spreading of these platforms remains unclear. No DIGIT-based system has been confirmed as affected at the time of writing this report. Nonetheless, the fact that the vulnerability existed, and for an unrecorded time duration, points towards the possibility of exploitation. This is compounded by the fact that DIGIT is broadly used as the foundational tech-supporting layer for many products and services, primarily by Indian government and various state government to deliver public services.
For instance, UPYOG, India’s national platform for online governance, was built under the National Urban Digital Mission, which comes under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). This Mission chose DIGIT as its foundation to deliver the intended services. UPYOG is offered to states as a reference platform for all of India’s 4,000-plus cities and towns, with 30 states and union territories signed on and rollout beginning in cities such as the eight Kerala urban local bodies that went live on it in 2023, followed by three in Chhattisgarh.
Database containing details such as property tax, trade licence, birth and death certificate, wage payment, health and court systems hold sensitive citizen data. A database-level flaw in a user and access control service could therefore expose identity records, financial records or case-related data. That is a risk assessment based on CERT-In’s description, and the agency has not said any of these systems were compromised.
What remains unknown:
- CERT-In has not said how many deployments run v2.9, or whether any have been attacked.
- eGov has not said whether it has notified state and municipal deployments directly, or how fast they are upgrading.

In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.
If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”
The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.
A long deployment runway
This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.
For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.
The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has de-notified and withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023) where medical colleges were liable to face penalty fines for violations of educational standards and infrastructure requirements at medical colleges.
Earlier reports in The Hindu stated NMC’s withdrawal of MSMER-2023 weakens accountability in medical education by removing provisions to fine individual faculty members and administrators up to ₹5 lakh for submitting false information. Although the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) can still penalise institutions up to ₹1 crore under separate regulations, institutional penalties may be less effective in deterring individual misconduct. Misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk.
The NMC justified the withdrawal by arguing that MSMER created overlapping assessment powers with MARB. However, scrapping the regulations entirely raises questions about the necessity of this move, particularly when non-compliance remains common and transparency in medical education is inadequate. Moreover, conflicting appeal deadlines under MARB regulations and the NMC Act could lead to legal disputes and delay enforcement. Ultimately, the NMC must clarify whether the existing regulatory mechanisms are being effectively enforced and whether their outcomes are publicly accessible without which the withdrawal of MSMER risks appearing to be a relaxation of regulatory oversight rather than a simplification of rules.
Medical experts have further warned that deterrence against practices such as ghost faculty and fabricated patient records would potentially expose students and institutions to greater malpractice and mismanagement. While some experts support the removal of regulatory duplication, they emphasise that effective oversight depends on rigorous verification, transparent reporting, consistent penalties and time-bound enforcement. The NMC must therefore demonstrate that MARB can enforce standards as effectively as the withdrawn framework; otherwise, regulatory rationalisation risks becoming a dilution of accountability.
The NMC has clarified that the MSMER introduced a parallel mechanism through which the undergraduate and postgraduate boards could assess institutions, thereby encroaching on the MARB’s mandate. While talking to The Hindu, NMC officials said the denotification is aimed at simplifying regulatory procedures and eliminating overlapping responsibilities, without compromising the quality of medical education.

It also works just fine with Qi2 and MagSafe chargers, and other magnetic accessories. The case is plain black, but you can order it with Dbrand skins for an extra $5. I went with the Ultramatte Teardown, but there are many colors and styles. This is my all-around favorite iPhone Duo case.
All that said, no case is perfect, and the hinge is tricky to protect. Dbrand chose a two-piece design: The iPhone slots into the main back part, and the front has tiny tabs you remove to stick it to your iPhone Duo with adhesive. I’m not a fan of using adhesive; it’s easy to remove, though you obviously lose some stickiness (you get an extra set of stickers in the box). I worry that the front may get pushed off over time as the hinge slides over it, but so far so good.
Famous for its origami-style folding folios, cases, and wallets, Moft is a brand I like. The Dynamic Folio works great because it’s a simple cover that attaches magnetically. It extends beyond the Duo’s dimensions, with a solid camera surround to provide a little protection. The cover opens and folds to act as a stand or serve as a comfortable grip. The stand works with the iPhone Duo open or closed in landscape or portrait, and is surprisingly stable.
While I love the functionality, the Dynamic Folio looks a little dull. I’m not sure how much protection it would provide in a fall, though there’s also a full-case version that the back of your iPhone Duo slots into, but it costs an extra $20. As much as I like this, it feels overpriced for what it is. Constantly folding the cover out of the way can get annoying, and I’m not sure how well it will age.
Slim and very good-looking, this Mous case has a back panel made with Aramid synthetic fiber, with a matte black surround that provides a little grip. It’s a one-piece design with its own flexible hinge (no adhesive required), and it doesn’t add too much bulk to the iPhone Duo. The buttons and port are easily accessible, and there’s a raised lip around the camera module and cover screen. The minimal hinge cover doesn’t interfere with opening and closing the phone.
The big downside is that the Duo’s hinge isn’t fully protected. If you’re unlucky enough to drop it on the hinge, you could end up with a big repair bill. It’s also relatively pricey. Mous does have a version with a hinge cover for an extra $10, and it also comes in different finishes, including walnut wood, leather, and speckled fabric, but I haven’t tried it yet.
Maybe the simplicity of a big, chunky, one-piece case appeals. Smartish has you covered with the Gripzilla. This iPhone Duo case protects the phone from every angle, with heavily reinforced corners providing serious drop protection and an indented hinge cover that makes it very comfortable and secure to hold. The finish is pretty damn grippy, though it doesn’t quite match Dbrand’s case above. It is thicker, though, with lips around the cover screen and camera. I’m confident your iPhone Duo would survive a fall while wearing this, and it’s relatively affordable.
While it’s a one-piece case, the actual hinge is two very slim bits of plastic, and the hinge cover slides over the top when you open it and feels a bit janky. The button cutouts are quite deep, and it can be a little tricky to access Touch ID. I tested the plain black version, which is very dull, with nothing to distract from the ugly chunkiness, but you can get versions with a back panel featuring flower blossoms, mountains, or a contrasting green color.
If you prefer something a little slimmer and cheaper, I also quite liked the Smartish Gripmunk ($30), and it comes in various finishes.
I didn’t love every iPhone Duo case I tried.
Aulumu Aduo Particle Case for $90: Super slim, with an Aramid fiber case that the back of the Duo snaps into, this case minimizes bulk. The cutouts are good, and there’s protection around the camera. I also quite like the pattern, with dots of color on the back. The problem is that the front part of the case is a different material in a slightly different tone, and it relies on adhesive to stick to the front (mine kept coming loose). There’s also no protection for the hinge.
UAG Mouve XTE Case for $85: I usually like UAG’s stuff, but this is another two-piece case that relies on adhesive for the front part, so there’s no hinge protection. While there’s a lip for the camera and the cover screen, the sloping width leaves no room for a screen protector. The potentially handy fold-out ring on the back for secure holding and deployment as a stand feels like cheap plastic. Most two-piece cases like this are very slim, but this has UAG’s trademark angular chunkiness, just without the actual protection. It’s a rare misfire for the brand.
Best iPhone Duo Accessories
There’s a world of iPhone Duo accessories out there, but these are the ones I’d pick based on my limited testing so far. Many of the picks in our best MagSafe accessories and best MagSafe chargers guides will also work well with the Duo.
I’m impressed by this screen protector, considering it’s only $20 for a two-pack. The application tool makes life easy, and you get a cleaning kit to make sure your iPhone Duo is dust-free before you begin (take your time). I got a couple of air bubbles, but they were easy to push out. It is slightly smaller than the actual screen to accommodate most cases, but cases with a thick front bezel will buckle up or lift the screen protector. If you don’t plan to use a case, choose a different screen protector.
Smartish also offers a privacy screen protector that’s just as easy to install. It’s a two-way privacy screen, meaning people to your left and right won’t be able to see what’s on your screen. If they’re close or in front of you and staring down, they’ll still be able to see what’s on your display.
A stand is more important than usual for the iPhone Duo, and you ideally want something that can prop it up when it’s open, so you can take advantage of the large inner display. This ring works well, offering an adjustable angle no matter which way you prop the Duo and whether it’s open or closed. It feels sturdy, with two adjustable hinges, and the magnets are strong enough that you can also hold it by the ring with confidence. It’s just a shame it’s so expensive.
Your iPhone Duo can serve as a handy notebook or sketchpad. If you use the USB-C cable that came with your iPhone Duo to plug in an Apple Pencil (USB-C), you can pair it, enabling you to scribble notes, annotate, or sketch on the cover screen or the larger inner display. Sadly, it doesn’t support the Apple Pencil Pro or other models, so make sure you get the Apple Pencil (USB-C).
All the MagSafe wallets I’ve tried are designed for regular iPhones, so part of them extends beyond the bottom edge of the iPhone Duo. This one is no exception, but it still works well as a fold-out stand, looks stylish, and fits up to three cards. You can prop the Duo in landscape or portrait, and open or close it when you turn the wallet sideways. This is our top pick, but you can find some alternatives in our best MagSafe wallets guide.
Best iPhone Duo Chargers
Apple’s iPhone Duo supports wired charging at up to 60 watts and wireless charging at up to 25 watts, but you only get the top charging rates with the right gear. For wired charging, you need a charger that supports USB PD 3.2 with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) rated at 60W or higher and a capable USB-C cable. For wireless charging, you need a charger that supports Qi2 25W. Other chargers will still work; they’ll just be slower.
This updated version of our favorite MagSafe power bank supports Qi2 25W, enabling the maximum iPhone Duo wireless charging rate. It also packs 10,000 mAh of power, enough for a full charge with change, has a handy kickstand to prop the Duo up, and sports an LED display that shows remaining power and other stats. It will extend below the bottom edge of the Duo, since it’s designed for regular iPhones, but that’s true of the current crop of MagSafe power banks.
As the best of the best wireless chargers, this is what lives on my nightstand. It can wirelessly charge the iPhone Duo at the maximum 25-watt rate, and it’s heavy enough that you can remove your phone one-handed. You can also attach the open iPhone Duo in portrait orientation (in landscape, it tilts to one side). There’s even a spot around the back for your wireless earbuds to charge.
If you prefer wired charging at the maximum 60-watt rate, I recommend pairing this cable (or the cable that came with your iPhone Duo) with the Anker Nano Charger Neo ($26) or Apple’s 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max ($39).

Around 83 cases of lung cancer were recorded every month across prominent government hospitals in the national capital in the last six and a half year period, with one patient succumbing to the disease every three days.
This information was provided in response to an RTI query to AIIMS, RML Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and the Delhi State Cancer Institute.
Under the Right to Information (RTI) Act, data regarding lung cancer cases and associated deaths between January 1, 2020, and July 31, 2026, were requested from the hospitals. Safdarjung Hospital only provided the number of lung cancer deaths but did not disclose the total number of cases.
A request was also made for data on patients who had never smoked. However, none of the institutes provided any data on it.
According to information provided in response to separate RTI applications filed by PTI Bhasha, 6,581 lung cancer cases were recorded across three of the four hospitals (excluding Safdarjung), averaging 83 cases per month. Across all four hospitals, 913 deaths were reported, which translates to one patient dying every three days.
The national capital is currently grappling with a severe air pollution crisis, an annual affair now in November, which is observed as the Lung Cancer Awareness Month.
Although health experts state that long-term exposure to air pollution increases the risk of lung cancer, it is not the sole cause. Smoking and genetic mutations are two of the other contributing factors.
The highest number of cases was recorded at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS). This central government hospital provided data for the period from January 2020 to March 2026, during which 4,860 cases of lung cancer were registered and 158 deaths occurred. This averages to approximately 65 cases per month, with two patient deaths occurring monthly.
According to data from the Delhi State Cancer Institute (DSCI), 1,613 cases of lung cancer were reported between January 1, 2020, and July 2026, resulting in 354 deaths. This translates to an average of 20 cases per month, with four patient deaths occurring monthly during this period.
The institute noted that in 2021, the disease was also diagnosed in two children, and over a span of about six and a half years, 351 women were found to be suffering from lung cancer. However, it did not provide a gender-segregated breakdown of the deaths.
Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital reported 108 cases of lung cancer during this period, including 47 women, with eight deaths recorded. Safdarjung Hospital reported 393 deaths among patients suffering from lung cancer during the same timeframe.
A senior doctor at the DSCI, speaking to PTI on the condition of anonymity, mentioned that the institute receives patients not only from Delhi but also from Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Bihar, and even Nepal.
Regarding the role of air pollution in Delhi on lung cancer cases, the doctor said the primary cause is smoking or exposure to tobacco smoke, though genetic mutations also play a role.
According to doctors, lung cancer has also been detected in non-smoking women; this is suspected to be linked to genetic mutations and pollution.
Doctors also said that the disease is often diagnosed only in its final stages, making treatment extremely challenging.
Dr Geeta Kadayaprath, a senior specialist at the Apollo Athenaa Women’s Cancer Centre, said that long-term exposure to polluted air—common in cities like Delhi—can increase the risk of lung cancer.
She noted that the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), under the World Health Organization, has classified outdoor air pollution and the particulate matter it contains as carcinogenic to humans.
She explained that PM 2.5 particles are so minute that they can penetrate deep into the lungs and, over time, cause damage to cells.
When asked about symptoms, Dr Vikas Maurya, a senior specialist at Fortis Hospital in Shalimar Bagh, explained that there are often no clear symptoms in the early stages.
However, potential warning signs include a persistent cough, coughing up blood, shortness of breath, chest pain, changes in one’s voice, unexplained weight loss, and recurring chest infections.
He further noted that the condition cannot be detected through a standard X-ray; instead, a CT scan is required for diagnosis.

Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.
Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”
A fourth engine
Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.
An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.
Some background
The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

- The claim that Etsy's new terms of service allows the company to train artificial intelligence technologies using artwork posted on its platform appears true at face value, although it's unclear whether the company has any plans to actually do that.
- Etsy's new terms of use state that the company and its third-party partners have the right to use content posted on its platform "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
- In response to backlash from vendors, Etsy said it does not and will not "use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity."
- The same statement gives examples of ways Etsy uses vendor content, such as creating advertisements using listings from artists, but it doesn't clarify whether Etsy plans to use AI or generative AI for those purposes. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
A rumor is spreading that global e-commerce marketplace Etsy updated its terms of service to allow the company to train artificial intelligence systems using artwork posted on the platform.
The allegations have caused an uproar in small business and independent artist communities, as many rely on Etsy to make sales. Artists with tens of thousands of followers have shared Instagram and X posts declaring that they had closed their Etsy shops over the company's new AI policies.
For example, one post with nearly 100,000 likes as of this writing claims that, in plain English, Etsy's terms of service allows it to "train generative AI on our artwork."
"They can package and resell that data to third parties," the post continued. "Stay on the platform, and your art is theirs to scrape. Sell. Train."
Etsy has, in fact, updated its terms of use with a new AI policy, which go into effect Dec. 16. The plain text of the updated terms of use states that any content posted on Etsy can be used "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
In response to the uproar, however, Etsy's vice president of customer operations, James Ossman, said in a Nov. 16 blog post (archived) that the company does not use AI to copy artwork, nor does it claim ownership over sellers' creations (emphasis theirs):
"We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers."
However, it's unclear whether Etsy might use AI to create content in ways that artists may consider as equivalent to an AI model being trained off of their work. For example, Etsy's statement says it may use seller content to feature listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns. Etsy has not clarified whether that means the company might use generative AI to create an advertisement that uses an artist's listing photo. 
We asked Etsy for further clarification and await a response. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
The changes to Etsy's terms of use come after the e-commerce marketplace released clearer restrictions on AI use in October.
"We recognize we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted. It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business," a blog post from Ossman said about those regulations.
Etsy's new terms of use, annotated
The updated language on AI is under Section 5, "Your Content," in Etsy's terms of use, which is available in full (archived) on the company's website.
Both the new terms of use and the older terms of use, which is in effect through Dec. 15, state that Etsy does not claim ownership over sellers' content, but that it has broad rights to use sellers' content for Etsy's own purposes (underlined emphasis ours): 
Content that you post using our Services is your content (so let's refer to it as "Your Content"). We don't make any claim to it, which includes anything you post using our Services (like shop names, profile pictures, listing photos, listing descriptions, reviews, comments, videos, usernames, etc.).
B. Permission to Use Your Content. By posting Your Content through our Services, you grant Etsy and third parties authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion a license to use Your content, including to operate, provide, improve, and promote the Services. We don't claim ownership of Your Content, but we have your permission to use it to help Etsy function and grow.
The "Your Content" section then goes on to explain what rights Etsy has over seller content posted on its platform. The older version of the document includes no mention of artificial intelligence. The newer version adds the sentence we underlined below:
C. Rights You Grant Etsy. (Here's the legalese version of the last section). By posting Your Content, you grant Etsy and, as authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion, third parties, a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, sub-licensable, perpetual license to use, display, edit, modify, reproduce, distribute, store, and prepare derivative works from Your Content. This allows us to provide the Services and to promote Etsy, your Etsy shop, other shops and listings, or the Services in general, in any formats and through any channels, including across any Etsy Services, our partners, or third-party website or advertising medium. […] This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.
Etsy acknowledges in its terms of use that providing the platform with these rights "sounds like a lot" but argues that it's "necessary for us to keep Etsy going." The company's examples for reasons why it might need these rights include resizing or enhancing seller listings to optimize them for its mobile app, translating descriptions into other languages and featuring seller listings in marketing campaigns.
While the new language states that creators may have opt-out rights, a review of the company's privacy policy and supplemental U.S.-specific privacy policy found no evidence Etsy sellers can opt out of AI training entirely. It does note, however that those in the United States have the right to opt out of sales of personal data. Different states also have different data privacy laws that may be applicable.
It is also worth noting that whether or not it's legal to scrape copyrighted content is an issue that's still being hammered out in the courts, so Etsy's statement that it does not have ownership over seller content does not necessarily mean it doesn't have the right to scrape that content.
Etsy's response to backlash
Etsy's Nov. 16 post about its changes to the company's terms of use provides several examples for how the company may use content to train AI models, but it doesn't appear to be a comprehensive list (emphasis theirs):
How we use your content to train AI models: We made an update to our terms that says Etsy and our partners may use member content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. This change is meant to clarify the ways we use AI in our marketplace.
We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers.
We will continue to focus on using AI to support sellers and improve the Etsy experience, and we're committed to being transparent about how we use this technology. Here are a few examples of how we are using AI on Etsy today:
- We train models to identify potentially fraudulent accounts and related listings, helping us investigate potential issues and protect our members.
- We use AI to understand the inventory across our marketplace, so we can help buyers find your items through search and provide them with tailored recommendations.
- We build AI-powered seller tools to help you run your business more efficiently, and better understand and meet your buyers' expectations.
Etsy's post also states that its terms of use "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models."
"We use security tools designed to detect and limit unauthorized scraping, and we are continuously improving our abilities to protect your content and keep Etsy safe," the statement said.
Notably, the statement does not make it clear whether Etsy itself or authorized third parties might be able to scrape Etsy content to train AI models. In fact, Etsy's terms of use specify that users cannot scrape any Etsy page for AI training "without our express permission."

Nations Championship: Steve Borthwick says England's All Blacks Tests 'World Cup practice' | Andy Farrell: Ireland still aren't World Cup contenders
Final weekend of Nations Championship takes place at Allianz Stadium; Ireland vs Australia on Friday (8.10pm), England vs New Zealand on Saturday (4.40pm), France vs South Africa in final on Sunday (4.40pm); coaches Steve Borthwick, Andy Farrell and Dave Rennie speak to media
Wednesday 25 November 2026 21:39, UK
Head coaches Steve Borthwick of England, Andy Farrell of Ireland and Dave Rennie of New Zealand speak to media ahead of the final weekend of the inaugural Nations Championship.
England, having come into the tournament under a cloud of pressure following the worst Six Nations display in their history earlier this year (four losses, fifth place), have stormed to victories over Australia, Japan and New Zealand this month.
Last week, Borthwick's side secured a record 25-point victory over the All Blacks at Allianz Stadium. With England finishing second behind France in the northern hemisphere standings and New Zealand runners-up to South Africa in the southern hemisphere table, the two sides are now set for an immediate rematch.
England face the All Blacks again at Twickenham on Saturday, with Borthwick viewing the latest clash as valuable preparation for the Rugby World Cup in Australia in 10 months' time.
"The nature of this tournament, it's a new tournament, is the understanding that international games have that level of jeopardy," Borthwick told the media on Wednesday.
"The consequence upon each of these games. This is an important step.
"It's a real positive step in this competition towards the jeopardy of being involved in World Cup games.
"In the World Cup, you want to be in situations where you're having to back up big games in multiple weeks.
"I think it's going to be an excellent Test match this weekend, a really tough Test match against a super dangerous New Zealand team.
"We're expecting New Zealand to come hard at the breakdown, and we're expecting them to really challenge us there.
"All our focus this weekend is we're expecting the very best of New Zealand. They're full of so much talent and so much experience. We know this is going to be a fierce Test match.
"We've got a young squad. We've got some players that are very experienced at the end of the spectrum and a lot of players that are young and haven't played against teams like New Zealand that often. So I think it was an important step in our development.
"This Saturday is another very important step. Each and every international experience we have is vital for the long-term development of this team."
Ireland's Farrell: We still aren't World Cup contenders despite win vs Springboks
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell began this Test window by telling the media that, unlike in 2023, this current Ireland side - based on performances to date - are not Rugby World Cup contenders.
What has followed this month is dominant victories over Argentina and Fiji in Dublin, followed by a stunning 20-17 success over double world champions South Africa last week.
Ireland face Australia at Twickenham on Friday, but Farrell reiterated his point that Ireland are not in World Cup-title conversations.
"No [Ireland are not World Cup contenders]," he said. "We took a step in the right direction last week, but that's got to continue to be that, hasn't it? To make sure that we keep feeling that way.
"That's always going to be the challenge [emotional challenge a week after win over Springboks].
"Plus, we have a six-day turnaround, and we play Scotland in the World Cup with a six-day turnaround as well. Getting yourself back up, that's the way you get some consistency in your performance, so it's pretty important.
"You are testing your depth, and you're always going to get that with four quality games over such a short space of time. But the Six Nations is five games, and then the World Cup is seven games if you've got any ambition, really.
"It's not ideal [shortage at No 8], but again, these are things that happen over a tournament, and that's what we've found this year.
"Obviously, from the start having so many experienced players in Caelan Doris and Jack Conan out - played plenty of times for us - and then we've lost a few as we've gone on.
"But you've got to be able to adapt with the squad that you've got, and you've been able to do that so far.
"It is what it is [Dan Sheehan's two-Test ban]. He had a fair hearing, and we move on."
All Blacks boss Rennie responds to calls for his sacking: 'Nature of the job'
New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie has overseen a first All Blacks defeat to Wales since 1953 and a record loss to England this month.
Such results have led to huge pressure and reports he should be sacked.
"I don't listen to anything. I don't read anything, so that probably helps," Rennie said.
"Look, it's the nature of the job, and it's the expectations of this role too.
"But international rugby now is really tight. You look at the recent results, and I think four years ago heading into a World Cup, Ireland and France were ranked No 1 and No 2, so things can change really quickly.
"It wasn't that long ago South Africa and us were No 1 and No 2. We're well aware of how tough it is, and England are a really good side.
"But we believe if we get our game right, we'll be competitive at the weekend.
"We're just excited to wear the jersey again and put on a performance that we're proud of and the country's proud of. We'll talk about fatigue next week.
"You want it to hurt, because we're all hurt after the weekend.
"Sunday's still a bit of a struggle, but you can't afford to sulk because you've got to look forward and think: 'How do we fix things?'
"Our job is to try and bring energy and connection and we're a really tight group. We want to get a result on the weekend for us, but also for the country.
"We're really appreciative of all the support we've got, especially after last week's performance. We're determined to rectify that."

AI is reshaping the media and marketing industries at warp speed.
Adtech and martech startups are raising millions of dollars from venture capital firms on the back of the AI wave.
Many of these companies are developing under-the-hood tech, such as agentic AI tools designed to streamline marketers' workflows and boost productivity. Others are working on creative platforms that let marketers create ads and even virtual influencers using generative AI. Some are working in new fields such as "generative engine optimization" (GEO), helping brands optimize their visibility in AI search results and to AI shopping agents.
The AI boom has also sparked a rush of mergers and acquisitions in the advertising space.
"Adtech has been innovating with real-time decisioning, identity, and all these component parts that in a much more automated world are very relevant," Sparrow Advisers cofounder Ana Milicevic told CMO Insider.
Business Insider has interviewed the founders of startups building tools to disrupt advertising and marketing with AI. These companies shared the pitch decks they used to impress investors and raise venture capital funding.
Read 23 pitch decks advertising and marketing AI startups used to raise millions:
Series B
- Vibe, an adtech platform for buying ads on streaming TV: $50 million (Vibe was acquired by Walmart in a deal that completed in August 2026. The Wall Street Journal reported the deal was valued at $1.4 billion, though Walmart declined to comment on the terms.)
Series A
- Azoma, a platform that helps brands get their products discovered by AI shopping agents: $11.2 million
- Daydream, a search engine optimization agency that blends AI agents with human expertise: $15 million
- FLORA, an AI creative tool for designers and artists that combines several large language models into a single interface: $42 million
- Fluency, an adtech startup that is working on AI agents to help automate ad campaigns across Meta, Google, TikTok, and more: $40 million
- Hedra, a generative AI video startup that's expanding its enterprise tools for marketers: $32 million
- Dig, a company that uses LLMs to help brands identify reputational risks and disinformation: $14 million

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

A 15 second-long clip has gone viral on X, showing a man kicking and attacking a woman holding a mic, seemingly performing was on-stage. This prompted the woman and several other men from the audience to retaliate.
The clip was shared by X user Ben-Yehuda (@Tal7yvwr) on November 21 with the claim that a Muslim man attacked a woman for not wearing a Burqa in the United States. The post garnered 5.4 million views and reshared over 3,000 times. (Archive)

The same clip was shared by X user Vivek Mishra (@Viveksagarbjp) with an identitical claim. This post received 1.1 million views and over 700 reshares. (Archive)

Several other users also shared the viral clip with similar claims. Below is a gallery of some of these posts:
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral video and its associated claim, we ran reverse image searches on some of the keyframes. We came across a video posted on Youtube on November 14 by a channel called ‘The Channel’ which shows a set of Chilean stand-up comedian Luis Slimming. At the 0:07 mark, the same attacker who appears in the viral clip, gets up on-stage and attacks Slimming. The rest of the video shows an altercation between the attacker and Slimming, and seemingly other members of his team or audience.
We found similarities in the attacker’s face, movement, clothes and pattern of action in both the viral clip and the original video. Below is a gallery comparing keyframes from the two:
We found an article by The Free Press Journal — Chilean Stand-Up Comedian Luis Slimming Attacked During Live Show; Violent Scuffle Caught On Camera — reporting that stand-up comedian Luis Slimming was attacked by a man during his live comedy show on November 12, at Hotel Antay in Arica city of Chile. This confirmed that the viral video is a digitally altered version of the attack on Slimming, replacing him with a woman.
A closer look at the viral video revealed several inconsistencies in the woman’s response to the attack, indicating that it might be generated using AI. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection tool Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 64% likely that the video is generated using AI.
To conclude, the viral video of a woman being attacked has been generated using AI by altering the video of stand-up comedian Luis Slimming, who was assaulted while performing on stage on November 12 in Chile. Thus, the claim that the woman was attacked by a Muslim man in the United State for not wearing a burqa is false and misleading.

On the heels of recent news reports on how keratin-based hair-straightening products containing glycolic acid derivatives led to severe kidney injury in women, researchers from Kerala have reported a series of cases wherein, the use of fairness creams has been linked to nephrotic syndrome.
(For top health news of the day, subscribe to our newsletter Health Matters)
In a study published in the latest issue of Kidney International (‘NELL-1 associated membranous nephropathy linked to skin fairness cream use — insights from an Indian case series’, ) doctors describe a series of 15 cases of Membranous Nephropathy, reported by Aster MIMS Hospital, Kottakkal, Malappuram district, that were traced to the regular use of fairness creams.
Heavy metal screening of the blood and urine samples of these patients revealed high levels of mercury, the toxic effects of which are well-known. An analysis of the fairness creams also showed that these contained high levels of mercury -- in some instances, 10,000 times above the permissible limit of 1 ppm.
Since 2021, Ranjith Narayanan, a nephrologist practising at two busy private hospitals in Kozhikode, had noticed a specific pattern in cases of membranous nephropathy diagnosed amongst his patients. They all had non-specific symptoms — fatigue, mild edema and frothy urine — but high levels of proteinuria, in the range of 6.5-22.2 g/day.
