You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.
One of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.
One way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.
Here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.
How to turn on and use Taptic Time on your Apple Watch
To enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.
That last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.
The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.
When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.
Who should actually use Taptic Time on an Apple Watch?
The honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.
The main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.
If your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

Job seekers want to show they're fluent in AI without suggesting they rely on it too heavily. Communicating that sweet spot can be tricky.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, said he commonly sees both over- and under-reliance in interviews — and it can be a costly mistake.
Brooker said it's increasingly clear when candidates haven't kept pace with how quickly the field has changed over the past year.
"It's very obvious when people haven't tried the tools, been building hands-on, been using this new technology, and spending time deeply understanding how it works," Brooker said.
He said it can be challenging, even as a leader, to keep up. It can also be difficult to differentiate between a trend and a meaningful update. Identifying that difference requires good taste and a lot of communication with others in the field, Booker said.
Personally, he said he dedicates eight hours a week to intentional learning, some of which he does in parallel with building. At least some of this time is set aside for experimenting with new techniques, new tools, papers, and keeping up with the long-term durable trends.
The other mistake Booker says he sees is over-relying on the tech. That involves a mindset of, "'I'm just going to ask AI to do this for me,'" or, "'I'm going to hand this question to my agent and answer it.'" Those applicants aren't thinking through answers and design questions.
"I want to hire people who can think," Brooker said. "I want to hire people who can deeply consider trade-offs. I want to hire people who can communicate and understand and engage with the technology."
Brooker said that simply typing in a problem and then asking an LLM or AI agent to solve it, "isn't a particularly useful or valuable skill." However, the VP said that it's "very useful and valuable" to know when to use AI and when to think for yourself.
His comments reflect a growing number of tech leaders who have said that judgment and taste are becoming the most important skills in the field, and that AI is increasingly automating work, leaving engineers with more time for higher-level decision-making.

Mumbai-based fintech startup Vegapay has raised $10 Mn (₹92.3 Cr) in a Series A funding round co-led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia and India and Prosus. The round also saw participation from existing investors Elevation Capital and Eximius Ventures. The funding round comprises both primary and secondary transactions, with over 40 employees getting an opportunity to sell a portion of their vested employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs). It will deploy the fresh capital to onboard more banks onto its credit line on UPI platform, introduce secured credit lines backed by fixed deposits, gold and mutual funds, and expand its credit card, prepaid card and forex card programmes. It also plans to strengthen its engineering and risk teams. Founded in 2022 by Gaurav Mittal, Himanshu Agrawal and Puneet Sharma, Vegapay provides a technology platform that enables banks to launch and manage Credit Line on UPI (CLOU), credit card and other credit programmes. Its platform allows banks to run multiple co-branded credit programmes, each with independent limits, pricing and rules. Banks can also deploy the technology on their own cloud infrastructure or on-premises. The startup claims to command a majority of India's Credit Line on UPI market as of November 2026. Its platform is live with YES BANK, Unity Small Finance Bank, Suryoday Small Finance Bank and BOBCARD. It also powers credit programmes for fintech and consumer-facing platforms, including Paytm, BharatPe, Kiwi UPI, Scapia and EbixCash World Money. Betting On Credit Line On UPI Vegapay's fundraise comes as Credit Line on UPI emerges as a new distribution channel for formal credit in India. The offering allows banks to provide customers with pre-sanctioned credit lines that can be used to make payments at UPI QR codes through existing payment applications, without requiring a separate credit card or app. While UPI has transformed India's digital payments ecosystem, the integration of credit into the payment network could create another avenue for banks to distribute lending products. Vegapay is positioning its platform as the underlying technology layer for banks looking to launch these products without building the entire infrastructure in-house. "UPI was India's payments revolution. Credit Line on UPI is the UPI moment for credit, and banks should lead it," said Gaurav Mittal, cofounder and CEO of Vegapay.

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Seven of India’s JioStar television channels, including popular Hindi-language entertainment channels Star Plus and Colors, are now streaming in the U.S. on live TV service Fubo.
Alongside Star Plus and Colors, the slate comprises Star Bharat, Colors Rishtey, Colors Cineplex, MTV India and English-language news channel News18 English.
The four general entertainment channels carry both fiction and non-fiction programming. Their libraries include popular dramas “Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi,” “Anupama” and “Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai,” as well as reality franchises “Bigg Boss,” “India Ke Top 1 Percent” and “Laughter Chefs.”
Colors Cineplex is the group’s movie channel, programming Hindi films that range from older Bollywood favorites to hits such as “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham,” “Tiger 3,” “Welcome” and “Dil Toh Pagal Hai.” MTV India adds its youth-skewing formats “Roadies,” “Splitsvilla” and “Hustle,” while News18 English covers news out of India.
Viewers can get the channels through two Fubo packs. The Hindi Entertainment & Cricket pack costs $34.99 for the first month as an introductory offer, rising to $39.99 a month after that. The JioStar pack is priced at $10.99 a month.
Amit Malhotra, head of international business at JioStar, said: “The opportunity for Indian entertainment internationally is no longer limited to taking individual shows or channels overseas. It is about building a distribution ecosystem through which the breadth of Indian television can travel. At JioStar, our approach is to bring the full spectrum of our content, from fiction and reality to cinema and youth entertainment, to South Asian families in the U.S. and to a wider audience who can connect with it.”
JioStar is pitching the move at the South Asian diaspora, for whom Indian TV is still a close tie to Indian culture, and also at a wider audience curious about the country’s storytelling.
Malhotra added that the Fubo launch gives JioStar a solid base in the U.S. as it puts together a broader international distribution network for its linear channels.
In September, JioStar’s streaming service JioHotstar launched in the U.K., Canada and Singapore, replacing Hotstar in those markets with a library of more than 160,000 hours of content in over 12 languages.

Bisleri International has maintained that its packaged drinking water is safe for consumption, disputing the findings of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which has sanctioned prosecution against the company after a water sample was declared unsafe following laboratory tests.
In a statement issued on Monday (November 23, 2026), the company said the matter related to a batch manufactured in September 2025 at its Goa facility, one of 143 plants in its network, and dated back about 14 months.
Bisleri said the FSSAI collected six samples from the facility on September 30, 2025, of which five met all applicable standards. The sixth sample recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Following an appeal by the company on November 22, 2025, the FSSAI referred the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. Bisleri said the referral laboratory found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit, but separately flagged the presence of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
The findings came after the initial laboratory examination had found the sample non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits, and declared it unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The referral laboratory also declared the sample unsafe, citing the detection of PAHs. Based on the laboratory findings, the FSSAI subsequently sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri.
Questioning the differing test results, Bisleri said the difference between the two sets of findings raised questions that it believed warranted clarification. The company said it arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, where the bromate level was also found to be within the prescribed limit.
Bisleri said it submitted the independent test results to the FSSAI’s Western Regional Office along with a formal letter dated February 2, 2026.
“We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed. To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website,” a company spokesperson said.
The company’s management is deciding on the next steps, the spokesperson said. The company said it maintained stringent quality controls, including more than 90 tests across its 10-step manufacturing process. It added that it would continue to cooperate with the FSSAI and address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process.

World champion D. Gukesh backed his choice of the London System against Uzbek challenger Javokhir Sindarov in their second FIDE World Chess Championship game, describing it as a “cool” opening despite the contest ending in a 20-move draw on Wednesday.
Unlike the hard-fought opening game, the second encounter proved a dampener for chess fans expecting another full-blooded battle. Gukesh failed to extract any advantage from the opening and opted for a quick draw by repetition after just 20 moves.
Speaking about his choice of the London System with the white pieces, Gukesh described it as a good opening. “Nowadays everything from both colours is playable, there is so much to explore because of the engines, I don’t think one opening is better than the other, I thought it would be a cool way to start,” he said.
The remark left chess followers speculating about whether he would return to the London System later in the tournament.
Sindarov said he had not expected the opening but was familiar with the variation. Asked why neither player could gain an advantage, Gukesh noted that “both are well prepared”. Sindarov, meanwhile, said both players had solid positions and it was not easy to make progress in the early middle game.
Asked whether, after the tension of the opening game, he would have preferred to get a result in his favour in the second, Gukesh was quick to say he would have liked both games to go his way.
The World champion, however, added, “It’s not easy, you try to create chances, sometimes you get, sometimes you don’t, we both spent months preparing, generally I feel fine, it’s a 14-games match and only two are over yet, overall games are fine and I feel energetic”.
Asked about the company he has during the match, Gukesh praised his friends Shikhar and Charmie, who are accompanying him along with his Polish second, Grzegorz Gajewski. He said he was very happy with the arrangements for the match.
Asked about the composition of his team, Gukesh said he would reveal the details later.
On why he chose not to continue playing instead of settling for a draw, Gukesh said it was not easy to find a way to put his opponent under pressure.
“I could not see a way to pose some serious problems for my opponent, and if I have to take some measures, I also have to take a certain amount of risk. You hope for your opponent to go wrong at some point but it is equally likely that you will get in to trouble. It’s about making some clever decisions”.
The third game will be played on Thursday. Sindarov could opt for a different opening, giving Gukesh an opportunity to showcase his preparation in another variation.

New Delhi- The Centre on Thursday informed the Delhi High Court that a Look Out Circular has been issued by the Mumbai Police against CJP co-convener Saurav Das, who was stopped at the airport from travelling to the United Kingdom.
The submission was made before Justice Amit Mahajan, who issued notice and sought a response from the Centre on Das’s plea challenging the government’s move to stop him from travelling.
The court listed the matter for further hearing on December 9.
During the hearing, the Centre’s counsel said a Look Out Circular (LOC) was issued against Das by the Mumbai Police on November 23 and that a show-cause notice was also issued to him and he is yet to respond to it.
Das’s counsel submitted that he was not made aware of any LOC, the reason for its issuance and its purpose.
The court was hearing a plea by Das, who was stopped from flying to the United Kingdom for an event at Oxford University, where he was slated to speak on the “cockroach movement”.
Das has alleged that he was stopped at the immigration counter at the Delhi airport before boarding his flight to London on the night of November 23.

FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.
The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."
"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."
A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.
The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."
"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.
Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.
He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.
"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.
In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.
In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."
"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."
Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.
Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

The Karnataka Cabinet has approved a comprehensive policy for the prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and social reintegration of burns survivors, paving the way for a Statewide network of specialised burns care facilities. Karnataka is the first State in the country to come out with such a policy.
The policy envisages setting up 15-bed burns care wards in district hospitals and government medical college hospitals, besides upgrading the Mahabodhi Burns Care Centre at Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), Bengaluru, as a Centre of Excellence.
Ritvik Ranjanam Pandey, Principal Secretary (Health), said the focus would now shift to implementing the policy. “With the Cabinet approval in place, the next step is implementation. We will work towards putting the various components of the policy in place,” he told The Hindu.
Expanding access to specialised care
Karnataka records an estimated 2.5 lakh to 3 lakh burns cases annually, according to the Cabinet note. However, specialised treatment, including intensive care and rehabilitation, remains concentrated in Bengaluru and Mysuru. The proposed district-level facilities are expected to address this gap.
Each 15-bed unit will comprise 10 general beds, three high-dependency unit beds and two intensive care unit beds. The wards will also have operation theatres for burns procedures, isolation facilities and physiotherapy services.
Mr. Pandey said the policy adopts a comprehensive approach covering emergency response, transportation, stabilisation, treatment, referral services and long-term rehabilitation. It also provides for standardised protocols for wound management, intensive care and surgical interventions. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation are to begin from the first day of treatment, wherever clinically appropriate.
BMCRI to be Centre of Excellence
The Mahabodhi Burns Care Centre at BMCRI will function as the State’s apex institution, providing specialised treatment, training, research and technical support to district-level facilities.
The proposed upgrade includes improvements to operation theatre and intensive care facilities, besides strengthening physiotherapy and rehabilitation services. Dedicated facilities for hydrotherapy, prosthetics, radiology and laser treatment are also envisaged.
The centre will undertake capacity-building programmes, develop treatment protocols, support telemedicine services and establish a State Burns Registry.
A hub-and-spoke model will link the Centre of Excellence with district-level units through standardised guidelines and referral protocols connecting primary, taluk, district and tertiary healthcare facilities.
Rehabilitation and social reintegration
Beyond emergency medical care, the policy emphasises the psychological and social consequences of burns. It envisages counselling, reconstructive surgery, social security and support for survivors to return to their families, education, employment and community life. The policy also provides for livelihood support and vocational rehabilitation to help survivors rebuild their lives.
The estimated one-time expenditure for establishing the 15-bed burns care wards is ₹100.95 crore, while ₹4.5 crore has been earmarked for upgrading the Centre of Excellence. The latter will involve a recurring expenditure of ₹1.2 crore annually.
Recognise disfigurement
Welcoming the policy, women’s rights activist and Aweksha co-founder Donna Fernandes, however, said it would have been more inclusive had it explicitly recognised disfigurement as a disability, making survivors eligible for disability benefits and compensation.
“We are disappointed that the policy has not included disfigurement as a disability,” she said, pointing out that survivors with severe facial injuries face social ostracism, humiliation and psychological trauma that cannot be captured through conventional assessments of functional disability. “Disfigurement is a disability. You cannot measure it, you cannot quantify it, and you cannot assign a percentage to it,” she said.
Harrassment and violence
Besides, the policy should also recognise that burns involving women are not necessarily accidental, but can result from domestic violence, dowry harassment and deliberate attacks by husbands or in-laws. Treating such cases merely as cooking or stove accidents overlooks the circumstances behind the injuries.
Ms. Fernandes further called for burns survivors to receive compensation and healthcare benefits on a par with acid attack survivors, as both groups suffer extensive skin and tissue damage, disfigurement and long-term consequences.
Recognising disfigurement as a disability and extending equivalent benefits to burn survivors would have strengthened the policy, she added.

Richard Hammond has revealed that the BBC sounded him out about getting back behind the Top Gear wheel for the show’s upcoming reboot.
The presenter said he declined the opportunity to return to the motoring show he helped turn into a global phenomenon alongside Jeremy Clarkson and James May.
Hammond disclosed the BBC’s approach during an interview with Times Radio on the day that Gordon Ramsay was unveiled as the new host of Top Gear.
“I did talk to them about Top Gear relaunching, and I’m sure they went to the others as well. They came to me, and [asked] was I interested? ‘No, I’m too old,’ [I responded],” Hammond said.
Watch on Deadline
“I’ve done it. I wouldn’t want to revisit it. That was our Top Gear, wasn’t it? We did it, the three of us, and when we left and went on together, it was the three of us. But that was our show.
“The BBC owns Top Gear and has had it for decades, and I think right now should be making a show that actually tells us what’s happening in the world of cars.”
Times Radio presenter Kait Borsay asked Hammond if he would be interested if Clarkson and May returned to Top Gear.
“We’ve done it. Let somebody else. We made our show in the way we did, and for our time,” he replied. “The BBC should be making a TV show that tells us, the consumers: This is what’s happening in the world of transport.”
Hammond hosted Top Gear between 2002 and 2015, before leaving the BBC with Clarkson and May and launching The Grand Tour on Amazon Prime Video.
Ramsay was announced as the next host of Top Gear four years after Andrew Flintoff’s crash. Ramsay will lead the series alongside a soon-to-be-announced lineup of co-presenters, with The Stig returning.
Filming will take place across the UK and around the world in 2027, with the Top Gear test track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home.
Ramsay said: “At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected – surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.”

In Lucknow, Kharge (left) stressed the need for collective work rather than verbal exchanges.
NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday finally broke silence on Imran Masood's aggressive attack on Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing in Uttar Pradesh.Speaking at an event in Lucknow, Kharge advised Masood to "focus on action rather than just words", as the Saharanpur MP's increasingly sharp remarks against ally Samajwadi Party (SP) have added to the strain over seat-sharing negotiations ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."... Imran Masood — whom I frequently hear on television, where he often speaks with great passion. However, we must focus on action rather than just words; the more we work together, the further we will progress. He is in Parliament, where he consistently fights for the party and strives to ensure that our positions are upheld," Kharge said.The Congress chief's remarks come amid growing friction between the two INDIA bloc allies, with Masood repeatedly questioning the SP's approach to seat-sharing even as discussions between the parties remain under way.
Masood questions SP's seat-sharing approach
Masood on Thursday questioned the rationale behind continuing seat-sharing discussions after the Akhilesh Yadav-led SP announced five candidates while negotiations with the Congress were still in progress."It is no alliance if one partner 'leaves' seats for the other after announcing its candidates," he said, raising questions about whether the Congress was being treated as an equal partner.The Congress MP also made it clear that he would remain with his party and would not accept a subordinate position in the alliance.
"What else should I say? You (SP) release the list. Then you leave the seats. Are we alliance partners or your servants? Did we ask you to leave these seats for us? We had discussed the matter, and now an order has been issued that we should not speak about those discussions," he said.Masood, who was involved in the seat-sharing discussions, argued that an alliance should involve joint decisions and announcements. He declined to comment on the SP's manifesto, which was scheduled to be released later on Thursday, saying he was unaware of the party's approach."It is their decision. How can I comment on it? The meaning of an alliance is that there should be joint press conferences and everything should be joint. If something else is happening here, I do not know about it," he said.Recalling the previous Assembly elections contested by the Congress and SP, Masood said his party had fought 107 seats when Akhilesh Yadav was the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh."Now, he is yet to become the chief minister," he added.
Earlier barbs had put SP on the defensive
Masood's latest remarks follow a series of public attacks on the SP leadership over the alliance arrangement. On Wednesday, he had used sharp expressions to convey his frustration with what he described as the SP's treatment of the Congress.In an interview with The Times of India, he questioned whether the SP wanted to fight the BJP or its own alliance partner."Aapki ladai mujhe samajh nahi aa rahi hai — BJP se ladni hai ya humse? Aap hamare gale par pair rakhkar, hamari kabar ke upar Taj Mahal banana chahenge, toh mera saans ghutega. Main toh haath-pair maarunga (I am unable to understand your battle … You want to fight the BJP or us. If you will want to stand on my neck and build a Taj Mahal on my grave, I will be suffocated. I will fight back)," he had said.Later, speaking to a television channel, Masood compared the Congress to zero, arguing that its presence multiplied the strength of an alliance partner by ten.
"If you don't understand our importance, then OK, Goodbye, Thank You," he said.The SP had largely refrained from responding to his remarks throughout Wednesday. However, his repeated criticism prompted some SP functionaries to question the Congress leadership's silence.A senior SP functionary told TOI that either the Congress leadership was choosing to ignore the statements or was unaware of what its leaders were saying. In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.
Modern governance, however, forgot what Ashoka and Virchow knew. It allotted people to one ministry, livestock to another and forests to a third, and pathogens, which recognise no such allocation of business, have exploited the gaps ever since. One Health, which the world marks on November 3, is the effort to recover that lost unity with the tools of the 21st century by bringing human, animal and environmental health into a common framework for research, surveillance and prevention. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, which regards the world as one family, resonates with this understanding of interconnected life.
This year the case makes itself. Lumpy skin disease (LSD) has returned to India. The September forecast from ICAR-National Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology and Disease Informatics’ early-warning system placed 219 districts across 28 states and Union Territories at risk, and Rajasthan had recorded more than 10,400 cases in 10 eastern districts by mid-September. In Siberia, a young technician at Irkutsk’s anti-plague institute died in early October, of what Russian authorities called pneumonia of unknown cause, amid reports of pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 people were placed under observation. Whatever the final diagnosis, Yersinia pestis, the organism of the Black Death, has never left us. It persists in rodents and their fleas, from the marmots of the Central Asian steppe to the prairie dogs of New Mexico and the rats of Madagascar.
Neither story respects a departmental boundary. LSD does not infect people, but it drains milk cans, household incomes and children’s nutrition. Plague is at once a problem of wildlife ecology, laboratory biosafety, clinical medicine and public trust.

Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.
To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”
But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.
That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.
The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.
“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she added, “I think we have a lot of ground to make up.”
When contacted for comment, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email that the agency’s records don’t support the decline reported by IIE, though it didn’t say whether its own data show lower enrollment by foreign students, and that President Trump should be credited for cracking down on rampant visa fraud.
“Institute of International Education’s ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” the DHS spokesperson said. “So far, [the Student and Exchange Visitor Program] has not experienced a 9% drop of foreign student enrollment.”
A recent independent analysis by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration of the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, a DHS database that has for more than 20 years monitored foreign students, found that international student enrollment declined by 6.3% between October 2025 and October 2026.
Concerns that the Trump administration would make it difficult for foreign scientists to enter or stay in the U.S. preceded the president’s inauguration. Since then, the administration has enacted travel bans affecting dozens of countries; instituted “extreme vetting” for visa applicants, including the review of social media profiles; and revoked more than 8,000 student visas. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also stepped up enforcement of alleged visa violations, including the recent detention of a Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who had been traveling home after presenting at a scientific meeting.
But many of the administration’s efforts to more tightly regulate international scholars have not come to fruition. That includes the attempt to end “duration of status,” a policy that for nearly half a century allowed students and postdoctoral researchers to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training. DHS’s proposed four-year cap would likely have forced the vast majority of new foreign life science students to apply for extensions to stay in the country given that, on average, it takes five to six years to earn a biomedical doctorate. But a federal judge found that the proposal violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations.
The Trump administration has also proposed a $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience; academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are often used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.
Even though these restrictions have not been enacted, they’ve left many foreign students with a clear sense that they aren’t wanted here.
“All these rules, it just made me feel like my immigration was a crime. That’s the biggest recurring feeling that I’ve had these past few years,” said a biomedical Ph.D. student at the University of Washington, who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You know what? I’m just here to study. I’m just learning, and I’m focused on my science. But it has felt very disruptive.”
There are growing signs that fear is impacting student decisions. A poll this summer from the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications fell 21%.
A more recent survey of 437 universities, including more than 200 in the U.S., found that nearly 60% of U.S. institutions reported lower graduate enrollment between August and October compared with the same period last year. Ninety percent of U.S. respondents cited restrictive government policies as a significant obstacle.
That trend isn’t unique to the U.S. The Global Enrollment Benchmark Survey found that nearly 80% of institutions in the United Kingdom, which has also instituted tougher immigration controls, reported reduced foreign graduate student enrollment. By contrast, nearly 60% of Asian universities that responded, including five Chinese institutions, said graduate enrollment had increased. It’s a shift that Aw says could have major implications for the global economy and the future of innovation.
“There is truly a global competition for talent,” she said. “China has made no secret that one of its most pressing priorities is international education and to bring as many talented students to its shores as they can from around the world. That used to be the United States.”

Rescuers battle tough conditions in flooded Indonesian mine
Rescuers are battling high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain while searching for miners believed trapped by flooding in an illegal gold mine
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Rescuers battled high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain Thursday searching for 10 miners believed trapped by flooding in an illegal gold mine where 16 bodies have been recovered.
The miners were digging for grains of gold late Monday when heavy rain caused the Ciseureuh River to overflow into a mine shaft in the Bogor regency of West Java province. Several people escaped from one section of the excavation before floodwaters filled the shaft, estimated to be about 100 meters (330 feet) deep, in a mountainous area south of the capital, Jakarta.
Authorities said they were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, and local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.
Police first received reports of trapped miners about 16 hours after the flooding occurred, and nearby state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.
The search and rescue team used submersible water pumps to suck water from the hole and tried to close off openings where groundwater seeped in.
West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said authorities believe at least 10 miners remain trapped as rescuers retrieved 16 bodies by Thursday.
“On the fourth day, the chances of finding survivors have become increasingly slim,” Rochmawan said. “But we will continue the search. At this point, it would be a miracle if anyone were still alive.”
Thursday’s search operation involving 325 personnel focused on two adjacent mine shafts, using rope-access techniques to reach victims, said Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency chief Desiana Kartika Bahari.
The flooded shaft was near facilities operated by PT Antam’s Pongkor gold mining unit, but the company said the incident was unrelated to its operations.
Informal mining is common in Indonesia, where thousands work in dangerous conditions. Miners face risks including landslides, flooding and tunnel collapses, while gold processing often involves toxic mercury and cyanide with little protective equipment.

New Delhi: Indian creditors may have to wait longer for easier access to overseas assets of debt-laden companies. As it fleshes out rules for the cross-border insolvency framework under the amended bankruptcy law, the government is parsing stakeholder suggestions to ensure the norms do not end up helping defaulters shop for friendlier foreign courts that could potentially put lenders at a disdvantage, two people in the know said.
The April amendments to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) provided for a formal cross-border bankruptcy mechanism, requiring rules and regulations to make it operational.
The framework, the people said, is now unlikely to be finalized this fiscal year, as it requires broader deliberations, although the government remains keen on the mechanism’s rollout as early as possible.
“Several aspects need careful examination before the rules can be finalized,” said the first person cited above, explaining why more deliberations are needed. “These include possible safeguards against misuse, protecting interests of domestic creditors and ensuring primacy of proceedings in India if most of the assets are located here.”
While a crossborder insolvency framework is much needed to improve recoveries for Indian creditors, its design calls for caution, given the differences in bankruptcy laws across jurisdictions. The framework, as per the amended IBC, is to be tailored around a United Nations model law with modifications to suit the Indian context.
There are fears that Indian defaulters may use the framework to invoke insolvency proceedings in a foreign country where the bankruptcy regime suits their purpose better, to short-change domestic creditors’ interests, said the people in the know.
While many countries follow a debtor-in-possession model, where the existing management retains control during insolvency resolution, India follows a creditor-in-possession model, where control passes to a resolution professional acting for creditors. Unscrupulous promoters may take advantage of this mismatch to the disadvantage of Indian creditors, said the first person cited above.
Insolvency case disposals can also be faster abroad than in India, where it took an average of 771 days to resolve a case as of September, against the IBC timeline of 330 days, including litigation time.
If a defaulter can therefore quickly obtain a foreign proceeding and then seek recognition of the case in India, the chances of shifting the centre of gravity of the case to another jurisdiction increase.
The people said that stakeholders are seeking safeguards and clear rules on when India will be treated as the ‘centre of main interest’ (COMI), or the main location of defaulters’ assets.
“The government is seized of the matter,” the second person said, adding that rules would be finalized keeping in mind the sensitivities of the matter.
Queries emailed to the corporate affairs ministry, which will firm up the rules, late on Tuesday remained unanswered until press time.
The rules and the risks
The UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency recognizes that one country has to proceed with the main insolvency case and others with the supplementary case, depending on the so-called ‘centre of main interest’.
Similarly, if a foreign country has already initiated insolvency proceedings against a particular defaulter to recover some of the assets located here, India, too, will have to cooperate with that regime.
There are apprehensions that Indian defaulters may try to move, at least on paper, their ‘centre of main interest’ to shift insolvency proceedings to their country of choice.
A crossborder framework assumes importance, as a stressed Indian corporate group may have subsidiaries and assets spread across countries. The absence of a formal framework makes it tough for Indian creditors to approach a foreign court, seek a stay on asset sales there, or obtain information.
The need for such a framework emerged during bankruptcy proceedings of Amtek Auto, Videocon Industries, Essar Steel and Jet Airways, where a range of issues, including asset location and complex crossborder procedures, delayed resolution.
Currently, the IBC provides for crossborder insolvency through bilateral agreements and letters of request issued by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to foreign courts under Section 234. However, this mechanism is prone to delays and uncertainty.
Factors at play
Anoop Rawat, partner and national practice head (insolvency & restructuring) at Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas & Co said the cross-border insolvency framework must factor in the difference between the Indian creditor-in-control model and the largely debtor-in-control model in jurisdictions, including the US, the UK and Singapore.
“This asymmetry creates potential misuse risks, such as forum shopping through artificial shifting of the centre of main interests, using a foreign filing to retain control, seek a stay and delay Indian proceedings, or move assets before recognition in India,” he said.
Yogendra Aldak, executive partner at Lakshmikumaran and Sridharan Attorneys, pitched for ensuring reciprocity for India in the rules.
“The government should consider this, particularly given the concerns over forum shopping, as a reciprocity test would help ensure that foreign proceedings do not get easy recognition here while Indian creditors face hurdles abroad,” Aldak said.
Vishal Gehrana, partner-designate at legal firm Karanjawala & Co, said the rules must ensure that a company cannot simply choose a convenient country to escape the consequences of its defaults. “The decision about which country’s courts should deal with the main insolvency proceedings must be based on the company’s genuine business operations and economic centre, and not on artificial changes made to suit the promote.”

'Best midfielder in the world' - where does Bellingham rank?
- Published
Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?
Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."
Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.
While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.
"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."
While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?
BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.
Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid)
Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.
He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.
He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.
He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.
When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.
He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.
Vitinha (Paris St-Germain)
While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.
But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.
The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".
He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.
Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.
"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."
Declan Rice (Arsenal)
Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.
He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.
Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.
The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.
He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.
Rodri (Barcelona)
The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.
It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.
The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.
His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

British drugmaker GSK’s subsidiary GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals (GSK India), as part of a strategy to sharpen focus on cancer therapies, on Tuesday announced the launch of monoclonal antibody-drug conjugate BLENREP (belantamab mafodotin) as a combination therapy for those with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma.

Beyond haematological and gynaecological cancers, GSK said it is focusing on lung and gastrointestinal cancers, and other solid tumours. It is currently conducting 15 oncology clinical trials, including studies evaluating dostarlimab in head and neck cancer and colon cancer, the company said.

Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Thursday (November 26, 2026) said political agendas of lawyers must not be masqueraded as professional duty, nor should judicial platforms be targetted for personal gains.
Constitution Day celbration, highlights on November 26, 2026
“Disagreement is not a weakness of constitutional democracy. A strong Bar must be able to question, challenge and disagree. Equally, a confident institution must have the capacity to engage with criticism without treating every disagreement as a challenge to its authority. What matters is that such engagement must remain guided by reason, professional integrity and respect for constitutional processes. If political agendas are masqueraded as professional duty or judicial platforms are targeted for personal gains — there stands the professional integrity impaired,” the CJI said in his address at the Constitutional Day celebrations organised by the Supreme Court Bar Association.
These responsibilities must also inform our response to the challenges facing the justice delivery system. The CJI acknowledged that pendency, delays and unequal access to legal representation continue to affect the experience of justice for many citizens.
“Behind every case number is a person awaiting the resolution of a dispute, the protection of a right or the vindication of a claim,” the CJI said.
The top judge said the responsibility to better the situation must be shared between the Bar and the Bench.
“Courts must continue to strengthen their processes and make justice more accessible. The Bar must contribute through focused and honest advocacy, responsible case management and professional discipline,” the CJI said.
Comment | Constitution is an inseparable part of our life journeys
Chief Justice Kant said the credibility of the justice system depended, in no small measure, upon the integrity with which its officers discharge their responsibilities.
The CJI said the professional obligation of an advocate extends beyond the immediate interests of the client. Candour towards the court, accuracy in presenting facts and authorities, and fairness in advocacy were equally important.
“The credibility of the justice system depends, in no small measure, upon the integrity with which its officers discharge their responsibilities,” the CJI said.
Correspondingly, the judiciary had an obligation to remain open to persuasion, engage seriously with the arguments advanced and ensure that decisions were supported by clear and principled reasoning.
“Judicial authority is an essential feature of our constitutional system. But public confidence in that authority must be continuously earned through independence, fairness and consistency,” Chief Justice Kant noted.

For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date.
The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements.
