Cleaning the Gomti: Lucknow's plan to stop sewage reaching the river
A drone survey has identified 45 drains discharging into the Gomti in Lucknow. The findings underpin a plan to intercept sewage, expand treatment capacity and improve connectivity.
The Gomti flows through Lucknow for around 30 kilometres, but keeping the river clean will require the city to tackle a problem that often remains out of sight: sewage flowing through drains and eventually reaching the river.
A drone survey conducted in Lucknow has identified 45 drains discharging into the Gomti, 12 more than the 33 recorded in Municipal Corporation records. The findings have prompted an action plan under the Namami Gange programme to tap the remaining drains, divert sewage to treatment plants and expand the city's treatment infrastructure.
The scale of the problem is significant. While Lucknow has 10 sewage treatment plants (STPs) with a combined capacity of around 629.5 million litres per day (MLD), a substantial volume of sewage continues to flow through drains that are either untapped or only partially tapped.
According to a state government release dated August 13, 2026, around 75 MLD of sewage from 12 drains has already been tapped, while five drains do not require tapping. The remaining 28 drains carry around 260 MLD and are yet to be fully addressed.
The findings also highlight the gap in sewerage connectivity. Of Lucknow's 7.52 lakh households, around 4.01 lakh, or 53.32%, are connected to the sewerage network.
45 DRAINS IDENTIFIED, 28 STILL TO BE ADDRESSED
The drone survey has given authorities a clearer picture of the number of drains flowing into the Gomti and the volume of sewage they carry.
Of the 45 identified drains, 12 have already been tapped, carrying approximately 75 MLD of sewage for treatment. Five drains have been identified as not requiring tapping.
That leaves 28 drains, either untapped or partially tapped, carrying an estimated 260 MLD of sewage. Addressing these drains is a central part of the proposed river rejuvenation plan.
The findings also point to the challenge of relying only on existing sewage infrastructure. Although Lucknow has treatment capacity of around 629.5 MLD across its 10 STPs, the city still has a substantial number of households outside the sewerage network and drains carrying sewage directly towards the river.
NEW STPs AND DRAIN NETWORKS PROPOSED
A pre-feasibility report for the rejuvenation of the Gomti proposes new sewage treatment infrastructure at several locations in Lucknow.
The plan includes proposed STPs with capacities of 160 MLD at Basant Kunj, 65 MLD at Wazirganj, 150 MLD at Jiamau and 65 MLD at Neelmatha.
It also proposes a nature-based treatment system at the Mastemau drain, along with smaller modular sewage treatment plants at Pipraghat, with a capacity of 750 kilolitres per day (KLD), and Ghaila, with a capacity of 100 KLD.
Apart from new infrastructure, the plan calls for upgrades to the Bharwara and Daulatganj STPs and repairs to connected drains.
The integrated Gomti rejuvenation plan was submitted to the National Mission for Clean Ganga on May 6, 2026.
SOME WORK COMPLETED, MORE TARGETED
Work on sewage treatment and drain tapping is already under way in parts of the city.
A 39 MLD sewage treatment plant under Namami Gange was completed on November 4, 2024.
The tapping of an untapped drain to treat 3.5 MLD of sewage at the Barikalan STP is targeted for completion in October 2026. Meanwhile, drains that are to be connected to the 50 MLD Loniyapurwa STP are expected to be linked by June 2027.
These projects are expected to help divert sewage away from the Gomti and ensure it is treated before being discharged.
However, the broader challenge will be to ensure that the proposed infrastructure is completed, existing treatment plants are upgraded and drains are effectively connected to the sewerage and treatment network.
WATER METRO ON THE GOMTI STILL AT STUDY STAGE
The state is also examining the feasibility of a Water Metro on the Gomti. The proposal, however, remains at the study stage and has not yet been approved.
While the idea could add another dimension to the river's use, the immediate challenge remains improving sewage management and preventing untreated wastewater from entering the Gomti.
The drone survey has highlighted the scale of the problem. The proposed rejuvenation plan now lays out a series of infrastructure projects aimed at addressing it. The impact on the river, however, will ultimately depend on how much of the untreated sewage is actually intercepted, treated and prevented from reaching the Gomti.

Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where modest brick houses and tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.
But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.
It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.
South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.
The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.
Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.
The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.
Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.
"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.
Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."
Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.
"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.
It "definitely just reminded me just how much kids are a lot smarter than they think they are," she adds. "They notice a lot more than they think they do."
Learning "Ubuntu"
Fortunately, Fiona's tale has a happy ending. Dreaming of becoming the next Miss South Africa, her character Lindani decides to try and raise the money she needs to enter a modelling contest by baking scones and selling them to her neighbors.
"She believes deep down inside that each one of her homemade scones has something special that makes them really delicious," Fiona writes.
In the end, Lindani makes enough cash to enter the contest. She comes in second place and is crowned "princess."
"She is happy because she has proved to herself that she can make a way when it initially seemed there was none," Fiona writes.
In real life, Fiona — also keen on modeling — is being raised in Alex by a single mom. Alex has high crime rates and poor government services like water and electricity. The young teenager is all too familiar with the problems, but she says there are good things about township life too..
"Alex is a crowded place, but when you're in Alex, you can learn a lot of things," she explains. "You can learn how to have Ubuntu."
Ubuntu is an African philosophy centering on community well-being and shared responsibility. As Fiona puts it: "Ubuntu is to help other people when they are in need."
Fiona, whose favorite subject at school is English, says she'd like to go to university, maybe to study medicine. And there's another dream too.
"One day, if I grow up, I want to build a big house that will be having a room with its own books," she says.
Homes without books
Fiona didn't grow up with books at home. Two-thirds of South African children don't have books at home, according to one study by UNICEF.
They won't necessarily find them at school either.
Only about 15% of public schools in South Africa have a functioning library, according to government data.
The dire state of child literacy has its roots in the home. Many children have weak early learning foundations, according to the UNICEF study, and they have no exposure to books before starting primary school.
"When I became the minister of basic education in 2024 I was confronted by the statistic of 80% of 10-year-olds who cannot read for meaning in any language," Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube told NPR.
The minister says the government is trying to tackle this problem by getting more kids into early learning programs.
"We're investing ten billion rand [$58 million] over the next three years on a massive haul out of early childhood development centers," Gwarube says.
Tebogo Selekane, an English teacher at Kwa-bhekilanga secondary school, says the weekend program at Read Alex has helped some of her students a lot. Two of her students have stories in the book.
"They are doing very well in reading," says Selekane. "There's a lot of change in them... they will respond back with confidence."
A country of storytellers
At the book launch, Wandile Mathe, a 21-year-old South African writer and joint coordinator of the project, says despite South Africa's poor literacy rates, the children he coaches come from a nation of storytellers.
"I think South Africans are natural storytellers," he says. "There's always gossip going around anyway."
"In the taxi, at the line, in a shop, wherever you go, there's always someone willing to tell you a story, whether about their personal life or the things that they're seeing around," he laughs. "We're huge social commentators. Nothing will pass by and we will not comment."
The kids who contributed to the book are true to this storytelling tradition, borrowing from their lives and what they see daily in the township. As well as Fiona's story about poverty and alcoholism, there are tales about peer pressure, dangerous men on the street, losing parents and inability to pay school fees.
But it's not all doom and gloom. The heroes and heroines all find ways to overcome the obstacles, learning important lessons and making friends along the way.
For example, one of the young authors, 13-year-old Anita Maloka, wrote a story about a rural girl who moves to Johannesburg to attend school and dreams of becoming a scientist. But the school is not what she hoped.
"Sometimes two students had to squeeze together on one chair. Textbooks were scarce," she writes. The family doesn't have the money to send her anywhere better though, so the character works toward earning a scholarship at a school that "has a real science lab and an entire room just for learning to program computers and building robots."
Like her character, Anita, who dreams of becoming a marine biologist, is also working toward getting a scholarship that will take her out of the township.
But she stresses that life in Alex is "not just about struggle."
"It's about children who want to travel, to explore and dream and make their dreams come true," she says.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Vishal Mathur is Technology Editor for Hindustan Times. When not making sense of technology, he often searches for an elusive analog space in a digital world.
Vivo X500 Pro Max’s photography masterclass, and also welcomes Apple loyalists
Vivo’s new flagship pairs stabilised 200-megapixel zoom lens with restrained, true-to-life Zeiss colour science, setting the photography bar for 2027 flagships
The smartphone camera, as an idea, is in an astonishing place. Not just the leaps in overall capabilities, but the smartphone space is defined by two very distinct approaches. Within that, there is a clear course correction happening as well, something I’ll illustrate, as we assess the latest flagship from Vivo, the X500 Pro Max. A 200-megapixel telephoto camera and the optional 200mm and 400mm equivalent lens options if you need that for long-range photography, offer good versatility to build with. But there are two contentions to weigh on.
We are in an era where flagships generationally have a tough time justifying pricing inflation with genuine forward experiential steps. The Vivo X500 Pro Max has managed that, resoundingly, particularly with the camera and the evolution of Origin OS. Secondly, there is the looming shadow of the Vivo X300 Ultra that was released a few months ago—brilliant across the board, be it the cameras, overall performance and in being an Android flagship as a collective. And if I may crystal gaze for a moment, the X500 Pro Max has a solid foundation to compete not just with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, but also an inevitable arrival of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max at some stage.
Also Read: From ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh: As flagship phones get 30% costlier, buyers rethink value
Pricing was therefore a complication. Vivo sees the X300 Ultra currently retailing for around ₹1,59,999 and slots the X500 Pro Max at ₹1,64,999 onwards. My question is this—how long does that remain on sale? On the point of the variants, there is a smaller window than usual between the 12GB+256GB spec and the ₹1,79,999 you’ll part with for 12GB+512GB. Go for the latter, if that’s within the realms of the budget. The Photography Kit bundle is currently with the higher spec, and that’s priced at ₹2,29,999. Difficult to have an opinion on pricing and value these days, as subjective as those matters are, considering smartphone makers have very little room due to component pricing inflation.
Cameras absolutely dominate the list of reasons as to why you’d consider a Vivo flagship phone, and it’s sensible to begin with that. The main camera is a 50-megapixel, a Sony LYTIA L910 sensor that’s 1/1/28-inch with 24mm focal length and gimbal-like (it is actually the CIPA 7.0 professional stabilisation standard) optical image stabilisation (OIS). The highlight here has to be the 200-megapixel telephoto, which is a 1/1.4-inch Samsung ISOCELL HP10 sensor with 85mm focal length and OIS. Completing the troika is a 50-megapixel ultra wide, which is a bit more humdrum, considering it’s a Samsung JN5 sensor from 2024, if memory serves me well.
The main camera, for starters requires you to tweak a setting from the outset. This by default pixel bins photos to 12.5-megapixel, which while great for saving space, does mean you’ll notice some pixelation if you crop or zoom in. I’d suggest selecting the 25-megapixel as the default setting for most photos you click, for a meaningful improvement as far as detailing goes. The other thing you need to do is set this to Zeiss Natural setting for colour saturation, for the most realistic processing.
Also Read: India’s smartphone market is shrinking, and phone prices have never been higher
Once you get the settings right, photography results are incredible across lighting conditions—in terms of detailing, colour reproduction and realism. When certain photos really need it, including those with complex natural lighting, the dynamic range really steps up to give that realistic representation of the moment you’ve tried to capture. Photos between 2x and 10x also don’t compromise anything on the finer elements of a photo.
A positive change that I continue to notice is the dialling down of the artificial detail boosting that had become apparent in the past couple of years. There is a natural flow to the gallery as you absorb the moments of a vacation later, rather than unnatural skies or a landscape that didn’t look this green. That said, some processing tweaks are needed to add a bit of realism to skin tones, which in moments, this phone tends to brighten up a smidgen more than necessary.
The star of the show is certainly the 200-megapixel telephoto, which allows you to get really close to the subject. And more often than not, without compromising on the details. I felt that a 50x or a 100x zoomed photo is much easier to manage on the Vivo X500 Pro Max with lesser shake and easier centering of the subject, than on a Samsung flagship or even the latest iPhone—that’s exactly the sort of result Vivo would have been looking to achieve with the elaborate OIS for this sensor.
Also Read:Tech is expensive, but is there light at the end of the tunnel?
Videos get a significant upgrade too. All cameras on the Vivo X500 Pro Max support 4K60 video recording resolution, in which the latter is the frames per second number. The main camera can also do 4K240 at 1x and 2x while the telephoto can also record at 4K120, as well as both can do 8K30 too. Dolby Vision, check. Log, check. Compared to photos, depending on how you’ve set up the elaborate filters and setting there, most videos have a bit more restrained colour. I believe the idea is to have a more neutral basis for video editing. Telephoto autofocus tracking will be very handy, more than you may realise initially, if you are recording a fast moving subject in the distance.
Everything about the Vivo X500 Pro Max is as you’d expect on a flagship which demands you part with top money. The design, for instance, takes a lot of inspiration from the X300 Ultra’s subtle dual-tone finish. The Eternal Black colour, for instance, has a glass fibre and spray-coated texture finish. I also notice a less profound ring around the camera island. Look at the back of this phone from a perfectly flat side view, and you’ll notice what Vivo calls the Tideline Design, where the area around the camera island is very gently raised compared to the lower part of the phone—they’re taking some cues from nature, a shore and how a tide interfaces with it.
I must note that the 7,800mAh battery has been incredibly well optimised. This is particularly true for standby battery frugality—leave a fully charged Vivo X500 Pro Max at 10pm and you’ll wake up to it at still 100% (or on some days, 99%) charge at 6am. Even during the day with active usage and apps working in the background, this is sipping charge very gently. Getting two days, with the battery reducing from 100% to 25%, is pretty much the way of life with a Vivo X500 Pro Max. Does this make it the most battery efficient phone in the current flagship lineup? I’d peg this ahead of the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.
Also Read:Gravity, dust and regret: The cost of repairing a foldable smartphone
Last but not least, are the improvements to Origin OS 78 that’s based on Android 17—and a thing worth noting here is how Vivo is making this versatile across devices, something we recently also noticed with the Vivo X Fold6 which specifically added utilities for the foldable’s display real estate. Here, you’re sure to find utility with a broader compatibility with Apple devices—Quick Share works with AirDrop, Office kit file transfers are compatible with Mac and iPad, Apple Watch will work with this phone, AirPods get Spatial Audio support and battery display within Origin Island and iCloud is baked into the File Manager app. There is a sensible realisation that Vivo must appeal to users who may otherwise also have some Apple devices within their reach.
Before you do part with the cash for the Vivo X500 Pro Max, chances are there will be a second glance at the spec sheet, particularly the Mediatek Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset choice. It is not a Qualcomm chip, will likely be your biggest contention. Vivo has, for a while now, bet on MediaTek’s chip for their flagships and results have been impressive. Nothing tells me it’ll be any different this time, because the Dimensity 9600 Pro feels absolutely capable of delivering a flagship experience—including sustained performance.
It is genuinely difficult to hold up anything as a shortcoming with the Vivo X500 Pro Max. Everything is generationally refined, the camera experience continues to stride, flagship level of performance and battery life, as well as the versatile option of the photography kit (this specifically, whether or not you buy it, is more subjective than anything else). Can I go so far as to say this is setting the benchmark for this year’s camera flagships? I’ll have to wait for Xiaomi’s latest flagship to pronounce my take on the matter, but Vivo and Zeiss as always have done enough to give this that substance. The Oppo and Hasselblad tonality and processing comes very close, but this may just edge it with the Zeiss Natural mode.
It is not that the Vivo X500 Pro Max doesn’t have room for improvement. The lack of Qi2 magnet integration means newer generation faster wireless chargers are off the agenda, till you get a case with those. Secondly, some may complain that the 90-watt charging speed is a step behind flagships, such as the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (100-watt), and they’d have a point. Last but not least, is the pricing. This generation of flagship phones demand top money, but are you getting that much evolution for your experience, compared to the flagship you may already be using? The answer, defines the decision.

Being a tech reviewer, my entire phone gallery is filled with hundreds of random screenshots. It also holds important photos of family moments, my pet, and a few other travel memories.
Because of this, my phone usually runs out of storage quickly. It also has a habit of running out at the worst possible time, showing storage-full notifications when I am about to capture something important.
I usually back up my photos to Google Drive using the Google Photos app. However, the free Cloud storage is already full.
With every Gmail account, Google offers 15 GB of free storage, which is now shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos. That storage. I wouldn’t prefer paying for more cloud storage, so I needed something that I could use to back up without paying for the cloud, and that is easy to sync between devices without manually transferring
While searching for options and thinking of building it myself, I found Syncthing, a free, open-source app that automatically transfers photos taken on your phone to your Windows PC or Mac. This is especially useful because, with a recent MacBook upgrade, I had gigabytes of unused storage.
It’s so seamless that once you take a photo on your phone, it automatically appears on your Windows PC or Mac without connecting a cable. It requires no monthly subscription and removes the friction of manually backing up files. It is also a free, open-source tool and works over Wi-Fi.
The best part is that it comes with flexible options. You can choose where photos are stored, back them up to an external hard drive, and configure it to keep copies even when you delete photos from your phone.
However, setting up Syncthing might be complex for beginners. So I created this detailed, comprehensive guide to help you set up Syncthing to automatically back up photos taken on your Android phone to either Windows or Mac.
Table of Contents
Before you begin, here are the minimum requirements for these steps to work
- You need an Android phone (I used a OnePlus 13R with Android 16)
- Ensure both are on the same Wi-Fi network for the initial setup.
- You need a Windows 10 or 11 PC, or a Mac
- Make sure your Mac or Windows PC has enough free space to back up your phone photos.
Install Syncthing-Fork on your phone
Step 1: Open the Google Play Store, search for the Syncthing-Fork app, and tap Install.
Step 2: Once the app is installed, tap Open
Step 3: The app welcomes you with an onboarding screen. Click Continue
Step 4: Next, you need to grant storage permission to the app. Tap the Grant Storage Permission button
Step 5: You will be taken to the file access settings of the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone. From there, enable the toggle that says Allow Access to Manage All Files.
Step 6: Next, you need to grant permission for battery optimization for the Syncthing-Fork app
Step 7: Next, tap Allow
Step 8: On the next screen, the app asks for location permission; you can skip it. Tap on the Continue option.
Step 9: On the next screen, the app asks for Notifications. The app uses notifications to alert you about device connections for the sharing required in the form of notifications. So you need to allow the app to send notifications. It also keeps the app running in the background.
Step 10: Tap Grant permission, then tap Allow to allow app notifications.
Step 11: That’s it; your app onboarding and setup are complete. Next, you need to download Syncthing on Windows.
Install Syncthing on Windows
Step 12: On your Windows PC, open any browser and go to the Syncthing downloads page. Scroll down and tap on the Syncthing Windows Setup option.
Step 13: Next, under the Assets section, download the installer
Step 14: Once the download is complete, click Open file
Step 15: Similar to mobile, you need to go through multiple screens to set up on Windows. There isn’t much to do; just click Next on the first five pages.
Step 16: Now, enable or disable additional tasks based on your needs. I recommend enabling automatic syncing when logging on and starting syncing after installation. Also, create a desktop shortcut to the Syncthing configuration page so that it will be easy to access in the future
Step 17: Once selected, click Next
Step 18: Finally, click Install to install it on your Windows.
Step 19: If the Windows Firewall block prompt appears, click Yes to the firewall rule
Step 20: Next, click Allow to continue installation.
Step 21: Once installed, click Finish. Make sure you enable the Syncthing configuration page.
Step 22: The configuration page opens in your default browser. The default browser security blocks access to the page. No need to worry; to bypass it, click Advanced on the warning page.
Step 23: Next, click Continue to 127.0.0.1
Step 24: Next, choose whether to send usage reports. I would suggest No.
Step 25: Next, click OK on the password notice
Install Syncthing on a Mac
If you are using a Mac, you can also set up Syncthing on your Mac to sync photos between your Android phone and your Mac. Follow the process below.
Step 26: On a Mac, open the Syncthing downloads page. Here is the link. On the downloads page, under the downloads section, click on the Syncthing-Mac OS link.
Step 27: Next, scroll down and download the .dmg file
Step 28: Click Allow to download
Step 29: Once downloaded, drag Syncthing to the Applications folder.
Step 30: Next, Open Syncthing on your Mac and allow local network access
Step 31: It opens in the default browser. Select No when the Allow Anonymous Usage reporting prompt appears. That’s it.
Connect your phone and computer
Next, connect your phone to Windows or Mac to start sharing photos. The process is similar on both macOS and Windows. For this demonstration, I am using Windows.
Step 32: Next, open the Syncthing page on your computer and click Actions at the top right.
Step 33: Click Show ID
Step 34: Syncthing shows the computer’s device ID as text and as a QR code. Scan the QR code with your phone to copy the device ID.
Step 35: Open the Syncthing-Fork app on your Phone and tap the Devices tab
Step 36: Tap the Add Device button
Step 37: Tap the QR code button, then scan the QR code shown on the desktop using your phone camera. If Android asks for camera access, tap Allow.
Note: If the QR code isn’t working, you can type the ID instead, or click Copy on the computer, send the ID to yourself in a chat or email, then paste it here.
Step 38: Next, check the device ID. Remember that it should match the ID on your computer screen.
Step 39: Give the computer a name. Tap Name and type a name you will recognize, such as Windows PC or My Mac or something that you can recognize.
Step 40: Once done, tap the check mark
Step 41: Within a minute, a yellow New Device box appears on the Syncthing page on your computer, asking you to connect your phone. It also displays a name; cross-check that the name is your phone’s model (mine is CPH2691). Then, click Add Device.
Note: If nothing appears after a few minutes, ensure both devices are on the same Wi-Fi, then reload the page. On a Mac, check that you have allowed local network access.
Step 42: Next, enter the phone name and click Save. You can enter any name that is easy to recognize, similar to how you name your desktop on your Android phone.
Step 43: Next, open the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone and check that the phone says Up to Date.
Share the Camera folder from your phone
Step 44: Next, choose the folder you want to back up. On the phone, tap the Folders tab, then tap the Add Folder button at the top right (the folder with a plus sign).
Step 45: Type the folder name. In this case, I am naming it a camera.
Step 46: Next, tap Directory to choose the folder on your phone.
Step 47: Android’s folder picker opens. If you want to back up photos from the camera, tap DCIM; this is the folder where phone cameras save photos.
Step 48: Next, tap the Camera folder.
Step 49: Finally, tap the Use this folder option
Step 50: Next, allow Syncthing to access the folder. Tap the Allow option.
Step 51: Next, under Devices, turn on the switch next to your computer’s name. This shares the folder with it.
Step 52: Next, choose the Folder Type. By default, it says Send & Receive. It means it also copies the images from your desktop to your phone. Keep it if you want to sync photos between both devices, or select Send Only in the next steps. Tap Send & Receive to open the list.
Note: Don’t skip this step. If you set up Send & Receive, deleting the backup copy on the computer also deletes the photo on your phone. So carefully choose an option.
Step 53: Open the list
Step 54: Tap Send Only
Step 55: Finally, tap Finish
Step 56: Next, tap the check mark to finish; remember that it shows as Unshared until the computer accepts it.
Accept the folder on your computer
Step 57: Now, on the computer, a yellow New Folder box appears once again. Click Add.
Step 58: Choose where to save the photos. In Folder Path, type where the backup should go. I used my Pictures folder. For instance, you can type the path: C:\Users\YourName\Pictures\Phone Backup. You can also save the photos on an external drive. You can enter the external drive path here.
Step 59: Next, click File Versioning. Make sure the photos you delete on your phone stay on the computer
Step 60:In the tab, click No File Versioning to open the list
Step 61: Here, choose the Trash Can File Versioning option. This means that when a photo is deleted on the phone, Syncthing moves the computer’s copy into a hidden .stversions folder inside your backup folder instead of deleting it.
Step 62: Next, under Clean out after option, set Keep Clean Out to 0. Zero means forever, so deleted photos are never removed from the computer.
Step 63: Next, click the Advanced tab.
Step 64:Under Folder Type, click Send & Receive to open the list
Step 65: Choose Receive Only. The computer now only receives from the phone and doesn’t transfer photos from your desktop to your phone. This is simialr to send only settings we enabled on the phone.
Step 66: Finally, click Save. Scroll down inside the window if you don’t see it, or switch back to the General tab.
Check that it works
Step 67: Next, your phone will start transferring photos to your computer. You will see an up-to-date status as a green dot next to the folder under Remote Devices. My 224 photos and videos (3.5 GB) took about two minutes over Wi-Fi. Keep both devices awake and on the same Wi-Fi until it finishes.
Step 68: You can also see the status on mobile too. On the phone, the Camera folder also says Up to Date and shows how many files it has sent.
Step 69: You can also test it by taking a photo with your camera app, then open Syncthing-Fork again. Within a few seconds, the folder shows the new photo’s name as the last file sent.
Step 70: To open the backup photos on Windows, open File Explorer and click Pictures in the left sidebar. On a Mac, open Finder and go to your Pictures folder.
Step 71: You can see a Phone Backup folder. Open it.
Step 72: You can find all backup images here.
Back up only on Wi-Fi
If you have limited data, make sure the phone backs up on Wi-Fi only, so it never uses your mobile data. Follow the steps to back up images only using the Wifi.
Step 73: In Syncthing-Fork, tap the menu button at the top left.
Step 74: Tap Settings
Step 75: Tap Run Conditions
Step 76: Keep Run on Wi-Fi on and leave Run on metered Wi-Fi off, so a large backup never runs over your phone’s hotspot
Step 77: Also, make sure Run on mobile data is off
Step 78: This is Optional: You can also enable backup only while charging, so it won’t affect your battery life; these services need to run in the background.
Automatically Back Up Your Photos Without the Cloud
This is how you can back up your photos from your phone to a Mac or Windows PC. This is especially useful if you have limited storage on your phone and don’t want to pay for cloud storage.
If you have free space on your Mac or Windows device, photos will be backed up automatically. The best part is that Syncthing also lets you back up photos to an external device connected to your computer, so all your photos are backed up without affecting your computer storage.
However, there are a few things to note. For the backup to work, make sure your phone and computer are on the same Wi-Fi, and that the Syncthing-Fork app shows a green dot at the top.
If you are using a Mac, allow local network access in System Settings (Privacy & Security > Local Network). If the backup stops after a while, the most likely reason is that Android has paused the app. To run the app again, open Settings, go to App Settings, and select the Syncthing-Fork app. In the battery settings, choose Unrestricted.
I have also noticed that sometimes the folder is out of sync on my computer. This is most likely because of the limited storage space on my Mac. To fix this, free up space and choose a folder on another drive on a Mac or Windows. If you are facing any other issues, comment below, and I will be happy to help you.

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”
He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.
This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Big Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.
For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”
Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.)
As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.
What started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”
The videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”
Meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he says. “So I got a kick out of it.”
Meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.
To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”)
Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.
Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”
Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)
What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”
Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.
So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.
Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Facebook users are sharing posts listing seven rules that U.S. President Donald Trump allegedly proposed to limit privileges for lawmakers in Congress.
These alleged rules included proposals like removing pensions for Congress members and requiring lawmakers to participate in the same government-run social services many Americans use, like Medicare for health care insurance and Social Security for retirement paychecks. Here's how the claim usually went, per these posts:
I'm in agreement with Fox News. I wonder how loud it'll get if Trump could pull this off. It will be interesting.
President Trump is asking everyone to share this, in three days, most people in the United States will have seen the message. This is an idea that should be passed around, regardless of political party.
The TRUMP Rules:
1. Tenure / No Pension. A Congressman/woman collects a salary while in office and receives no pay when they're out of office. And no more perks go with them.
2. Congress (past, present, & future) participates in Social Security. All funds in the Congressional retirement fund move to the Social Security system immediately. All future funds flow into the Social Security system, and Congress participates with the American people. It may not be used for any other purpose.
3. Congress must purchase their own retirement plan, just as ALL Americans do.
4. Congress will no longer vote themselves a pay raise. Congressional pay will rise at the ok same rate as the COLA for monthly Social Security recipients minus 1% if having a budget balance deficit.
5. Congress loses their current care system and participates in the same health care system (Medicare) as the American people.
6. Congress must equally abide by all laws they impose on the American people (i.e. NO MORE INSIDER TRADING!!!).
7. All contracts with past and present Congressmen/women are void. The American people did not make this contract with Congressmen/women. Congress made all these contracts by and for themselves.
Serving in Congress is an honor and privilege, NOT a career.
The Founding Fathers envisioned citizen legislators should serve their term(s), then go home and go back to work … not get all kinds of freebies. Term limits of 2 terms and treat them like a regular citizen!
You will need to copy and paste.
I AGREE SO IM SHARING!
Note:
This should be done immediately!!!
Thank you! Copy/Paste and shared
Meanwhile, Snopes readers asked about similar posts and searched the website for verification.
The above text is a copypasta — a copy-and-pasted internet hoax common on Facebook. As Snopes previously reported, variants of this particular copypasta have spread online since at least 2009, when a version of the rules listed above were labeled "The 28th Amendment" and attributed to business magnate Warren Buffett.
Internet users circulated it as the "Congressional Reform Act of 2017" during Trump's first term and the "Congressional Reform Act of 2025" in 2025, during his second term.
Fox News, which the copypasta cited as its source, has never reported on "The TRUMP Rules" as of this writing, per a search of the news outlet's website (archived). Trump has also not mentioned or posted about this particular copypasta online, according to two databases that track his social media output (archived, archived). The White House webpage for news releases didn't reference these supposed rules. Finally, a search for "The TRUMP Rules" on Google returned no credible and relevant results treating the list as a legitimate proposal (archived).
Thus, we have rated this claim false.
The so-called reforms listed in the act also include a mixture of rules that already exist and proposals that would actually change existing policy. Here's a breakdown of what these supposed reforms would and would not change:
Do Congress members receive pensions?
Congress members, like most federal employees, are eligible for a pension. Here are the pension eligibility requirements, according to the Congressional Research Service:
Members of Congress are eligible for a pension at the age of 62 if they have completed at least 5 years of service. Members are eligible for a pension at age 50 if they have completed 20 years of service, or at any age after completing 25 years of service. The amount of the pension depends on length of service (as measured in months) and the average of the highest three years of salary. By law, the starting amount of a Member's retirement annuity may not exceed 80% of his or her final salary.
Do Congress members pay into Social Security?
Per our previous reporting, Congress members have paid into Social Security since 1984, when they first became eligible for Social Security benefits.
Congress members first elected in 1984 or later are covered automatically under the Federal Employees' Retirement System, which other government workers use, and can decline coverage.
Aside from Social Security, lawmakers elected before 1984 can be covered under the Civil Service Retirement System; a separate pension plan, CSRS Offset, which is a mix of CSRS and Social Security; or Social Security alone. Lawmakers also pay into these plans — how much they pay and which plans they pay into differs based on when they were elected.
Can Congress members give themselves a raise?
Congress members can vote for a pay raise as dictated by the Constitution, but the raise doesn't take effect until the next election due to the 27th Amendment.
Technically, a law passed in 1989 grants Congress an automatic cost-of-living pay raise, but lawmakers have blocked those pay increases from taking effect for years. Rank-and-file members of Congress, who receive $174,000 annually as of this writing, have not increased their pay since 2009.
Do Congress members have own health care system?
Under the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly known as Obamacare, lawmakers must give up the insurance coverage previously provided to them via the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and buy health insurance through a plan or exchange created under the act. The Office of Personnel Management has also dictated that members of Congress must purchase through DC Health Link, a program offered under the ACA.
Members of Congress also pay into Medicare and are eligible for it, just like any American.
Are Congress members allowed to participate in insider trading?
Congress members are allowed to trade stocks, but legally, they're not supposed to conduct insider trading. The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 — known as the STOCK Act — prohibits members of Congress from using "any nonpublic information derived from the individual's position … or gained from performance of the individual's duties, for personal benefit."
Critics argue the STOCK Act failed to stop insider trading, however, and no member of Congress has been prosecuted for insider trading under the STOCK Act as of this writing — although policy experts have said there's been "persistent credible allegations" of insider trading since the act passed.

Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

Can you play GTA 6 from an external hard drive on PS5 or Xbox Series X/S?
Rockstar’s behemoth takes up a lot of storage space.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of the year by some distance, having racked up $3.79 billion in pre-orders and day-one sales. On PlayStation 5 alone, more than 39 million unique players took control of dual protagonists Jason and Lucia on opening weekend, making it the biggest game debut in the 32-year history of PlayStation.
There will be many other folks who want to play the game and haven't had a chance to jump in yet. One thing they should note is that, with a hefty install size, GTA 6 will take up a significant chunk of their PS5 or Xbox Series X/S storage space.
You might be wondering whether you can install GTA 6 on an external hard drive to avoid having to delete other games and data from your console. You can move GTA 6 to your external storage when you're not playing it. However, to run the game locally, you'll need to have it installed on your system's built-in storage, an SDD you've installed in your PS5 or a compatible NVMe expansion card that's plugged into your Xbox.
As with many other recent games, GTA 6 needs to take advantage of the fast-loading capabilities of the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. The consoles are unable to load data for these titles quickly enough from an external hard drive over a USB connection. For the same reason, disc-based PS5 and Xbox Series X games are installed onto system storage before you can play them. The PS5 can run PS4 games from external storage, though. Likewise, an Xbox Series X/S can run older Xbox One and Xbox 360 titles directly from an external hard drive.
That said, there is a way to play GTA 6 without first having to free up a whole lot of console storage space. It's possible to stream the game from the cloud on Xbox Series X/S. There are two things to note if you'd like to go with that option, including that Xbox just brought in new cloud gaming time limits. Game Pass subscribers get up to 15 hours of cloud gaming included each month. You can pay extra for more access. Also, GTA 6 is limited to Xbox Series S graphics settings on Xbox Cloud Gaming.
On the PlayStation side, cloud streaming works on PS5 and PlayStation Portal if you're a PlayStation Plus Premium subscriber. There are no cloud gaming time limits on PS Plus. You'll also need to purchase GTA 6 for PS5 or Xbox Series X/S to stream the game from the cloud, as it's not included in the PS Plus or Game Pass libraries — and it probably won't be for quite some time.

EXCLUSIVE: Netflix will not be returning to the murky underworld of Amsterdam Empire.
Deadline understands that a second season of the Dutch series starring Famke Janssen is not currently planned due to scheduling issues.
Amsterdam Empire launched two years ago and is one of the streamer’s most high-profile shows to come out of the Benelux region.
X-Men and GoldenEye star Janssen, who also exec produced, played Betty Jonkers, the former pop star wife of a coffee-shop mogul who has spent his life fighting against criminals, competitors and Dutch laws to become the biggest of them all. When his affair with a well-known journalist comes to light, it turns out his most dangerous enemy has been living under his roof all this time.
The show clocked up just over 10 million views in its first nine months according to Netflix’s What We Watched reports. After premiering in October 2025, it spent two weeks in Netflix’s non-English language top 10 and five weeks at number one in The Netherlands.

India rejects US excess capacity claims, says no structural overcapacity in any sector
“The Notice is currently under examination,” the ministry said, adding that India had engaged constructively throughout the investigation.
The government of India on Wednesday said it was examining a notice issued by the United States Trade Representative (USTR) in a probe into manufacturing capacity across 14 economies, including India, and reiterated that the country does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.
In a statement issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the government said it had taken note of the notice of determination and request for comments issued by the USTR under Section 301 of the US Trade Act.
“The Notice is currently under examination,” the ministry said, adding that India had engaged constructively throughout the investigation.
Deep Dive
The Department of Commerce had stated, in its response to the notice of initiation and subsequent proceedings, that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector, the statement said.
India also reiterated that trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of the ongoing negotiations for the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA).
“The Government of India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement,” the ministry said, referring to the framework announced on February 2 and the joint statement issued on February 7.
US report targets India's manufacturing policies
The USTR's 189-page report, released on Wednesday, has built its case around India's flagship manufacturing programmes, including Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.
The report describes India's manufacturing policies as an effort to expand production beyond what market demand would support. It concludes that India's “acts, policies, and practices” concerning manufacturing capacity are unreasonable and burden US commerce.
The USTR estimates that raising manufacturing's share of India's GDP to 25%, as envisaged under Make in India, would require about $500 billion in additional output at 2025 levels.
India has rejected the allegations throughout the eight-month investigation, arguing that it is building manufacturing capacity to meet domestic demand and reduce dependence on certain countries for critical inputs.
In its submissions, India said production rises and falls according to orders and market conditions, rather than being directed by the government. It also argued that Make in India and PLI should not be viewed as schemes to create manufacturing capacity unrelated to demand.
India participated in confidential consultations with the USTR during the investigation. Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal had also rejected the charge at the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee in October, saying India “does not have structural excess capacity” in the sectors identified.
Tariff proposal and trade deal talks
The USTR has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods under the Section 301 investigation. The rate could fall to 17% if India signs a trade agreement with Washington.
The report focuses on sectors such as steel, solar, health and information and communications technology (ICT), and also flags India's labour laws, market access barriers and growing imports of inputs from China.
The proposed tariffs exempt generic medicines in dosage form, hundreds of drug ingredients when used in pharmaceuticals, and patented drugs.
Written comments on the proposed tariffs are due by January 5, 2027, while hearings are scheduled to begin on January 25.
India and the US have been negotiating a bilateral trade agreement since February 2025. The two countries announced a framework for an interim deal in February, with Washington outlining an 18% reciprocal tariff on a range of Indian goods.

Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.
"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.
Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.
The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.
But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.
Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.
"They are a keystone species for maintaining the páramos and play a key role in water production," he says. "But most frailejons are in trouble,"
When explorers first spotted the shrubs mysteriously protruding from the mountain fog centuries ago, they reminded them of hooded monks. Hence the name frailejon, which is Spanish for "big friar."
The long, thin leaves of some species bend toward the sky and resemble palm fronds. Many are stout in the middle because, rather than falling to the ground, their dying leaves slump down to form a brownish outer shell to their trunks.
The Muisca Indians, who once populated the area, considered frailejons to be sacred guardians of the water. When he first came across the plants as a teenager in Colombia, Diazgranados says: "I became completely captivated."
By contrast, Moreno, 53, who runs the frailejon greenhouse, used to be one of the plant's predators. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the central Colombian town of Monguí, Moreno and neighboring farmers knew little about them and chopped them down to make way for potato fields and cow pastures.
"We viewed them as a nuisance," Moreno says.
Later, while employed by a coal mine, he was injured during a cave-in and vowed to work above ground in the fresh mountain air.
On his own he began studying páramo ecosystem that he'd grown up in, started his greenhouse and began leading tourists and volunteers on expeditions to replace the frailejons that had been wiped out.
"I felt inspired to do something to protect the páramos," he says.
Elsewhere, Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have gotten involved in reforestation campaigns after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejons.
Yet many average Colombians have learned about the plant's importance through an enormously popular cartoon character called Ernesto Pérez. Shaped like a frailejon, he exhorts people to conserve the flora and fauna of the Andes, similar to the way Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the U.S.
In fact, several of the volunteers Moreno is guiding up the mountain say the cartoon and its earworm theme song introduced them to the frailejon.
"The song is very contagious," says Nicolás Coronado, 25, who works for a Bogotá-based plastics company, and is carrying a 6-inch frailejon that he will plant in the páramo.
The hike takes the group up to an altitude of 11,000 feet, past streams, waterfalls and lagoons. Underfoot, the ground is damp and spongy. The area is a state park and frailejons dot the landscape. But there are also barbed-wire fences erected by farmers and a half dozen cows grazing on the mountainside.
Moreno and his assistants show the volunteers how to dig shallow holes, then add a bit of shredded tobacco as fertilizer, before nestling the tiny frailejons into the soil.
Their survival is no sure thing. Many die in the cold, harsh climate and those that take hold grow just a few inches per year.
To help them along, the volunteers hold an impromptu ceremony, with one member reciting a prayer to connect with the mountain spirits and another blowing on a conch shell.
By now, some volunteers have grown attached to the frailejons that they've carried up the mountain and have bestowed names on them. Among them is biologist Julieta Barba has baptized hers "Gerry," in honor of her mother.
After patting some dirt around the plant's roots, she says: "I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo."

Quick Answer
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia is about more than personal misconduct. It raises serious questions about conflicts of interest, abuse of power, and Silicon Valley’s habit of excusing tech leaders. His departure sends a vital message: no amount of genius, wealth, or market success should place anyone above accountability.
So Jensen Huang will not be returning to Nvidia, in spite of a groundswell of support. And though it might shock some tech bros, I think it is the best thing that could have happened to tech.
The tech world witnessed one of its most dramatic unravelings this month, perhaps the most significant one in years, if not decades. All was going smoothly; AI was still the sun the tech world was revolving around, and one of the biggest planets revolving around it was Nvidia. The company was not just in on living, breathing, and thriving on AI development but at the center of bettering AI for others, as it manufactured AI chips.
When current affairs become… well, current affairs
It all came crashing down when a report was published in The New York Times, revealing news of an affair. This was not the run-of-the-mill gossip that’s seen in the scandal section in tabloids, but news that changed the trajectory of Nvidia and possibly AI.
Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (unrelated, although having the same surname), a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company. Alice was suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence. Megaspeed was one of the major buyers of Nvidia’s AI chips, and, as per reports, it diverted chips worth USD 2 billion to China against regulations, although both Megaspeed and Nvidia deny any wrongdoing.
Following the news, A LOT went down. Huang seemed to swing into damage control and issued an apology for the affair, promising cooperation with an investigation into it. The tech world thought the worst was over. After all, what could make this worse? Then the New York Times, on 11 November, released a report citing another extramarital affair. This time it was reported that he was in a relationship with Nvidia’s Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang. After trying to save face and his 41-year-long marriage (Jensen Huang is married to Lori Huang), Huang had to resign and leave his post as CEO at Nvidia on 12 November.
But this is not the story of a person’s personal slip-ups, or the extra-marital affair story that much of the media is making it to be. It is actually much bigger than that.
It’s not about infidelity, but about power and misconduct
While Huang has received a fair deal of criticism for his conduct, he has received a lot of support too, especially from Silicon Valley, where it seems that when there is a tech billionaire in question, the rules that apply to the rest of the world cease to apply to them. If you build an important enough product, accumulate billions of Dollars, and build some political connections, what would otherwise be a big no-no suddenly becomes negotiable, and the boundaries around right and wrong start to get hazy.
Affairs and flings are nothing new to the world of tech in particular, or the world of celebrities in general, but this case is more than just a personal lapse of judgment. Had Huang’s affair(s) been something that had happened outside of the workplace or if he had fallen for someone who had nothing to do with tech (an actress, an influencer, a trapeze artiste, et al.), this would have been an entirely different conversation. But his intimate relations with his employee and a customer – and the fact that we are being asked to overlook them – shine a light on what might be wrong with the inherent culture at not just Nvidia but in Silicon Valley.
While most concerns have revolved around Alice Huang being a Chinese spy and sensitive AI technology crossing borders, allegations which have not yet been proved, what is clear beyond doubt is that Huang misused his position as the CEO of one of the biggest companies in the world, on both the client and employee side.
In both of his affairs, Huang was the person of power, with Alice Huang and Kimberly Powell. The client in question bought billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips from Nvidia, and given her intimate relationship revelation with Huang, it would be difficult to rule out that the business deals made between the two were in no way influenced by the relationship. We are not even getting to the part of Alice Huang being a Chinese spy, and whether she managed to get sensitive information and AI chips from Jensen Huang for China, which would give China the AI leverage it needs to get ahead of the US in the AI race. Even if she was “just another client,” does it not still remain a bother that a person who has been hailed as a tech demi-god could not control his urges long enough to get through business? Similarly, his second affair with a senior employee working at Nvidia who directly reported to him, and, as per reports, was promptly promoted during her time at Nvidia, does bring up some very serious questions about preferential treatment, conflict of interest, and company power dynamics.
This is not about Huang’s infidelity, but his ability to make sound decisions. A lot of the evidence suggests that in a situation where he could misuse his position of power, he did. It was not just his moral compass that was compromised, but his professional one too. The fact that this happened, and that the former Nvidia CEO has still received a lot of support, not only raises concerns about the culture at Nvidia, but also about the overall priorities of Silicon Valley.
When the stock market decides where to draw the line
Since Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a number of executives, tech CEOs, and even the US President himself have come out in support of him. Media channels have had extensive discussions on the matter, and many have marked the (so far) two affairs as a “personal lapse of judgment” and think Huang’s potential as a tech genius outweighs his failings. Elon Musk has compared his exit as “it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak”, while other leaders like Sam Altman, Steven Chen, Tim Sweeney and many more have pushed for his comeback. President Donald Trump has said he would “not mind” seeing Huang reinstated as CEO, and Musk has even offered to hire him.
Now, there is no doubt that Jensen Huang is a genius who has built one of the most important businesses in the world of tech. Many fear that without him, Nvidia would tank, and this would have a devastating impact on AI. However, since the reports of his affairs have come out and his resignation, Nvidia’s stock has taken a nosedive, and so have many other AI stocks. In fact, many are predicting that Huang’s exit might burst the AI bubble, which, for obvious reasons, is way worse for the tech world in general than any lapse in professional and moral code of conduct. Accountability seems to count for little as long as the stock market is doing well.
Time to take the Tech God pedestal away?
Given this groundswell of support, the easy decision for Nvidia would perhaps have been to let Jensen Huang walk back in as if nothing happened and sit back and see the share prices spike. It actually seemed likely, and Huang himself had posted on X (where he was given a free blue tick by Elon Musk), offering to make a comeback if the board considered it would be in the best interest of the company. However, on 18 November, Nvidia ruled out the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. And while this led to groans of disappointment from many of the tech bros, we actually think it was the right call to take.
