While a company has responsibilities towards its shareholders, it also has to keep its employees and clients in mind. Share prices cannot be used as an automatic defense against misconduct, especially at the highest level. Unfortunately, over the past few decades, tech brilliance has been placed on a pedestal, giving a handful of people immunity from general human misconduct. Bouts of bad temper, abusive behavior, and so much more are often turned a blind eye to because a person is perceived as a “Tech God,” a person who is part of the genius crowd that is building a better, brighter future for us all. But recent times have revealed that many of these tech gods whom we have trusted, and largely exempted from strict governance or interference, cannot even follow simple, basic rules that govern mere mortals. And these handful of people, who cannot even follow the basics, are sitting in boardrooms and are now deciding the future of billions of people, even those who have not opted for an AI-laden future or are not even aware of what AI is.
Jensen Huang’s conduct – and the support he has received – now raises the question of whether the people we were told are tech geniuses are as reliable and trustworthy as the narrative around them has painted them out to be. Or are they just a bunch of power-hungry, wealth-accumulating techies who have way too much autonomy for comfort?
The Huang affair (pun intended) marks an important phase in modern tech. While we still do not know how it will all end – there are endless conspiracy theories doing the rounds – we do hope it will teach many in the tech world not to turn a blind eye to “personal and professional misconduct,” just because a person is seen as a genius and is perceived to be good for the world in general and the stock market in particular.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

“Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: The Immersive Adventure,” the upcoming theatrical adaptation of the hit Johnny Depp movie, is getting ready to set sail.
The production, which is due to open in London early next year, has now shared behind-the-scenes rehearsal footage as the cast practice their sword fighting and rig-climbing skills.
Directed by Olivier-winner Matt Costain, the show sees George Maguire step into the iconic boots of Captain Jack Sparrow opposite Phil Daniels (“Quadrophenia”) as Captain Barbossa, Lily Blunsom as Elizabeth Swann, Harrison Wilde as Will Turner and Gleanne Purcell-Brown as Anamaria.
Alex Payne is fight director.
The rehearsal footage shows the cast and crew brandishing their swords and soaring through the air in what is set to be Secret Cinema’s most ambitious show ever.
The production is set to launch on March 10, with previews from Feb.16, at Secret Cinema’s new flagship venue in Greenwich Peninsula, just a stone’s throw from where the films were shot. It is currently due to run through June 6.
The sets also promise to be epic with two-time Emmy winner Jason Sherwood — known for live broadcasts of the Oscars — as production designer and Kait Kerrigan, who wrote the book for Broadway’s “The Great Gatsby,” as theatrical adaptor.
Music supervisor is Olivier-winner Alan Williams, costume designer is Susan Kulkarni and hair and make-up is by Helen Keane.
Secret Cinema, which is owned by TodayTix, is known for bringing films to life with 360-degree immersive elements to make audiences feel as though they have stepped through the screen. “Pirates” will break somewhat with tradition by weaving specially curated clips from “The Curse of the Black Pearl” – the first film in the Disney franchise – throughout the theatrical storytelling experience rather than screening it in full.
“We’ve taken everything Secret Cinema does best and pushed it further than ever before, creating a new kind of theatrical experience where the story doesn’t just happen in front of you – it happens all around you,” said Merritt Baer, Secret Cinema’s artistic director and producer and president and co-founder of TodayTix Group. “This is exactly the kind of show we’ve been building towards and opening it in our new home at Greenwich Peninsula makes it even more exciting.”

Government, parliament and judiciary must have mutual respect and not overreach: Shanmugam
Senior Minister K Shanmugam said the government must respect court decisions even when they differ from its policy objectives, and seek legislative changes through parliament where necessary.
SINGAPORE: The government, parliament and judiciary must mutually respect each other and maintain clear boundaries, refraining from overreach, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Thursday (Nov 26).
He added that the government bears primary responsibility for making these boundaries clear in the Constitution and legislation.
"Mutual respect has to start from the government. It requires the government to understand what the rule of law means, and to accept and respect it," said Mr Shanmugam in his hour-long speech.
This does not mean that the executive and the judiciary will always agree, he added.
Mr Shanmugam, who is also Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs, was giving the closing address at the Global Rule of Law Conference a day after Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon’s keynote speech at the same event also brought up the need for each branch of government to "stay within its lane" while engaging in dialogue with one another.
Held at the Shangri-La Singapore hotel, the audience included chief justices, judges, lawyers and scholars from over 20 jurisdictions as part of the Singapore judiciary's bicentennial celebrations, marking 200 years of the rule of law in the island nation.
MUTUAL RESPECT
Stating that he had not discussed with the Chief Justice what to say at the conference, Mr Shanmugam said he realised later that their speeches on the rule of law had some overlaps and ran along similar philosophical lines.
The senior minister said each institution - the government, parliament and the judiciary - has to understand the limit of what it should do and not overreach, because "overreach often invites a reaction, and that is not good".
Referring to how founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew used to give tutorials about contract law to his Cabinet ministers, Mr Shanmugam said this was because he understood the fundamental principle that a small country with no natural resources would be trusted only if its word was good.
“Respect for the law was deeply ingrained in our founding in our leadership. It is an approach that successive governments have sought to maintain and … is deeply understood by all the four prime ministers of Singapore,” said the senior minister.
There is also “considerable continuity in the leadership of our legal institutions”, he said, adding that there have only been four law ministers – including incumbent law minister Edwin Tong – and four chief justices since Singapore’s independence.
When it came to matters which the executive and the judiciary do not always agree on, Mr Shanmugam said there will be occasions “where the courts interpret the law in a way that is different from the government's policy objectives".
"When that happens, the government must respect the court's decision. But if it considers that the law needs to be changed, it must go back to parliament, explain its position, and seek legislative change."
He added that such situations can be quite rare.
Recently, the government proposed legal changes for reformative training or jail to be the default sentencing options for young offenders convicted of scam-related offences.
This followed a September High Court ruling in which a panel of judges including Chief Justice said reformative training or imprisonment should not be the default sentence in such a situation.
The government later disagreed with the court. Mr Shanmugam told parliament at the time: "This is not the time to go soft."
While the senior minister did not bring up this example In his closing address on Thursday, he said mutual respect is also much easier to maintain when each institution has clarity on where its powers begin and where they end.
"Where the boundaries are unclear, the courts may find themselves having to decide questions with far-reaching policy consequences," said Mr Shanmugam.
He then cited foreign cases where the courts have directed governments on matters of policy, such as what type of fuel should be used in public buses or what numerical limits should be imposed on prison populations.
“Perhaps these situations arose because the relevant constitution or legislation gave the courts a broad role in protecting rights without clearly defining the limits of judicial intervention in matters of policy,” said Mr Shanmugam.
In another case in the United Kingdom, he noted how a tribunal had ruled in favour of a Nigerian man who appealed against his deportation after he was jailed for false imprisonment of the woman.
The man later violently raped another woman less than three years later.
“Cases like this illustrate the difficult consequences that can arise when questions of immigration and public safety are determined through the court process,” said Mr Shanmugam.
While the court was not wrong to apply the law as they understood it, he noted that such decisions can have consequences well beyond the parties before the court, affecting public safety and those who have no voice in the proceedings.
The point is that among other things, such a situation could lead to public dissatisfaction and a “general loss of trust in institutions”, including the judiciary, he said.
SECTION 377A EXAMPLE
Turning to Singapore, Mr Shanmugam cited how the 2023 repeal of Section 377A of the Penal Code, which criminalised sex between men, was handled in Singapore.
He said that in the lead-up to the repeal, the government sought to maintain a balance between the desire of the majority for Singapore to be a socially conservative society with heterosexual families, and making sure that there was space for the LGBT community to live their lives and contribute to society.
The government then came up with what Mr Shanmugam called "a somewhat messy compromise" of neither repealing Section 377A nor enforcing it, because of the concern that the issue, if forced, would divide and polarise society.
When a case came up before the Court of Appeal in 2022 challenging the constitutionality of Section 377A, the court began its judgment by setting out the limits of its own role, said Mr Shanmugam.
The court said differences of this kind were better mediated through politics and not litigation, and that parliament was best placed to devise a pluralistic vision that accommodated divergent interests.
The petition was dismissed without the court having to decide whether Section 377A was in fact unconstitutional.
Mr Shanmugam said it was interesting that both he and Chief Justice Menon had used this same example in their speeches.
"An academic writing about this case might well conclude that the court found an elegant way to avoid deciding the substantive question and leave it to the political process," he said.
While most governments would have preferred that the courts dealt with such cases, Mr Shanmugam said Singapore's government decided to "act to find a way forward".
Section 377A was later repealed by parliament.
Mr Shanmugam said Singapore's society as a whole could have been worse off if the Court of Appeal had struck out Section 377A, and the consensus and trust built on compromise could not have been achieved.
EXCEPTIONS TO THE RULE OF LAW
The senior minister pointed out that Singapore has exceptions to the rule of law, which are necessary as they “paradoxically” strengthen and support a stable society with the rule of law.
"The legitimacy of this legislation ultimately rests on public confidence that the powers will be exercised responsibly and not arbitrarily," he said.
The Internal Security Act (ISA), for example, allows the Minister for Home Affairs to order preventive detention on the grounds of national security or public order.
The exercise of preventive detention powers under the ISA has been challenged in Singapore's courts, but it was made clear that the courts cannot go into the assessment of the government's considerations.
Over time, the government added extrajudicial safeguards. For example, if a detainee appeals against his detention, the appeal goes to an independent advisory board chaired by a Supreme Court judge, who is appointed by the president.
The minister can disagree with the advisory board, but the president has the final say and can overrule the minister.
JUDICIARY MUST BE PROTECTED
Mr Shanmugam also spoke at length about the importance of protecting the prestige and standing of the judiciary from public attacks.
Judges, unlike politicians, cannot go out and publicly defend themselves against attacks on their integrity, he said.
The government has a primary responsibility to protect the judiciary from such attacks, whether or not they agree with the judgment.
Even when there is strong public unhappiness, the government is to defend the independence and integrity of the judiciary, said Mr Shanmugam.
If the government feels strongly about the issue, it should change the law and not criticise or attack the courts in parliament or in public, even if it is "politically opportune" for the government to do so.
“Criticising the judiciary might get the government some short-term points, but the long-term damage is to the judiciary and the country as a whole,” he said.
He used the example of the 2018 Court of Appeal decision in the City Harvest Church criminal breach of trust case.
The decision, which meant the directors would not face a higher sentence, caused much public angst and unhappiness, perhaps even outrage, said Mr Shanmugam.
"Many felt that the church leaders should have faced heavier penalties," he said. "You know, the man in the street has a certain common wisdom."
Online comments alleged, among other things, that the judges had let them off lightly because they were rich. Mr Shanmugam said he decided to make a ministerial statement in parliament to make it clear that such comments were "quite unacceptable".
He also said that judges should not be personally attacked or have their integrity impugned just because people do not agree with their decision.
The government also made it clear that those who continued to make such comments would be prosecuted.
Mr Shanmugam said the government chose not to defend Mr Edwin Tong, then counsel for the appellants and now Law Minister, in parliament.
This was because he was entitled to defend himself as a politician, he said.
He said judgments can be criticised, but baseless attacks on the integrity and impartiality of judges should not and cannot be allowed.
On protecting the prestige and standing of the judiciary, Mr Shanmugam said the rule of law does not exist in a vacuum, but that it is implemented by people.
Therefore, good lawyers are needed in the judiciary, in the Attorney-General's Chambers and across different branches of government, including law enforcement agencies and the Ministry of Law.
Remuneration is an important part of this, he said, adding that for the very best people, any move to the public service will involve financial sacrifice.
"In general, to run a system properly with good people, you need to ensure a fair remuneration. These are deliberate policy choices that the government has made and defended publicly," he said.
"If we want a strong legal system, we must be prepared to invest in the people who operate it."
INTERNATIONAL RULE OF LAW
Mr Shanmugam also made reference to what the United States' Secretary of State said recently about the rule of law in the international law context.

Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
- Published
It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.
He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.
In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.
During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.
Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.
One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.
"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.
Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.
One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.
Dark infatuation
Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.
After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.
But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.
On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.
Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.
In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a sourced motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".
By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."
Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.
Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.
He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.
Covering tracks
After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".
One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".
Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".
Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.
"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.
The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.
Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.
On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.
There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.
His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."
Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.
It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.
Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.
Lamarre faces life in prison
By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.
"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."
"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."
He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.
Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.
The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.
Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
- Published
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.
When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.
The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".
It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".
It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.
It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.
The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.
The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.
Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.
Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".
According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.
She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.
Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.
In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".
In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.
She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.
However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.
The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."
The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.
Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.
The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing, and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”
State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.
“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?
Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.
Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.
“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”
This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.
But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.
In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.
“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.
“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.
But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.
“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.
To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.
One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.
One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.
“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.
Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved the first drug to treat limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers.
The drug, developed by BridgeBio under the name ribitol and marketed as Welgemda, is specifically approved for patients with LGMD 2i/R9, a subtype the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and another 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
BridgeBio said Monday it will charge insurers $75,446.58 for a 28-day supply of medicine — meaning the price will be just a hair under $1 million per year.

Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.
If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.
Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.
Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.
How to change your TV's refresh rate to 24fps to achieve a film look
There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.
In your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.
It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

Seeing a rise in caesarean deliveries in India -- from 8.5% in 2005 to 21.5% in 2021 -- which is well above WHO-recommended levels, researchers are calling for policy measures, including more regulation in private healthcare, in an analysis published in The Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia journal.
Study highlights
Delivering a baby via a caesarean section (C-section) involves making a surgical cut in the mother's abdomen and uterus.
The researchers, including those from the Institute of Public Health Bengaluru and Christian Medical College in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, said that while a medically indicated C-section is vital to preventing maternal and newborn mortality, rates of caesarean deliveries exceeding 10 per cent in the population are not linked with reduced mortality -- as noted by the World Health Organization.
An unjustified caesarean delivery is related to longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs, with babies born through the procedure known to be at an increased risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes and allergies, among other health problems. The team reviewed 75 previously published studies -- mostly from India, followed by Bangladesh and Pakistan -- and examined factors in the countries' health systems contributing to caesarean procedures in the population.
Financial concerns
The authors said that an avoidable caesarean delivery can be financially stressful for families across South Asia, where a substantial fraction of deliveries occur in the private sector.
For example, out-of-pocket expenditures for a C-section in India will cost around Rs 43,000 in private hospitals, and around Rs 8,500 in public ones, suggesting that avoidable caesarean deliveries unnecessarily burden the healthcare system and families, they said.
Limited regulation and insurance coverage were among other factors associated with increased C-section rates. Decision-making at the healthcare provider's level was influenced by financial incentives, medico-legal concerns and scheduling convenience, the researchers said.
Driving factors
Mother's education, socioeconomic status and age, and family preferences were found to be individual and community-level factors driving an upward trend in caesarean deliveries.
Caesarean deliveries in Bangladesh are estimated to have increased from 18 per cent in 2011 to 45 per cent in 2022, while those in Pakistan rose to 20 per cent in 2018 from about three per cent in 1990. Data from national surveys were analysed for arriving at the figures.
The authors said that caesarean deliveries are being resorted to at nearly double the rates since 2000, with one in every five births involving the surgical procedure.
Coordinated policies needed
C-section rates in Asia rose from 4.4 per cent in 1990 to 19.5 per cent in 2014, with south Asia reflecting similar upward trends seen across the continent, they said.
"The review highlights the need for coordinated policy responses across levels, including payment reforms, regulatory oversight, and improved antenatal counselling, to ensure (C-section) use aligns with clinical need rather than socio-economic or institutional pressures," the authors wrote.

Sonia Gandhi, in her recently published memoir, recalls being advised surgery for suspected breast cancer in 2010. Since she is a prominent public figure, she wonders, in her book, whether she was entitled to even a modicum of privacy with regard to her health. Her account assumes renewed significance following a recent petition before the Madras High Court that inquired about the health of Kolathur MLA V.S. Babu (now deceased). These episodes expose a fundamental legal tension between the privacy politicians may want about their health, and the accountability they owe their constituents in a democracy. Does the public’s right to information justify waiving or limiting an office-holder’s medical confidentiality? How should a democracy reconcile these competing interests?
Medical information is among the most sensitive forms of personal information. A diagnosis may reveal not merely someone’s present condition but also their reproductive history, genetic predispositions, psychiatric illness or future health risks. Disclosure can invite discrimination, political exploitation and public speculation. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. Holding public office does not automatically extinguish this protection. A politician receiving treatment need not publish laboratory reports. Nor does a disability establish an inability to govern. State intrusion needs lawful justification, not curiosity.
The Constitution does not prescribe a general medical-fitness requirement for occupying high public office. Article 58 sets eligibility conditions for the President but requires no medical-fitness certificate. Article 65(2) allows the Vice-President to perform presidential functions when the President cannot do so through absence, illness or another cause. The Constitution recognises presidential illness but does not specify a detailed procedure or medical authority to determine contested incapacity. This distinction between eligibility to assume office and capacity to continue functioning deserves closer scrutiny.
For legislators, Articles 102 and 191 prescribe disqualification when a person is of ‘unsound mind’ and stands so declared by a competent court (not by a medical board). Section 16(1)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, similarly provides for disqualification from electoral registration (by court not medical board). For Supreme Court judges, Article 124(4) permits removal on proof of incapacity, while the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, provides a procedure that may involve a Medical Board. Article 317(3)(c), governing Public Service Commission members, permits removal for unfitness arising from ‘infirmity of mind or body’.

NorthEast United hit back close to the half-hour mark as Moyano displayed exquisite ball control, trapping dead a deft lobbed pass from Nikhil Barla. Escaping the Delhi backline, the Spaniard cut back inside to fire a low shot past Nora Fernandes at the near post.
With the scores level at half-time, there was drama in the 55th minute as Lalrinliana Hnamte’s goal was ruled out.
Rodriguinho’s mazy run ended with him hitting the deck after being blocked by Eneko Satrustegui, but Hnamte was alert to the loose ball and slotted home. However, the decision went against Delhi as Hnamte was deemed to be offside.
In the 77th minute, Alaaeddine Ajaraie thought he had scored a screamer from distance to put NorthEast in front, only for the officials to rule it out for a foul in the build-up involving Macarton Louis Nickson.
The home crowd was in full voice towards the end as NorthEast piled on the pressure, with Ajaraie involved in creating more chances, but SC Delhi managed to hold fort at the back. (Bloomberg) -- Record flooding from king tides is inundating the California coast Wednesday, compounded by a Pacific storm that’s contributing to flight delays in San Francisco.
Tuesday’s high tide of 8.23 feet (2.51 meters) was the largest ever recorded in the city during the month of November. Wednesday’s high tide may surpass it, said Sebastian Westerink, a US National Weather Service meteorologist in Monterey.
“Today and tomorrow around noon are going to be the worst,” Westerink said. “Then it is going to start lowering from there.”
About 145 flights through San Francisco International Airport were delayed Wednesday, according to FlightAware, a tracking site.
Flood warnings remain across San Francisco, much of the Bay Area and the Pacific coastline. Gauges on Wednesday in Santa Barbara and San Diego recorded their highest tides ever, the weather service said, breaking records set about a month ago.
Rough seas and dangerous swells have been spotted along California’s shores. Authorities in Marin County north of San Francisco issued a “shelter-in-place” order to residents in the Calles area of Stinson Beach as waves push past the beach. There’s also an evacuation warning in Stinson Beach — a community of 541 people — as large waves are expected through 2 p.m. local time.
Evacuation warnings are in effect more than 300 miles (483 km) south in Ventura County. The alerts encompass waterfront neighborhoods recently fortified with protective berms.
California’s king tides, the highest predicted tides of the year, recur when the sun, moon and Earth align and the moon is closest to Earth. This year, they’re arriving after El Niño helped raise sea levels and powerful waves battered the state’s coastline, damaging roads and destroying homes.
Travel has become dangerous at times: King tides have forced road closures and shut down portions of the Pacific Coast Highway in Orange County, south of Los Angeles.

- The claim that the Pentagon cannot account for $2 trillion in taxpayer money is based in truth but missing some context.
- It is more accurate to say that the Pentagon cannot comprehensively account for about $2.14 trillion worth of assets, based on a November news release from the Department of Defense about its annual department-wide audit. As of this writing, DOD remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit.
- We have left this claim unrated for several reasons, including the fact that the department is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing.
- Congress passed an act in 2023 mandating that by 2028 the Pentagon must obtain a clean audit, a term used to describe when auditors find no issues with an organization's financial records. The Pentagon celebrated the progress made toward that goal in 2026, despite significant issues remaining.
- Federal auditors also told Snopes that even the departments and services without clean audits could still accurately account for most of their assets.
Social media users claimed in mid-November that the U.S. Department of Defense is unable to account for $2 trillion in taxpayer funds.
"The military is unable to account for $2 trillion in tax payer money, but somehow forgiving student loans would be 'unfair to the American tax payer,'" one post on Facebook read. Users shared similar posts on X and other platforms.
This rumor began after the Department of Defense released its annual agencywide audit Nov. 16. The Pentagon said in a news release that more than 56% of the department's assets received a "clean audit," meaning auditors from the department's Office of the Inspector General and from independent public accounting firms found no issues with the agency's financial records for that percentage of its assets:
For the first time in Department history, clean audit opinions will cover more than 56 percent of DoW [Department of War, the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense] assets and over 90 percent of its liabilities. These figures include audit opinions expected in January and February of FY 2027.
The Pentagon has $4.87 trillion in assets, according to its fiscal year 2026 financial report (Page 19). In other words, about 44% — or about $2.14 trillion — of its assets, or resources owned and controlled by the Defense Department, are not comprehensively and cleanly accounted for.
We have left this claim unrated as the Department of Defense is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing, as DOD notes. Those audits combined is what determines the Pentagon's departmentwide audit opinion.
The lack of a clean opinion also does not necessarily mean that the Pentagon has no idea where its assets are — just that it can't keep a detailed, transparent record of how it moves money around. Furthermore, reader opinions may differ on whether $2 trillion in assets are the same as $2 trillion in taxpayer money, given that the amount those assets cost at the time of purchase may be different from their current value.
In an email following the publication of this story, the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General said DOD services and agencies without clean opinions can still "accurately account for most of their assets."
"For example, the military services can accurately account for military equipment and munitions but have challenges accounting for some general equipment and inventory for the Joint Strike Fighter and other programs," the email said. "There is no direct reference to $2 trillion being unaccounted for in the DoW OIG financial statement audit reports."
DOD did not immediately respond a request to explain the exact details behind its 56% calculation.
A related rumor circulating online claimed the Pentagon can't account for $31 billion worth of F-35 aircraft parts. That's a reference to a real Government Accountability Office report — separate from the audit — that found DOD's "records of its F-35 parts are outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete." The OIG's audit echoed that conclusion, finding that DOD "has not yet established an accurate, complete, or financially reportable population of F-35 property, nor implemented an IT environment capable of supporting reliable reporting."
DOD celebrates audit progress, despite major issues
Overall, DOD received a "disclaimer of opinion" rating, which means the condition of the agency's accounting is so poor, it is impossible to assess its financial records.
However, it is worth noting that the percentage of assets accounted for in 2026 is technically progress for the Pentagon, which remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit. The Pentagon has received a disclaimer of opinion rating on every departmentwide federal audit since they began in 2018.
"This is a really big deal for us," said Jules W. Hurst III, the department's undersecretary and chief financial officer, in DOD's news release. "For the first time, by February 2027, we will have clean opinions on a majority of our assets and over 90% of our liabilities."
A clean opinion, or clean audit, means auditors have found no issues with an organization's financial records. At least one fund that the Pentagon oversees, the Medicare Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund, received the first clean opinion in its history this year.
The department's Office of the Inspector General said in the introductory memo to its report that while the Pentagon's disclaimer of opinion rating remained the same, the Department of Defense has taken "deliberate steps" to meet a congressional requirement to receive a departmentwide clean audit by 2028. For example, DOD has increased spending on auditing and overhauled its strategy toward a clean audit.
The Government Accountability Office, which has had the Department of Defense's financial management on its "high risk" list for fraud and management since 1995, said in May that DOD's "renewed focus" on a clean audit was "encouraging." However, the office said the new strategy's efforts to consolidate standalone audits of agencies under DOD oversight "potentially risks limiting accountability and transparency."
In fact, the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General said that while the audit results seemed to suggest fewer material weaknesses — in other words, severe issues that result in a high risk of inaccurate financial reporting — that reduction comes from consolidation, not from actual resolution of the problems.
For more on the DOD's history of spotty financial records, see our in-depth look examining what the Pentagon's audit ratings actually mean.

The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this “smoke taint” adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.
That’s why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.
As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of “dry hopping” (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.
All beer contains hops, a key flavoring agent that also imparts useful antimicrobial properties. (Beer spoils quickly without them.) Brewers mash and steep grain in hot water, which converts all that starch into sugars. This is traditionally the stage where hops are added to the liquid extract (wort) and boiled to give the beer that hint of bitterness. During the boiling process, a portion of the resins (alpha acids) in hops isomerize into iso-alpha acids. That chemical rearrangement of the molecules is what produces bitterness. Yeast is then added to trigger fermentation, turning the sugars into alcohol.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.
