The Indian Association of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (IAPEN), Chennai Chapter, adopted the Sarcopenia Declaration at Beyond Calories 2026, its national gastrointestinal nutrition summit organised in association with SIMS Hospitals in Chennai on November 25.
The declaration calls for early screening for sarcopenia, setting protein intake targets, regular strength exercise and early mobilisation and rehabilitation after illness, including post-intensive care follow-up.
It also emphasises professional education, India-specific research and the development of diagnostic cut-offs suited to Indian populations. It urges policymakers to include sarcopenia in national healthy-ageing and non-communicable disease programmes, particularly focusing on rural and low-income communities.
Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of muscle mass, strength and function. It can occur with ageing and is accelerated by inadequate nutrition, physical inactivity and chronic diseases. It increases the risk of falls, fractures, disability, delayed recovery from illness or surgery and loss of independence.
Doctors at the summit cited data showing that 43.6% of Indians aged 60 and above have sarcopenia, with 19.4% having its severe form. They noted that the condition also affects younger people, particularly those with chronic illnesses, poor nutrition and sedentary lifestyles.
The summit featured talks by specialists in surgical gastroenterology, critical care and nutrition.

Singaporean doctor remanded in Melbourne before sentencing for filming over 800 women in toilets
A three-day pre-sentence hearing that ended on Thursday (Nov 26) examined Ryan Cho’s remorse, rehabilitation and risk of reoffending ahead of his sentencing on Feb 12, 2027.
SINGAPORE: A Singaporean trainee doctor was taken into custody on Thursday (Nov 26) after the end of his three-day plea hearing in a Melbourne court where he had admitted to secretly filming more than 800 medical colleagues across three Australian hospital toilets.
The defence and prosecution crossed swords during Thursday’s hearing over 29-year-old Ryan Cho's remorse and rehabilitation prospects.
Cho will return to court for his sentence on Feb 12, 2027.
Cho's lawyer, Belinda Franjic, reportedly told the court that her client had expressed "genuine remorse" and that he has taken steps towards rehabilitation. 
"He got caught up in his own voyeuristic fantasies and it seems he simply didn't turn his mind to the impact on the victims," she said, as quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). 
Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson argued that Cho was full of self-pity rather than remorseful to his victims, the Australian Associated Press reported.
Mr Gibson added that Cho's rehabilitation prospects were “guarded” after a psychiatrist found his risk of sexual recidivism was moderate to high.
Judge Gabriele Cannon questioned whether Cho had cared about his victims.
"He knew through his training the importance of privacy and dignity and treating people in a respectful way," she said, as quoted by ABC.
Cho had pleaded guilty to recording 3,042 videos of 874 unsuspecting victims using the toilets and bathrooms at three Melbourne hospitals, Australian media outlets reported.
Between 2024 and 2025, he secretly filmed the victims at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, Royal Melbourne Hospital and the Austin Hospital, using a phone hidden in a mesh bag.
He also filmed two young girls who were the daughters of a hospital worker, according to reports from news outlets Australian Associated Press and ABC.
Cho also blocked other hospital toilets and tampered with locks to funnel victims to his desired location.
Separately in 2021, he also stalked his housemate and recorded more than 3,000 videos of the woman and her friends.
The court heard that Cho elaborately categorised the recorded files into folders on his laptop and sorted his edited videos according to victims and under separate tiers.
He was caught after an employee at the Austin Hospital noticed a mesh bag containing clothes and a mobile phone, which had been left recording in a staff toilet cubicle in July last year. The junior doctor was subsequently handed more than 900 charges.
But his lawyers and prosecutors struck a deal to "roll up", or combine, charges when he agreed to plead guilty, resulting in Cho facing 13 charges, ABC reported.
His medical registration has been suspended, preventing him from practising as a doctor in Australia.
DETERMINING SENTENCE A "DIFFICULT" TASK: JUDGE
Cho had pleaded guilty to four counts of producing intimate images, two counts of stalking, producing and possessing child abuse material, four counts of installing an optical surveillance device and failing to comply with police directions, ABC reported.
Each count of producing an intimate image carries a maximum penalty of three years' jail.
Judge Cannon told the court on Thursday that the three-year ceiling made sentencing Cho "difficult", as he was entitled to a discount for an early guilty plea and she would have to consider other mitigating factors, according to the ABC report.
Cho is expected to be sentenced for each individual offence. The judge will be required to set a "base" sentence and can stack a portion of each subsequent charge or order they be served concurrently, the article said.
Crown prosecutor Gibson reportedly defended the decision to combine Cho's charges, saying the Singaporean would otherwise have faced "hundreds of charges".
Over the three-day hearing, several of Cho's victims stepped forward to detail the impact their former colleague's actions had left on their lives. They slammed his behaviour as "disgusting", labelling him a "sexual predator" and "perverted creep".
Australian media outlet news.com.au reported that the man remained expressionless and stared straight ahead as he heard the accounts of his former co-workers.
The outlet quoted a victim who shared the horror she felt after she was told pictures of her had been found on Cho's hard drive: "I’d never met him, never even seen him and yet he was storing images of me at my most vulnerable."
Another nurse told the court she now tried not to drink water so she would not need to use the Royal Melbourne Hospital’s bathrooms during her 12-hour shifts.
One oncology nurse, Courtney Whelan, who was working at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, waived her right to anonymity and told reporters earlier this week that "the place where she protected the dignity of others became the place she lost her own", news.com.au reported.
She broke down in tears as she revealed she now suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression.
"NOTHING OF THIS SCALE": DEFENCE
Cho's lawyer, Ms Franjic, reportedly told the court that her client's offending "beggars belief" and was unprecedented in Victoria as there had been "nothing of this nature and nothing of this scale".
She argued that her client, who has diagnosed schizoid personality and voyeuristic disorders, did not understand his actions would cause harm, the Australian Associated Press reported.
The victims were "never supposed to be alerted" and Cho likely did not think they would ever find out and therefore reasoned he did not cause them harm, the report said.
Cho had instead told a psychiatrist that the police had caused distress to the victims instead because they alerted them to his offending.
Mr Gibson was quoted by ABC saying that while Cho's crimes invaded his victims' privacy, his actions also affected the wider healthcare community as the victims needed time off work.
"It is extraordinary to think that having spent years studying and being on the precipice of a successful career and future … that he would risk it all in this way," Mr Gibson reportedly said.

Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
- Published
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.
As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024.
Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus.
Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London.
Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party.
Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown.
Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty.
Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee.
Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down.
Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party.
The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

A video has gone viral across social media platforms with the claim that a group of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangha (RSS) activists vandalised a restaurant in West Bengal.

The 25-second-long clip shows a mob breaking glass panes and ransacking the space. The caption, written in Hindi, says when the owner asked for payment, the RSS members accused the restaurant of wrongly serving them chicken.
The same clip was shared by X user @yadavanoop08, with the claim that certain “RSS goons caused a ruckus” at a restaurant in West Bengal after they were asked to pay their bill. (Archive)
पश्चिम बंगाल के ड्यूर्विंग होटल में RSS के कुछ गुंडों का हंगामा,
होटल द्वारा बिल मांगने पर RSS के गुंडों ने ये आरोप लगाकर दुकान में तोड़फोड़ करने लगे कि खाने में चिकन दिया गया है।

Several other users also shared the video with identical claims on X.
Fact Check
In order to determine the veracity of these claims, first, we ran a reverse image search on some of the keyframes of the viral clip. This led us to images of a restaurant called Durbin Bangla located in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Below is a comparison of a frame from the viral video and an image of the restaurant we found online.
The viral video also contains footage of the incident shot from outside the restaurant. We examined keyframes from this clip and compared them with photographs of the outside facade of the restaurant available online. See below:
These comparisons prove conclusively that the restaurant shown in the viral clip is not in West Bengal, but in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Further, the viral clip shows a police officer in a green uniform in the midst of the chaos. This matches the uniform worn by Bangladesh police.
A keyword search then led us to several news reports (The Daily Star, The Financial Express and Dhaka Tribune) on a mob attack and vandalism at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka’s Mohakhali on November 13, 2026.
The Daily Star reported that a disagreement over a vacant seat at the restaurant eventually escalated into a heated conflict, followed by a clash with the restaurant employees and vandalism at the restaurant.
To sum up, the viral video is from Bangladesh. It shows an incident at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka. The claim that a group of RSS members is seen vandalising a restaurant in Bengal over non-payment of bill and being served chicken is false.

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, was set on fire late on Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.
Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.
During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.
On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.
Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.
At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since 10 November, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday, the bank said.
On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

“The construction work for the medical college on the Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) new campus in Ramanagara is progressing rapidly. The tender for the medical college in Puttur has been finalised, and the construction will commence shortly. We will apply to the NMC to start these colleges from 2027-28 with a capacity of at least 50 seats,” Medical Education Minister Sharan Prakash Patil said.
“There is also a proposal to start medical colleges in Vijayapura and Kolar districts. The cabinet will decide on that soon,” he added.
The government has decided to start a medical college in every district of the State. There are 25 now. If colleges are established in Ramanagara, Puttur, Vijayapura, and Kolar districts, only Tumakuru, Bengaluru Rural, and Udupi districts will have to have a government medical college of their own.
Currently, there are 76 medical colleges in the State, comprising 25 government and 51 private institutions, with a total of 15,745 seats available for the 2026-27 academic year. If the Ramanagara and Puttur colleges are approved for the next academic year, with 50 seats each, this will go up to 78 colleges with 15,845 seats.
Will NMC approve this year?
The NMC has rejected the State’s applications for starting medical colleges in Kanakapura and Ramanagara four times from 2023-24 to 2026-27, for want of infrastructure, including teaching and non-teaching staff. Will the commission approve the proposals this year at least is the moot question.
In this context, the State government decided to construct a medical college and hospital in Kanakapura at an estimated cost of about ₹550 crore, and the construction work is in progress. However, the work of the medical college planned to be built on the proposed Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) campus in Ramanagara is only 70% complete. Therefore, the government has decided to start the medical college using the district hospital.
“The construction of medical college on the RGUHS new campus in Ramanagara will be completed soon. Consequently, steps have been taken to shift the university to the new campus within the next three to four months. Meanwhile, the construction of a medical college and hospital in Kanakapura is progressing rapidly, and once the work is complete, a proposal will be submitted to the MNC for the commencement of the college,” Mr. Patil said.

When discussing cervical cancer, what often gets left out is that it is one of the most preventable of cancers. Despite this, cervical cancer continues to be a cause of thousands of deaths among women every year, not only in India, but in many parts of the world. In many such cases, the condition is detected far too late, leaving limited room for intervention. The issue therefore, is not a gap in science, but a gap in awareness
The main culprit in cervical cancer is a virus that is very common, human papillomavirus, or HPV for short. HPV primarily spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, most often during sexual intercourse. The virus is so widespread that virtually everyone, both men and women, at some point in their lifetime, will be infected without even realising it. More often than not, the immune system gets rid of the virus without causing any damage.

The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle. Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.
It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.
“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”
That’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.
Mouse in the House
From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach—you get the idea. There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of New York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.
The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.
It's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.
I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.
Thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.
The asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.)
The horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.
Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as New York, that's incredibly valuable.
You should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.
Che Carina!
Turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you quickly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in New York City is 25 mph.
But as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.
The sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.
The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.
New Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.
As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the city; anything longer will give you range anxiety. That trip over the bridge? I went from Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Lower Manhattan and back (around 12 miles). The indicated remaining range went from 46 miles to 30 by the time I got home.
Recharging takes around five hours from zero to full, and the charging cord is built into the car near the passenger-side door. Annoyingly, the 10-foot cable isn't retractable, so you awkwardly have to stuff it back into the door frame when you're done. But the bigger issue is the length. And the standard AC plug. EV charging stations don't typically have AC outlets like the ones in your home. And 10 feet is far too short to reach any apartment or residence in New York City.
I bought a 50-foot extension cord and ran the cable from my outdoor parking spot to my backyard outlet. It worked perfectly well, but I'm also an outlier, with access to a parking spot and a backyard. Most people don't have those luxuries, so you'll need your own solution.
Initially, after my first ride with the Topolino, I was apprehensive. It felt like I was sitting in a plastic box on wheels, with a blaring sound that wouldn't stop, and every big bump sending a shock into my body. After a week, I was driving the thing everywhere, hand dangling out the half-window, fist-bumping other drivers in bumper-to-bumper traffic, and parking in the tiniest available spots around Brooklyn. Now, a week without the little mouse, I miss it dearly.
It's far from the perfect city car. There are small things I would change to improve the overall rideability. And like the Fiat 500e, it's way too expensive. But as someone who likes their car to stand out, I find so much of what's available in the US market uninspiring. The Topolino breaks the mold. We need more small cars like it.

Nasdaq-listed Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has criticised rival AI companies for promoting slogans such as “human control and agency” and “AI should be just a tool” without adequately addressing the risks of increasingly autonomous systems. In a lengthy post on X, Amodei accused some rival CEOs of using human agency as a commercial and political pitch without meaningfully differentiating their products or confronting the trade-offs involved. “What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in,” he wrote. Amodei’s comments came in response to an Axios report examining differences among AI leaders over whether humans should voluntarily hand some decision-making authority to superintelligent AI systems. The report said some Anthropic employees believe humans will, and in certain cases should, hand over authority to such systems once they become demonstrably better at making critical decisions. It also cited public pushback from Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who have emphasised retaining human agency. Amodei rejected suggestions that he supports handing governance to AI, calling it “a terrible idea”. He said AI must remain subject to legitimate democratic processes and that human self-determination should not be sacrificed for efficiency or security. Governance Versus Task Automation Amodei argued that the debate conflates two distinct issues – handing governance to AI and using it to automate specific tasks. While greater automation could drive advances in medicine, transportation, energy, and software, he flagged concerns over job displacement, AI systems autonomously developing more powerful successors, and the reliability of AI-led research into keeping systems aligned with human intentions. He also cited Anthropic’s stance on autonomous weapons, saying the company had refused to allow its existing models to be used for such weapons despite the threat of legal sanctions. Amodei argued that rival companies offer broadly similar automation capabilities, questioning whether their public messaging on human control reflects substantive differences in how their products work. Calls To Slow Development In September, Amodei published an essay titled ‘We Must Pace The Frontier’, urging AI companies to slow advances in model capabilities so that safety measures and research could keep pace. The proposal drew public support from Altman, Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis. Their backing highlighted broad agreement on the need to manage AI risks, even as their companies continue to compete to build more capable systems. In a separate development, Altman announced on X yesterday that OpenAI is testing ‘Private Inference’, part of its OpenAI Private Intelligence offering, with a small group of customers. He said stronger privacy protections would make frontier AI useful for a wider range of work. OpenAI also offers zero data retention (ZDR) with private safety processing, which enables automated safety reviews without giving its personnel access to the underlying content. OpenAI describes Private Inference as using confidential computing and verifiable controls to protect information during processing.

Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.
Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.
First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.
According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.
Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.
My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.
When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

WhatsApp is finally offering scheduled messages
You’ll be able to schedule a text, photo or video message up to 14 days in advance.
WhatsApp is introducing what it says is one of the most-requested features from users: scheduled messages. This option will be available globally in the coming weeks and it'll support text, photo and video. Sibling app Instagram has offered scheduled messages since 2024, so this is a long overdue update.
You'll be able to schedule a WhatsApp message to send between 10 minutes and 14 days in the future. Scheduled messages will work in both one-on-one conversations and group chats.
Once the feature is available on your account, you can schedule a message by pressing and holding the send button. You'll then be able to pick a date and time to transmit your message. The recipients won't know that it's a scheduled message as it'll look like any other update to them.
This is a very welcome feature. One of the few things I genuinely like about email (other than it being a truly decentralized means of communication) is being able to schedule replies. I don't really need anyone to know that I'm actually hashing out an email to them late at night. I usually schedule it to send the next morning so I don't seem like someone who works too much even though I definitely work too much.
WhatsApp suggested some other ways scheduled messages might be useful, such as to wish someone luck just before a test or job interview, or to make sure they receive a happy birthday message right when it's midnight for them (especially if you're not in the same time zone). You'll be able to see all of the messages you've timed up to send in the future and delete them if you change your mind. WhatsApp said that, as with all other personal messages, scheduled messages are end-to-end encrypted, so only you and the recipient(s) can read them.

From its origins as a racing game called Race ‘n’ Chase to billion-dollar sales records, GTA has a fascinating history. Here are 11 surprising facts about the franchise, including Hollywood connections, hidden ghosts, clever anti-piracy tricks, celebrity lawsuits, and its Scottish roots.
After more than a decade of waiting, Rockstar Games has finally launched perhaps the most anticipated game in the recent history of gaming. Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6). It has been barely a few days since the game hit the stands and the Web, and it already has the world (gaming and non-gaming too) in its grip, and is setting sales records.
Its release means saying goodbye to the legendary “we got (this/something) before GTA 6” meme, but GTA 6 is already carving a place for itself in the franchise’s history, a history marked by crime, cars, and chaos and a lot of other things that even diehard fans might not be aware of.
From celebrity lawsuits to ghosts and many controversies, the world of GTA is filled with insane stories. So even as you set yourself up for another session of GTA 6 or wait for your copy of the game to download, or just turn your nose up at “crazy gamers who will line up for anything”, here are eleven amazing facts you might not know (but should know) about the legendary Grand Theft Auto franchise.
Table of Contents
It was originally supposed to be a racing game (and called Race’n’Chase)
It may look completely different today, but GTA was originally supposed to be a fast-paced, addictive racing game called “Race ‘n’ Chase.” Development of the game got underway in the mid-nineties, but the developers did not quite get things right. Early models had car-crashing issues and coding glitches that made police cars ram into player cars aggressively, instead of just chasing them. This, of course, took away its traditional racing game feel. But during testing, players enjoyed this glitch and chaos, so the developers decided to move away from a “Race n Chase” sort of setup and decided to create an open world action-oriented game. They called it Grand Theft Auto (GTA). The rest, as they love to say, is history.
Play the OG GTA online and free of cost
Want to experience the original Grand Theft Auto that was released in 1997? Well, you can actually play it for free online in a browser at https://www.playdosgames.com/online/grand-theft-auto/. Just make sure you have a keyboard handy, as it struggles with touch controls.
Thank you, Tony Montana! GTA: Vice City was inspired by Scarface!
Even the greatest video games have to draw inspiration from somewhere, and in the case of GTA: Vice City, inspiration came from Brian De Palma’s 1983 crime classic, Scarface. The developers used the movie as a blueprint to showcase how Miami looked back in the 80s. The protagonist in the game also follows a very similar arc to the protagonist in the film, the iconic Tony Montana, and even has a location similar to that of Tony Montana’s (Scarface’s protagonist) infamous mansion in it.
GTA has a lot of Hollywood in it…but is not too fond of stars
GTA has not just drawn inspiration from Hollywood, but has also featured many famous actors from it. The game has cast a number of actors, comedians, and musicians to either play themselves or voice a character. A key reason for hiring musicians and comedians to play themselves in the game or be a part of an extensive radio or DJ set is to make the city in the game feel even more real and lived in. Famous actors like Ray Liotta, Samuel L. Jackson, Burt Reynolds, and many more have been a part of the franchise. This tradition lives on with GTA 6, as this time around actors Dylan Rourke and Manni Perez have voiced the two leads of the game.
That said, problems with a number of high-profile stars (most notably Burt Reynolds) led Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to say in an interview with Vulture “We don’t bring in name actors anymore because of their egos and, most important of all, because we believe we get a better sense of immersion using talented actors whose voices you don’t recognize.”
The Ghost Town of GTA 3 that is ‘out of bounds’
Imagine having a small part of the game that you cannot explore? Well, that is exactly what the Ghost Town in GTA 3 is. It has nothing to do with gameplay, lacks the general collision mechanism of the game, and yet it exists. The ‘out of bounds’ area was actually designed as part of GTA 3’s opening cinematics and was put away from the main map, and kept in the game only for the intro scene. However, players found their way to the location using glitches and modifications, although they could not interact with it like the rest of the game. Before Vice City, there was Ghost City in the GTAverse.
Punishing pirates, the GTA way
By the time GTA 4 was released in 2008, the GTA franchise had become insanely famous. And with great celebrity and terrific sales comes…great piracy. As pirated and unauthorized units of the game became a problem, Rockstar Games used some very creative countermeasures to punish/ annoy those who bought pirated copies of the game. Unauthorized copies ended up with constant drunk effects on the camera, sudden and auto acceleration, broken mission scripts, damaged cars, and more, which were put in place to make the pirated game actually feel pirated. You do not pirate a gangster game easily!
Macabre and moving Easter eggs
The GTA franchise is laden with Easter eggs, but two of the most amazing ones are found in GTA 5. What makes them special is the attention to both detail and sentiment. These are not your run-of-the-mill “press this key and your car changes into Superman” or “use this key combo to start driving on Mars” kinds of easter eggs, but much more somber and sensitive ones.
In GTA 5 between 23:00 and 00:00, you can actually find a translucent figure at the peak of Mount Gordo. There is a flat rock where the ghost of “Jolene Cranley-Evans,” who was said to have been killed by her husband, Jock Cranley, appears around midnight. Jock had pushed her off the mountain peak, which is also why, when the player goes near the ghost, it disappears and “Jock” written in blood appears on the flat rock!
The other Easter egg is not as eerie but definitely heartbreaking. A small dog can be seen sitting quietly next to the grave of his owner in the Pacific Bluffs cemetery between 10:00 am and 11:00 am. This is the game paying tribute to a real grieving dog, Greyfriars Bobby, a 19th-century dog who guarded his owner’s grave for 14 years.
Watch the moon in GTA 5!
It was not just the easter eggs that were amazing in GTA 5. Rockstar Games upped their detail game (pun intended) by several notches, paying attention to the tiniest of details. The best example of this is the moon in the game. Yes, the moon. The moon in GTA 5 does not remain the same through the gameplay and actually goes through proper lunar phases– something many players might not even notice during regular gameplay. So you get full, crescent, waxing gibbous, and other phases of the moon while playing the game. Now, that’s one moonshot that worked.
GTA and controversies go hand in hand, and even the Guinness Book agrees
Ever since its release in 1997, the GTA franchise has been surrounded by controversies. And these have only gotten bigger with each new version. Celebrities like Lindsay Lohan, Karen Gravano, Michael Washington have filed lawsuits against Rockstar Games’ parent company Take-Two Interactive, for modeling its characters on them.
The game has also attracted a lot of criticism for its alleged glorification of violence and sexual themes – GTA: San Andreas was hit by the Hot Coffee controversy in 2004, when developers left explicit, sexual interactive code in the game instead of deleting it. They had disabled the code, but players used mods to access it, which allowed them to make the main character (CJ) have sexual encounters with characters after inviting them for coffee. The franchise had over 4,000 news stories published in July 2008, all related to violence, crime and misogyny perpetration. It is hardly surprising that it has been recognized as the most controversial video game franchise in history by Guinness World Records. Of course, millions still love it. But that is another story…
Generating the kind of revenues that make Hollywood envious
GTA games generate the kind of revenue that Hollywood blockbusters can only dream of. GTA 5 hit one billion USD in retail sales within three days, making it the fastest entertainment property overall to hit that milestone at that time. And GTA 6 seems to have followed in its footsteps. While no official figures have been released, it is estimated that nearly 25 million copies of the game were sold on the first day, and its earnings come to around 3.8 billion USD. Just for context, Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey has made USD 1.8 billion at the box office at the time of writing.
It is made in Scotland!
It might be released by a US company (Rockstar Games) and might feature US cities in its gameplay, but Grand Theft Auto is actually made in Edinburgh, Scotland, by Rockstar North, which was previously known as DMA Design, a company that was incorporated in Dublin. So yes, believe it or not, the game that many consider to be classically all-American was actually made by the Brits. And that too, by the ones that wear kilts. Bravehearts, truly.

Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened after meeting at CFB Wainwright
Nurse treating soldiers is being harassed, Opposition leader says in House of Commons
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says one of his constituents — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — is having her employment threatened because she met with him.
In an unusual speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege is being breached.
Last month, Maureen Carpenter was photographed speaking to Poilievre following the fire that killed five soldiers and wounded 38 others on Oct. 17. Poilievre said she is under contract with Calian Health, a government contractor, and works as a nurse.
"Maureen spoke to me on base, with the permission of the unit commander. I had the permission of the base commander to be there. She talked about caring for our men and women on the shift that night, that horrendous night," said Poilievre.
An online post from Oct. 20 shows Poilievre meeting with medical staff at CFB Wainwright Health Services. Online comments identify the woman in the photo as Carpenter, which was confirmed by Poilievre's office.
(Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)
"We owe Maureen as well as colleagues like her, our greatest gratitude. That is what I conveyed in our conversation. Instead, Maureen tells me that she's been threatened by Calian Health, all because she spoke to her local member of Parliament."
Poilievre is the MP for Wainwright, Alta., residents. The base is part of his federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot.
He said, following the meeting, Carpenter was subject to a complaint and threatened — told by her boss that if her term contract was not already coming to an end, she would be put under the microscope by the company's legal department.
"The implicit message was that her contract would no longer have any chance of renewal, something that she had taken for granted before that point," Poilievre said.
Neither Calian nor Carpenter responded immediately to a request for comment.
Poilievre said Carpenter was told she violated the company's policy by meeting with her MP. He said there is no such policy — there is a rule against speaking to the media, but nothing prohibiting speaking to a member of Parliament.
He said being able to speak to an MP is a right guaranteed under the Charter, and a requirement in order to ensure Canadians get good government. During the conversation, he said they discussed better support for mental health following the fires.
He said they did not discuss her company or workplace.
Poilievre said that when he heard from Carpenter, he raised the issue with the minister responsible. His office later confirmed he meant Defence Minister David McGuinty.
McGuinty's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"My intention was not for this to be politicized. I simply wanted it to be solved," Poilievre said.
"Based on his original assurances, I had hoped the minister would put Calian in its place … but her family is indicating that the problems have worsened and there is no end in sight."
Poilievre moved a motion to refer the matter to the procedure and House affairs committee for investigation.
"Ideally though, the government and Calian will instead simply say sorry and fix the problem," he said. "But until and unless that happens, my ability to represent my constituents has been interfered with and you must denounce this conduct."

Even as Christian communities continue to face attacks allegedly from Hindutva groups across various parts of West Bengal, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) state president Samik Bhattacharya on November 15 issued a warning to Christian missionary school, saying it they were found promoting “anti-India activities”, they would not be allowed to function.
“If any Christian missionary school, due to religious reasons, promotes anti-India activities, we will not let that school run,” he said while addressing a gathering at Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary celebrations in New Alipore, Kolkata.
“Guardians should become alert that an official at a school placed a Pakistani flag on the table of his chamber… in a school here in Kolkata. Please correct yourselves… We will let this happen in West Bengal no matter how powerful they are. All Christian missionaries can take to the streets; we are not opposed to any religion, but sitting in our state, in our country, we will not let you insult saffron [colour]… We will not allow it.”
Prior to issuing the warning, Bhattacharya claimed that a woman BJP worker was prevented from entering a “prestigious school in Kolkata” for wearing a saffron saree. “A prestigious school in Kolkata…I am not naming the school right now because a few days later I will sit outside its gates. One of our sisters, our BJP worker who was seen wearing saffron attire…was told [by the school] that ‘wearing these saris, you cannot come to school, you cannot pronounce the name of lotus flower while teaching the students.’ This is happening in the land of Kolkata where several eminent personalities have walked,” he said.
He further went on to insinuate that Christians were continuing to uphold British mentality in India. “It’s been 75 years since the British left the country, but the mentality has not left. You have come here; you are holding your establishments; you are Catholics, you are Protestants; you can propagate your religion. But remember, this government is not Babur’s government. This government is not trying to uphold British legacies. West Bengal has an independent government,” he said.
A report published by The Telegraph stated that the BJP president alleged that a reputed college in Kolkata was carrying out religious conversions in Asansol forcibly through “allurements”. “There is an obhijato (elite) college in Kolkata whose principal is carrying out religious conversion in Asansol. This cannot be allowed to continue. This is not the government of the Trinamool Congress, this is not the Left Front government…We are against political intervention in any educational institution. We want schools to create their own curriculum,” the report quoted him.
Bhattacharya, however, did not name any Christian missionary schools or colleges or provide any evidence behind the severe allegations he levelled against the community.
Upon being asked about Bhattacharya’s allegations against Christian missionaries, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on November 17, Tuesday, told the media, “…I get information on this and verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed, if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally, we will withdraw the NOC given to the institute.”
Murshidabad, West Bengal: On a Christian missionary school in Kolkata bars a teacher from wearing a saffron sari, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari says, “…I will verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed—if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally…”

Christian Bodies Condemn Remarks, Issue Statements
The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in a statement on November 18 reacted to Bhattacharya’s statement saying “sweeping accusations without evidence” maligned a peace-loving community and endangered social harmony, and demanded “specific facts, accountability, and immediate legal action”.
BCP posed eight questions to Bhattacharya and the state administration, questioning the lack of legal action against alleged perpetrators of illegal conversion, if any, and the silence over recurring vigilante attacks on Christians. It asked why attacks and vandalism of prayer meetings by ‘militant groups’ had not been condemned, whether such groups were allegedly being used to intimidate Christians, and sought the status of FIRs filed in connection with alleged threats and attacks against the community in the state.

The BCP also demanded documentary evidence of alleged conversions in Christian-run educational institutions, pointing out that millions studied in these schools, and urged ruling party leaders educated in missionary institutions to share their experiences.
The association further questioned the administration’s silence on around 50 alleged attacks on Christian prayer gatherings over the past four to five months, contrasting it with their vocal responses to issues like an official allegedly displaying a Pakistani flag or wearing a saffron saree, without conclusive evidence.
Concerns Ahead of Christmas
Following Bhattacharya’s remarks, Paritosh Canning, moderator of the Church of North India and bishop of the Calcutta diocese, on Sunday sought chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s intervention against the rising number of attacks against the Christian community in West Bengal. Issuing a statement under the banner of Bengal Christian Council, he urged Adhikari to take appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of Christians, churches and places of worship, to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed right of practising one’s faith.
“Our concerns are not without reason. Reports of attacks, intimidation and disruption of Christian religious activities have emerged from several districts of Bengal…These reported incidents include attacks on priests, pastors and worshippers, vandalism of churches and crosses, disruption of prayer meetings, intimidation of Christian families and interference with religious activities,” the statement read.
“These developments have caused considerable anxiety and apprehension among members of the Christian community. West Bengal has traditionally been a land of communal harmony…With Christmas approaching, the apprehensions of the Christian community have become particularly serious…the prevailing atmosphere of insecurity has raised genuine concerns about whether Christians will be able to observe their religious services and celebrate Christmas without fear or disruption,” the statement added.
Condemning Bhattacharya’s remarks, representatives of BCP and the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools held a joint press conference on November 16, Monday. Representatives of the associations dismissed the allegations of forceful religious conversion as baseless. They demanded that Bhattacharya name the two institutes and provide evidence to back his claims against Christian missionaries.

“A viral video has recently come to our attention. While we cannot verify its authenticity at this moment, the remarks recorded in it feature four grave allegations: claims of widespread religious conversions, an accusation that a…principal is involved in conversion activities; an allegation regarding a person wearing a saffron sari coming to a school; and a sweeping insinuation that even though the British have left, Christian missionary school administrators continue to carry a ‘British mentality,” read a statement by the representatives.
“At a time when vigilantes and hooligans are taking the law into their own hands across various districts — vandalising and launching brutal attacks on peaceful prayer meetings under the false pretext of forced conversions and desperately trying to build a fabricated narrative — the Christian community is both shocked and deeply angered to hear such an incredible, hate-mongering and aggressive speech from a usually balanced and sagacious leader like Samik Babu,” it added.
Speaking to Alt News, Moloy D’Costa, secretary of the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools and vicar-general of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Calcutta, said, “The comments made by Mr Bhattacharya are vague. Every school has its own dress code, and there is no universal colour code. The authorities should either provide evidence or identify specific institutions and take appropriate action against them, rather than making general statements that vilify an entire community and a network of institutions.”
D’Costa also pointed out, “Several leaders in the party attended Christian missionary institutions; have they converted to Christianity? Converting to Christianity is a lengthy process. Simply visiting a church or sprinkling water is not part of that process. Accusations of forced conversion are being made from all sides, yet not a single case has been reported where anyone has been proven guilty of such actions.”
National Christian Council (NCC) state general secretary Arpan Rana strongly condemned Bhattacharya’s remarks on Christian missionary institutions, stating that “sweeping allegations without evidence” risk fostering suspicion and hostility towards the Christian community.
Rana told Alt News that Christian institutions were primarily invested in “education, humanitarian service, moral development and nation-building, not forced religious conversion,” adding that students from diverse religious backgrounds have studied in these institutions without abandoning their faiths. “Thousands of students from Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have received education from these institutions while preserving their respective religious identities,” he said.
He also termed the portrayal of Indian Christianity as a legacy of British colonialism ‘historically misleading’, noting that Christianity existed in India long before colonial rule. “We expect scholarly arguments backed by evidence, not broad political claims. If any institution is found to engage in unlawful conversion, we support impartial investigations, but the entire Christian community should not be collectively accused,” he added.
Akin to other Christian associations in the state, Rana, on behalf of the NCC, urged the state government to protect Christian institutions, churches and communities, and ensure they can celebrate Christmas peacefully.
As precautionary measures, the BCP also advised churches to inform local authorities about upcoming programmes, establish a community alert system, ring church bells thrice if suspicious groups enter church premises, immediately notify police, and install CCTV cameras at vulnerable points. It also urged members to seek legal aid from BCP, maintain discipline and peaceful conduct, refrain from retaliation, and involve neighbours of all faiths and civil society members in Christmas celebrations to foster communal harmony.
Alt News has been documenting instances of hate crimes against the Christian community in West Bengal since early this year. Instances of violence, attacks, vandalism, and intimidation have often been carried out by Right-wing groups including Bajrang Dal, Vishva Hindu Parishad, and others, against individuals practising Christianity, house churches, and small Christian communities. However, in most of the cases we have reported, police action has been sparse, with fresh instances of harassment emerging regularly.

South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
South African pharmaceutical company Biovac says it aims to dramatically increase its vaccine production by the end of 2028 with help from a 75-million euro loan from the European Union's investment bank
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- South Africa’s Biovac said Wednesday that a new manufacturing facility aims to dramatically increase African production of vaccines by the end of 2028 to help reduce the continent’s heavy reliance on imported doses.
Africa needs more than 1 billion vaccine doses a year, but only around 1% of them are manufactured on the continent, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Biovac, a public-private pharmaceutical company that's part-owned by the South African government, distributes or does end-stage production for vaccines for polio, tuberculosis, tetanus and other diseases.
It's also seeking regulatory approval to start end-to-end production of an oral cholera vaccine by late 2028, company officials said.
It would be the first cholera vaccine manufactured entirely in Africa and only the second vaccine produced end-to-end on the continent, following a yellow fever vaccine produced by Senegal's Pasteur Institute.
Biovac acquired the base technology for its cholera vaccine from the International Vaccine Institute in South Korea, Biovac CEO Morena Makhoana said. He added that the vaccine is currently undergoing clinical trials and the company expects to have initial safety and efficacy data by June.
Biovac plans to upscale its overall vaccine production by building a new manufacturing facility next to its current base in Cape Town with support from the European Union's investment bank.
The bank has lent Biovac 75 million euros ($82 million) to help finance the new production center and European Investment Bank Vice President Ambroise Fayolle visited Biovac on Wednesday.
“It is important because we believe in science and we believe the benefits can reach beyond vaccine production,” Fayolle said, adding that health resilience should be a global priority.
Biovac chief operations officer Mark MacNaughton said the new facility would give the company the potential to produce around 150 million vaccine doses a year. That would include 30 to 40 million doses of the new cholera vaccine, if it is given regulatory approval, Biovac said.
Cholera, a waterborne bacterial disease, kills thousands of people every year in Africa. A global shortage of cholera vaccines from around 2022 caused the suspension of immunization campaigns in parts of Africa, epitomizing how reliant the continent of more than 1.5 billion is on imported vaccines.
The World Health Organization reported more than 7,000 cholera deaths in Africa last year, the most in more than two decades.
Cholera vaccination campaigns on the continent only restarted this year.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, African governments were left at the back of the vaccine queue and had to scramble to secure doses.
The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Congo, which has killed more than 5,000 people, is another indication of how desperately Africa needs to increase its local vaccine production, health officials have said.
The African Union has set a target for the continent to produce 60% of its vaccines by 2040, though that's seen as a steep challenge.

One group of scientists has successfully trained a single species of wasp to successfully recognize human faces in an artificial laboratory setting. Other researchers have conducted experiments showing that a different species of wasp has the ability to recognize the faces of other wasps.
Expert say there are around 150,000 known species of wasp. Therefore, it is improper to apply the findings of the experiments to all wasps without further research. We found no evidence that wasps will remember a human face following chance encounters.
Among the animal kingdom, wasps have a pretty bad reputation. To the general public, they are often thought of as the bee's angrier, more aggressive cousin, with a more painful sting to boot.
Adding to people's fear of wasps is a rumor that has spread for years, which warns that they can remember people's faces. One concerned reader even got in touch to ask, "Can wasps remember faces?"
The claim seemingly alludes to the common perception that wasps are aggressive in nature. Some posts even imply they seek revenge against their enemies, including humans.
To figure out whether the rumor is all buzz, no sting, Snopes spoke to experts who have researched wasps and their facial recognition capabilities.
We found no evidence suggesting wasps remember human faces following chance encounters, but researchers told us about one experiment that trained a single species of wasp to successfully recognize human faces in an artificial laboratory setting. Given how many different species of wasp there are, it would be wrong to apply this finding to all wasps without further research. As a result, this claim is mostly false but with an element of truth.
First, some context
There are thousands of different species of wasp, according to Elizabeth Tibbetts, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Michigan. Princeton University Press puts that figure at roughly 150,000 known species.
Despite their public perception, Tibbetts said most species don't sting at all, though yellowjackets and hornets are exceptions. A wasp's social environment also changes dramatically from species to species. While some live in large nests and have a bee-like hierarchical social structure complete with a queen (this being a feature of eusociality), many species live completely solitary lives.
As a result, it would be improper to universally apply any characteristic to all wasps (some species even feature wingless females). The research pool, which is small to begin with, on wasps identifying and remembering faces — human or otherwise — only focuses on a few species. The studies have found relatively solid evidence of those species' facial recognition abilities, but it would be incorrect to apply any findings to all the thousands of wasp species without more research. 
Can wasps remember human faces?
Adrian Dyer — an associate professor of physiology at Australia's Monash University, who studies the cognitive capabilities of various animals, including bees and wasps — has trained both the western honey bee (Apis mellifera) and the common wasp (Vespula vulgaris) to recognize images of human faces, utilizing a test that is also used to check facial recognition capabilities in humans.
In his 2017 experiment with common wasps, Dyer's team presented two platforms to the wasps, each featuring a different human face. One platform rewarded the wasps with a droplet of sugar, while the other punished them with a droplet of quinine hemisulfate, which tastes bitter to the insects. The wasps repeatedly trained with the rewards for several days. Then, the team removed the rewards and ran the tests again. The wasps chose the face they had learned would reward them with sugar quite consistently, even when the reward was absent, and even when they were presented with new alternative faces. The only time they tripped up was when the faces were turned upside down.
Speaking via phone call, Dyer said his experiment was more of a testament to the creatures' learning abilities than anything else, though. His studies were performed in a lab setting, and recognizing human faces was not a natural ability — the bees and wasps needed to be specifically trained, instead of having an innate system for facial recognition, like humans do. (Scientists have found some facial recognition abilities in babies as young as a few hours old, he said).
So, if you've ever swatted a wasp away, the research does not suggest that it can simply look at you, remember your face and track you down a few days later. "The wasps are acting in the way they evolved to act," Dyer said. "They are not trying to seek revenge."
Some wasps can recognize faces of nest-mates
Tibbetts' research mainly focuses on Polistes fuscatus, the northern paper wasp. It is a common species in the eastern United States that forms nests near humans and wooded areas. They do sting when threatened, but Tibbetts said the wasps are more docile than one might think. "I didn't get stung until after I completed my PhD," she said via phone call.
At the beginning of her research career in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Tibbetts said she noticed something interesting about the paper wasps she was studying — they all had different facial and abdominal markings, sometimes behaved in selfish ways and had individual personalities. Their social dynamics, she added, are incredibly complex and interesting.
Tibbetts wondered whether those social dynamics meant the wasps were also aware of the physical differences between individual members of their species. So, she gave some of the wasps makeovers, using paint to alter each one's facial appearance. Then, she returned the wasps to their nests and recorded their behavior.
At first, nest-mates acted more aggressively toward the wasps with painted faces, by lunging and biting at them. Perhaps they thought the wasps with painted faces were impostors? No, according to Tibbetts. Studies show numerous species of wasp use chemical signals to identify their nest-mates and will quickly chase out or attack an impostor, but none of the wasps with painted faces were chased out in Tibbetts' experiment. All were accepted back into the nest.
But within two hours of being reintroduced, the aggressive behavior towards the wasps with painted faces died down. The wasps had adjusted to their nest-mate's new look. Tibbetts concluded that the wasps were using the facial markings to recognize each other, and the aggressive behavior she saw represented the wasps attempting to determine where the face-painted wasp fit in the social hierarchy.
In the years since Tibbetts first published her findings in 2002, she has continued to study the impressive cognitive and social abilities of the paper wasp. "Their capacity has really shocked me," she said. 
In one follow-up study, Tibbetts found northern paper wasps will "socially eavesdrop" on others, changing how they interact with a nest-mate after they have seen that nest-mate fight. In another, she found the wasps were better at identifying whole faces than partial faces, suggesting they could be learning faces by taking in all the information at once — the same way humans do. In a third study, Tibbetts described raising hybrid hives of three different, related paper wasp species. No matter their surroundings, P. fuscatus continued to perform well on facial recognition tasks, but remarkably, P. metricus, one of the other species, seemed to learn some basic facial recognition abilities when raised alongside P. fuscatus.
It is clear these small insect brains are a lot more complex than they might initially appear. Dyer said the findings are so important because they show it does not take a large, mammalian brain to perform complex tasks. "Think of a bee as a million neurons floating in space," he said. In comparison, human brains have somewhere between 50 and 100 billion neurons.
