Man, 39, ID'd as victim of fatal shooting in midtown Toronto home invasion: police
Michael Eckert was confronted by a suspect before he was shot, police say
A man killed in a midtown Toronto home invasion early Wednesday is being remembered as a talented musician who "always led with his heart," according to a longtime friend.
Police have identified the man who was fatally shot as Michael Eckert, 39.
Emergency crews responded to reports of a shooting at a residence in the St. Clair Avenue West and Poplar Plains Road area at around 2:40 a.m., according to a Toronto police news release Wednesday afternoon.
An unknown number of suspects forced entry into the residence, police said. One of the suspects was confronted by Eckert, shot him and fled the home, police said. Eckert was taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Staff Sgt. Shain Griffin with 53 Division told CBC News early Wednesday morning the victim was the homeowner's son.
Police identified the victim of a shooting during a home invasion in midtown Toronto Wednesday as Michael Eckert, 39, of Toronto. (Toronto Police Service)
Toronto police Det. Sgt. Alan Bartlett said at a news conference earlier Wednesday that there is no evidence to suggest the family was targeted.
"I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be, not only to the residents of that community, but to the residents of the city of Toronto as a whole," Bartlett said.
There were four residents inside the home at the time but no one else was injured, he said.
This is Toronto's 37th homicide of the year, according to police.
Bartlett said Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw assured him that every resource available will be provided to investigators and "no expense will be spared."
He said police do not yet have details on the number of suspects, any descriptions or what vehicles may have been used.
He urged anyone with surveillance video or anyone who saw anything between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. to contact police.
Victim was a 'loving and caring person': friend
Galen Pelley, a friend of Eckert, said he knew him for about 20 years after they met studying music at Humber College. He said they made music together ever since they met and he felt Eckert was like a brother to him.
"We're all still in shock," Pelley said Wednesday. "We can't believe that this would happen to anyone, let alone someone that we all cared about and who cared for so many himself."
Pelley said Eckert, the youngest child in his family, had two sisters and two brothers and did more than his share of taking care of others. He was also an uncle, he said.
"Mike always led with his heart, both on stage and off stage," he said. "He had an affinity for drummers and I always thought guitarists wrote the best songs."
Pelley described Eckert as a "gentle giant" who was an avid reader and a humble, "loving and caring person."
"He spoke louder through his music than he ever would off stage or in person," he said.
Eckert's instrument of choice was the pedal steel guitar, he said.
Eckert performed at the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary as back up for Blue Rodeo this month, Pelley said, adding: "He's gone too soon and that was a real moment for him to flourish."
'Far too many' home invasions in Toronto: city councillor
Coun. Josh Matlow told reporters outside the home Wednesday there have been "far too many" home invasions in the city and that it needs to be a top priority to address residents' concerns.
"There's a feeling amongst Torontonians that far too often people go to bed at night worrying about whether or not they'll wake up to somebody in their home," Matlow said, adding there's work to do in the community to support "very scared" residents.
He said he has offered Demkiw his "complete support" during the investigation. He urged people to not jump to conclusions.
MPP Stephanie Smyth, who joined Matlow, said police do what they can to investigate incidents, but that more needs to be done to address the fear residents feel.
Coun. Josh Matlow and MPP Stephanie Smyth spoke to reporters outside the scene of a fatal home invasion on Wednesday. They shared their condolences for the victim's loved ones and reassured residents they will do their best to address fears. (Paul Smith/CBC)
"They can talk about the stats all they want, but the bottom line is people are afraid. And the one place you should not feel afraid is in your own home," she said.
Matlow added that "it's shameful" to hear that many residents in the neighbourhood and nearby areas have hired private security to safeguard their homes. Smyth said there needs to be stronger deterrence for such crimes, such as harsher penalties.
"People have to do what they feel is the right choice to ensure the safety of their family," Bartlett said in regards to some people hiring private security.
When asked what tips he had for residents regarding a potential home invasion, he said people should call 911 immediately and that Toronto Police Service "provides the best that it can in terms of public safety services."
"Oftentimes we can't provide the why, we simply don't know. What my promise has been to the victims' family is that we'll do our very best to provide the who."
Incident follows Bridle Path home invasion last month
The incident comes nearly a month after a home invasion and shooting sent a family of four adults in Toronto's Bridle Path neighbourhood to hospital. Police arrested one suspect in Ottawa last week and are looking for two others.
Police have been investigating and patrolling to deter home invasions in parts of the city after seeing a rise in incidents earlier this year, Demkiw said in remarks to the Toronto Police Service Board back in July.
- 4 hospitalized as Toronto police investigate home invasion, shooting at Bridle Path home
- CBC Investigates Here's where home invasions are happening in Toronto and what's being done to prevent them
He said the service launched the initiative in areas that saw the largest increase in home invasions, which includes 22, 32 and 53 Divisions. The 22 division covers neighbourhoods in central and southern Etobicoke, 32 operates in central and western North York, and 53 Division covers central and midtown Toronto.
"We continue to put our people and our resources where we see challenges, and where we hear concerns from our communities," Demkiw told the police board.
Home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year in Toronto, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.

Buying a new TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.
Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.
For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.
Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.
What Size TV Should You Buy?
The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.
Should You Buy an Art TV?
I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.
Should You Pick an OLED or RGB TV?
TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.
Which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.
Best Overall TV
Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) Specs
| Display type | Mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 144 Hz | 
| Operating system | Tizen OS | 
| Connectivity | Wireless One Connect Box: HDMI 2.1 (x5), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Google Assistant, Amazon Alexa, Samsung Bixby | 
| Speaker layout | 2.0.2 channel | 
I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.
The Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.
Extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.
Best Budget TV
TCL QM7L Specs
| Display type | QD Mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 144 Hz | 
| Operating system | Google TV | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x2), HDMI 2.0 (x2), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Google Gemini, Amazon Alexa | 
| Speaker layout | 2.1 channel | 
TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast issues when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.
A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.
Best RGB TV
LG Micro RGB Evo Specs
| Display type | RGB Mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 120 Hz (165 Hz with VRR) | 
| Operating system | Web OS | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa, Google Gemini, LG AI Voice ID | 
| Speaker layout | 2.2 channel | 
Samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released new RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests,I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.
Another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.
Best OLED TV
Samsung S95H Specs
| Display type | QD-OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 165 Hz | 
| Operating system | Tizen OS | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa, Samsung Bixby | 
| Speaker layout | 4.2.2 channel | 
Samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.
Perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim shows like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.
It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.
Best Budget OLED TV
Roku Pro Series OLED Specs
| Display type | OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 120 Hz | 
| Operating system | Roku OS | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Roku Voice, Google Assistant, Amazon Alexa | 
| Speaker layout | 2.0 channel | 
The company famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.
I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.
Best Budget Art TV
Amazon Ember Artline Specs
| Display type | QLED | 
| Refresh rate | 60 Hz | 
| Operating system | Fire OS | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x1), HDMI 2.0 (x3), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa | 
| Speaker layout | 2.0 channel | 
The Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV shows.
Art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.
Image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.
Best Gaming TV
Sony Bravia 9 II Specs
| Display type | RGB Mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 120 Hz | 
| Operating system | Google TV | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x2), HDMI 2.0 (x2), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Google Gemini, Amazon Alexa | 
| Speaker layout | 2.2.2 channel | 
While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.
I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.
The Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.
Honorable Mentions
Hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.
LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.
Other TVs We’ve Tested
Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while shows and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.
Sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.
Sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That said, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.
TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.
TCL RM9L RGB Mini-LED: The TCL RM9L RGB TV is huge and hugely expensive. The $6,000 85-inch is the smallest and cheapest model you can get, and it is generally outclassed by the LG Micro RGB Evo.
What We’re Testing Next
The WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given past performances from LG C and G-series TVs, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades in this guide.

The Maharashtra state cabinet on Wednesday, 25 November, has approved free foodgrains for 42.30 lakh farmers in 33 drought-affected districts in the state, PTI reported. This was announced in a statement by Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis.
The benefit will be available for three months, to farmers not covered under the National Food Security Act or receiving benefits under the APL-Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) scheme, it added.
Further, the state proposed amendments to two laws to strengthen accountability in public service delivery and expedite recovery of money lost in financial frauds.
Under the foodgrain scheme, eligible farmers who are not covered under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) or receiving benefits under the APL-Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) scheme will get:
The cabinet proposed amendments to the Right to Public Services Act to impose penalties of up to ₹25,000 on officials responsible for unjustified delays in delivering government services and setting up divisional-level tribunals to expedite cases of financial fraud.
It also approved the introduction of a bill to amend the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999, to speed up the attachment and sale of assets belonging to fraudulent financial establishments and individuals and facilitate repayment to defrauded investors.
Dedicated MPID tribunals will be established at the divisional level, with cases required to be disposed of within 90 days of filing.
The cabinet also sanctioned ₹5,548 crore for the Narmada-Tapi River-linking Project (NTRLP) in Nandurbar district.
The NTRLP envisages constructing six diversion barrages and is expected to provide irrigation benefits to around 26,526 hectares in the region. It will also generate 11.50 MW of electricity.
In another decision, the cabinet approved amendments to the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966, to introduce a Revenue Court Case Management System for quasi-judicial proceedings in the revenue department, according to the release.
The amendments will also provide for a “one district, one appeal” mechanism to expedite disposal of cases.

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
- Published
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

Jeremy Conway — an artiste’s agent, and a titan of the industry with an unerring eye for the stars of the future — died earlier this month aged 87. His client list was legendary, a rollcall that included Anthony Hopkins, Brian Cox, Helena Bonham Carter, Benedict Cumberbatch, Claire Bloom, Greta Scacchi, Noma Dumezweni, Joanne Froggatt, and David Harewood,.
Over 50 years ago, Conway founded his eponymous agency. In 1980, Nicki Van Gelder joined him, adding her name to the shingle. There were just three of them in the office then, and when John Grant joined in 1994 there were nine. “We are now 32!” Grant recently told Deadline of the company that’s now a powerhouse called Conway Van Gelder Grant. Grant confirmed that Conway — “his friend and mentor” — had died on 1 November this year. Conway was CVGG’s principal partner until he retired in 2015.
In a tribute penned for Deadline, Bonham Carter, who’s still with the agency, recalled a note she had written for Conway’s retirement party thanking him “for my career.” She meant it. She continued, “I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost [1983’s A Pattern of Roses] and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he said somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train.”
Watch on Deadline
Conway wasted no time. He fired off a message to Trevor Nunn suggesting that he consider Bonham Carter for the title role in Lady Jane, Nunn’s film about Lady Jane Grey, the 16th-century “Nine Days Queen”. Next, Conway took Celestia Fox, Merchant Ivory’s casting director for a jolly supper, where he advocated Bonham Carter for the role of Lucy Honeychurch in their upcoming production of A Room with a View.
During this period, Grant remarked, “Jeremy represented several of each cast of the Merchant Ivory Films.” Anthony Hopkins and Bonham Carter both starred in Howard’s End, while Hopkins went on to make Remains of the Day. Cross-referencing the Merchant Ivory catalogue, it’s possible to discern that, over a period of three decades, scores of CVGG artistes populated their films.
I met Conway many times over the years — at first nights, at Oscar-night soirées in Hollywood — and every now and then we’d have lunch. He once explained that, as the son of Colonel Charles Maxwell Orr Sawers, a colonel in the 9th Royal Deccan Horse who served in India and Burma, he knew all about “getting work done and just getting on with it.” I found that comment from Conway in a red Silvine notebook, one of hundreds that I forgot to throw away. The army-brat background, I think, gave Conway that carpe diem attitude, but it was cloaked by his avuncular bearing.
But he was definitely getting on with it when he got his hands on Ted Tally’s screenplay for The Silence of the Lambs. And he was getting stuff done when suggested that the film’s director Jonathan Demme go and watch Hopkins in David Hare and Howard Brenton’s play Pravda, which opened at London’s National Theatre in May 1985. The part of Hannibal Lecter won Hopkins his first Academy Award.
Conway loved actors. I would often catch him at plays well into their runs, featuring thespians that he didn’t represent. He wasn’t out to poach them; he just wanted to watch great performances.
Born David Maxwell Sawers, Conway attended Radley College in Abingdon, in Oxford. After that, he studied drama at the Guildhall School of Music & Drama., which is where he met his life-long partner Neville Phillips, with whom he entered into a civil partnership in 2005. Parts in Z Cars, early episodes of Doctor Who and stage roles followed, but Conway enjoyed watching the likes of Judi Dench, Maggie Smith and Hopkins at the Old Vic rather more than treading the boards himself.
Deciding to become an agent, he joined forces with former Royal Academy of Dramatic Arts-trained actor-turned-agent Norman Boyack. Together they formed Boyack and Conway, where their roster included John Thaw, Sheila Hancock and Edward Hardwicke. When Boyack decided to leave the business, Conway set up on his own, representing Hopkins, Susan Penhaligon and Trudie Styler, then an actress, early on in her career.
Once Van Gelder joined, the business grew. Grant observed that Conway was “definitely one of the first agents in London to represent European and world film actors from various countries. As wide a range as Romania, Scandinavia, Germany, France and India. Notably Jesper Christensen, Lars Mikkelsen — who’s still with us — and Om Puri.”
Aside from his film, theatre and television passions, Conway loved to cook and entertain, and he would regularly host dinner parties at the weekend, inviting the good and the great of the entertainment world. Grant added that he was a keen gardener and collector of art and artefacts. “He was also an avid reader,” Grant marveled, “and somehow found time to read many books alongside a large volume of scripts. He had an encyclopedic knowledge of plays and could frequently be heard discussing why someone was specifically right for a role.”
For over a decade Conway was a board director of the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, where he was first in line to scoop up tomorrow’s stars. He was also long associated with Bafta, having been a member for 60 years.
A better-than-thriving CVGG is Conway’s legacy; he always had one eye on the future by partnering with Van Gelder and Grant. How he went to bat for all his actors mattered most. I remember being on the set of Guy Ritchie and Matthew Vaughn’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels when Jason Flemyng inched his way over to me for a chat and he was almost in tears as he told how Conway had saved his life by “giving me a career”.
That’s precisely the side of Conway’s character that Bonham Carter reflected on in her tribute to her beloved agent, which I’m posting in full below…
“I think for Jeremy’s retirement party I wrote a note saying, ‘Thank you for my career.’ I meant it. I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he said somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train.
“Jeremy was my industry parent. He was my champion. And patron. My enthusiast. He was bossy, impatient, and had formidable energy and appetite for all things life had to offer. He had great taste. His house, when I last saw him, was brimful of paintings and objects of beauty. He loved his job and he loved it for the culture of it — the plays, the acting, the life, art, the people. His interest and curiosity was acute.
“Of course, most of our relationship was conducted on the phone. He had a great, handsome, fully resonant telephone voice. He had trained as an actor and would always intone, ‘CON-sonants, Helly!’
“One of my favorite poets, Mary Oliver, ends one of her poems, by saying, ‘I don’t want to end up having simply visited this world.’ Jeremy didn’t just visit it, he ate it, and he tasted it. He explored, and he made people’s careers and opened doors, and he grew an agency from seed that lives and thrives.
“His legacy and his children are the agency and all those he impacted, people whose lives would be utterly different without him. His family of connections and tentacles of influence over decades in the industry is like a tree with many roots, an old oak that will far outlive us all.
“I think of him with huge love and gratitude. I was all his idea. All his fault.”

- However, there is no evidence Trump bought $3 million of the company's shares before Huang's return and then traded on this insider knowledge for a $300 million profit, contrary to social media posts.

- The Financial Times estimated that Trump made anywhere from $1.3 million to $15 million on Nvidia shares after Huang's return, based on data through September. A claim is spreading that U.S. President Donald Trump bought $3 million in Nvidia shares before convincing the company to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, which increased the value of its shares by 9,000%, allowing Trump to make a $300 million profit.
The rumor circulated on X, Facebook and Threads.
If Trump had traded on his knowledge of Huang's return before it was public, that would be insider trading, which is illegal.
It's true that Trump has millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares. Trump also said he persuaded Nvidia to bring back Huang, who was removed by the company's board after admitting to several affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. (Subsequent reporting from reputable outlets such as The Wall Street Journal suggests U.S. officials now believe their initial intelligence on the alleged spy was erroneous.)
However, there is no evidence Trump purchased $3 million in shares shortly before Nvidia reinstated its CEO on Nov. 23. In fact, the president's required financial disclosures for October and November are not yet available because of the lag in reporting, making it impossible to rate this claim as of this writing. A Google search returned no indication that any reputable news outlet has reported on leaks or documentation specifically showing that Trump bought $3 million in Nvidia stock in November.
Even if Trump did purchase $3 million in Nvidia stock, the math behind these posts makes no sense. Nvidia's stock rose a little over 30%, not 9,000%, after Huang was reinstated. (A hypothetical 9,000% increase in value for $3 million worth of stock would result in $270 million in gains; a 30% increase results in $900,000 in gains.)
The White House has repeatedly told Snopes and many other news outlets that there are no conflicts of interest with the president's stock holdings. In April, Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, told Snopes the following in an emailed statement:
President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000. Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.
The White House did not return a request for comment about Trump's financial stake in Nvidia.
Below, we break down the possible origin of the claim and what Trump's financial disclosures actually reveal about his Nvidia stock holdings:
Origin of claim
It's possible this claim originated from a separate rumor that an anonymous person bought $3.4 million worth of Nvidia options, which is not the same as stock trading. Options trading involves buying and trading on contracts that give someone the right to buy or sell a stock at a certain price on a certain date, rather than buying stock outright. In other words, it allows people to bet on a company's future stock price.
The New York Times reported that the rumor about the anonymous trade appeared to come from an X user called @MrMikeInvesting who claimed to be a stock and options trader, but the Times spoke to three firms who track options activity who said they had no evidence that the trade happened.
"Two said that the size of the purported trade was so large that it was nearly impossible," the Times reported.
The Times also said the rise in value of the contracts matching the parameters of the post was, in fact, roughly 9,000%, according to data from the firm Market Chameleon. However, the total value of those contracts would have been closer to $8 million, not more than $300 million.
How much has Trump invested in Nvidia?
Information about Trump's investment portfolio is available in the Office of Government Ethics' searchable database for public officials' financial disclosures.
Financial disclosure forms do not record the exact value amount for each investment. Instead, the forms report trades using ranges. For example, a trade might be reported within the range of $50,001 to $100,000.
A search for the word "Nvidia" in Trump's 2026 annual financial disclosure, which was published in June, returned 73 transactions. His most recent monthly financial disclosures with data from July, August and September all show purchases and sales of Nvidia stock. A Snopes review of these documents found that each trade ranged from thousands to millions of dollars. 
Multiple reputable outlets have reviewed Trump's financial disclosures in depth to attempt to estimate the president's Nvidia stock holdings and the effect of Huang's removal and reinstatement on the president's portfolio.
The Washington Post reported that Trump held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, although the "actual value range was probably higher because Nvidia's share price rose between the end of 2025 and the end of August."
The Financial Times determined that Trump made anywhere from $1.3 million to $15 million on Nvidia shares after Huang's return, based on data through September — and could have lost up to $42 million on the value of his shares before Huang's return on Nov. 23.
Meanwhile, a CNBC analysis found that Trump's transactions on Nvidia shares — both purchases and sales — were worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million as of the end of August. By the time Huang was reinstated on Nov. 23, Trump's stake, based on the value reported in August, would have been worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million, according to CNBC.

Prosus-owned fintech company PayU India swung to an adjusted EBITDA profit of $12 Mn in the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), compared to a loss of $1 Mn in the year-ago period, driven by growth in its lending business. However, adjusted EBIT remained negative at $3 Mn, although this was an improvement from a loss of $15 Mn in H1 FY26. The bottom line improvements come despite a 3.3% decline in its revenue to $384 Mn from $397 Mn in the last year period. However, disclosing the numbers, Prosus said PayU's revenue grew 6% in local currency, excluding the impact of mergers and acquisitions (M&A). Excluding strategically cancelled merchant accounts, revenue growth stood at 13% and transaction volumes grew 20% in local currency. The development comes as Prosus reported a mixed performance across its India portfolio, with the Dutch technology investor also disclosing an 8.6% fully diluted stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech startup Navi following a $100 Mn investment. Separately, it recognised a $103 Mn impairment on an unnamed listed equity-accounted investment in its Indian ecosystem. The distinction is important as PayU has been exiting merchant accounts that do not meet its profitability requirements, affecting reported payments revenue but improving the quality of its business. PayU's Credit Business Drives Profitability PayU's payments business continued to account for the larger share of its revenue, contributing $265 Mn in H1 FY27. However, payments revenue declined 12% YoY in dollar terms, or 4% in local currency, reflecting the timing of the Diwali festive season and strategic merchant exits. Despite the revenue decline, the payments segment's gross margin improved to 25% from 23% in H1 FY26. In contrast, PayU's credit business’ revenue grew by 24% YoY to $119 Mn. This business also turned adjusted EBITDA positive, recording a profit of $10 Mn against a loss of $3 Mn in the year-ago period. Credit revenue grew 36% in local currency. The lending business accounted for around 31% of PayU's total revenue during the period, compared to 24% a year earlier. Its credit assets under management (AUM) also grew 20% YoY. Prosus Completes $100 Mn Navi Investment At a group level, Prosus disclosed that it completed its $100 Mn investment in Navi in November 2026, acquiring a 9.1% ownership stake in the fintech company. The investment follows approval from the Competition Commission of India (CCI). Prosus said it would account for Navi as an equity-accounted investment, citing the significant influence it holds through board representation. Based on the $100 Mn investment and the fully diluted ownership percentage, the transaction implies an equity valuation of approximately $1.2 Bn for Navi, as per Inc42’s calculations. Separately, Prosus recognised a $103 Mn impairment on a listed equity-accounted investment in its India ecosystem during H1 FY27, following a significant decline in the investment's market value relative to its carrying value. The investor attributed the broader market pressure to factors including higher oil prices, elevated global interest rates and a weaker rupee. Prosus reported total impairments of $136 Mn on equity-accounted investments during the period. Of this, $103 Mn related to the listed investment in its India ecosystem, while the remaining $33 Mn was associated with unlisted investments in its other ecosystem. To note, this impairment reflects a reduction in the carrying value of Prosus' investment and does not represent a loss incurred by the portfolio company itself. The disclosures come as Prosus continues to reshape its portfolio through investments, operational improvements and capital allocation. The company reported 59% growth in ecosystem revenue to $5.7 Bn in H1 FY27, while ecosystem adjusted EBITDA stood at $492 Mn, compared to $530 Mn in the year-ago period. In India, Prosus said that its ecosystem now reaches more than 500 Mn annual users and processes around 450 Mn orders a month, with PayU's payment infrastructure embedded across several portfolio businesses.

A Delhi Police cyber team has busted an alleged organised cryptocurrency fraud syndicate. In a statement, additional deputy commissioner of Police for Delhi’s South-West district, Kumar Abhishek, said that the cyber team has arrested four members of the syndicate, including alleged mastermind Atul Meena. The arrests come after a trader approached the Police in connection with a phishing scam that drained 4,985 USDT, valued at around ₹5 Lakh, from his wallet back in June. The victim had allegedly attempted to sell USDT via a P2P transaction on crypto exchange Binance on June 6 when a purported buyer convinced him to move the discussion to WhatsApp. The victim claims to have then unsuspectingly clicked a phishing link that granted unauthorised wallet access to the syndicate, resulting in the entire balance being transferred. Afterwards, the victim filed a complaint with the Police and a case was registered in the matter on July 2. Using call records, IP logs and WhatsApp data, the officials traced the suspects’ operations to Rajasthan’s Alwar, where they were recruiting local youth to join the alleged syndicate on a profit-sharing basis. The recruits allegedly procured SIM cards and set up WhatsApp accounts to source USDT sellers. Once sellers responded, their numbers were passed to Meena to execute the phishing pitch. Abhishek said that the cyber team raided Meena’s hideout in Alwar and also arrested three of his associates from Jaipur – Jagmohan Meena, Narender Kumar Meena and Manish Meena – before ultimately apprehending Atul near Dhaula Kuan in Delhi. Besides the four arrests, they also recovered ₹1.6 Lakh in cash, 11 mobile phones, one iPad, one Wi-Fi router and six SIM cards during the course of the probe. Police said the complainant has been refunded the entire sum and they are examining the transaction logs and exchange wallets to identify the accounts linked to the syndicate. This comes as law enforcement agencies scrutinise the Indian crypto ecosystem over links with organised criminal rings. Earlier this month, the ED provisionally attached around ₹14.2 Cr worth of assets linked to crypto platform HashPe, alleging it was operating a fraudulent crypto-based Ponzi investment scheme. Five Bengaluru-based platforms also came under the directorate’s scanner in June when ED searched their premises and froze their accounts having ₹6 Cr worth assets in total. The ED then had said that these platforms used VDAs to enable unauthorised cross-border transactions. This comes as the regulatory treatment of cryptos remains an ongoing debate in India. While the government does not recognise cryptocurrencies as legal tender, crypto platforms have to strictly comply with money laundering regulation. At the same time, income from VDAs attracts 30% capital gains tax and 1% TDS. Policymakers have been cautious to introduce a legal framework around crypto given concerns over money laundering, terror financing, cyber fraud and offshore capital flows. Earlier this year, at a meeting of the parliamentary standing committee on finance to discuss the same, senior government officials told the panel that they consider the sector “high-risk”.

Amazon is on the hook to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after losing its legal battle against the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The US District Court for the District of Maryland ruled in favor of the CPSC, which argued that Amazon is a distributor of goods, not a logistics provider, making it responsible for carrying out recalls of third-party products.
Amazon loses its latest attempt to get out of handling more recall notices
A court ruled in favor of the US CPSC’s argument that Amazon is responsible for recalled products that other companies sell on its platforms.
Amazon sued the CPSC in March 2025 after the agency ordered Amazon to recall over 400,000 “Fulfilled by Amazon” products that pose a “substantial product hazard,” including faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers without electrocution protection, and children’s sleepwear that doesn’t meet federal flammability standards.
As a result, Amazon will be required to implement the following measures, initially outlined in the CPSC’s January 2025 order:
Notification:
On the day CPSC publishes the recall releases, Amazon must notify the public by posting the recall releases to Amazon.com; notify original purchasers directly via email and by providing information regarding the recalls on each purchaser’s “Your Orders” page.
Amazon must provide one round of notice of the recalls to Fulfilled by Amazon participants that sold the subject products.
Incentive to Remove Products from Commerce:
Amazon must issue a full refund in the amount of the purchase price to any consumer who submits proof of destruction or disposal of a subject product.
Maintaining Records of Recalls:
Amazon must maintain the recall releases on the “Recalls and Product Safety Alerts” webpage on amazon.com for a minimum of five years.
Amazon must submit monthly progress reports for five years and maintain records of its actions to comply with the Order for the same period.
Amazon didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Two potential vaccines against the deadly Ebola strain gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo are set to enter trials in the outbreak's epicentre next week, the World Health Organisation announced earlier this week.
There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the explosive outbreak declared in May, triggering an international public health emergency.
A total of 5,568 deaths out of 11,376 cases have been confirmed in the vast central African country's worst-ever Ebola outbreak, according to the WHO.
"We expect two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus to begin testing as early as next week," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a press conference at the UN health agency's headquarters in Geneva.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC is a single framework that can test the safety, efficacy and ability to trigger an immune response of multiple vaccines. The trial uses ring vaccination: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, kicked off the Tumaini trial on October 23, at the full-scale Phase 3 level, to determine if it also offers any protection against Bundibugyo.
Different vaccine types
The trial will now also incorporate the two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which have both gone through earlier-stage, smaller-scale Phase 1 clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab developed by the University of Oxford; the other, mRNA-1469, was developed by the US-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Meg Doherty, head of the WHO's science for health department, said Phase 2 clinical trials with the candidate vaccines are scheduled to begin on November 26 or 27 in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province at the epicentre of the outbreak.
If the safety and immune response data from the Phase 2 trial pass the next stage of review, the candidate jabs can move forward to a full-scale Phase 3 trial.
Children paying 'terrible price'
Doherty said that more than 140 people were enrolled in the Tumaini trial, with thousands of contacts ultimately expected to sign up. The trial will also eventually expand beyond the current single site in Bunia.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
Tedros said 400 to 500 new cases were still being reported every week, with two-thirds of confirmed deaths still taking place outside Ebola treatment centres.
"Children are paying a terrible price. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths," he added.

New York state bans AI chatbot toys for kids
Companies violating the five year ban will face a $15,000 per day fine.
New York governor Kathy Hochul has signed into law a five-year ban on the sale of AI chatbot toys, including dolls and robots that use the internet to converse with children. The new law comes with some teeth, including steep daily fines for each violation enforced by the state's attorney general.
"Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul said in a statement. Calling herself New York's first "mom governor," Hochul said the new measure was "deeply personal."
The governor's press release cited the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested chatbot toys marketed to children aged three to 12. Some of the toys talked about sexually explicit subjects and provided advice that could create a fire hazard in homes. The toys had few or zero parental controls and the longer the conversation, the more safety limits weakened. Some toys could even record a child's voice or scan their face.
"AI chatbots in children's toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk," said New York attorney general Letitia James.
Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation, according to the governor's office. James added that her branch would "not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won't allow our children's health to become the collateral damage of big tech."
Hochul and New York State legislators recently enacted another law called "AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors," prohibiting unsafe chatbot features for children under 18, with civil penalties of up to $25,000 per infraction. Hochul also signed an executive order this summer, issuing a one-year ban data centers using 50MW or more.
Anti-AI measures were a politically popular during US midterm elections, as Americans voted to restrict the country's data center boom. Data centers were the subject of 45 ballot measures in 10 states and 39 measures were passed to restrict the facilities in some form.
In a statement, Amazon said the products it sells must follow US laws. Canada·THE FIFTH ESTATE
After 18-year-old’s online exploitation and death, mom wonders why police didn’t search devices right away
Police apologize for not 'properly' communicating offer to 'further this investigation'
WARNING: This story contains references to suicide, abuse and graphic material that may be upsetting to some readers.
A grieving mother in St. John's says she and her family were left to find their own evidence after police didn't investigate signs her teen was being exploited by a sadistic online network, despite RCMP in the province being the first police force in Canada to warn parents about the threat more than two years ago.
The family — who CBC News is not identifying for fear of retaliation by online predators — reached out to the fifth estate earlier this year after seeing the program's investigative documentary about 764 — an online network of violent extremists that targets vulnerable minors. It also tries to coerce them into sending sexually explicit messages and images, doing self-harm — including carving their predators' names into their skin as a sign of devotion — and even killing themselves.
The mother says her teen, who we are referring to by the initial J, was being exploited in a similar manner and died by suicide in April at the age of 18.
J was an 18-year-old in Newfoundland who loved sunrises, sunsets, their family and their dog. They died by suicide in April. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Since their death, J's mother says she has been left to scour her child's devices and journals and has found evidence of multiple usernames exploiting her child, utilizing similar tactics used by members of 764, including sexual exploitation and pressure to self-harm.
While police were aware of J's victimization after J attempted suicide in June 2025, J's mother says police did not take J's devices for analysis then or after J died by suicide this past April.
Following an interview with the fifth estate, Sgt. Brent Perry, who runs the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit, reached out to J's mother. He apologized for not "properly" communicating the force's "offer/ability to further this investigation" and has since taken the devices for review.
An inner world of exploitation
J's mother is speaking out now, she says, to find justice for J.
"I feel like this is my role now as J's mom … so the world can see what happens online because a lot of us are blinded to it and J's not here to tell the story themselves."
J left behind multiple phones and journals for their family in which they outline the extent of their online exploitation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
J's vulnerability can be seen in journal entries, drawings and videos they left behind. In one recording, when J was 15, J speaks about their struggles with mental health, suicidal ideation and self-harm.
J's journal entries also reveal a window into a sadistic online world where J's vulnerability left them targeted and trapped.
According to their mother, J — who loved sunrises, their family and their dog deeply — was struggling with their gender identity during the pandemic and began to spend more time isolated in their room on their phone.
It was only after a suicide attempt in June 2025 that J ended up in hospital and disclosed they had been exploited online by several individuals who had pushed them to record and share images of them self-harming and attempting suicide.
J's mother said she was shocked by what her child shared.
"J explicitly said: ‘They told me to do this, they told to kill myself, they told me to cut myself. They told me, you know, they made me do it. I had no choice. They knew where we lived.'"
For what would have been J's 19th birthday in August, the family placed a purple bench in memory of the teen, at a spot where they enjoyed watching the sunset. (Submitted by J's family)
J's mom called Canada's national tipline, Cybertip.ca, which alerted police. An officer from the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit came to the hospital and interviewed J.
But according to their mother, a few months later, an officer informed the family that without more information, the investigation was stalled.
Previous police warning
Just a year before, Newfoundland and Labrador RCMP was the first police department in Canada to warn the public about violent online networks that went by names like 764 or CVLT — groups targeting vulnerable children as young as eight on popular social media, gaming and streaming platforms.
At the time, police warned caregivers about how members of the group often invite minors to private chatrooms where they sexually exploit and groom them — for the main purpose of gaining clout within the group.
Since that advisory, the unit has been investigating at least half a dozen cases in the last year. In June, the unit held a news conference to alert the public of another 764 victim in the province.
Despite the growing awareness, and J's case bearing the hallmarks of 764's exploitation, J's mother says her child's online abuse was not flagged as another potential case.
J's mother says she can't understand why her child's case wasn't examined more closely given the RCMP had issued the 764 alert just a year before police became aware of J's exploitation.
"When it came to the 764 and knowing that my child was only a year after that and nothing was done — like it was basically dismissed and said: ‘This is it, there's nothing we can do….' Like, why didn't they take this more seriously? Why didn't they ask to see [the] devices?"
Instead, the family says after J's death, an officer told them to reach out if they found any evidence themselves.
J had several devices and in a note left behind included passwords and pointed to where the family could find phones, computers and journals documenting the abuse they endured.
With the help of family members, J's mother spent weeks poring through J's journals, combing through accounts and chats as well as images and videos and found evidence of multiple individuals exploiting her child.
"Why do I, as a parent who just lost my child, have to go through all of this looking for that explicit content? You know, like it's, to me that's torture."
J's mother has kept a number of J's personal belongings close, including the teen's baby blanket. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)
When asked why a family in that situation would be left to gather evidence of their dead child's exploitation, Perry said he could not speak about individual cases. But he acknowledged his empathy for the family.
"I'm a father myself and that issue is very much alive to me," Perry told the fifth estate.
"I'll reiterate that if a family has information that they believe would be of interest to the police to investigate, our door is always open to investigate and hear what information they have."
764 offshoots continue to evolve
Understanding how to tackle the larger problem of 764 and its offshoots is still in its infancy, says Marc-André Argentino, an extremism expert with Public Safety Canada who has been tracking 764 and affiliate groups since 2022.
Argentino says 764 and its offshoots continue to evolve from a loose network urging minors to self-harm to pressuring members to commit acts of public violence.
"This is not fictitious. And it is as bad as we are saying. And actually it is worse."
764 and its related groups draw inspiration from a satanic neo-Nazi movement called the Order of Nine Angles (O9A). (CBC)
Argentino has spent much of his time in the last year training thousands of front-line workers around the world, including 2,000 police officers in Canada, to recognize signs of 764.
"We have a challenge talking about 764 and the network simply because of the type of harms and criminal acts that are perpetrated, the extreme nature of these acts," he said, adding that the fact youths are often behind the violence is hard for many to comprehend.
As the threat escalated, Canada was the first country in the world to designate 764 a terrorist threat in December 2025.
Since then, police have made multiple 764-related arrests across the country, including in Quebec City, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, as well as identifying several victims in British Columbia.
In an email, a spokesperson for the RCMP said while it cannot share how many 764 cases are being investigated, the "threat is evolving and increasingly involves young people."
Calls for legislation
At a recent event in Ottawa, parents, young people and advocacy groups called on the federal government to implement its online harms legislation, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), which was tabled in June 2026.
The bill is designed to implement age-appropriate protections and safeguards for younger users, including safer design features and measures to reduce children's exposure to harmful material and high-risk online interactions. The bill is expected to become law next year.
J's mother says the legislation can't come soon enough.
She has spent hours going down dark online corners hoping to hold someone accountable and find justice for her child.
Police apologize, take devices
In the email to J's mother that was sent a day after the fifth estate interviewed Perry, he offered to support her analysis of J's devices "to further her search for answers."
Sgt. Brent Perry is in charge of the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary’s integrated internet child exploitation unit. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Perry added that "it has recently come to my attention that our offer/ability to further this investigation was not communicated properly and for that I offer my sincere apology."
The email, sent in June, was the first significant development since J's death in April. In that time, J's mother had found evidence to share, including images of who J claimed was their main predator and messages offering money in exchange for J to carve a name into J's skin.
The RCMP has since asked J's mother to bring in everything she found — including J's devices.
"I provided whatever information I possibly could," she said.
Her voice breaking, she added that she could feel J working through her "to keep me going, to push further and to keep searching. I so badly want justice."
Police have since copied most of the devices and told her the investigation could take months.

A sharp sell-off in South Korean stocks took an emotional turn on Tuesday when financial television anchor Kim Ah-hyun struggled to hold back tears during a live broadcast, as she watched a Samsung Electronics-linked leveraged investment product plunge more than 15% in a single session.
The moment, which has since spread across social media, came as South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index suffered one of its steepest single-day declines this year. The index fell 6.16%, shedding 308.52 points to close at 4,697.51 on November 25, wiping out the previous session's gains and marking its lowest closing level since January 13.
Kim, who hosts Seoul Economic TV's financial programme 'Kim Ah-hyun's Golden Stocks', was discussing the difficult conditions facing investors when a chart showing a 15.21% fall in a single-stock leveraged product linked to Samsung Electronics appeared on screen.
She fell silent for several seconds, lowered her head and appeared visibly emotional before looking towards the production team for assistance. The broadcast subsequently cut away from the chart.
The sharp fall in the KOSPI came after a strong rally a day earlier, when the index had gained 4.79% amid renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence stocks following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return to his position.
However, the mood changed sharply on November 25. Falling US chip stocks and reports that Washington could impose fresh tariffs on 16 economies added to investor anxiety, triggering heavy selling across Seoul's markets.
The KOSPI opened nearly 4% lower, briefly triggering a temporary halt in programme trading sell orders. It later touched an intraday low of 4,672.55 before recovering slightly towards the close.
South Korea's two biggest semiconductor companies bore much of the damage. Samsung Electronics shares fell 9.87%, while SK Hynix plunged 11.05%. Foreign investors sold a net 1.8993 trillion won, worth approximately $1.4 billion, in South Korean shares.
In a subsequent livestream, Kim explained that her reaction came after hearing repeated accounts of retail investors suffering substantial losses.
She described her emotions as 'tears of anger' and urged investors not to lose hope despite the difficult market conditions.
The incident struck a chord online, with footage of the broadcast circulating widely on overseas social media platforms.
The sharp sell-off has also prompted South Korean authorities to consider additional support for the stock market.
According to reports, the South Korean government is examining an expansion of its securities market stabilisation fund, which currently stands at 10.76 trillion won, or around $8 billion. The Korea Development Bank has reportedly approached 25 financial institutions to assess their capacity to contribute more funds. No final decision on the expansion has been announced.
There was some relief on November 26, when the KOSPI recovered after the previous day's steep losses. The index rose 0.3% to close at 4,711.21, while Samsung Electronics gained 0.4% and SK Hynix advanced 2.2%.
Investors also kept an eye on the Bank of Korea's interest rate decision, looking for signals on the direction of monetary policy amid the market turbulence.

California warns of flooding as king tides peak over Thanksgiving
- Published
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.
While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.
Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.
The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

29 miners believed trapped by flooding in an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia
Rescuers are searching for 29 miners believed trapped by flooding in an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Rescuers were searching Wednesday for 29 miners believed trapped by flooding more than a day earlier in an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia.
The miners were digging for grains of gold when heavy rain caused the Ciseureuh River to flow into the shaft Monday in the mining area in Bogor regency of West Java province. Authorities have not confirmed if anyone escaped, and there was no information on the miners’ condition.
The shaft was estimated to be about 100 meters (330 feet) deep in a mountainous area south of the capital, Jakarta. The search-and-rescue team deployed after the flood was reported early Wednesday brought in submersible water pumps to suck the water from the hole and tried to close off openings where groundwater seeped in.
“Water inside the hole has not yet receded and is expected to take a long time to drain,” Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency chief Desiana Kartika Bahari said in a statement. “Depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are among the factors being considered in determining the search strategy so personnel can operate safely.”
Informal mining operations are common in Indonesia, providing a tenuous livelihood to thousands who labor in conditions with a high risk of serious injury or death.
Landslides, flooding and collapses of tunnels are just some of the hazards facing miners. Much of gold ore processing involves highly toxic mercury and cyanide and workers frequently use little or no protection.

Conspiracy theorists claimed the video served as evidence that "lizard people" walk among us. Wright reportedly told the New York Post that he's "obviously" a human.
A video circulating online appears to show a man rolling his eyes in a so-called "reptilian" fashion while standing behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a news conference.
The clip, which was posted on X, Facebook and other platforms, reignited a decades-old conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly hold positions of power, which Snopes has previously reported on.
Snopes readers wrote in to ask if the video was real or generated using artificial intelligence.
This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.
Wright's eye roll is visible in multiple credible livestreams of the news conference in question, which Mamdani held on Nov. 20 to announce a plan to shutter Rikers Island, the city's largest jail, by 2032.
For example, Wright's eye roll is visible at the timestamp 1:51 in a YouTube livestream posted by the official New York City mayor's office account, whereas USA Today's livestream shows the eye roll at 1:54.
There's no evidence that the livestreams in question were enhanced using AI, nor would there be any reason to do so.
According to the New York Post, Wright said he has "no idea what was going on in that video."
"Obviously I'm a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he reportedly told the Post. "I can't speak to any reptiles or aliens."
