Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.
On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.
Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.
Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.
"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.
Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."
"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.
The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.
Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed
Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.
The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.
The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.
The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.
"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.
He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.
"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."
Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.
Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

Streaming has changed how Indian authors write, and a screen option can pay a writer more than several editions of a book ever will, publishers, producers and creators said during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.
The session, “From Print to Pixel: The Transmedia Paradigm,” was moderated by journalist Mayank Shekhar. On stage were Priya Kapoor, editorial director of Roli Books; South African filmmaker Tarina Patel, founder and CEO of Tarina P Productions; Rajiv Chilaka, founder and managing director of Green Gold Animation; Raghav Chandra, a retired Indian Administrative Service officer, novelist and founder director of the Bhopal Literature and Art Festival; and Prakash Magdum, former managing director of the National Film Development Corp. (NFDC).
Kapoor, who has commissioned and edited titles including “Black Warrant,” “Dongri to Dubai” and “Taj Mahal Foxtrot,” said that since streamers arrived in India, writers have become aware their books can travel beyond the page.
“We definitely get submissions where you read it and you know that somebody is 100% thinking of a film adaptation, and others who are writing because they had a book in mind,” Kapoor said.
Production houses and directors in Mumbai call Roli from time to time with briefs that track the trends – a young adult story, say, or mythology, which is in vogue now. A while back, they wanted hard-hitting non-fiction.
Then there are writers who have already optioned or sold a screen story and come to Roli for a book version, because the deal needs underlying IP. “It’s essentially a screenplay that’s been summarized into a book, and that is where the trouble begins,” Kapoor said.
“Black Warrant” took a far less conventional route. Former warden Sunil Gupta, recently retired from Delhi’s Tihar jail, walked into Kapoor’s office with Praveen Jain, a former chief photographer at The Indian Express, and spent an hour telling stories. Gupta couldn’t write, so a legal intern named Satyabhan recorded and transcribed sessions built on Kapoor’s questions, and Sunetra Choudhury, author of the prison book “Behind Bars,” came on board as co-writer. The chapters followed the way Gupta remembered events rather than any episodic plan, though the show’s writers later told Kapoor the structure suited them.
Gupta, the protagonist of both book and series, is very happy with the result, Kapoor said. “He goes for the shooting also, he goes for the premieres, he’s a star.” He made a point of flagging scenes that never happened, and Kapoor has told him the filmmakers are allowed those creative liberties.
The money gap between the two industries is wide. In Indian English-language publishing, Kapoor put a bestseller at 5,000 copies, and a hit adaptation does not change that much. “Our reading audience is not our watching, viewing audience,” she said. A screen deal, though, can pay an author more than five or 10 editions of a book would, even when the project never gets made.
Chilaka’s “Chhota Bheem” took the opposite path, starting on TV and spreading outward. The character borrows only the strength of Bheem from the Mahabharata, transplanted into an ordinary village kid. Over 18 years, Green Gold has made more than 1,000 episodes, over 100 TV features, around five feature films and four spinoffs, with some 2,000 characters and more than 1,000 licensed products. Chilaka put the business done on the property at more than INR10 billion ($112 million).
The Netflix spinoff “Mighty Little Bheem,” which reimagines the hero as a baby, is among the streamer’s top preschool shows internationally, Chilaka said. Green Gold made it without dialogue. “So we gambled with that, and the gamble paid off,” he said. The show also leaves out Bheem’s father, which Chilaka said drew a strong response from single-mother households in North and South America.
Coming next year is “Sing with Bheem,” a musical spinoff series. A stage musical bowed last month at the Royal Opera House in Mumbai, a Chhota Bheem cafe is open in Hyderabad with seven or eight more planned across India, and the character has fronted public campaigns in West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and on Western Railways.
The franchise grew out of insecurity, Chilaka said. Green Gold was a 20- to 30-person studio making an animated “Krishna” while 17 other studios worked on their own Krishna projects. It sold the film to Cartoon Network, but animation budgets never covered production costs, so Chilaka planned for home video, comics, merchandise and birthday parties from the start, and modeled his ensemble on “Friends” so every child could find a match.
“Sustaining is still okay, we’ve done it for 18 years, but getting another hit like that is the biggest challenge because we’ve done so well,” Chilaka said.
Patel, whose credits include “Mandela’s Gun,” has mostly built films from firsthand accounts rather than books. Her current project is a real-life story set against boxing and apartheid, for which she optioned what she judged the best of five or six books on the subject. Announcing it brought out a string of claimants waving documents, followed by a long, stressful stretch with entertainment lawyers.
“If it’s a public figure, anyone can tell the story. Irrespective of whether there’s a family, there’s an estate, their books, anyone is entitled to tell the story of a public figure,” Patel said. Diaries, personal photographs and other private family material still require access, she added.
Chandra said the Bhopal festival, now eight editions old, programs a session or two on literature to cinema each year, with past editions covering “12th Fail,” “Bandit Queen” and “The Railway Men.” He pointed to universality and contemporary relevance as what carries a book to the screen. His own novels, “Scent of a Game” and “Kali’s Daughter,” drew interest from a prominent director just before COVID that went nowhere. At the session he showed an AI-generated pitch deck built from a “Scent of a Game” subplot about the last wild cheetahs in India, put together by a junior colleague in about 15 minutes.
Magdum, who headed the National Film Archive of India during Mahatma Gandhi’s 150th birth anniversary, has been mining archival footage of Gandhi for a book, Shekhar said. Magdum recalled how Fox Movietone crews hauled sound equipment by bullock cart to a Gujarat village to film Gandhi with sync sound shortly after India’s first talkie, “Alam Ara,” opened on March 14, 1931.
“A book is a very private kind of a thing. You are imagining in your own world whatever is the writer creating,” Magdum said, adding that an adaptation works when the director captures the soul of what the writer meant.
Asked for their favorite book-to-screen adaptations, Magdum and Patel both picked “Slumdog Millionaire,” drawn from Vikas Swarup’s novel “Q&A.” Patel, a friend of Swarup’s, said he wrote it while posted in Cape Town and that screenwriter Simon Beaufoy’s love story turned it around. Chandra chose “Omkara” and “The Guide,” Chilaka the “Harry Potter” and “The Lord of the Rings” films, and Kapoor “The English Patient.”

The UK government’s antisemitism tsar is probing the BBC.
John Mann told the Today programme he has opened an investigation to see how “widespread” Jewish staff’s “feeling of discomfort” is within the corporation. According to The Times, whistleblowers have already told him they consider the BBC a “hostile environment.”
Mann said his investigation should complete by Easter before he reports back to the broadcaster. He invited “anybody who is Jewish inside the BBC past and present with something to say” to come forward and speak with him.
On Today, he said he had already heard from employees who had read about the investigation in The Times just three hours prior. Rather than listeners or viewers, he said the probe concerns “the lived experience of Jewish staff past and present at the BBC,” and will “report facts, not opinions.”
Watch on Deadline
Deadline understands the BBC has not yet been notified about Mann’s investigation. Mann has been the UK government’s adviser on antisemitism for seven years.
In the wake of October 7, antisemitism has been an issue the BBC has struggled to get to grips with. At times, this has spilled out in the open. Last month, one of the exec producers behind Oscar-winner Mr. Nobody Against Putin was reported to have settled with the BBC for £400,000 ($523,000) over antisemitism claims, although an internal BBC investigation did not uphold her complaint. “I think I made too much noise about being a Jew inside the BBC,” Lucie Kon told The Telegraph a few weeks ago.
A BBC spokeswoman said: “We take any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC. We have introduced compulsory training on antisemitism for all our staff and we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have. We are determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted.”

Easy daily use. Lots of LEDs and medical-grade lasers. Simple to wear. FDA-cleared tech. Results started to appear within a month.
TIRED
Must be used consistently. Portable battery is an extra $99.
The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.
I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.
However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.
The Scientific Crown
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.
Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)
The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.
If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.
Growth Spurt
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.
During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.
The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.
Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.
A Hairy Situation
In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.
The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)
Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

India reclaimed the top spot among emerging market peers in October, overtaking Vietnam despite trailing it on five of the seven indicators tracked by Mint’s Emerging Markets Tracker (EMT). A narrower gap in exports, currency performance and stock market capitalization, coupled with a substantial lead in import cover, helped India edge ahead.
India’s overall score stood at 73.6 out of 100, against Vietnam’s 70.1. The decisive factor was import cover, where India’s 9.9 months of reserves stood well above Vietnam’s 1.8 months. Improvements in India’s relative performance on exports, currency and market capitalization also helped narrow the gap, despite Vietnam retaining the lead on these indicators.
India’s exports grew 45% year-on-year in October, below Vietnam’s 53.8%. However, the gap narrowed considerably from September, when India’s exports grew 22.9% against Vietnam’s 39.5%. Similarly, the rupee remained flat against the dollar month-on-month, while the dong’s appreciation slowed to 0.4% in October from 0.6% in September.
India’s stock market capitalization declined 3.2% month-on-month in October, a steeper fall than September’s 2.2%. However, Vietnam’s performance deteriorated more sharply, with its market capitalization declining 2.8% in October after rising 2.7% in September.
India’s lead on import cover—the number of months of imports a country’s foreign exchange reserves can finance—also proved significant. While India’s import cover stood at 9.9 months, Vietnam’s remained at just 1.8 months, giving India a substantial advantage on this indicator.
Malaysia delivered the strongest export performance and inflation print among the peers. However, weakness across several indicators, including the manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), import cover, currency performance and stock market capitalization, pulled its overall ranking down.
India’s scorecard
India retained its strong position on GDP growth, at 7.8%, trailing only Vietnam and giving it a structural advantage over the other countries. Its export growth also improved significantly, reaching 45% in October from 22.9% in September and making it the third-best performer among its emerging market peers. However, the improvement can partly be attributed to a low base in the previous year. Sustaining this momentum will be crucial to maintaining India’s ranking in the months ahead.
Manufacturing activity remained resilient, although the PMI eased to 54.7 in October from 55.1 in September. India nevertheless ranked second among the 12 countries on this indicator.
Import cover deteriorated to 9.9 months from 10.6 months in September as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) allowed state-owned oil companies to source dollars directly, easing pressure on the spot market but depleting foreign exchange reserves. Despite the deterioration, India’s relative performance on import cover remained strong.
India continued to lag its peers on currency performance and stock market capitalization in October. While RBI measures helped keep the rupee flat against the dollar, several other countries recorded currency appreciation.
India’s stock market capitalization declined significantly during the month, with the benchmark Sensex shedding 2.02% on average. However, 10 of the 12 countries recorded a decline in market capitalization, amid a pullback in global artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor stocks, rising oil and inflation pressures, and elevated bond yields. India was therefore a laggard on this indicator, but not an outlier.
Inflation emerged as a bigger pain point for India in October, with the print breaching RBI's upper tolerance limit of 6%. Relative to their respective central banks’ targets, India’s inflation deviation was significantly sharper than that of most other countries. Only four countries recorded a larger deviation from their inflation targets than India did.
The outlook
The outlook for India remains mixed. GDP growth is expected to slow marginally to around 7.6% in July-September from 7.8% in the previous quarter. Elevated inflation could prompt another rate hike of 25-50 basis points in December, while import cover may deteriorate further as foreign exchange reserves are down 0.6% in November so far.
However, a significant jump in foreign equity investments and the rupee’s appreciation against the dollar in November so far could improve India’s relative position. India recorded net foreign portfolio investment (FPI) of $16 billion through 25 November, while the rupee appreciated 1.8%, supported by RBI measures, the return of foreign investors to Indian markets and lower crude oil prices.
The Sensex has risen 10.5% month-on-month in November so far, with mid-cap and small-cap stocks also gaining. This came even as stocks linked to AI continued to shed value. The divergence could give India a relative advantage going forward, as the country appears to be benefiting from the “anti-AI” trade.

Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.
A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.
Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.
Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Significant defeats
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.
Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.
Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.
One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.
What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.
IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.
The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.
For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".
Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.
In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.
It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.
In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.
It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.
There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.
Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.
"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."
Taliban v Sharaa
The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.
He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.
Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.
Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.
According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.
The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.
Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.
African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.
There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.
With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.
Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".
That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.
History lessons
Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.
After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.
In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.
"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.
But not everyone is changing tactics.
IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.
And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.
Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.
The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the vehicle had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs.
The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its massive blockbuster Dupixent, an inflammation-targeting drug approved in nine indications. The company, where Belén Garijo took over as CEO earlier this year, had been vocal that it was looking for takeover targets with late-stage or even commercial assets that fit with its existing focus in immunology and rare diseases.
Sanofi is paying $175 per share for New Jersey-based Insmed, through a combination of debt financing and cash. Insmed’s share price was roughly $120 before Bloomberg reported last week that the deal was in the works, which sent the stock up.

- For years, people have shared various explanations for the origin of the name "Black Friday," the common term for the popular shopping day just after Thanksgiving.
- There's no hard proof of who first used the term, or why. But the evidence indicates it emerged in 1950s and 1960s Philadelphia, and specifically among workers whose jobs required them to face the hordes of holiday shoppers that filled the city's streets and stores.
- Some say the name came from the day marking the moment shop bookkeepers switched from red ink (representing losses or debts) to black (representing profits). We didn't find any evidence for that explanation before the 1970s.
- Since the 2010s, a third explanation has circulated: that the name originally referred to Black slaves, who were allegedly sold at a discount nationwide on the day after Thanksgiving. There is no historical evidence to back up this version of the etymology..
Why do we call the day after Thanksgiving "Black Friday"? The popular term for the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season — typically marked by retailers offering steep discounts — is easy to remember, but the reason for the name isn't obvious. Making things more confusing, social media posts offer a range of different explanations, with some crediting the name to overwhelmed police officers (archived) and others saying it has roots in the history of slavery in the U.S.
Below, we'll walk you through the evidence for how the modern Black Friday took shape, as well as some myths about the name that emerged over time:
History of the term
According to the Oxford English Dictionary, which has an extensive entry on the term, English speakers have attached the adjective "black" to the name of a day of the week to "denote a specific past date associated with disaster, defeat, ruin, etc." since the 1570s. The specific term Black Friday first appeared in print in 1610 when schoolchildren used the phrase to refer to any Friday on which exams took place.
Starting in the 1860s, the term took on an economic connotation when stockbrokers and journalists applied it to two notorious financial panics, one in the U.K. in 1866 and one in the U.S. in 1869.
It's not clear exactly when Americans began to use the phrase to denote the day after Thanksgiving, which takes place the fourth Thursday of November. However, as multiple researchers and reporters have noted in their own investigations into the history of the term, the earliest known published appearance of the phrase to describe that specific day was in an article in a November 1951 issue of Factory Management and Maintenance, an industrial trade magazine.
That article, titled "Tips to Good Human Relations for Factory Executives," contained a section titled "What to Do About 'Friday-After-Thanksgiving'" that began:
"Friday-after-Thanksgiving-itis" is a disease second only to the bubonic plague in its effects. At least that's the feeling of those who have to get production out, when the "Black Friday" comes along.
This article made no mention of holiday shopping; it simply acknowledged that factory workers who were scheduled to work the day after Thanksgiving frequently called in sick, leaving the factories short-staffed. In other words, the article's author used the term Black Friday in the same way English speakers had been using it for centuries already: to refer to an especially bad day.
The earliest evidence for the term being used as shorthand for an exceptionally busy shopping day marking the start of the holiday season rush came about a decade later. Between the 1960s and the 1990s, two competing origin stories emerged to explain the term's modern use.
According to one story, Philadelphia police and/or retail employees coined the term to describe what was, for them, a reliably frustrating workday, whereas the other story credits shop owners and bookkeepers for the name, who chose it because, on that day, entries in their account ledgers went from red, signifying debt or losses, to black, signifying profits.
In the 2010s, a third explanation for the name gained traction on social media, in which it was claimed that Black Friday reflected the discounted auctions of Black slaves that, before the abolition of slavery in the U.S., were allegedly held on that day. As we found when we investigated this claim in 2013, it was not supported by any concrete proof and made little sense in a historical context.
Philadelphia police, taxi drivers and retail employees
As multiple writers who have investigated the history of Black Friday have noted, the available evidence suggests that the association of the day after Thanksgiving with holiday shopping began in and around Philadelphia in the 1950s.
At first, residents of eastern Pennsylvania referred to the resulting surge in sales and traffic as "Big Friday" — at least in print, as multiple newspaper articles from the 1950s attest. According to a 1960 article in the Philadelphia Inquirer, the annual shopping boom resulted, at least in part, from that newspaper's annual tradition of running local retailers' first holiday ads of the season on Thanksgiving Day.
https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-philadelphia-inquirer/158986966/
Article from Nov 25, 1960 The Philadelphia Inquirer (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania)
Over the following years and decades, Philadelphians who had jobs that required them to interact with the onslaught of shoppers — specifically, retail workers, taxi and bus drivers and police officers — came up with another, less cheerful term, according to newspaper reports of the era. That term was Black Friday.
In a 1970 article, for example, a Philadelphia traffic patrolman told the Philadelphia Inquirer that "policemen and cab drivers" called the day Black Friday because it was "supposed to be the worst day for traffic out of the whole year."
Similarly, five years later, The New York Times — in its earliest use of the term Black Friday to describe the holiday, according to the newspaper's official X account — credited "Philadelphia police and bus drivers" with inventing the term. That article also noted that out-of-town traffic from fans traveling to see the Army-Navy football game, traditionally held in Philadelphia the Saturday after Thanksgiving, contributed to the road and around town.
And in 1985, a manager at Wanamaker's, a Philadelphia department store, told a reporter for the Evening Sun in Hanover, Pennsylvania, that his employees called the day Black Friday because it was "really a tough day on them … the analogy is to a black cloud hanging over them."
Red to black
As the term Black Friday caught on, journalists and executives in the retail world began to point to a more positive explanation for the term. Interviewed for the same 1970 Philadelphia Inquirer article mentioned above, a Wanamaker's public relations director told the reporter that the "only thing black" about the day was "the color of the ink used to record it in the store ledgers."
The P.R. director was referring to the accounting custom of using black ink to report profits and red ink to report losses or debts. In other words, he meant that Black Friday got its name because it was profitable for companies.
Over the following decades, as Black Friday spread beyond the Philadelphia area, that story came to eclipse the explanation that the day's nickname originated from exasperated police officers and retail workers. In 1980, for example, a reporter for the Times Leader in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, wrote:
Since most businesses do 70 percent of their sales between now and Christmas, this is obviously the time when all the money is made, putting the stores "in the black."
Similarly, in 1989, a reporter for the Press of Atlantic City, New Jersey, wrote that Black Friday "supposedly received its name because it's the day American retailers post a profit, or, in accounting lingo, break into the black, for the year."
The explanation that the name Black Friday refers to the day's profits is reasonable on its surface, but as the journalist Kevin Drum concluded when he looked into the history of the bookkeeping explanation in a 2011 blog post, it ultimately holds less water than the explanation that the term originated from frustrated Philadelphia-area police, taxi and bus drivers and retail employees who had to face the crowds at work that day.
One of several pieces of evidence Drum cited for this conclusion was an email he received from a woman who said she had briefly worked at Wanamaker's, the department store, in 1971. In the email, the woman wrote:
The feeling of impending doom me to this day. The experienced old ladies that had worked there for years called it "Black Friday." I'm quite sure it had nothing to do with store ledgers going from red to black.
Slave sales
Decades after the first published examples of the term Black Friday emerged as shorthand for the annual shopping holiday the day after Thanksgiving, a new alleged explanation of the term's origin appeared on social media, where it circulated largely in meme form starting around 2013. According to this new explanation, the "Black" in Black Friday originally referred to Black slaves, who were allegedly sold at a discount nationwide on the day after Thanksgiving.
As we found when we investigated the claim in 2013, there was no historical evidence to support this explanation. In fact, Thanksgiving only became a national holiday in October 1863 — 10 months after Abraham Lincoln ended legal slavery in the U.S.'s remaining slave states by issuing the Emancipation Proclamation.
Furthermore, as we noted above, there is no evidence that the term Black Friday was associated with shopping until the middle of the 20th century, 100 years after the Emancipation Proclamation.
Although the slave sale explanation makes little historical sense and has been the subject of multiple independent debunkings beyond our own, it has still continued (archived) to circulate (archived) on social media for more (archived) than a decade.
In one notable example, the singer Toni Braxton posted (archived) the claim in meme form on her Facebook account in November 2014, commenting: "No Black Friday for me …"
In summary, the available evidence does not tell us exactly who first called the day after Thanksgiving Black Friday — or why. However, newspaper reports from the middle of the 20th century strongly suggest the term first emerged in and around 1950s and 1960s Philadelphia, and specifically among police, cab and bus drivers and retail employees whose jobs required them to face the hordes of holiday shoppers that filled the city's streets and stores.
Either way, their choice of the term Black Friday was grounded in centuries of English speakers using it to denote a particularly disastrous or unfortunate day — a likely reason why, by the 1980s, retail executives began to promote their own more positive explanation of the name.

Amid rising demand for paneer during the wedding season, authorities in Uttar Pradesh have busted an alleged adulterated paneer manufacturing unit in Raebareli, where a laundry-product optical whitener was allegedly used to make the dairy product.
The Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) raided the unit in Aghaura village, under Bachhrawan police station limits, on Monday night. An FIR has been registered against the owner, Dhirendra Paswan, and six workers under Sections 264 and 265 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to a Times of India report.
Officials allegedly found Ranipal optical whitener, refined palmolein oil, citric acid and caustic soda being used to manufacture paneer under unhygienic conditions.
“We have collected samples of all the chemicals used in making adulterated paneer, besides samples of milk and paneer. Around 1,500 litres of milk and over three quintals of paneer were destroyed,” Vineet Kumar Pandey, assistant commissioner, FSDA, told TOI.
Pandey said the wedding season, which drives up paneer demand, creates opportunities for such units to make money by supplying adulterated products.
Consumption of non-food-grade optical whiteners may cause gastrointestinal irritation, nausea and vomiting, depending on their chemical composition and concentration. Caustic soda, meanwhile, can cause severe burns to the mouth, throat, oesophagus and stomach if consumed in sufficiently high concentrations, Pandey warned.
He added that even permitted ingredients such as citric acid and palmolein could constitute adulteration when used to pass off a product as genuine dairy paneer.
Samples collected during the raid will undergo laboratory testing to determine the extent of adulteration.
Earlier this month, the Food Safety and Drug Administration Department in Mathura intercepted 2,500 kg of contaminated and suspicious paneer being brought into the border district from Rajasthan.
Ordering the destruction of the entire consignment, the officials sent samples for testing and arrested the driver of the vehicle transporting the product, they said.
Assistant Commissioner (Food) Jatin Kumar Singh said that given the high demand for khoya and paneer for sweets prepared during the Diwali season, large quantities of substandard khoya, paneer and other food items are being brought into Mathura from neighbouring states -- Rajasthan and Haryana as well as from other districts.
Singh said that on Thursday, the department received information that a large quantity of substandard, synthetic paneer was being transported to Mathura from the Kaman tehsil of Rajasthan's Deeg district.
Acting on the information, two teams were deployed along different routes and around 1.30 am (on the intervening night of Thursday and Friday), they intercepted a suspicious pick-up van near Bathen Gate in the Kosi Kalan area on the Delhi-Agra National Highway.

Hong Kong marks deadly fire anniversary with flowers and tears following gov warning
Hong Kong residents have remembered the victims of the city's deadliest fire in decades by offering flowers and prayers
HONG KONG -- Hong Kong residents on Thursday remembered the victims of the city's deadliest fire in decades by offering flowers and prayers days after the government warned them to be cautious about commemorative activities and to avoid being exploited by people it said had ulterior motives.
The blaze engulfed seven high-rise buildings in Wang Fuk Court on Nov. 26, 2025, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others in a disaster unimaginable in the wealthy financial hub known for its safety and modernity.
A year on, many fire survivors were still grieving their losses despite life pushing them forward to adjust to their temporary housing, arrange funerals for their loved ones, clean up their belongings retrieved from charred homes and decide on resettlement plans.
At a park near the apartment complex in Tai Po in the north of Hong Kong, a steady stream of residents laid flowers, snacks and toys to pay tribute. Some returned to the familiar area and gazed at their old homes. Others were seen crying.
Survivor YN Chi still remembers her escape from the complex a year ago, saying she wouldn't be alive if she had left five minutes later. She feels frightened when she thinks about it.
“My greatest wish is to deliver the truth for those 168 victims,” she said. “They are truly innocent. It's tragic."
The tragedy is a sensitive issue in the Chinese territory, and not everyone feels free to speak about it.
As the first anniversary approached, Hong Kong's No. 2 official, Eric Chan, said last Friday that the government would allow all lawful commemorations but reminded residents to choose carefully what to take part in and not to be exploited by others to engage in disruptive acts. Without identifying anyone, he said some people spoke plainly online that they hoped to use this opportunity to organize people to come out or carry out acts of disruption.
Echoing that, China’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office on Tuesday urged vigilance against attempts to “use the disaster to stir up chaos."
It said the government's response demonstrated its decisive action in advancing reforms with efficiency and pragmatism. Many residents have gradually emerged from the shadow of the tragedy and are grateful to the government and society, it added.
But Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the city government responded to the fire “by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability.”
Kai Chou, who studies in Tai Po, saw the flames from afar when the blaze broke out and, as a Hong Konger, he felt compelled to commemorate the victims in a tragedy that involved human-made mistakes. He said it was needless for the government to urge residents to guard against those with ulterior motives and questioned if it was treating residents as “terrorists.”
“You made mistakes too, and yet even when we're just trying to mourn, you still have to say things like this," the 18-year-old Chou said.
Grace Chan, a non-Tai Po resident who offered a flower, told reporters with tears in her eyes that Hong Kong has changed and she could not digest it.
Hong Kong Journalists Association Chairperson Selina Cheng noted on Threads Wednesday that local journalists faced challenges in their anniversary coverage, saying a local television station had not broadcast its own report.
On the eve of the anniversary, the Hong Kong office of China's Foreign Ministry emailed foreign news outlets, including The Associated Press, to provide information about the aftermath of the fire for reference, saying the government was taking seriously the weak links in building maintenance and fire safety regulations exposed by the fire, and that it was committed to pursuing reform and investigations.
Beyond Tai Po, religious commemorations were held across the city, including a Wednesday Mass that drew hundreds, including bereaved families.
At a cathedral in Hong Kong's downtown, the names of the 168 victims were read out one by one. Jenny Lam, a pastor who lost three family members in the fire, said that on many sleepless nights, she thought about how those who remain should live on. She later realized they needed to live well.
“It's not about forgetting our pain," she said. "But rather ... to continue experiencing the beauty of this world on their behalf.”
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the blaze, said she pondered where the victims lived and how their families would feel when she heard their names.
Lo had anticipated the government would hold commemoration activities, saying its apology was already late and doing so would show it was truly walking alongside them.
“There was disappointment, but I won't place any expectations on it anymore,” Lo said.
Eric Chan, the official, earlier told a radio show that the authorities did not hold commemorations because other similar activities were already being organized.
An investigation found the blaze was likely caused by a lit cigarette and spread rapidly through non-fire-retardant scaffolding material. The report blamed faults in the complex's renovation work and oversight deficiencies by several government departments.
Just a month ago, Hong Kong leader John Lee and officials bowed in apology, while his housing minister resigned.
Da Chung, a former Wang Fuk Court resident who attended the Mass, said that she was learning to make peace with it, but it was not easy for everyone. She could feel the sadness of those who lost their families during the event.
“Their grief hangs in the air,” she said.

Bengaluru-based digital lending startup Finnable has raised ₹405 Cr ($43.8 Mn) in a Series C funding round led by Bharat Value Fund (BVF), which invested ₹150 Cr in the startup. The round also saw participation from Pratithi Investments and NK Squared, along with existing investors TVS Capital and MEMG Family Office. Finnable will deploy the fresh capital to expand its lending portfolio, strengthen its tech stack and forge new partnerships across the lending ecosystem. Founded in 2015 by Nitin Gupta, Viraj Tyagi and Amit Arora, Finnable is a personal loan platform offering quick, paperless loans ranging from ₹25,000 to ₹10 Lakh. It primarily serves mid-income salaried professionals earning between ₹15,000-50,000 per month. Finnable has scaled its lending operations significantly, with its consolidated assets under management (AUM) stood at over ₹4,600 Cr as of this October. The startup also reported a profit after tax (PAT) of ₹51 Cr in the first half of FY27, surpassing the ₹46 Cr profit it recorded for the entire FY26. The startup didn't disclose its top line performance for the period. The bottom line growth came at the behest of expansion beyond personal lending. The NBFC began offering loans against property in June 2025, although the product remains at a relatively early stage. The latest fundraise comes a year after Finnable announced a ₹500 Cr equity raise led by Z47 and TVS Capital. Prior to that, the company raised ₹30.5 Cr in a Series B round. India's Digital Lending Opportunity Finnable's latest fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in India's retail credit and digital lending market, particularly as lenders look to serve borrowers who remain underserved by traditional banking channels To note, around 8 Cr aspirational borrowers accounted for 79% of India's 14 Cr retail credit originations between January and March 2026, according to Equifax India's recent report. These borrowers represented ₹19 Lakh Cr of the total ₹24 Lakh Cr in retail credit originations during the period. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also reported a 22% YoY increase in NBFC retail lending in August, compared with 13.6% growth a year earlier, Finnable said. With India’s fintech sector projected to reach $250 Bn in revenue by 2030, lending tech startups are expected to contribute over 53% of that growth.

Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty) Explainer World Chess Championship 2026: Gukesh Dommaraju v Javokhir Sindarov match questions, answered When does it start? Who’s tipped to win? And why isn’t Magnus Carlsen playing? We (mostly) have the answers Play through 22 famous world championship games Jump to When and where is the World Chess Championship? Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Where do they rank internationally? Who is the current world No 1 in chess? How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Who are their seconds? What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? What is the schedule and how does the match work? How can I watch the World Chess Championship? What else should I know? India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here.
