Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels. All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India. What else should I know? The World Chess Championship is typically held every two years, though this schedule has varied over time. A 1993 schism between the International Chess Federation (Fide) and the Professional Chess Association (PCA), a breakaway organization formed by Kasparov and British grandmaster Nigel Short, ushered in an era of competing world championship titles. The title was reunified in 2006 when Kramnik held off Bulgaria’s Veselin Topalov 6-6 (2½-1½) amid a bizarre cheating row over bathroom visits known as Toiletgate. Robert Sapolsky, a biologist and neuroscientist at Stanford University, says an elite chess player can burn up to 6,000 calories a day while playing in a tournament, three times what an average person consumes daily. Karpov infamously lost 22lbs (10kg) during his grueling world title encounter with Kasparov in 1984 before it was called off controversially after five months and 48 games due to concerns over player health. Chess has enjoyed a sustained pop-cultural resurgence since the pandemic, a boom that reached Broadway with last year’s reimagining of … Chess, the cult-classic Cold War musical featuring songs by Abba’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus. Starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, the revival centered on a love triangle involving American and Soviet grandmasters loosely inspired by Fischer and Boris Spassky’s epochal 1972 encounter in Reykjavík (with secondary nods to Karpov and Viktor Korchnoi). Critics were less enthusiastic – the Guardian’s two-star review called it a “messy Broadway revival” that wasted its catchy songs – but the Grammy-nominated cast recording that came out in April goes dumby hard and Michele’s snub for a Tony nod was the worst blunder since Ding’s 55 Rf2?? in Singapore. That Sindarov is even playing for the world title is a historic achievement. His victory came two years after Gukesh became the youngest Candidates winner at 17, then the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. Together, they represent the youngest pairing ever to play for the world title by some distance. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12. He helped the country win its first Chess Olympiad gold medal in Chennai in 2022, when Uzbekistan went unbeaten against a field of 186 teams. They followed it with a bronze in 2024 before another gold on home soil in Samarkand last year, cementing the nation’s place among the sport’s leading powers. And yes, that was him among the Uzbek fans supporting the White Wolves as they made their Fifa World Cup debut last summer in the US. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row. Cambodia hosts Chinese military for largest Golden Dragon joint exercise yet
Cambodia and China have started joint military exercises aimed at strengthening cooperation between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- China and Cambodia launched their eighth joint military exercise on Wednesday, seeking to strengthen ties between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia. Cambodian military spokesperson Thong Solimo said the drills are the largest since the exercise began in 2016.
The 15-day Golden Dragon-2026 exercise will end on Dec. 9. Its stated focus is counterterrorism, humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and disaster relief.
The drills are part of Beijing’s broader push to expand its regional influence. Cambodia consistently backs Chinese foreign policy, while Beijing is its most important ally and benefactor. Chinese aid and investment have helped fuel Cambodia’s rapid economic growth in recent decades.
The United States, China’s main rival for influence in the region, has expressed concern over the military ties between Beijing and Phnom Penh. Cambodia suspended its joint Angkor Sentinel exercise with the United States in 2017, after the last drills in 2016. Following efforts by both sides to improve military relations, the exercise is set to resume next February.
Beijing has helped fund an expansion of the Ream Naval Base on Cambodia’s southern coast, raising concerns it could become a strategic outpost for the Chinese navy in the Gulf of Thailand. Cambodia has repeatedly denied any agreement granting China special privileges or the establishment of a foreign military base.
Cambodian leaders have said warships from all friendly countries are welcome to dock at its new upgraded facility, provided they comply with certain conditions. In January this year, the U.S. warship USS Cincinnati arrived at Ream, marking the first time a U.S. Navy warship has docked at the facility since its Chinese-funded renovation was completed in 2025.
According to Cambodia's state broadcaster TVK, three Chinese vessels arrived at Ream earlier this week to take part in the Golden Dragon exercise. The opening ceremony was presided over by Cambodian Defense Minister Tea Seiha and Rear Adm. Liu Sumin, commander of China's Guangzhou Naval Base.
Tea Seiha said the exercise does not aim to threaten or provoke the security of any third country, but is purely for the purpose of strengthening global security and humanitarian relief. Liu Sumin echoed the point, saying through an interpreter that “Its content does not target any third party, nor is it related to the regional situation or any specific security issues.”

At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.
Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.
"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.
The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.
The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.
"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.
Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.
The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.
Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.
Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.
While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."
Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.
"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"
Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.
"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."
One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.
"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."
Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.

The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.
A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.
The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.
Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.
Lack of awareness
Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.
“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.
Vulnerable group
A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.
Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.
“The patients had used fairness creams and noticed symptoms related to kidney disorders. They probably had membranous nephropathy, and since they sought medical help at a very early stage, treatment was possible,” says Dr. Mathew.
The symptoms
Swelling in the legs and face and frothing in the urine are some of the signs people need to be wary about, the doctor adds.
Much has changed in the beauty industry, with social media driving trends, says Liji Coleenz, a make-up artist and salon owner in Kochi with 20 years of experience.
“Even teenagers fall prey to the beauty aspirations set on social media. Our fixation with fairness is troublesome. We can never aspire to have Korean skin and need to be comfortable in our skin,” she maintains.

According to a survey by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% of people in the majority of age groups. The Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025 was released on Monday (November 23, 2026).
It showed that children aged 12-59 months had 42% anaemia prevalence, adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46%, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23% anaemia prevalence, whereas women of reproductive age had 56% prevalence.
The survey also found that mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden.
“SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in the SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat,” said Rajiv Bahl, secretary, Department of Health Research.
The report noted that about half of anaemic women, including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls, and children, have mild anaemia, indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men, and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia, said the release issued by the Union Health Ministry.
SAMPADA represents one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex, and physiological groups.
“A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates,” the release said.
Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls, and children, said the report.
The micronutrient assessment showed that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden, highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia, including infections, hemoglobinopathies, and inflammation related to chronic disease.
However, the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating a limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.
Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia. SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under-five children, adolescent girls, and women of reproductive age, while adolescent boys, men, and the elderly have a low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0.
“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required,” said Bharati Kulkarni, director, ICMR-NIN.

Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs
MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election.
On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living.
The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions, hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little.
These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face.
House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.
Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.
Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.
Academics and policymakers trace the origins of the problem to the 2008 financial crash. Home construction plummeted following a building boom that helped fuel the country's housing bubble. Large-scale investors began buying property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation years later.
Both Sánchez and his main opponent, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, have promised to enact measures if elected to financially help first-time home buyers.
That's the share of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 who were still living with their parents in 2025, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute. Almost half of those between 26 and 34 cited an inability to pay rent or buy a home as the reason why.
Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas.
Analysts say the rental supply in these areas has diminished due to a combination of factors, including population growth driven by immigration and tourism.
In cities and holiday hot spots, short-term and tourist accommodations on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com have proliferated, reducing the available rental stock.
That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidized or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.
In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.
“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”
That was the last time Spanish real wages peaked when adjusted for inflation.
Spain’s economy has substantially outgrown the eurozone average since Sánchez took office in 2018, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Spanish economy is expected to expand by an estimated 2.6% this year, more than double the eurozone's projected growth of 1.2%, according to the EU.
Even so, real wages have barely budged.
Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labor force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.
“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”
Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.
That's how much the cost of food increased between 2015 and 2025. While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, other costs have also increased while Sánchez has been in office.
To soften the impact of price rises, his government has at various times reduced value-added taxes (VAT) on food, subsidized energy and provided financial assistance.
Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”
Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticizing Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.
Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.
“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

Electronics design and manufacturing startup Elecbits is in talks to raise fresh capital in the range of $12-15 Mn in a fresh funding round led by PE firm Xponentia Capital, sources familiar with the development told Inc42. Existing investors, including Nexus Venture Partners, are also likely to participate in the round. Inc42 reached out to Elecbits and Xponentia Capital for comments on the proposed fundraise. However, neither responded to queries at the time of publishing this story. The capital to be raised is yet to be finalised. Founded in 2019 by Saurav Kumar Singh and Nikhil Rawat, Elecbits operates a full-stack electronics design and manufacturing platform, helping businesses take hardware products from concept and prototyping to manufacturing and delivery. The startup offers services across the electronics manufacturing value chain, including printed circuit board (PCB) design, firmware development, component sourcing, PCB fabrication and assembly, quality control and final product manufacturing. It also operates Elecbits XOR, an AI-powered electronics engineering and manufacturing platform that offers instant quotations, component intelligence, supply chain visibility and risk management tools. The platform aims to simplify the traditionally fragmented electronics manufacturing ecosystem by bringing engineering, procurement and manufacturing workflows under one roof. Elecbits caters to businesses across digital payments, power electronics, IT hardware, automotive and consumer electronics. It claims to work with over 200 companies, including Panasonic, Schneider Electric, Motherson, Maruti Suzuki, Urban Company, Zetwerk and Ola Electric. The startup positions itself as a vertically integrated manufacturing partner for companies looking to diversify their supply chains beyond China under the China+1 strategy. In December 2025, Elecbits raised $5.5 Mn in a Series A funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners. The round also saw participation from SE Ventures and Riverwalk Holdings. The fresh fundraise comes amid growing investments in India's electronics manufacturing ecosystem, supported by government initiatives such as the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS). As India looks to deepen its domestic electronics manufacturing capabilities and reduce reliance on imports, startups building design, engineering and component supply chain capabilities are looking to capitalise on the opportunity. For Elecbits, the proposed $15 Mn round could provide additional capital to expand its manufacturing capabilities, strengthen its technology platform and scale its enterprise business.

Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy alleged that the country had reached a situation where instead of the Constitution determining who should govern, those in power were attempting to decide who should be allowed to vote.
Addressing a public meeting after participating in the ‘Samvidhan Raksha March’ organised by the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee (TPCC) on Constitution Day on Thursday (November 26, 2026), he alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah were conspiring to secure a fourth consecutive term for the Bharatiiya Janata Party (BJP) at the Centre by deleting voters’ names.
The march, organised on the call of the All India Congress Committee (AICC), began at the Ambedkar statue on Tank Bund and proceeded to the Indira Gandhi statue on Necklace Road in Hyderabad. Mr. Revanth Reddy, Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka, TPCC president B. Mahesh Kumar Goud, AICC in-charge B.M. Sandeep, Ministers, MPs, MLAs, MLCs and senior Congress leaders participated.
Mr. Revanth Reddy said the Constitution, shaped by the vision of Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and B.R. Ambedkar, had provided equal voting right to all. He reminded that women in the United States were denied voting rights for several decades despite the country gaining independence much earlier, while Dr. Ambedkar had ensured universal adult franchise in India.
Ideological battle
Mr. Revanth Reddy said the country was witnessing an ideological battle between the legacy of Mahatma Gandhi and that of Nathuram Godse. While the Gandhi family — including Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra — were fighting to protect the country and its Constitution, the BJP was following the legacy of Godse, he alleged.
Calling upon people to stand with the Gandhi family and the Congress, Mr. Revanth Reddy said the party that had fought for India’s independence would continue to exist for another 100 years. The BJP, which he described as a party formed for power, had no comparable history, he said.
Mr. Mahesh Kumar Goud alleged that the BJP was organising counter-rallies because it could not tolerate the public response to the Congress’s Constitution protection campaigns. He said the Congress would continue to enjoy the support of people despite such counter-mobilisations.
AICC incharge for Telangana B.M. Sandeep said the history of the Congress and that of independent India were inseparable. He alleged that the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) had played no role in the freedom struggle and that constitutional values had come under pressure over the past 13 years.

440 players, three days, one venue - the Nations Championship logistics logjam
- Published
Earlier this year, when planning their Nations Championship finals week, Argentina's staff had a request.
Would their hotel in Shepperton allow the team to scorch a patch of the hotel garden for an asado – a traditional Argentine barbecue, in which meat on a low grill is cooked over a bed of hot charcoal?
Japan were also making arrangements. The Brave Blossoms had a special rice cooker shipped over to supplement the kitchen facilities at their Kensington base.
Such are the countless details that go into an unprecedented logistical juggle.
The maths makes the bottleneck clear.
The Nations Championship brings together more than 550 players and support staff from the world's top 12 teams for six matches funnelled into three days and just one venue - Twickenham.
The new tournament has made new, unprecedented demands on organisers.
The first was to find enough accommodation in one corner of London, on a notoriously busy shopping weekend, kicked off by Black Friday sales.
A block booking was therefore made back at the start of the year to secure beds in hotels from Brentford, Guildford, Cobham and beyond.
Not all those establishments had experience of hosting elite rugby teams.
So, chefs and team nutritionists convened to ensure that the hotels were braced with sufficient supplies of eggs, chicken and the rest, to cater for the high-energy, high-protein diets of rugby's best players.
The demands continue.
While their fellow hotel guests might hit the sights, Nations Championship sides hit the pitch.
Individual, private training facilities have had to be sourced for each team, with pitches hired out at local clubs, schools and universities.
Teams were given the choice of hotels and training grounds based on their world ranking at the start of the tournament in July, with world number ones South Africa nabbing the Teddington base that usually hosts England's opponents on a regular autumn internationals weekend.
The choice is all the more important given the logjam of matches means teams will do their eve-of-match captain's run session at their training ground, rather than, as traditional, at the match venue.
To get their players, staff and equipment between hotel, training base and Twickenham itself, organisers have given each team use of four vehicles; a team bus, a people carrier, a van for training kit and a truck for moving scrum machines and other heavy items.
Once they finally do arrive, Allianz Stadium, which has hosted Sevens, double-headers and schools finals days in the past, has enough changing rooms to comfortably accommodate four teams at once.
The higher-ranked team is given the home dressing room in each fixture.
Had England lost to New Zealand last weekend, they would be in the unfamiliar away dressing room. Victory however bumped them up to fourth, the All Blacks down to fifth and secured their usual spot.
Even if they dodge the traffic however, there is tunnel congestion to be dealt with.
The first match on each of the three days kicks off three and half hours before the headline fixture.
Barring extraordinary levels of intervention from the Television Match Official, the final whistle should blow in the first fixture before the team buses for those involved in the second arrive.
However, with post-match media duties, feeding and debriefing to be done, a window between five minutes and half an hour after kick-off in the second fixture has been identified for the teams involved in the first to make a hassle-free getaway.

One team has asked for permission to break with protocol. Scotland's players may stay to watch the South Africa v France grand final (16:40 GMT) as a squad social event after their own play-off against Argentina on Sunday (13:10).
Twickenham's ground staff are confident that, despite forecast rain on Saturday, the Allianz Stadium pitch will still be in good shape by the sixth match in 48 hours.
The pitch was relaid in the summer with a hi-tech reservoir installed below the surface to help precisely control drainage.
What happens in the stands is less predictable.
"We sell out at 99.9% of England men's games and we have a very clear picture of what we need to order for those," says Nils Braude, the managing director of the Twickenham Experience.
Nations Championship finals weekend will be different. Filling the 82,000-capacity Allianz Stadium, with only a week's notice on which teams will be playing when, has proved trickier.
It is estimated that Italy v Fiji and Ireland v Australia - Friday's double-header - may play out to a half-full stadium.
Braude is dealing with different numbers, demographics and demands.
"If you are a member of the public that doesn't get to go to rugby very often, now is your chance to come in," he adds.
"We are anticipating it is going to be much more akin to a general event-goer or a Red Roses game, so a more family orientated, mixed generational crowd.
"That causes a bit more just thinking about what we order
"New fans generally arrive a bit earlier than a rugby fan who has their habits well established.
"The new fans tend to eat more, particularly if it's a long day. If they are arriving an hour or two before the first game and leaving an hour after the last game, they are here for a significant amount of time.
"So having enough food on site to satisfy that demand is a key.
"As for drinks, we're known for serving a lot of Guinness, and so we can always do that. But we are anticipating a crowd that tends to look for more cocktails, Proseccos, non-alcoholic drinks and soft drinks, so we do ramp those up a little bit for these type of games."
While the stadium's bars, which number close to 80, are loaded with enough drink to see out the first two days of the Nations Championship, there are beer kegs stored in the car parks around the stadium in place to fill any unexpected shortfall.
Equally Twickenham's partner breweries and suppliers are on alert to truck in more if required.
That restocking is part of a 24-hour operation that will be in place across the Nations Championship finals weekend.
Chefs tend to be first on site from around 05:00, with a central kitchen preparing meals for the stadium's hospitality suites. After the match has taken place and the crowd has cleared, the cleaning crew descend.
They will work through the stadium seat by seat in the couple of hours after the final whistle and then to concourses and removing empties, rubbish and hospitality table linen.
Deliveries happen overnight to take advantage of an empty venue and the clearer roads around it.
For a stadium keen to host more events throughout the year, it is also a chance to show its consideration for residential neighbours, even on compressed timeframes.
The crash of glass recycling and reversing beep of forklift trucks will be restricted to certain hours.
Braude is also keen to ensure his own team get the rest and recovery they need over a weekend that comes on the back of a busy autumn.
But alongside the challenges, there is an opportunity.
"It's exciting," says Braude. "It is certainly an event that shows up. You can really flex your muscles as a venue when you have these type of events."
Brawn and brain is being deployed well beyond the white lines this weekend.

Where big U.S. unions stand on Trump's Canada tariffs
U.S. labour movement has long supported targeted tariffs, but unions criticize Trump's approach
While U.S. President Donald Trump insists his tariffs will bring a boom in factory jobs, the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers are largely skeptical of his approach.
Nowhere is that skepticism more apparent than organized labour's view of Trump's tariffs on imports from Canada.
Despite their long-standing support for targeted tariffs as a tool for protecting U.S. jobs, the leaders of some of the biggest unions in the U.S. are calling on the Trump administration to take a different approach to Canadian products.
Brian Bryant, international president of the IAM Union, formerly known as the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, says he'll take that message directly to Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, at a meeting scheduled for early December.
"We're in favour of strategic tariffs where they're used appropriately to correct bad behaviour," Bryant told CBC News. "Canada's not the problem here."
Bryant says the Trump administration is applying tariffs haphazardly and should focus its attention on countries that pay cheaper wages.
The IAM Union is particularly concerned about the Trump administration's tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, Bryant says.
"We have many manufacturers in aerospace, general manufacturing, shipbuilding that are dependent and reliant on that," he said. The Trump administration should not be "adding to their costs for those because that's going to jeopardize our members' jobs."
Progress in tariff talks
Canadian officials and their U.S. counterparts have said in recent weeks the two sides are making progress toward a trade deal.
While the Carney government is seeking as much of a reduction in tariffs as possible, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has said Canadians should not expect a deal that brings zero tariffs.
Unions in the U.S., some of whom represent significant numbers of Canadian workers, are watching the talks closely and urging the Trump administration to shift its position.
Roxanne Brown, international president of the United Steelworkers (USW), signed a joint letter with Bryant this summer calling on the White House not to impose the threatened 50 per cent tariffs on some $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.
The international president of the United Steelworkers, Roxanne Brown, centre, is surrounded by union representatives during a Sept. 15 news conference in Laval, Que., addressing tariff and trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
"We had great concerns about the impacts those tariffs were going to have on our members' jobs," Brown told CBC News. "We wanted to be on the record to really push back against those tariffs."
Trump went ahead with the additional tariffs, which apply to a range of Canadian products including wood products, alcohol, cheese and sporting goods.
Steel tariffs need study, says USW
When it comes to steel production, the USW supports tariffs on what Brown calls "bad actors," countries that unfairly subsidize their industry or engage in dumping of cheap steel.
"There should be a clear study into that dynamic between the United States and Canada. If it doesn't exist, the tariffs shouldn't exist," Brown said.

India has administered more than one crore doses of the HPV vaccine to 14-year-old girls under its national vaccination campaign in less than nine months, covering nearly 87% of the identified annual target, the Health Ministry said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
The nationwide HPV vaccination campaign, launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in February this year, provides free, voluntary and single-dose vaccination to 14-year-old girls at designated government health facilities with parental consent.
The annual target cohort comprises around 1.2 crore girls, based on Registrar General of India (RGI) 2021 population estimates.
Six States — Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh, and Bihar — have achieved 100% coverage of their identified target populations, the Ministry said.
Among other States, Assam has recorded 95.63% coverage, followed by Telangana (95.28%), Karnataka (93.16%) and Uttarakhand (90.17%).
Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan have crossed the 80% mark with 86.21% and 85.23% coverage, respectively.
Kerala has recorded 77.02% coverage, Tamil Nadu 76.12%, Odisha 74.90% and the Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu 72.99%.
In absolute numbers, Uttar Pradesh leads with more than 29.33 lakh girls vaccinated, followed by Bihar with over 13.70 lakh and Gujarat with more than 7.75 lakh, according to the Ministry.
The milestone reflects coordinated efforts by the Centre, States and Union Territories, district administrations, healthcare workers, teachers, parents and local communities, it said.
The campaign has also focused on community engagement and dissemination of science-based information on HPV vaccination, with healthcare professionals, including paediatricians, gynaecologists, and specialists from institutions such as AIIMS, helping address concerns about vaccine safety and effectiveness.
The U-WIN digital platform is being used for real-time monitoring, beneficiary tracking and digital vaccination records. It also enables parents to book vaccination slots and download digital certificates.
The Ministry said programme managers can use the platform to identify coverage gaps and eligible girls who are yet to be vaccinated, besides helping in planning and resource allocation.
HPV vaccination is considered an effective preventive intervention against infections with high-risk types of human papillomavirus, which are responsible for the vast majority of cervical cancer cases.
More than 800 million HPV vaccine doses have been administered globally, while nearly two decades of scientific research and real-world experience have demonstrated protection against vaccine-targeted HPV infections and associated precancerous conditions, the Ministry said.
All vaccination sessions under the campaign are conducted at designated government health facilities under the supervision of trained medical officers, with access to 24x7 healthcare arrangements for assessment and management of rare adverse events following immunisation.
The Ministry said it would continue working with States, district administrations, healthcare professionals, educational institutions and communities to address coverage gaps and reach all eligible girls.
Parents and guardians of eligible 14-year-old girls have been encouraged to visit designated government health facilities or use the U-WIN platform for information and vaccination slot booking.

Zverev was asked about the latest accusation while representing Germany at the Davis Cup Final 8.
“It’s not a court case. What is it called? It’s not a lawsuit. It’s a statement that I’m supposed to have made. In my opinion, I didn’t,” he replied. “To be honest, I’m not really into it that much right now, so I don’t really know too much about it. But, no, I’m not too concerned about it, to be honest.”

Zverev was asked if he was misquoted by L’Equipe.
“I think I’m innocent. I’ve spoken about it enough,” he said. “I’m really done talking about that subject because it’s been, what, five years ago? Six years ago? So I’ve spoken enough about it.”
Zverev’s Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, said in a statement last week that they were formally served with Patea’s lawsuit.
“Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit,” Zverev’s lawyers said. “If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion” protected by the German constitution.
They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.
Patea’s lawyer, Michael Scheele, said Zverev’s claim over his innocence “triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client.”
He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honor had been violated.
“Quite apart from the fact that Zverev’s claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form,” he said. “Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement.”
Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and he be fined up to 250,000 euros ($275,000) every time if he does.
Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing.
The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organizations.
Zverev this month ascended to the No. 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two Grand Slam titles this year. He was beaten by Carlos Alcaraz in the championship match of the ATP Finals on Sunday.
Germany faces Britain in the Davis Cup quarterfinals on Thursday.
Zverev previously denied abuse allegations from another former girlfriend, Olga Sharypova, who first made the accusations in 2020.
The allegations prompted the men’s professional tennis tour, the ATP, to investigate her claims. It ended 15 months later, in January 2023, with the ATP saying there was “insufficient evidence” to substantiate the claims.
